(p-2608) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-A'raf (the Chapter of the Heights)

Abu al-Shaykh Ibn Hayyan narrated from Qatadah, who said: "Al-A'raf is Meccan (*Makki*, revealed in Mecca), except for the verse ﴿Ask them about the town﴾ [al-A'raf: 163]. From here to ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 172] it is Medinan (*Madani*, revealed in Medina)."

Its verses number two hundred and six.

(p-2609) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad.﴾

The discussion of the opening letters of the chapters, and the scholarly positions regarding them, has already been presented at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[2] ﴿A Book revealed to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast about it, that you may warn thereby, and as a reminder for the believers.﴾

﴿A Book﴾ "That is: this is a Book ﴿revealed to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast about it﴾, meaning: let there be in you no tightness of breast from conveying it, for fear that they would deny you, or that you would fall short in discharging its right."

Indeed, he (ﷺ) feared his people, their denial of him, their turning away from him, and their harm. So his breast would become constricted from the conveying, and he would not be at ease with it. Thus Allah gave him security and forbade him from concerning himself with them.

Al-Nasir said: This interpretation is supported by His words, exalted is He: ﴿So perhaps you will leave out some of what is revealed to you, and your breast will be constricted by it, lest they say, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?"﴾ [Hud: 12], and so on. ﴿that you may warn thereby﴾ "That is: by the Book sent down, the polytheists, that they may believe. ﴿and as a reminder for the believers﴾" That is: an admonition for them.

The specification of the reminder to the believers is to indicate that the warning is specific to the polytheists. And the warning is placed first because it is more important given the context.

(p-2610)

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[3] ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other than Him as protectors. Little do you remember.﴾

His words, exalted is He, "﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾" are an address from Him, exalted is He, to all the morally responsible (mukallafun) people, commanding them to follow what has been sent down, which is the Qur'an. By "what has been sent down" is meant the Qur'an and the Sunnah, adhering to its generality, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 3-4].

Admonition:

Al-Suyuti (Sayyid al-Iklil) said: Some have cited this as evidence that the permissible (mubah) is commanded, because it is among what Allah has sent down, and we have been commanded to follow it. End of quote.

I say: This is an excessive deduction and a cold over-profundity. May Allah have mercy on the one who said: "When the whiteness becomes intense, it becomes leprosy."

﴿And do not follow other than Him as protectors﴾, meaning: do not follow protectors other than Him, exalted is He, from among the jinn and mankind, who would lead you to worship idols, desires, and innovations.

﴿Little do you remember﴾, meaning: you are not admonished except a little, as you are not affected by it and do not act upon its requirement, and you abandon His religion and follow other than it. Then Allah, exalted is He, warned them of His punishment if they do not follow what was sent down to them, with His saying, glorified is He:

The commentary on the Lord's saying:

[4] ﴿How many a town have We destroyed; so Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were taking their midday rest.﴾ [5] ﴿So their cry was not but that they said, "Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 4–5]

﴿How many a town have We destroyed⦆ — i.e., We intended to destroy it because of its opposition to what was sent down to them. ﴿So Our punishment came upon it⦆ — i.e., the punishment from Us came upon its people. ﴿By night⦆ — i.e., while they were spending the night, like the people of Lot. Baytutah (spending the night) means entering into the night, i.e., at night before they reached morning. ﴿Or while they were taking their midday rest⦆ — i.e., resting at midday, like the people of Shu'ayb. The meaning: Our punishment came upon it unexpectedly, while they were not anticipating it — at night while they were asleep, or by day while they were resting at the height of noon. All of this is at a time of heedlessness. The intended meaning is that the punishment came upon them at a moment of their heedlessness, without any preceding sign indicating the time of the descent of the punishment. In this there is a warning and intimidation for the disbelievers, as if it were said to them: Do not be deceived by the causes of security and ease, for when the punishment of God descends, it descends all at once. A parallel to this verse is the Lord's saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are sleeping?⦆ [al-A'raf: 97] ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are playing?⦆ [al-A'raf: 98]?

Then the Exalted expounded their worldly punishment by a declaration of their otherworldly punishment, through His saying, glorified is He:

The commentary on the Lord's saying:

[4] ﴿How many a town have We destroyed; so Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were taking their midday rest.﴾ [5] ﴿So their cry was not but that they said, "Indeed we were wrongdoers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 4–5]

﴿How many a town have We destroyed⦆ — i.e., We intended to destroy it because of its opposition to what was sent down to them. ﴿So Our punishment came upon it⦆ — i.e., the punishment from Us came upon its people. ﴿By night⦆ — i.e., while they were spending the night, like the people of Lot. Baytutah (spending the night) means entering into the night, i.e., at night before they reached morning. ﴿Or while they were taking their midday rest⦆ — i.e., resting at midday, like the people of Shu'ayb. The meaning: Our punishment came upon it unexpectedly, while they were not anticipating it — at night while they were asleep, or by day while they were resting at the height of noon. All of this is at a time of heedlessness. The intended meaning is that the punishment came upon them at a moment of their heedlessness, without any preceding sign indicating the time of the descent of the punishment. In this there is a warning and intimidation for the disbelievers, as if it were said to them: Do not be deceived by the causes of security and ease, for when the punishment of God descends, it descends all at once. A parallel to this verse is the Lord's saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are sleeping?⦆ [al-A'raf: 97] ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are playing?⦆ [al-A'raf: 98]?

Then the Exalted expounded their worldly punishment by a declaration of their otherworldly punishment, through His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion of the words of the Exalted:

[6] ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers.﴾

﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾: that is, those to whom the messengers were sent, namely the nations. He will question them about what they answered their messengers, as He says: ﴿And on the Day He calls to them and says, "What was your answer to the messengers?"﴾ [al-Qasas: 65]. ﴿And We will surely question the messengers﴾: that is, about what answer they were given, as the Most Glorified says: ﴿On the Day Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was your response?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. The purpose of the questioning is the rebuke and reproach of the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 7:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[7] ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent.﴾

﴿Then We will surely relate to them﴾ — i.e., to the messengers and to those to whom they were sent, what came from them. ﴿With knowledge﴾ — i.e., knowing their circumstances, both the apparent and the hidden. ﴿And We were not absent﴾ — i.e., from them, nor from what occurred from them.

(p-2612)

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[8] ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth. Then those whose scales are heavy—it is they who are the successful.﴾

﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth﴾ — i.e., the weighing of deeds and the distinguishing between their heavy and light, on the Day when Allah will question the nations and their messengers, is (based on) justice. ﴿Then those whose scales are heavy﴾ — i.e., their good deeds in the scale ﴿it is they who are the successful﴾ — i.e., those who are saved from wrath and punishment.

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿And as for those whose scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, for that they used to wrong Our verses.﴾

﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾ — i.e., his good deeds in the scale — ﴿those are the ones who have lost themselves﴾ through punishment ﴿for that they used to wrong Our verses﴾ — i.e., they used to disbelieve.

Remarks:

The first: al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): This verse mentions the scale (al-mizan), and belief in it is obligatory. End.

Al-Imam al-Ghazali said in (al-Madnun): The soul is attached to the body like a veil that screens it from the realities of things. With death the covering is lifted, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We have removed from you your covering, and your sight today is sharp﴾ [Qaf: 22]. What is disclosed to it is the effect of its deeds, of what brings it near to God, exalted is He, and what distances it, and these are the measures of those effects, and some of them are more effective than others. It is not impossible in the power of God, exalted is He, that He should set up a cause by which creatures know, in a single instant, the measures of deeds in relation to their effects in bringing near and distancing. The definition of the scale is that by which excess is distinguished from deficiency. Its examples in the perceptible world vary: among them is the familiar balance, and among them is the steelyard for weights, the astrolabe for the movements of the heavens and the times, the ruler for measures and lines, and the prosody (arud) for the measures of the movements of sounds. The true scale, when God, mighty and majestic, represents it to the senses, represents it by whatever examples of these He wills or others. The reality of the scale alone exists in all of that, and it is that by which excess is known from deficiency; its form is determined for the sense at the time of shaping and for the imagination at the time of representation, and God, exalted is He, knows best the kinds of shapings He determines. Affirmation of all of that is obligatory. End.

The second: What is placed in the scale on the Day of Resurrection. It has been said: deeds, although they are accidents, God, exalted is He, will transform them on the Day of Resurrection into bodies.

Al-Baghawi said: This is related from Ibn Abbas, as it came in (al-Sahih): "The Cow and the Family of Imran will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds, or two shades, or two flocks of birds in ranks."

Among that in (al-Sahih) is the story of the Qur'an, that it "comes to its companion in the form of a pale-colored young man, and says: Who are you? He says: I am the Qur'an, which kept you awake at night and made you thirsty during the day."

And in the hadith of al-Bara' (in the story of questioning in the grave): "The believer is approached by a young man of good color and good scent, and he says: Who are you? He says: I am your righteous deed." And he mentioned the opposite regarding the disbeliever and the hypocrite.

So the apparent deeds in this world, in accidental forms, appear according to this view in the afterlife in essential forms, suited to them in goodness and ugliness. Sins and disobediences take on bodily form there and are imagined in the form of fire. Upon this is understood His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the properties of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies﴾ [al-Nisa: 10], and likewise the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning one who drinks from a vessel of gold and silver: "He is only swallowing the fire of Hell into his belly." There is no remoteness in this; do you not see that knowledge appears in the world of images in the form of milk?

It has also been said: the scrolls of deeds are what is weighed, and the hadith of the card supports it. Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound, and Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abd Allah ibn Amr, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A man of my community will be called out before the heads of all creatures on the Day of Resurrection. Ninety-nine registers will be unfolded for him, each register as far as the eye can reach. He will say: Do you deny any of this? Have my recording angels wronged you? He will say: No, my Lord! He will say: Do you have an excuse or a good deed? The man will be awed and say: No, my Lord! He will say: Yes, indeed, you have a good deed with Us, for there is no injustice upon you today. A card will be brought out for him in which is written: (I bear witness that there is no god but God, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and His Messenger). He will say: My Lord! What is this card with these registers? It will be said: Indeed you will not be wronged. The registers will be placed in one pan and the card in the other pan, and the registers will rise up, and the card will weigh heavier."

It has also been said: the doer of the deed is weighed, as in the hadith: "A fat man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and he will not weigh the wing of a gnat before God. Then he recited: ﴿So We shall not set up for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾ [al-Kahf: 105]."

In the virtues of Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you wonder at the thinness of his shins? By Him in whose hand is my soul, they will weigh heavier in the scale than Uhud."

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: It is possible to reconcile these narrations, by saying that all of them are sound: sometimes the deeds are weighed, sometimes their place is weighed, and sometimes their doer is weighed. And God knows best.

Abu al-Su'ud said: It has also been said: weighing is an expression for fair judgment and just rule, and this is the view of Mujahid, al-A'mash and al-Dahhak, and many of the later scholars chose it, on the basis that using the word "weighing" in this sense is common in language and custom by way of metonymy. They said: the scale is only intended as a means to know the measures of a thing, and the measures of the deeds of servants cannot be shown by that, because they are accidents that have passed away, and even if they remained, they would not accept weighing. End. And its origin is from al-Razi.

In (al-Inayah) it is said: Some interpreted weighing as meaning judgment and just rule, or the matching of them with their recompense, from their saying: wazanahu, when he equalled it. It is either a metonymy or a metaphor, by comparing that to the weighing characterized by lightness and heaviness, in the sense of abundance and scarcity. The well-known position of the People of the Sunnah is that it is a literal reality in its familiar meaning. End.

For the majority of the earliest generation acted upon these apparent meanings without interpretation.

In (Fath al-Bayan): As for those who find it remote to take these apparent meanings in their literal reality, they have brought no proof from the Shari'ah to support their remoteness; rather, the most they have clung to is mere rational improbabilities, and there is no proof in that for anyone. If it is not accepted by their minds, it has been accepted by the minds of people whose minds are stronger than theirs: the Companions, the Successors and their Successors, until innovations came like the dark night, and each said whatever he wished, and they put the Shari'ah behind their backs. Would that they had brought rational rulings upon which the intelligent agree and whose acceptance is unified. Rather, each faction claims upon reason what agrees with its desire and suits what it and those who follow it hold, so their intellects contradict one another according to the contradiction of their doctrines.

Every fair-minded person knows this. Whoever denies it, let him purify his understanding and his reason from the taints of partisanship and sectarianism, for if he does so, the dawn will shine for his eyes.

The mention of weighing and the scale has occurred in several places in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿And We shall set up the just scales for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in anything﴾ [al-Anbiya: 47], and His saying: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful﴾ [al-A'raf: 8], ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves in Hell, abiding eternally﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 103], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, God does not wrong an atom's weight﴾ [al-Nisa: 40], and His saying: ﴿And as for one whose scales are light﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 8] ﴿his mother will be the abyss﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 9].

The hadiths on this subject are very numerous and are recorded in the books of the pure Sunnah, and what is in the Book and the Sunnah suffices without others, so no attention is paid to anyone's interpretation or distortion of them, in light of the words of God, exalted is He, and the words of His truthful and believed Messenger; the morning light needs no lamp. End.

Its summary: the basic principle in unqualified usage is the literal meaning, and one does not turn away from it to the figurative except when it is impossible, and there is no impossibility here.

The third: If you say: Does God, mighty and majestic, not know the measures of the deeds of servants? Then what is the wisdom in weighing them? I say: In it are wisdoms:

Among them: manifesting justice, and that God, mighty and majestic, does not wrong His servants.

Among them: testing creatures by belief in this in the world, and establishing the proof against them in the hereafter.

Among them: making servants aware of what good and evil, and good deed and bad deed, they have.

Among them: manifesting the sign of happiness and wretchedness.

Its parallel: He, exalted is He, recorded the deeds of servants in the Preserved Tablet, then in the pages of the guardian angels assigned to the children of Adam, without the possibility of forgetfulness befalling Him, glory be to Him and exalted is He. Thus in (al-Lubab).

Abu al-Su'ud said: If it is said: the responsible person on the Day of Resurrection is either a believer that He is Wise, exalted above injustice, so His wisdom suffices him regarding the qualities and quantities of deeds, or he denies this, and then he does not accept that the preponderance of some deeds over others is due to specific properties returning to the essences of those deeds, but rather ascribes it to God, exalted is He, manifesting it to him in that way. Then what is the benefit of weighing?

It is answered: The state is disclosed on that day, and all things appear in their realities as they are, with their attributes and conditions in themselves, of goodness and ugliness and other things. They shed the borrowed forms through which they appeared in the world, so no one who witnesses them retains any doubt that they are the very ones that existed in the world, and that each of them has appeared in this existence in its true form, entailing its qualities, and nothing contrary to that comes to his mind. End.

(Al-Razi had preceded him in something similar.)

When God, exalted is He, commanded the people of Makkah to follow what was sent down to them and forbade them to follow other than it, and explained to them the bad outcome of following other than it through destruction in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, He reminded them of the various kinds of His blessings, to encourage them to follow His command and prohibition. So He, glory be to Him, said:

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[10] ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of living (ma'ayish), but little do you give thanks.﴾

﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth﴾ — that is, We made for you therein a place of settlement and a dwelling; or We gave you dominion therein and empowered you to dispose of it.

﴿And made for you therein means of living﴾ — ma'ayish is the plural of ma'ishah, which is that by which one lives: food and drink and other things. Or it is that by which one attains these, such as trade, agriculture and crafts.

﴿but little do you give thanks﴾ — the discussion of this is like that in His saying, ﴿little do you remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 3], which has passed shortly before. The concluding phrase (al-tadhyil) is brought to explain the bad state of those addressed and to warn them: that is, We did not bestow these upon you except so that you would give thanks by following what We have sent down to you, and by abandoning the following of others besides Us, so that you would obtain the means of living of everlasting felicity.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 11:

Then Allah, Exalted is He, explained His favour upon Adam, which extends to his descendants, and made clear to them the enmity of Iblis (Satan) and the envy he concealed toward their father, so that they would beware of him and not follow his ways, by His saying, glory be to Him:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[11] ﴿And We certainly created you and then fashioned you; then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated.﴾

"﴿And We certainly created you and then fashioned you; then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated.﴾" This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will create a human from clay from black mud altered"﴾ [al-Hijr: 28] ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. The opening of this verse with the oath and the particle of emphasis, as in the one before it, is an indication of the utmost care given to its content.

Abu al-Su'ud said: He attributed the creating and the fashioning to the addressees, although what is meant by them is the creation of Adam, peace be upon him, and his fashioning, definitively, in order to fulfil the due right of the context of bounty and to emphasise the obligation of gratitude upon them, by way of allusion that they have a share in his creation, peace be upon him, and his fashioning, since these two are not among the qualities restricted to him; rather they are among the matters that extend to all his offspring, since all are created within his creation, according to his pattern, and made after his likeness. Thus it is as though they were the one to whom his creation and fashioning were attached. That is: We created your father Adam from clay, not yet fashioned, then We fashioned him in the most wondrous form and the best proportion, which has passed on to you all. End of quotation.

On the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:

[12] ﴿He said, "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?" He said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾

﴿He said﴾: "Glory be to Him and exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾" That is, from prostrating, as it occurs in Surah Sad. The "lā" (not) is redundant (mazīdah), serving to draw attention to the fact that what is being rebuked is the abandoning of prostration, and to emphasise and confirm the meaning of the verb it precedes. This is like His words: ﴿so that the People of the Scripture would not know﴾ [al-Hadid: 29]. It is as if it were said: "so that the knowledge of the People of the Scripture would be established," and "What prevented you from making prostration certain and binding it upon yourself?"

Some scholars (muhaqqiqun) hesitated over how the negating "lā" can confirm the affirmation of a verb while giving the impression of its negation. Al-Shihab [al-Khafaji] inclined to the view that it does not confirm it absolutely, but only when it accompanies a negation, whether preceding or following, explicit or implicit, as in ﴿not of those who have earned Your anger, nor of those who are astray﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7], and as here. In that case it confirms the attachment of the prevention to it. This is the end of his words.

It has also been said that "What prevented you" is to be understood as "What moved you and what called you," either metaphorically or by implication (tadmin).

Al-Raghib [al-Isfahani] said: al-man' (prevention) is the opposite of giving, and it may also be used in the sense of protection. The meaning is: "What protected you from not prostrating?" It is not hidden that the question about what prevented him from prostrating, while He knew the answer, is for rebuke and to expose his obstinacy, disbelief, and arrogance, and his pride in his origin and his belittling of the origin of Adam (peace be upon him). This is made clear by His words: ﴿He said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ Ibn Kathir said: "This is among the excuses which are greater than the sin." This is the end of his words.

He said this, and did not say "He prevented me from such-and-such," in order to answer the question directly, because in this sentence he gave, as an independent statement, what indicates the prevention, namely his belief that he is better than him. The superior does not do such a thing to the inferior, together with what is contained in it of denying that someone like him should be commanded to prostrate to someone like him. The sentence therefore contains an answer by way of a demonstrative syllogism (qiyas istidlali), and it is of the foolish style, as in the story of Nimrod.

He gave a reason for his claim of superiority and excellence, namely his assertion that the element of fire is superior to the element of clay, because fire is a luminous substance (jawhar nurani) while clay is dark (zulmani). The accursed one was indeed mistaken in restricting excellence to what is from the standpoint of matter and element, and in neglecting what pertains to the agent (al-fa'il), as His words indicate: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My two hands?﴾ [Sad: 75], that is, without intermediary; and in terms of form, as He drew attention to with His words: ﴿and I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ [Sad: 72]; and in terms of ultimate purpose, which is the essence of the matter. For this reason He commanded the angels to prostrate to him, because He had shown them that he knew more than they did about what the matter of the caliphate on earth depends upon, and that he had special qualities not possessed by others.

In sum, a thing is ennobled by its matter, and also by its agent, its purpose, and its form. All three belong to Adam (peace be upon him) and not to Iblis, so his error became clear.

In al-Lubab it is said that the enemy of Allah, Iblis, did not know the truth of the matter and missed the path of right guidance, because it is known that the essence of fire is lightness, recklessness, rising, and agitation. This is what moved him, together with his prior wretchedness, to arrogance against prostrating to Adam (peace be upon him) and to belittling the command of his Lord, and so it brought him to ruin and destruction.

The essence of clay, however, is steadiness, deliberation, patience, forbearance, modesty, and carefulness. This is what called Adam (peace be upon him), together with his prior happiness, to repent of his sin and to ask his Lord for pardon and forgiveness.

It is related from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you." Narrated by Muslim.

Note:
Ibn Jarir narrated with a sound chain from al-Hasan regarding His words ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾ that he said: "Iblis analogised, and he was the first to analogise." He also related with a sound chain from Ibn Sirin who said: "The first to analogise was Iblis, and the sun and moon were not worshipped except through analogies."

For this reason, those who held that a general text may not be restricted by analogy (qiyas) have argued from this verse, since otherwise Iblis would not have deserved this severe censure.

Al-Razi said: The proof of the necessary connection is that His words to the angels ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 11] are a general address encompassing all the angels. Then Iblis excluded himself from this generality by analogy, namely that he was created from fire, and fire is nobler than clay, and whoever's origin is nobler is himself nobler, and the nobler may not be commanded to serve the lower. The evidence for this is that this ruling holds in all similar cases, and there is no meaning to analogy other than this.

It is established that when Iblis restricted the general text by this analogy, he deserved blame, and that was only because such a restriction is not permissible. Furthermore, the verse contains evidence for this from another angle: when Iblis stated this analogy, the Exalted said: ﴿So descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾ [al-A'raf: 13]. So Allah described him as arrogant after relating to us that analogy which necessitates restricting the text. This indicates that whoever tries to restrict the general sense of a text by analogy is being arrogant towards Allah.

This verse also shows that arrogance towards Him, the Exalted, necessitates severe punishment and expulsion from the company of the friends of Allah. It is established that restricting a text by analogy is impermissible, and this is the meaning of what al-Wahidi transmitted in al-Basit from Ibn Abbas, that he said: "Obedience was more fitting for Iblis than analogy. He disobeyed his Lord and analogised. The first to analogise was Iblis, and he disbelieved through his analogy. Whoever analogises religion by some of his own opinion, Allah will join him with Iblis." This is what al-Wahidi transmitted in al-Basit from Ibn Abbas, and al-Razi cited it.

Many reports have come from the early generations (al-salaf) condemning analogy, among them what has preceded from al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and Ibn Abbas, and from Masruq who said: "I do not measure one thing against another, lest my foot slip after it has been firmly planted."

And from al-Sha'bi: "Beware of analogy, for if you adopt it you will make the forbidden lawful and the lawful forbidden. I would rather sing a song than say something by my own opinion."

The hafiz Ibn Abd al-Barr, may Allah have mercy on him, cited many reports of this meaning in Jami' Bayan al-'Ilm wa Fadlih, and he said: "Those who deny analogy have argued with these reports and their like." They said regarding the hadith of Mu'adh that its meaning is that he should exert his opinion according to the Book and the Sunnah. Dawud [al-Zahiri] spoke against the chain of the hadith of Mu'adh and rejected it on the grounds that it is from "the companions of Mu'adh" who are unnamed. The hafiz Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "The hadith of Mu'adh is sound and well known; it was narrated by trustworthy imams, and it is the basis of ijtihad and of analogy upon the principles." He then said: "The rest of the jurists, regarding these reports and what is like them in condemning analogy, have said that it refers to analogy without a principle, or to analogy by which a principle is rejected, and to speaking about the religion of Allah on the basis of conjecture. Do you not see the words of those who say: 'The first to analogise was Iblis'? Because Iblis rejected the basis of knowledge by corrupt opinion. Analogy is not permitted by anyone who holds it except in returning branches to their roots, not in rejecting roots by opinion and conjecture. When a text from the Book or a report is authentic, analogy is nullified." [Cf. the verse:] ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36]. And what principle is stronger than the command of Allah the Exalted to Iblis to prostrate, when He knew what Adam was created from and what Iblis was created from? Then He commanded him to prostrate to him, and he refused and became arrogant for a reason that does not prevent Allah from commanding whatever He wills. So this and its like is not lawful and not permissible. As for analogy upon principles, and judging one thing by the ruling of its like, no one among the early generations disagrees about this. Indeed, every one of those reported to have condemned analogy is found to have upheld sound analogy as established. None denies this except an ignorant person or one who feigns ignorance, opposing the early generations in rulings."

Masruq al-Warraq said:
"Before today we were in ease regarding the religion, until we were afflicted with the people of analogies.
They stood up from the market when their gains dwindled, and they resorted to opinion at the time of poverty and destitution.
As for the Arabs, they are a people with no gifts for them, and among the clients are the signs of the penniless."

Abu Hanifa met him and said: "You have satirised us; we will satisfy you." So he sent him dirhams, and Masruq said:
"When the people of a city challenge us with a rare and unusual ruling,
we bring them a sound analogy, firm, of the weave of Abu Hanifa.
When the jurist hears it, he memorises it and records it with ink in a page."

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: These verses reached one of the people of hadith and reasoning of that time, who said:
"When the man of opinion disputes in defence of analogy and brings some foolish innovation from himself,
we bring them the word of Allah concerning it and noble, outstanding reports."

Thus Ibn Abd al-Barr related it in Jami' Fadl al-'Ilm. He has in it, in the chapter on "what has come concerning the condemnation of speaking about the religion of Allah by opinion and analogy without a principle," extensive discussions worth consulting.

Among what he mentioned there: the people of hadith went to excess regarding Abu Hanifa and exceeded the limit.

He said: The reason that causes this, in their view, is his introducing opinion and analogy alongside reports and giving them weight. Most scholars say: "When a report is sound, reasoning is nullified." Abu Hanifa rejected many akhbar al-ahad (single-transmitted reports) by a possible interpretation, and many of this was preceded by others, and he was followed in it by similar ones among those who held to opinion. Most of what is found from him in this regard was his following the people of his region, like Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and the companions of Ibn Mas'ud. But he and his companions were immersed in deducing rulings for new events and answering them by their own opinion and preference.

A great disagreement with the early generations arose from them concerning this.

Then he said: I know of no scholar who does not have an interpretation of some verse or a doctrine concerning some sunnah, by which he rejected another sunnah with a permissible interpretation or a claim of abrogation. But Abu Hanifa has a great deal of this, while it is found in others only rarely.

It is related from al-Layth ibn Sa'd that he said: "I counted seventy issues against Malik ibn Anas which all oppose the Sunnah of the Prophet (ﷺ), in which Malik spoke by his own opinion." He said: "I wrote to him advising him about this." This is a summary of the words of Ibn Abd al-Barr.

Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah mentioned in one of his fatwas that it was narrated from Ali and Zayd that they both argued by analogy. So whoever claims the consensus of the Companions (i.e., the Sahabah) on abandoning reasoning by opinion and analogy absolutely has erred, and whoever claims that there is no issue on which any of them spoke except by opinion and analogy has erred. Rather, each of them spoke according to the knowledge he had: whoever saw the indication of the Book mentioned it, and whoever saw the indication of the balance (mizan) mentioned it. This is the end of his words.

Ibn Taymiyyah (may Allah have mercy on him) said in another fatwa: "The Companions used to argue in most of their issues by the texts, as is well known of them. They also exerted their own opinion and spoke by reasoning, and they argued by sound analogy as well. Sound analogy is of two kinds:

One of them: that one knows there is no difference between the branch and the root except a difference that has no effect in the law. As was established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the Sahih, when he was asked about a mouse that fell into ghee, he said: 'Throw it away and what is around it, and eat your ghee.' The Muslims are agreed that this ruling is not specific to that mouse and that ghee. For this reason, the majority of scholars said: whatever impurity falls into any oil, like a mouse that falls into olive oil, or a cat that falls into ghee, its ruling is the ruling of that mouse which fell into the ghee."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 12 (part 2 of 2):

[p. 2627] Whoever among the Literalists (*Ahl al-Zahir*, the adherents of the apparent meaning of the texts) says that this ruling applies only to a mouse that falls into ghee has erred. The Prophet ﷺ did not restrict the ruling to that case. Rather, when he was asked about it, he gave a ruling on it. When a question is asked about a specific case or a particular type, and the mufti answers it, the answer is particular to what was asked. It is not restricted to that ruling alone. A similar example is that he ﷺ was asked about a man who had entered the state of ihram for the 'umrah while wearing a robe perfumed with *khaluq* (a saffron-based scent). He said: "Take off the robe that is perfumed with *khaluq*, and do in your 'umrah what you would do in your hajj." He answered concerning the robe. Had he been wearing a shirt or something similar, the ruling would have been the same, by consensus (*ijma'*, the agreement of the scholars).

The second type of analogy (*qiyas*, reasoning by analogy) is this: a text states a ruling for a particular attribute (*ma'na*) that is also found in other cases. If some proof establishes that the ruling is linked to the attribute shared by the original case and the new case, and he equates the two, this is a sound analogy. The Companions and the Successors who followed them in excellence used both of these types, and both belong to the understanding of what the Lawgiver intended. The derivation of a ruling from the Lawgiver's words depends on knowing that the wording is authentically from him and on knowing what he meant by it. When we know his intent, if we know that the ruling is for the shared attribute and not for an attribute specific to the original case, we establish the ruling wherever the shared attribute is found.

If we know that he intended to restrict the ruling to the subject of the text, we prohibit analogy. Just as we know that the Hajj is restricted to the Ka'bah, that the obligatory fast is restricted to the month of Ramadan, that facing direction in prayer is restricted to the direction of the Ka'bah, and that the obligatory prayers are restricted to the five, and similar cases, it is impermissible here to extend the stated rule to something else.

When the Lawgiver specifies a place or time for worship, such as the Ka'bah or the month of Ramadan, or specifies some words or actions, such as the recitation in prayer, bowing and prostration, and even the specific takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") and *Umm al-Qur'an* (al-Fatihah), then extending what is not specified to them resembles the situation of the people of Yemen, who dropped the specification of the sacred months and said: "What is meant is four months of the year." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The postponement [of sacred months] is only an increase in disbelief by which those who disbelieve are led astray. They make it lawful one year and make it forbidden another year to correspond with the number that Allah has made sacred﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:37]. Equating the lawful with the forbidden, both stated in the texts, is of the same kind as the reasoning of those who said: ﴿Trade is just like interest, but Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:275].

Likewise is the analogy of the polytheists, who equated carrion with what was slaughtered and said: "Do you eat what you kill yourselves, but not what Allah kills?" Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you. And if you obey them, indeed you would be polytheists﴾ [al-An'am 6:121]. These are corrupt analogies. Every analogy that a text shows to be corrupt is corrupt. Whoever extends one stated ruling to another stated ruling that contradicts its ruling has a corrupt analogy. Whoever equates two things without the attributes that are relevant in the ruling of Allah and His Messenger has a corrupt analogy.

However, some analogies are known to be sound, some are known to be corrupt, and some have not been clarified. Whoever rejects analogy absolutely is wrong. Whoever argues by an analogy that contradicts the Law is wrong.

Whoever argues by an analogy for which no proof has been established as sound has argued by something whose soundness is not known. This is like someone who relies on a report from an unknown man whose reliability is not known. Thus, textual and rational proofs are divided into what is known to be sound, what is known to be corrupt, and what is suspended until a proof establishes one of these. The term "text" (*nass*) is sometimes used for the words of the Book and the Sunnah, whether the wording's indication is definitive or apparent. This is what is meant by the saying of whoever says: "The texts encompass the actions of the responsible persons (*mukallafun*)."

"Text" is also used for what is definitive in its indication and admits no contrary, such as His saying: ﴿That is ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:196], and: ﴿Allah is the One who sent down the Book with truth and the balance﴾ [al-Shura 42:17]. The Book is the text, and the balance is justice. Sound analogy belongs to the category of justice, for it equates like with like and distinguishes between unlike. The indication of sound analogy agrees with the indication of the text. Every analogy that contradicts the indication of a text is a corrupt analogy. There is no text that contradicts a sound analogy, just as there is no clear rational judgment that contradicts sound transmitted evidence. Whoever is deeply versed in the legal proofs can derive most rulings either from texts or from analogies. Thus it is established that each of the text and the analogy indicates this ruling, as we have mentioned in the examples. Analogy indicates the prohibition of every intoxicant, just as the text indicates it. Allah prohibited wine because it causes enmity and hatred among us and turns us away from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. The Qur'an indicates this meaning, and this meaning is present in all intoxicating drinks. There is no difference between one drink and another. Therefore, distinguishing between the shared types within this genus is a distinction between like things and a departure from the requirement of sound analogy, just as it is a departure from the requirement of the texts. They themselves acknowledge that their position is contrary to analogy, but they say: "We have narrations that agree with it, and we follow them." They also say: "The name 'wine' did not encompass every intoxicant." They erred in understanding the text, although they are mujtahids (qualified jurists exercising independent reasoning) who are rewarded for their effort. Knowing the general and specific scope of the terms found in the text is part of knowing the limits of what Allah sent down to His Messenger. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The Bedouins are the worst in disbelief and hypocrisy and most likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:97]. The discussion of the preference between those who reject analogy and those who affirm it would be long to survey, and this context does not allow a fuller exposition than this. And Allah knows best. Here his words end, and may Allah have mercy on him.

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[13] ﴿He said: "Then get down from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein. So go out; indeed, you are among the debased."﴾

﴿He said﴾: God Almighty says to Iblis (Iblīs), ﴿"Then get down from it"﴾, meaning: because of your disobedience to My command and your departure from My obedience. Most of the exegetes hold that the pronoun refers to Paradise (al-Janna), and the pronoun is used before its mention because it is well known that he was one of its inhabitants.

Ibn Kathir said: "It is possible that it refers to the station in which he was, from the higher dominion (al-Malakut al-A'la)." (End of quote.)

Al-Mahayimi (al-Mahāyimī) also limited himself to this, saying: "﴿Then get down from it﴾, that is, from the rank of angelhood to the rank of the elements (al-ʿanāṣir). ﴿For it is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾, that is, it is not valid or proper, for it is the place of the obedient and the humble." (p-2631) ﴿So go out﴾ is an emphasis on the command to descend, following from its cause. ﴿Indeed, you are among the debased﴾, that is, among the abased and those of humiliation before God Almighty and before His friends.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[14] ﴿He said: "Reprieve me until the day they are resurrected."﴾

﴿"Reprieve me"﴾: that is, give me respite and do not cause me to die. ﴿"until the day they are resurrected"﴾: that is, Adam and his offspring from the graves.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[15] ﴿He said, "Indeed, you are of those reprieved."﴾

﴿He said﴾: "That is, Allah said to him" ﴿Indeed, you are of those reprieved﴾: "That is, of those deferred until the second blowing of the Trumpet."

Ibn Kathir said: He, exalted is He, granted him what he asked, because of the wisdom, will, and volition that He has in this, which cannot be opposed or prevented, and there is no one who can reverse His judgment.

The Imam Abu Sa'd al-Muhsin ibn Karama al-Jashumi al-Yamani said in his tafsir (al-Tahdhib) (p-2632): If it is asked, "What is the purpose of his request, given that he is expelled and cursed?" our answer is his knowledge of the Exalted's goodness toward His creation, both those who obey and those who disobey, so the sin he committed did not prevent him from asking. If it is asked, "Did He address him with this?" we say: that is possible, and it is also possible that He commanded an angel and the angel addressed him with it. If it is asked, "Is it permissible to answer the supplication of a disbeliever?" we say: there is a difference of opinion on this.

The first view: It was said that it is not permissible, because it is an honour and a exaltation (according to Abu 'Ali), and for this reason it is said, "So-and-so's supplication is answered." His being granted respite is not in the sense of answering his supplication, because he is cursed, and because he did not ask in a manner of humility.

(p-2633) The second view: It is permissible to answer his supplication for the sake of his correction, because it is an act of grace (according to Abu Bakr Ahmad ibn 'Ali). But this is not the correct view. If it is asked, "If he is granted respite, would that be an incitement to disobedience?" we say: No, because he did not know the appointed time (p-2634), so it is not an incitement, given that he considers the coming of death upon him to be possible. Also, when the Exalted informed him that He would cause him to enter the Fire and cursed him, he knew that he would never choose faith.

If it is asked, "What is the benefit of granting him respite?" we say: It is a grace (lutf) for him, because it enables him to rectify his affair.

Does anyone go astray through him? Abu 'Ali said: No, because of the Exalted's saying: ﴿You will not seduce [anyone] against Him﴾ [al-Saffat: 162] (p-2635) ﴿except him who is to burn in Hell﴾ [al-Saffat: 163]. Also, if anyone went astray through him, his remaining would be a corruption, and Allah, exalted is He, would not grant him respite. As for Abu Hashim, he permits that someone could go astray through him, and that it would be like an increase in desire. It is also permissible that it is a grace in several respects: first, that the responsible person, when he refrains from evil despite his whispering, his reward is greater. Second, the Exalted made us aware of his enmity, and the intelligent person strives to enrage his enemy and distress him, and that is only through obedience to his Lord. Whoever obeys him, it is from his own self that he is brought, not from his Lord. End of al-Jashumi's words, and this is in accordance with the principles of the Mu'tazila.

The discussion on the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the explanation of a verse's meaning) of His saying, Exalted is He:

[16] ﴿He said: "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path."﴾

﴿He said: "Because You have led me astray"﴾: "That is, You caused me to go astray from guidance, or You decreed my misguidance (*ghiwaya*)." The *ba'* (بِ) here is for swearing an oath, as in His saying, ﴿He said: "By Your might, I will surely mislead them all."﴾ [Sad: 82], meaning: "I swear by Your leading me astray." It has also been said that it carries the meaning of the particle of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*), that is, "on account of Your leading me astray." ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them﴾: "That is, for Adam and his offspring, lying in wait, just as highwaymen sit by the road to ambush travelers." ﴿Your straight path﴾: "That is, Your upright road, which is the path of truth." Its meaning is: "I will not cease from corrupting them." The word *ṣiratak* (صِراطَكَ) is in the accusative either as an adverb of place (*ẓarfiyya*) or by the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-jarr*, the omission of the governing preposition, from the grammatical analysis of i'rab).

(p-2636)

The Discussion of the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[17] ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left. And You will not find most of them grateful.﴾

"﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left﴾ That is, from all four directions. This is a figure of speech for his intent to mislead and lead them astray by whatever means he can, by coming at them from the four directions from which an enemy customarily attacks. For this reason he did not mention above and below.

﴿And You will not find most of them grateful﴾ That is, not using their powers, their limbs, and what Allah has bestowed upon them in the path of obedience and drawing near to Allah.

He said this on the basis of the signs he observed, by way of conjecture, as in His saying: ﴿And Iblis did indeed confirm his assumption about them, and they followed him, except for a group of the believers﴾ [Saba': 20]. Imam Ahmad narrated from Sabrah ibn al-Fakih, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, Satan sat in wait for the son of Adam on his paths. He sat in wait for him on the path of Islam, and said: Will you embrace Islam and abandon your religion and the religion of your fathers and forefathers? He said: So he disobeyed him and embraced Islam. Then he sat in wait for him on the path of emigration (hijrah) and said: Will you emigrate and leave your land and your sky? Indeed, the likeness of the emigrant is like the horse in its tether. He said: So he disobeyed him and emigrated. He said: Then he sat in wait for him on the path of jihad and said to him: It is the struggle of self and wealth; you will fight and be killed, the woman will be married off and the wealth divided? He said: So he disobeyed him and struggled. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Whoever of them does that and dies, it is incumbent upon Allah to admit him to Paradise; or if he is killed, it is incumbent upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, to admit him to Paradise; and if he drowns, it is incumbent upon Allah to admit him to Paradise; or if his mount throws him, it is incumbent upon Allah to admit him to Paradise."

The Hafiz said: There has come in a hadith a seeking of refuge from Satan's domination over the human being from all of his directions (p-2637), and Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would not omit these supplications when he entered the morning and when he entered the evening: O Allah, I ask You for pardon and well-being in my religion and my worldly affairs, and my family and my wealth. O Allah, conceal my faults. O Allah, protect me from before me and from behind me, and from my right and from my left, and from above me, and I seek refuge in Your greatness from being seized from beneath me." It was also narrated by al-Bazzar from Ibn Abbas.

Benefit:

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates that he (Iblis) asked for respite, and that Allah granted him respite, and we have already explained what has been said concerning it. It indicates the intensity of his enmity toward the children of Adam and his eagerness to lead them astray. It indicates that most of the children of Adam are not grateful. It indicates that misguidance is the act of Iblis, and acceptance of it is their act, for which reason He attributed it to them and blamed them for it; and if it were a creation of His, that would not be valid. End of quote. The discussion of such matters is well known.

Then Exalted is He emphasized upon Iblis the curse, the expulsion and the removal from the station of the Exalted Assembly, by His saying, glorified is He:

(p-2638)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 18:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[18] ﴿He said, "Get out of it, reviled and expelled. Whoever follows you among them – I will surely fill Hell with you all."﴾

﴿He said, "Get out of it, reviled﴾ — with a hamza in the well-known recitation, from (dha'ama) (to belittle and blame), when one despises and censures someone. It was also recited as "madhum" (مَذُومًا) with a dammed dhal and a silent waw, and this may be a lightened form of the hamzated word by transferring the vowel of the hamza to the silent letter and then deleting the hamza; or it may be from the weak-lettered root, whose analogous form would be (madhim) like (mabi'), except that the waw was substituted for the ya', in the manner of their saying (makul) for (makil) and (mashub) for (mashib).

﴿expelled﴾ — driven away and cast out. ﴿Whoever follows you among them﴾ — the lam in it is for introducing an oath, and its answer is ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾, meaning: whoever among the jinn and mankind obeys you, I will surely fill Hell with your disbelievers, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Go, and whoever follows you among them – indeed, Hell is your recompense, a full recompense."﴾ [al-Isra: 63].

Al-Jashami said: He said that because none will be in Hell except Iblis and his party of devils, and the disbelievers and wicked among mankind who submitted to him and abandoned God's command for his command. So He gathered them together in the address. If it is asked: why did He make Hell narrow and make Paradise wide? We say: because Hell is a prison, while Paradise is an abode of dominion. If it is asked: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you﴾? We say: as a kindness, so that the responsible person follows the prophets rather than the devils, and as a kindness toward Iblis and his party, since it is the utmost in restraint and prohibition.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates a threat for whoever follows Iblis, and that He will fill Hell with them. This requires a condition, namely that one does not repent, or that there is no greater obedience with him. And it indicates the humiliation, expulsion and cursing of Iblis because of his disobedience, as a warning against the likes of his condition.

(p-2639)

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[19] ﴿And, O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And, O Adam﴾ — i.e., "and We said, O Adam." ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ — i.e., the Garden of eternity (Jannat al-Khuld), or a garden on the earth.

Al-Jashami said: This story has already been mentioned, and the benefit of repeating it is that the Qur'an was revealed over some twenty-three years, circumstances arose, and delegations came, so the story was repeated so that whoever had not heard it might hear it, as a means of guidance and kindness. For the repetition of a single story in several places, in different wordings, each of which is at the utmost of eloquence, is among the aspects of the Qur'an's inimitability. ﴿So eat from wherever﴾ — i.e., from every place ﴿you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers﴾ — i.e., lest you become among those who wronged themselves.

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[20] ﴿Then Satan whispered to them, to expose to them what was concealed from them of their private parts. And he said, "Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels or become of the eternal."﴾

﴿Then Satan whispered to them﴾: that is, Iblis, with the eating of the tree, presenting the benefit to them in imagination. ﴿to expose to them﴾: that is, to reveal to them. ﴿what was concealed﴾: that is, what was hidden. ﴿from them of their private parts﴾: that is, their nakednesses. The lam in ﴿to expose﴾ is either the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), because he did not know that it would come from them, meaning the outcome of his whispering was that he exposed their private parts; or it is the lam of causation and purpose (lam al-ta'lil wa al-gharad), which is its original use, based on his conjecture or his knowledge by some means.

Note:

In the verse there is evidence that uncovering the private parts is among grave matters, and that it is repugnant to human nature; for this reason it was called sau'ah (shameful thing), because it distresses its possessor.

Al-Hakim said: Some people have taken the verse as evidence for the obligation of covering the private parts, and that this was in the law of Adam, peace be upon him.

Al-Qadi said: There is no evidence in the verse for obligation, because it contains nothing except that they did that.

Al-Asamm said: In the verse there is evidence that they both disliked being naked, even though there was no third person with them. In that there is evidence for the ugliness of nudity, even if no one is present with the one who is naked, except out of necessity.

﴿And he said, "Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels or become of the eternal."﴾ That is: except out of aversion that you become ﴿angels﴾, or ﴿become of the eternal﴾: that is, of those who do not die and remain dwelling in the Garden.

Those who held the superiority of the angels over the prophets have used this as evidence, since they committed that act out of desire to attain what was mentioned. Whoever did not hold this view replied with the possibility that this incident occurred before Adam's prophethood. And even if it occurred after it, perhaps Adam desired angelhood for strength, power and capability, or for the nature of the essence, by becoming a luminous substance (al-Razi pointed this out).

Al-Nasir said: It does not follow from Iblis's belief in this, and his whispering that the angels are more excellent, that the matter is so in the knowledge of God, exalted is He. Do you not see that Iblis reported that God forbade them from the tree so that they would not become eternal or become angels, and in that he was a liar and a falsifier? So there is no evidence in it then. The verse does not contain anything requiring God's confirmation of Iblis in that, nor His affirmation of him in it. Rather, the verse was concluded with what indicates that he lied to them and deceived them, when God said: ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 22]. Perhaps his preference of the angels over prophethood is part of his deception. End.

Al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): I say: I am still amazed at those who begin to derive evidence from this verse, when the speech in it is what God related from the words of Iblis in the context of condemning him for lying, deception, falsehood and fraud. Evidence is only drawn from the words of God, or from speech that He related from some of His prophets. If it is not that, it is speech that He related while accepting it and confirming it. End.

Moreover, it was read as (malikayn) with a kasrah on the lam, as Ibn 'Abbas and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir used to read it. Al-Wahidi said: Iblis only came to them from the direction of kingship. This is indicated by the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ [Taha: 120]. End.

An irregular reading may be an explanation of the widely transmitted one, as is well known, and with this the objection of al-Razi here is dispelled.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[21] ﴿And he swore to them both, "Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisors."﴾

﴿And he swore to them both﴾ means: he swore an oath to them both. ﴿Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisors﴾ means: in this matter.

Ibn Kathir said: That is, he swore to them by Allah regarding that, until he deceived them. And the believer may be deceived by Allah. End of quote.

From Qatadah: Only the believer is deceived by Allah. And it is reported from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that whenever he saw in his slave obedience and good prayer, he would free him. So his slaves would act in that way seeking manumission. It was said to him: "Indeed, they deceive you." He said: "Whoever deceives us by Allah, we allow ourselves to be deceived by him."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 22:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[22] ﴿So he lured them with deception. And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves some leaves of the Garden. And their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?"﴾

﴿So he lured them with deception﴾ "That is, he enticed them. Its origin is the thirsty man who lowers a bucket (yudalli) into the well to drink of its water, but finds no water in it, so he is one who lowers himself into it with deception. Thus, lowering (tadliyah) was used in place of enticing toward what brings no benefit. In it is an indication that he brought them down by this from a high rank to a low station, for tadliyah and idla' mean sending something down from a high place to a low one. It was said: the meaning of dallahuma is that he emboldened them by his deception, and the original is (dallalahuma), and ad-dall and ad-dalalah mean boldness, as the poet said:

"I think forbearance has emboldened my people against me, and sometimes the forbearing man is considered ignorant."

So one of the two doubled letters was changed into a yā'.

﴿And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾ That is: punishment and the ill consequence of disobedience seized them, so the clothing fell away from them, and their nakedness became apparent to them.

As-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): Some of them used it as evidence that whoever tastes wine has disobeyed, end of quote.

This is an adherence to the apparent meaning here, for dhawq is the existence of taste in the mouth, and it is evident that it may be used to refer to a small amount of eating, and this is what is meant here, because in another verse eating was explicitly mentioned in it. ﴿And they began to fasten﴾ That is, they began to patch and stick one leaf upon another ﴿over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ That is, in order to cover themselves with it.

Al-Jashami said: it indicates that covering the private parts was part of the law of Adam, peace be upon him. And some people have used the verse as evidence for the obligation of covering.

Al-Qadi said: There is nothing in the verse that necessitates obligation, since there is no more in it than that they did that.

Al-Asamm said: It also indicates that covering is part of the nature of Adam and Eve, and that they disliked nakedness even though there was no third person present, so in that is evidence of the ugliness of exposing oneself except when there is need.

﴿And their Lord called to them﴾ That is, He reminds them of the earlier prohibition, the command, and the warning to avoid Satan ﴿"Did I not forbid you from that tree"﴾ That is: from eating from it ﴿"and tell you that Satan is to you a clear enemy?"﴾

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 23:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[23] ﴿They said, "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾

"﴿They said, 'Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves'﴾" i.e., we have harmed them by disobedience. "﴿And if You do not forgive us﴾" i.e., what has passed. "﴿And have mercy upon us﴾" i.e., by accepting repentance and its acceptance. "﴿We will surely be among the losers﴾" i.e., we will surely be among those who have lost all the perfections they had attained. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said, concerning His words "﴿Our Lord, we have wronged﴾" and the rest of the verse: they are the words that Adam received from his Lord.

A subtle point (lata'if):

Al-Jashami said: It is said that Adam, peace be upon him, was made happy by five things: he acknowledged the sin, he regretted it, he blamed himself, he hastened to repentance, and he did not despair of mercy. And Iblis was made wretched by five things: he did not acknowledge the sin, he did not regret it, he did not blame himself but attributed the matter to his Lord and so did not repent, and he despaired of mercy.

The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[24] ﴿He said: "Go down, some of you an enemy to others. And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time."﴾

﴿He said: "Go down"﴾ — i.e., from the Garden to anywhere other than it. Abu Muslim said: its meaning is "go." It is addressed to Adam, Hawwa' (Eve), and Iblis.

Ibn Kathir said: The principal parties to the enmity are Adam and Iblis. That is why He said in Surat Ta-Ha: ﴿He said: "Go down, both of you, from it, all together"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123], and so on. Hawwa' follows Adam, and the serpent, if the report of it is authentic, follows Iblis.

The exegetes have mentioned the places where each of them descended. The sum of those reports goes back to the Isra'iliyyat (narratives traced to Israelite sources), and God knows best their authenticity. Had there been any benefit in specifying those places, one that returns to the responsible persons in matters of their religion or their worldly affairs, God Exalted would have mentioned it in His Book, or His Messenger (ﷺ) would have. End of quotation.

﴿some of you an enemy to others. And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾ — i.e., settlement, or a place of settlement. ﴿and provision﴾ — i.e., enjoyment and livelihood. ﴿for a time﴾ — i.e., until the end of your appointed terms.

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[25] ﴿He said: "Therein you will live, therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth."﴾

﴿He said, "Therein"﴾ — that is, the earth — ﴿you will live﴾, i.e., you will subsist. ﴿And therein you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾ — that is, on the Day of Resurrection for recompense, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more﴾ [Ta-Ha: 55].

Then, glorified is He, reminded them of His favor in settling them in the abode and the place of residence on the earth, and in clothing them with garments with which they cover their private parts, after He had stripped them of the garment of Paradise. This was because of their need, after the descent, for clothing and livelihood. So He, glorified is He, said:

"The discussion of the words of Allah, the Exalted:

[26] ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts, and as adornment; but the clothing of righteousness — that is best. That is among the signs of Allah that they may remember.﴾

"﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing﴾ meaning what is worn of garments and other things.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He made what is on the earth to be sent down from the sky, because He decreed and wrote there (i.e., He decreed and apportioned for you), and His decrees and apportionment are described as descending from the sky, inasmuch as they are written in the Preserved Tablet.

Abu al-Baqa' said: Since feathers and clothing grow by means of rain, and rain descends, He treated what is the cause (the rain) as if it were the means (the sending down)... End of quote.

(p-2645) Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya said in a fatwa of his concerning the meaning of 'descent': There is no need to take the word out of its well-known linguistic meaning, for clothing does descend from the backs of livestock. Glorified is He, Who bestowed favour upon them with what they benefit from livestock in clothing and furnishings. This, Allah knows best, is the meaning of His sending it down: He sends it down from the backs of livestock, namely the coverings of livestock made of wool, fur and hair, from which the children of Adam benefit in clothing and finery. He has indeed sent them down upon them. Most people on earth clothe themselves with animal hides, which serve to ward off heat and cold, and these are greater than what is made of cotton and linen.

﴿that covers your private parts﴾ — i.e., that conceals your nakedness which Iblis intended to expose from your two parents, until they were compelled to stitch leaves over themselves, though you have no need of that. ﴿And as adornment﴾ — its conjunction may be either a conjunction of attributes, in which case the clothing is described by two things: covering the private parts and beautification. Thus 'feathers' here means adornment, for it is the adornment of birds, and the word is used metaphorically from that. Or it may be a conjunction of one thing with another, meaning: We sent down two kinds of clothing, clothing for covering and clothing for adornment, in which case there is an ellipsis of the described noun, i.e., clothing that is 'rīsh' (having feathers), and rīsh is a word shared between the noun and the verbal noun.

Ali ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn Abbas, and al-Bukhari related from him, that 'rīsh' means wealth. Many of the early scholars also related this. Ibn Taymiyya said: Some exegetes applied to it the word 'wealth', and by it they meant a specific kind of wealth. Ibn Zayd said: beauty. It is also read as 'rīshan'. Ibn al-Sikkit said: 'al-riyāsh' is the household goods, whatever is of clothing or stuffing of bedding or covers; and 'al-rīsh' is goods and property, and it may apply to garments without other property. One says: 'innahu la-hasan al-rīsh', i.e., good garments. End of quote.

One says: 'rāsha fulān', meaning he gathered feathers, which is wealth and furnishings. 'Rāsha al-ṣadīq' means he fed him, gave him drink and clothed him; its origin is from rīsh, as if the poor destitute man has no ability to rise, like one whose wing has been clipped; and whoever you have shown kindness, you have 'rishtahu'. Thus in Taj al-'Arus.

Benefit:

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Umama, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever acquires a new garment and wears it, and when it reaches his collarbone says: 'All praise is due to Allah who has clothed me with that by which I cover my nakedness and adorn myself in my life,' then he takes the old garment and gives it in charity, he will be under the protection of Allah, under the guarantee of Allah, and in the care of Allah, alive and dead." It was related by al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.

(p-2647) Imam Ahmad also narrated from Abu Matar that he saw Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, come to a young boy and buy from him a shirt for three dirhams, and he wore it down to between the wrists and the ankles, saying as he wore it: "All praise is due to Allah who has provided me with finery by which I adorn myself among the people, and by which I cover my nakedness." It was said to him: "Is this something you narrate from yourself or from the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "This is something I heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at the time of clothing: 'All praise is due to Allah who has provided me with finery by which I adorn myself among the people and by which I cover my nakedness.'"

When Allah, the Exalted, explained the outward covering and its adornment, He alluded to the covering of the inward defects and its adornment by His words ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ — i.e., the fear of Allah, or faith, or good bearing; all are close in meaning. Its nominative is by way of the inceptive, its predicate being the clause ﴿that is best﴾, or 'best', with 'that' as its attribute, as if it were said: the clothing of righteousness, the one indicated, is best.

Al-Mahayimi said: Because the outward is the place of people's gaze, while the inward is the place of the Truth's gaze, and inward defects are more shameful than outward nakedness.

Al-Qashani said: The clothing of righteousness is the attribute of scrupulousness and caution, from the attributes of the soul; "that is best" because it is among the pillars of the laws, being the root and foundation of religion, like protective measures in treatment. End of quote.

Abu Ali al-Farisi said: The meaning of the verse: the clothing of righteousness is better for its wearer when he takes hold of it, and nearer to him to Allah, than the garments and finery with which he adorns himself. He said: The clothing is attributed to righteousness just as it is attributed to hunger in His words: ﴿So Allah made them taste the clothing of hunger and fear﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]. End of quote.

(p-2648) That is, it is a metaphor, both implicit and imaginative, by imagining for righteousness a state resembling clothing, which encompasses the whole body according to scrupulousness and fear of Allah, just as clothing encompasses the wearer; or it is of the type of 'the lujayn of the water' (a metaphor for the water's sheen). Nafi', Ibn Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction with ﴿clothing﴾.

﴿That﴾ — i.e., the sending down of clothing ﴿is among the signs of Allah﴾, indicating His grace and mercy upon His servants ﴿that they may remember﴾ — i.e., His blessing upon them, so that they recognise its greatness and give thanks for it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This verse comes by way of digression following the mention of the exposure of the private parts and the stitching of leaves over them, to display the favour in what He created of clothing, and because of the humiliation and disgrace in nakedness and the exposure of the private parts, and to signal that concealment is a great gate of righteousness.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates the magnitude of Allah's blessings through these favours which He enumerated. Ali ibn Musa al-Qummi held that it indicates the obligation of covering the private parts. Others said it does not indicate that; the apparent meaning is only the bestowal of favour through it, in that it wards off heat and cold, covers the private parts and gives adornment. As for its being obligatory, that is remote. Even if its obligation were established for them, we would need a fresh proof for its obligation in our law; and its obligation in this law has been established by widely-transmitted report and consensus, so there is no need to refer to another law.

It also indicates that Allah, as He bestowed the blessings of this world, bestowed the blessings of religion, for the closer view is that the clothing of righteousness is knowledge and righteous action. Thus He joined to the blessings of this world the blessings of religion by which success with reward is attained, so both blessings of the two abodes are obtained."

The discussion of the words of God, Exalted is He:

[27] "O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise, stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts. Indeed, he sees you, he and his soldiers, from where you do not see them. Indeed, We have made the devils allies to those who do not believe."

"O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you": i.e., let him not deceive you away from entering Paradise by stripping from you the garment of the Sharia and of piety, so that he removes you from the sight of God, with His mercy upon you. "As he removed your parents from Paradise": an adjectival clause describing an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., let him not tempt you with a temptation like the removal of your parents. "Stripping them of their clothing": i.e., the apparent, by means of the stripping of the garment of piety. "To show them their private parts": i.e., the apparent ones that indicate the hidden shame. The clause "stripping" (yanzi') is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) either from "your parents" or from the subject of "removed" (akhraja), meaning: he removed them while stripping their clothing, in that he was the cause of their being stripped. The form of the present tense is used to make the scene present to the mind.

Two notes:

The first: al-Suyuti said in al-Iklil: "This verse has also been cited as evidence for the obligation of covering the awrah, and whoever holds that the awrah is only the two private parts has used these two verses as evidence."
