He mentioned crime (jurm) alongside being deprived of entry into Paradise, and wrongdoing (zulm) alongside punishment with the Fire, which is more severe than the deprivation mentioned, as an alert that it is the greatest of crimes. Then the Exalted followed His threat with His promise, according to His custom in His Noble Revelation, so He said, glorified is He:

(p-2688)

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[42] ﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide eternally.﴾

"﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide eternally.﴾" Abu al-Baqa' said: "Those who believed" is the subject (mubtada'), and concerning the predicate (khabar) there are two views:

The first: "﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾," with the implied meaning "(from among them)," so the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) has been omitted, as it is omitted in His saying: ﴿And whoever is patient and forgives, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [al-Shura: 43].

The second: that the predicate is "﴿Those are the companions of Paradise﴾," and "﴿We do not burden﴾" is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridh) placed between them. End of quotation.

Several of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) restricted themselves to the second view. They said: The secret (sirr) of the parenthetical clause is to encourage the pursuit of what leads to everlasting bliss by showing how easily it can be attained and how facilitated its acquisition is. What made it fitting is that righteous deeds were mentioned before it; that is, when it is known that the basis of obligation (taklif) is capacity, the desire for that pursuit increases, since it is attained through what contains ease and not hardship.

A subtle point:

Al-wus' (capacity) is what a person can do with ease and sustain. This is the statement of al-Razi, drawing on the words of Mu'adh concerning the verse ("its ease, not its hardship"). He said: As for the utmost effort of strength, it is called juhd (exertion), not wus'. Whoever thinks that wus' means exerting maximum effort has erred.

I say: In the Qamus: al-wus' (which may be vocalized with three vowels) means wealth/means (al-judda) and strength (al-taqah), like al-si'ah. And in it: al-juhd is strength (taqah, and may be vocalized with a damma) and hardship (mashaqqah). End of quotation.

Ibn al-Athir said: al-jahd (with a fatha) means hardship, and it was said: exaggeration and utmost limit; and with a damma, it means capacity and strength. It was said: they are two dialects for capacity and strength, but for hardship and utmost limit, only the fatha is used. End of quotation. From this it is known that what al-Razi adopted is a view of the lexicographers, not a consensus.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 43:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[43] ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this. And we would not have been guided if Allah had not guided us. Certainly did the messengers of our Lord come with the truth." And they will be called, "This is Paradise; you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do."﴾

"﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾" That is: We will extract from their hearts the causes of hatred, envy and enmity, or We will purify their hearts of them, so that among them there will be nothing but mutual affection and compassion. The past tense form is to announce its certainty and firm establishment.

Its establishment is ﴿rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who has guided us to this"﴾, that is, to that for which this is the reward, that is, to the causes of this exalted station, by sending the messengers and granting success in acting.

﴿And we would not have been guided if Allah had not guided us﴾ That is: we would not have been directed to that deed whose reward is this, had Allah not granted us success through His proofs, His kindnesses and His care.

﴿Certainly did the messengers of our Lord come with the truth﴾ That is: so we were guided by their guidance. Al-Zamakhshari said: they say that, that is, "Praise be to Allah," etc., out of joy and delight at what they have attained, and savoring the speaking of it, not as drawing near or worship, just as you see someone who has been granted good in this world speaking in such terms, unable to refrain from saying it, out of happiness and gladness.

﴿And they will be called, "This is Paradise; you have been given it as an inheritance for what you used to do"﴾ That is: you have been given it because of your deeds in the world. So "inheritance" is used metaphorically for giving, and it is used figuratively in that sense to indicate that the cause is not an obligating one, even though it is a cause in outward terms, just as inheritance is ownership without earning, even though kinship, for example, is a cause of it. Based on what has been established, it cannot be said that this contradicts what is established in the two Sahihs from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Know that none of you will enter Paradise by his deed!" They said, "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said, "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy and grace."

It does not need an answer, nor is it necessary to say that the "ba'" here indicates exchange and not cause. This is the fulfilment of the promise of rewarding the obedient, not by entitlement and merit, but purely by His bounty, exalted is He, like inheritance. So said al-Inayah.

Imam Muslim narrated from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will call out: Indeed, for you is that you will live and never die; indeed, for you is that you will be healthy and never fall ill; indeed, for you is that you will be young and never grow old; indeed, for you is that you will enjoy bounty and never be miserable." That is the meaning of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they will be called, "This is Paradise"﴾, and so on.

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[44] ﴿The companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire: "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true. Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" They will say, "Yes." Then a caller will announce between them: "The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers."﴾

﴿The companions of the Garden will call out﴾: i.e., when they have settled in their abodes. ﴿to the companions of the Fire﴾: rebuking (p-2691) and humiliating them. ﴿saying, "We have found what our Lord promised us to be true"﴾: since we have attained these lofty ranks. ﴿"Have you found what your Lord promised to be true?"﴾: concerning your being brought down to the lowest of the low, on account of your arrogance toward the signs and the messengers. ﴿They will say, "Yes"﴾: i.e., we have found it to be true. ﴿Then a caller announces﴾: i.e., calls out. ﴿between them﴾: i.e., between the two groups, so that they may hear it, increasing the gloating of one group and the regret of the other. ﴿"The curse of God is upon the wrongdoers"﴾.

The commentary on His words, exalted is He:

[45] ﴿Those who bar (others) from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter.﴾

﴿Those who bar (others) from the way of Allah﴾ "That is: they prevent themselves and others from His upright religion, which He made clear through the tongues of His messengers, for its knowledge and for the prosperity of both abodes. ﴿And seek to make it crooked﴾ "That is: they seek to introduce deviation and inclination into it, away from what it is upon, so that no one follows it."

﴿And they are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾ "That is: they deny the meeting with Allah in the Hereafter and do not believe in it. Therefore they are unconcerned, and they commit what is objectionable in speech and action, for they do not hope for a reckoning for it nor a punishment. So they are the worst of people."

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[46] ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the A'raf (the Heights) are men who recognize each by his mark. And they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you." They have not entered it, though they are hoping.﴾

﴿And between them is a barrier﴾ means: between the two groups there is a wall and a screen, or between Paradise and Hellfire, to prevent the effect of each from reaching the other.

This barrier was called a wall in the verse: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them with a gate. Its inner side will have mercy, and its outer side will face torment﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And upon the A'raf are men﴾ means: upon the heights (a'raf) of the barrier, its battlements and its upper parts, which is the wall erected between them. A'raf is the plural of 'urf, a metaphorical use taken from the 'urf of a horse (its mane) and the 'urf of a rooster (its crest). Anything raised above the ground is an 'urf, since by its elevation it is more visible than what is low.

The exegetes have related many statements about the men of the A'raf, from the Successors and others, that they are the excellent among the believers, or that they are the martyrs, or the prophets, or a people who were harmed in the way of Allah, who looked down upon their enemies in order to gloat over them, so they recognized them by their marks, and they greeted the people of Paradise with peace. The wording, because of its ambiguity, allows all of this, since the context indicates the high rank of these people, especially by making their station the A'raf, which are the heights and the eminences, as has been mentioned earlier. All those mentioned are deserving of this, and Allah knows best.

﴿They recognize each﴾ means: from among the people of Paradise and the Fire, ﴿by his mark﴾ means: by their sign, which Allah has informed them of, such as the whiteness and blackness of the face.

**Benefit:**

Al-simā (the mark) is both a short vowel form and a long form, and al-simah and al-simiyā' (with their vowels) both mean "sign."

Al-Qadi said: al-simā is of the pattern fi'la, from "sāma ibilahu" (he let his camels graze, marked), when he sent them out to pasture marked, or from "wasama" with metathesis, like al-jāh from al-wajh. End of quotation.

Ibn Durayd restricted himself to the second view.

﴿And they call out﴾ means: the men of the A'raf ﴿to the companions of Paradise﴾ means: when they see them from their heights, and they have recognized from their marks that they are the people of Paradise, ﴿"Peace be upon you"﴾ by way of supplication and greeting, or by way of informing them of their deliverance from what is hateful.

The first view is the one transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, in what al-'Awfi related from him. He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Allah placed them in that station so that they might know those in Paradise and in the Fire, and so that they might recognize the people of the Fire by the blackness of their faces, and seek refuge in Allah from being placed with the wrongdoing people. And in that state they greet the people of Paradise with peace. ﴿They have not entered it, though they are hoping﴾: the pronouns in both clauses refer to the companions of the A'raf. The first clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw, and the second is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yadkhuluhā" (they enter it). That is: they called out to them while they had not yet entered Paradise, being in a state of hoping to enter it, awaiting it.

Al-Jushami, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is said: If the companions of the A'raf are the excellent among the believers, why is their entry delayed? We say: They hastened to the pleasure of gloating over their enemies, and though their entry is delayed, it is because of the manifestness of their merit and the nobility of their path to their stations. End of quotation.

In my view it is not far-fetched that the clause ﴿They have not entered it, though they are hoping﴾ is a circumstantial clause from "the companions of Paradise." That is: they called out to them with peace while they were, in their station, in hope of entering Paradise, bringing them good news of safety and success from the punishment, indicating that the men of the A'raf precede others in entering Paradise and that their stations are higher than others. And Allah knows best.

Abu Mijlaz held that the two pronouns refer to the companions of Paradise. That is: the people of the A'raf called out to the companions of Paradise with peace, while the companions of Paradise had not yet entered it and were hoping to enter it. This is a good view. The first clause is then a circumstantial clause from the object, which is "the companions of Paradise," and the second is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "yadkhuluhā."

The discussion of the words of God, Exalted is He: "And when their sights are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say: Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."

﴿And when their sights are turned﴾ — that is, the sights of the People of the Heights (al-A'raf) or of the People of Paradise.

Al-Jashami said: He said "turned" (ṣurifat) because their gaze toward the People of the Fire is a gaze of enmity, so they do not look except when their faces are turned toward them. As for the People of Paradise, their faces are toward them in joy at them, so it needs no effort. It was also said: because they, together with the People of Paradise, are distant from the People of the Fire, so they need to turn their sights toward the companions of the Fire.

Then al-Jashami said: The verse indicates the obligation of avoiding wrongdoers in this world, so that one is not with them in the Hereafter. End quote.

﴿toward the companions of the Fire﴾ — that is, toward Jahannam. ﴿They say﴾ — out of their intense fear, seeking refuge in God: ﴿Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people﴾ — that is, in the Fire.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The description of them with wrongdoing, rather than the torment and evil condition they are in at that time, which is what calls for the supplication, indicates that what they fear is not the torment itself alone, but what entails it and leads to it of wrongdoing.

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted: [48] ﴿And the companions of the heights will call out to men whom they will recognize by their marks, saying, "Your gathering did not benefit you, nor did that which you used to be arrogant about."﴾

"﴿And the companions of the heights will call out to men﴾" meaning: from among the great ones of the people of misguidance. "﴿whom they will recognize by their marks﴾" that is, by the signs which identify them, even if their forms have changed. "﴿Saying, 'Your gathering did not benefit you﴾" that is: your multitude, or your gathering of wealth by which calamities are warded off. "﴿Nor did that which you used to be arrogant about﴾" against the truth, or toward the creation. It was also read as (tastakthirun), from abundance, meaning: from the followers whom one seeks help from in repelling calamities.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: That is, your gathering, your clan, and your audacity against the truth did not benefit you, nor did your arrogance. This is either a negation or a rhetorical question of rebuke, and it is more eloquent and more silencing. Then they looked toward the Garden and saw among the weak ones, whom the disbelievers used to belittle in the world and claimed that God would not single them out over them in the world, the people of the heights say to them:

The Interpretation of His, Exalted is He, Words:

[49] ﴿Are these the ones of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy? "Enter the Garden; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve."﴾

﴿Are these﴾ "the weak among the believers ﴿of whom you swore that Allah would not grant them mercy﴾" — by elevating their ranks in the Hereafter. So there they are in the Garden, enjoying and delighting themselves, and in its gardens they are made joyful. As for His, Exalted is He, words: ﴿Enter the Garden; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve﴾, meaning: no fear will be upon you from the punishment descending upon the disbelievers, and you will not grieve as the disbelievers grieve over the loss of bliss. This [saying] is either from the words of the People of the Heights, who confer among themselves about entering the Garden after the rebuke of the people of the Fire, so one of them says to the others: "Enter the Garden"; or it is from the speech of the People of the Heights to the believers, meaning they say to them: "Enter the Garden"; or it is a continuation of the address of the People of the Heights to the men, as if it were said to them: "Look at these whom you swore that Allah would not grant them His mercy — how they have attained it, since it was said to them from His, Exalted is He, side: Enter the Garden." In any case, the sentence is built upon an omitted saying, for brevity, since it is known.

A subtle point:

Al-Zamakhshari explained the secret of their being held back on the Heights and then admitted to the Garden in the most eloquent exposition, and he said, may Allah have mercy on him: "It is said to the People of the Heights: 'Enter the Garden,' and that is after they have been held back on the Heights, and they have looked at the two groups, and recognized them by their marks, and said what they say."

The benefit of this is the demonstration that the reward is in proportion to the deeds, and that advancement and delay are according to them, and that no one is preferred before Allah except by his precedence in action, and no one is left behind with Him except by his lagging in it; and that the hearers may be eager for the condition of the foremost and strive to win their prize; and that they may picture that on that Day every person is known by his mark, which made him deserving of being branded with it from among the people of good and evil, so that the wrongdoer restrains himself from his wrongdoing, and the doer of good increases in his goodness; and that they may know that the sinners are rebuked by everyone, until the least of people in deeds. End.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the humiliation of the people of the Fire and their asking the people of Paradise for some of their drink and food, after the arrogance they had shown toward them, and after they had sworn that Allah would not show them mercy, and that they would not be granted that. He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[50] ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise: "Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided you." They will say: "Indeed, Allah has forbidden both of them to the disbelievers."﴾

"﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise: 'Pour upon us some water'﴾ i.e., of that with which Allah has provided you, to cool the heat of the Fire and thirst."

Al-Jashami said: They used the word "pouring" (al-ifada) because the people of Paradise are higher in place. "﴿Or some of what Allah has provided you﴾" i.e., of the foods and fruits. "﴿They will say: Indeed, Allah has forbidden both of them to the disbelievers﴾" i.e., He withheld them from them, because He had bestowed blessings upon them in the world, but they did not give thanks for them, so He denied them His blessings in the Hereafter. Thus the prohibition is a prohibition of withholding, not a prohibition of worship (taʿabbud). Then He described the disbelievers with His saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 51:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[51] ﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play, and whom the worldly life had deceived. So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾

"﴿Those who took their religion as amusement and play﴾" i.e., of what Satan had made attractive to them.

Al-lahw (amusement) is everything that turns one away from the truth, and al-la'ib (play) is every false matter. That is, their religion in reality is nothing but that, since it is their habit and their constant practice. "﴿And the worldly life had deceived them﴾" with its hasty adornments, so they did not act (for the Hereafter). "﴿So today We will forget them﴾" i.e., We will leave them as one who is forgotten, so We will not show them the mercy We show to those who work for the Hereafter. "﴿As they forgot the meeting of this their day﴾" i.e., as they behaved toward its meeting like those who forget, not bringing it to their minds and not caring about it.

A subtle point:

Al-Shihab said: "﴿We will forget them﴾" is a figure of speech. It likens His treatment of these people to the treatment of one who is not regarded or attended to, so he forgets him, because forgetting is impossible for God Most High, i.e., because nothing escapes His knowledge, as He said: "﴿In a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾" [Ta-Ha: 52]. Forgetting is frequently used in the sense of abandoning in the language of the Arabs. It is also valid here, so it would be a genuine metaphor (isti'arah tahqiqiyyah) or a free metonymy (majaz mursal). Likewise their forgetting of the meeting with God, since they had not been remembering God so as to have Him forgotten. He likened their not bringing to mind the meeting with God and the Resurrection, and their lack of concern, to the state of one who knew something and then forgot it. The kaf here is not for comparison but for causation, though there is no obstacle to it being for comparison too. End of quotation.

(p-2697) And He, exalted is He, said: "﴿And as they used to deny Our signs﴾" i.e., just as they used to deny that they were from God Most High.

al-Tirmidhi related from Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A servant will be brought on the Day of Resurrection, and Allah will say: 'Did I not give you hearing, sight, wealth and children, subject to you the cattle and the tilled land, and leave you to lead and to rule over others? Did you not think that you would meet this your day?' He will say: 'No!' Then He will say to him: 'Today I forget you as you forgot Me.'"

In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in Muslim: "The servant will meet his Lord, and He will say: 'O so-and-so! Did I not honor you, make you a leader, marry you, subject to you the horses and camels, and leave you to lead and to rule over others?' He will say: 'Yes, my Lord!' He will say: 'Did you think that you would meet Me?' He will say: 'Indeed I forget you as you forgot Me!'"

When He, exalted is He, informed of their loss in the Hereafter, He mentioned that He had removed their excuses in this world by sending the Messengers and sending down the Books. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[52] ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe.﴾

"﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed﴾ That is: We made clear in it the beliefs (i'tiqadat), the rulings (ahkam), and the matters of the Hereafter, in detailed and explicit exposition. ﴿with knowledge﴾" That is: knowing how We detail its rulings, its admonitions, its narratives, and all its other meanings, until it came as something firmly structured, upright, and free of crookedness. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He has sent it down with His knowledge﴾ [al-Nisa: 166]. ﴿Guidance﴾" That is: an indication that directs them to the truth and saves them from error. ﴿And mercy﴾" That is: it saves them from the punishment, because of what it contains of proofs and the removal of doubts. ﴿For a people who believe﴾" Because they are the ones who take full advantage of its benefits.

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted:

[53] ﴿Do they await anything but its final outcome? The day its final outcome comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth. So are there any intercessors for us who might intercede on our behalf, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?" They have certainly lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them.﴾

﴿Do they await anything but its final outcome?﴾ That is: they only await what its matter will come to, namely the clarification of its truthfulness through the manifestation of what it declared of promise and threat. Al-Shihab said: "Here (al-naẓar) carries the meaning of (al-intiẓar, waiting), not the meaning of seeing." And al-ta'wil (final outcome, consequence) means the consequence and what actually comes to pass, which is its original meaning, and it is also applied to interpretation (tafsir). The meaning is: before the occurrence of what is certain, they are like those waiting for it, because every coming thing is near, so they are on the verge of encountering what they were promised. Thus it is not asked: "How can they await it while they deny it?" For even though they deny it, they are in the position of those waiting and in their ruling, in that those conditions will certainly come upon them. ﴿The day its final outcome comes﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, because it is the Day of Recompense and the outcome to which their affairs lead. ﴿Those who had forgotten it before will say﴾ means they abandoned it as one abandons what is forgotten, at the time when remembrance would have benefited them, so they did not believe in it at the sight of the punishment. ﴿The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth﴾ means: with what is actual of the beliefs, the promise and the threat. ﴿So are there any intercessors for us who might intercede on our behalf﴾ in removing the punishment. ﴿Or could we be sent back﴾ to the place of action ﴿so that we might do other than what we used to do﴾ of denial, frivolity, play, and the deeds of this world.

He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have certainly lost their souls﴾ by directing their deeds toward disbelief. ﴿And what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾ means: what they used to fabricate has vanished from them, namely that their deities would be their intercessors with God, and they knew that in their claim they had been liars.

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the disbelievers and their worship of other than Him, He argued against them, making clear through His acts that there is no deity besides Him, with His saying:

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 54 (part 1 of 8)**

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[54] ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days; then He established Himself above the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which pursues it swiftly, and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command. Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command. Blessed is Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾

"﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾" meaning: indeed, your Master, your Owner, and your Manager, whom you must worship, O people, is the One who brought into being the substances of the heavens and the earth within the span of six days.

(p-2700) Concerning this verse there are several issues:

The first: al-Shihab said: "Yawm (day) in the language means any period of time. If this is what is meant, then the meaning is six periods, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day﴾ [al-Anfal: 16]. If the customary meaning is intended, which is the time from sunrise to sunset, then the meaning is within the span of six days, because the day only came into being after the creation of the sun and the heavens, so a noun must be understood as elided." End of quote.

In Sharh al-Qamus: the day is from sunrise to sunset, or from true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq) to sunset, and the second is a legal (shar'i) definition according to most scholars.

It is transmitted from al-Fasi, its commentator, that for the astronomers (al-munajjimin) the day is from one sunrise to the next, or from one sunset to the next.

Then al-Zabidi said: "It is also used in the sense of unrestricted time. Ibn Hisham transmitted this, and related it from Sibawayh regarding the expression (I, today, will do such-and-such), for they do not mean a specific day but the present time." He said: "On this basis they interpreted His words, exalted is He: ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]."

(p-2701) Then he said: "Yawm may be used to mean time in general, and from this is the hadith: 'Those are the days of harj (chaos),' meaning its time, and it is not restricted to daytime to the exclusion of night." End of quote.

The use of yawm to mean unrestricted time is the same as the meaning of unrestricted time mentioned before it, as is evident. The apparent position is that its application to the customary sense and to unrestricted time is linguistic in both cases, as the commentator of al-Qamus transmitted both, contrary to the apparent sense of al-Shihab's words above. So verify this.

The second: Ibn Kathir said: "God, exalted is He, informs that He created the world, its heavens, its earth, and what lies between them, in six days, as He informed of this in more than one verse of the Qur'an. The six days are: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, and on Friday the whole creation was gathered, and on it Adam, peace be upon him, was created. They differed regarding these days: is each day like these days, as is the common understanding, or is each day like a thousand years, as Mujahid and the Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal explicitly stated? This is also narrated through al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

As for Saturday, no creation occurred on it, because it is the seventh day, and it was named al-Sabt (Saturday) from sabt, which means cutting off (rest). As for the hadith which the Imam Ahmad related in his Musnad from Abu Hurayrah, who said: 'The Messenger of Allah ﷺ took my hand and said: Allah created the clay on Saturday, created the mountains in it on Sunday, created the trees in it on Monday, created the harmful things on Tuesday, created light on Wednesday, scattered the living creatures in it on Thursday, and created Adam, peace be upon him, after the afternoon prayer on Friday, the last of creation, in the last hour of the hours of Friday, between the afternoon prayer and the night.' Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj related it in his Sahih, and al-Nasa'i through more than one chain. It includes all seven days, while God, exalted is He, has said: in six days. For this reason al-Bukhari and other memorizers of hadith spoke about this hadith and considered it to be from the narration of Abu Hurayrah from Ka'b al-Ahbar, not raised to the Prophet (marfu'). And Allah knows best." End of quote.

I have explained this matter at length in my commentary on al-Arba'in al-'Ajluniyyah.

The third: al-Qadi said: "The creation of things gradually, despite the ability to bring them into being all at once, is evidence of choice (al-ikhtiyar), that is, if it had been by necessity (al-ijab), it would have occurred all at once. It also encourages deliberation in affairs."

As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿then He established Himself above the Throne﴾. Know that istiwa' occurs with several meanings for which the word is shared. It comes in the sense of settling (al-istiqrar), as in: ﴿and it settled on al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44]; and in the sense of intending (al-qasd), as in: ﴿then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. Whoever finishes a matter and intends something else has "istawa" to it and toward it. Al-Farra' said: "The Arabs say: istawa ilayya yukhasimuni (he turned toward me, disputing with me), meaning he turned to me." It also comes in the sense of taking control (al-istila'), the poet said:

"Bishr has taken control over Iraq."

Another said:

"When we rose above them and took control over them, we left them felled for the vulture and the hawk."

It also comes in the sense of height (al-'uluw), and from it is the verse: ﴿And when you and those with you have settled upon the ship﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28], and from it is this verse.

(p-2703) Al-Bukhari said at the end of his Sahih, in the Book of Refutation of the Jahmiyyah, in the chapter on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And His Throne was upon the water﴾ [Hud: 7]: Mujahid said: "istawa" means "'ala 'ala al-'Arsh" (rose above the Throne). End of quote.

In the book al-'Uluw by the memorizer al-Dhahabi: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: "I heard more than one of the exegetes say: ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], meaning: He rose high (irtafa'a)."

Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that it means "irtafa'a" (rose high), and he said: "In all its occurrences it means 'alaa wa irtafa'a (ascended and rose high)." I say: there is no need for excessive elaboration on this, for istiwa' is not unknown, even if its modality (al-kayf) is unknown.

The Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal related in his book al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyyah, from Shurayh ibn al-Nu'man, from 'Abd Allah ibn Nafi', who said: Malik ibn Anas said: "Allah is in the heaven, and His knowledge is in every place; nothing is devoid of it."

(p-2704) Al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Wahb, who said: "I was with Malik when a man entered and said: 'O Abu 'Abd Allah! ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], how did He establish Himself?' Malik lowered his head, and sweat seized him. Then he raised his head and said: ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], as He described Himself, and it is not said: how. The how (kayf) is negated from Him, and you are a person of innovation (bid'ah)."

In another narration he said: "The modality is not conceivable, and the istiwa' from Him is not unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking about it is an innovation."

The memorizer al-Dhahabi said in al-'Uluw, after citing this: and its text is:

"This is the statement of the People of the Sunnah entirely: that the modality of istiwa' we do not conceive, rather we do not know it; its istiwa' is known as He informed in His Book, and it is as befits Him. We do not delve deeply nor show off, nor do we engage in its implications, by negation or affirmation; rather we keep silent and stop, as the early generations (al-salaf) stopped. We know that if it had an interpretation, the Companions and the Followers would have hastened to clarify it, and they would not have been able to affirm it, pass it on, and remain silent about it. And we know with certainty, along with this, that Allah, may His majesty be exalted, has no like in His attributes, nor in His istiwa', nor in His descent, glory be to Him and exalted is He above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation."

Then al-Dhahabi said: The Imam, the eminent scholar Abu Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn Muslim ibn Qutaybah al-Dinawari, author of famous works, said in his book Mukhtalaf al-Hadith: "We say regarding the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿There is no private conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7], that He is with them, knowing what they are upon, just as you say to a man whom you have directed to a distant land: 'Beware of negligence, for I am with you,' meaning that your negligence is not hidden from me. How is it permissible for anyone to say that Allah, glory be to Him, is in every place, by indwelling in it, along with His words: ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] (p-2705) and along with His words: ﴿To Him ascends the good word﴾ [Fatir: 10]? How does something ascend to Him while He is with it? And how do the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him while He is with them?" He said: "If these people returned to their natural disposition (fitrah), and to what their essences were constructed upon regarding knowledge of the Creator, they would know that Allah, mighty and majestic, is the Most High and the Exalted, and that hands are raised in supplication to Him, and all nations, Arab and non-Arab, say: Allah is in the heaven, if they were not left upon their natural dispositions." End of quote.

Then al-Dhahabi also said, from Yazid ibn Harun, the Shaykh of Islam, that he was asked: "Who are the Jahmiyyah?" He said: "Whoever claims that ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] is contrary to what is settled in the hearts of the common people (al-'ammah), then he is a Jahmi."

Al-Dhahabi said: "By the common people he means the majority of the community and the people of knowledge. What has settled in their hearts from the verse is what the discourse indicates, along with their certainty that the One who established Himself: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. This is what has settled in their sound natures and correct minds. If He had a meaning beyond that, they would have spoken of it, and would not have neglected it. And if any of them had interpreted istiwa', the resolve would have been strong to transmit it, and if it had been transmitted, it would have become well known. If there is among the ignorant and foolish any who understands from istiwa' what implies deficiency, or analogy of the witnessed to the unseen, or of the created to the Creator, then this is rare. Whoever utters that is rebuked and taught, and I do not think any of the common people would affirm that in himself. And Allah knows best." End of quote.

(p-2706) The shaykh, the imam, the knower, the exemplar of the knowers, Shaykh 'Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, may Allah sanctify his spirit, said in his book Tuhfat al-Muttaqin wa Sabil al-'Arifin, in the chapter on the differences of schools regarding the attributes of Allah, mighty and majestic, and in mentioning the disagreement of people about pausing at His words: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. Ishaq said: "in knowledge," and he went on to say: "Allah, exalted is He, is by His essence upon the Throne, His knowledge encompasses every place, and the pause according to the people of truth is at His words 'except Allah'."

This has been transmitted from Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This pause is good for one who believes that Allah is by His essence upon the Throne and knows what is in the heavens and the earth. He went on to say: "A group of those who deny the istiwa' of the Lord, mighty and majestic, paused at His words: ﴿The Most Merciful, above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] and began with: ﴿established Himself﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] ﴿to Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ [Ta-Ha: 6]. They intend by this to negate the istiwa' by which He described Himself, and this is an error on their part, for Allah, exalted is He, established Himself upon the Throne by His essence."

And he said in his book al-Ghunyah: "As for knowing the Creator through signs and proofs in summary, it is that you know and are certain that Allah is One, the Unique." He went on to say: "No place is devoid of His knowledge, but it is not permissible to describe Him as being in every place. Rather it is said that He is in the heaven above the Throne, as He, glorified is His praise, said: ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and His words: ﴿Then the Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [al-Furqan: 59], and He, exalted is He, said: (p-2707) ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10]. And the Prophet ﷺ judged the Muslim status of the slave-girl when he said to her: 'Where is Allah?' and she pointed to the heaven." And the Prophet ﷺ said in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "When Allah created the creation, He wrote a book concerning Himself, and it is with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy has overcome My wrath."

In another wording: "When Allah, glory be to Him, finished creating the creation, He wrote concerning Himself in a book, and it is with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy has preceded My wrath."

It is appropriate to affirm the attribute of istiwa' without interpretation, and that it is the istiwa' of the Essence upon the Throne, not in the sense of sitting and contact, as the Mujassimah and the Karramiyyah said, nor in the sense of height and elevation, as the Ash'ariyyah said, nor in the sense of taking control and domination, as the Mu'tazilah said, because the Law did not come with that, and it was not transmitted from any of the Companions, the Followers, or the righteous early generations of the People of Hadith regarding that. Rather what is transmitted from them is taking it (p-2708) in its unrestricted sense.

It has been transmitted from Umm Salamah, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, regarding the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿The Most Merciful established Himself above the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]: "The modality is not conceivable, the istiwa' is not unknown, affirming it is obligatory, and denying it is disbelief."

Al-Qasimi, *Mahasin al-Ta'wil*, commentary on surah 7, verse 54 (part 2 of 8):

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj narrated it from her, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in his *Sahih*, and likewise in the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him).

Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah have mercy on him) said shortly before his death: "The reports about the attributes are to be passed on as they came, without likening (*tashbih*) and without denial (*ta'til*)." He also said, in the narration of some of them: "I am not a man of *kalam* (speculative theology), and I do not see *kalam* being applied to any of these matters. Whatever is in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or in a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), or from his Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), or from the Successors, [is acceptable]. As for anything beyond that, discussing it is not praiseworthy. So it should not be said regarding the attributes of the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, 'How?' or 'Why?' Only a doubter says that."

Ahmad (may Allah be pleased with him) also said, in another narration from him in a different place: "We believe that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is above the Throne in whatever manner He wills and as He wills, without limit and without a description that any describer can reach or any limiter can define," on the basis of what was related from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Ka'b al-Ahbar, who said: Allah, the Exalted, said in the Torah: "I am Allah, above My servants. My Throne is above all My creation, and I am upon My Throne, governing My servants by it. Nothing of My servants is hidden from Me."

That Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is upon the Throne is mentioned in every Book revealed to every Prophet sent, without modality (*bila kayf*).

Also, Allah the Exalted, in what has never ceased to be, is described with loftiness, power, dominion, and prevalence over all His creation, including the Throne and other than it. Therefore *istiwa'* is not to be understood as anything other than that. *Istiwa'* is one of the attributes of the Essence, according to what He has informed us of, affirmed, and emphasized in seven verses of His Book and in the authentic Sunnah. It is a necessary attribute of Him and befitting to Him, like the hand, the face, the eye, hearing, sight, life, power, and His being Creator, Provider, Giver of life, and Causer of death, which are also attributes of Him. We do not step outside the Book and the Sunnah. We recite the verse and the report, we believe in what is in them, and we entrust the modality of the attributes to the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic (p-2709), as Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna (may Allah have mercy on him) said: "As Allah, the Exalted, described Himself in His Book, its *tafsir* is its recitation. There is no *tafsir* for it other than that. We do not burden ourselves with anything beyond that, for it is unseen (*ghayb*), and the intellect has no room to grasp it." We ask Allah, the Exalted, for pardon and well-being, and we seek refuge in Him from saying about Him and His attributes what He and His Messenger (peace be upon him) have not informed us of. End of al-Jilani's words, may his secret be sanctified.

Abu Isma'il al-Ansari narrated in *Dhamm al-Kalam wa Ahlihi* from Abu Zur'a al-Razi that he was asked about the *tafsir* of ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and he became angry and said: "Its *tafsir* is as you recite it: He is upon His Throne, and His knowledge is in every place. Whoever says other than this, upon him is the curse of Allah."

It is also related from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hatim, who said: "I asked my father and Abu Zur'a about the creed of the People of the Sunnah regarding the fundamentals of religion, and what they had found the scholars holding in all the regions, and what they themselves believed about that. They said: 'We found the scholars in all the regions, in Hijaz and Iraq, Egypt and Syria, and Yemen, and it was part of their creed that Allah, blessed and exalted, is upon His Throne, separate from His creation, as He described Himself, without modality, encompassing everything in knowledge.'"

**Notes:**

**First: On the invalidity of interpreting *istawa* as *istawla* (to seize dominion):**

The Imam Abd al-Aziz ibn Yahya al-Kinani, companion of al-Shafi'i (may Allah the Exalted have mercy on both of them), said in his book *al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyya*: "The Jahmiyya claim that the meaning of *istawa* is *istawla*, from the Arabic saying 'So-and-so *istawa* over Egypt,' meaning he seized it." He said: "It is said to them: Is there any creature of Allah's creation over which a period of time passed during which it was not under His dominion? If they say no, it is said to them: whoever claims that is a disbeliever. Then it is said to them: You are bound to say that the Throne passed through a period during which Allah was not dominant over it. That is because He informed us that He, glory be to Him, created the Throne before the heavens and the earth, and then seized dominion over it after creating them. So you are bound to say: during the period when the Throne existed before the creation of the heavens and the earth, Allah was not dominant over it in that period." He then mentioned a lengthy discussion establishing loftiness and arguing for it.

(p-2710) Ibn Arafa said in *al-Radd 'ala al-Jahmiyya*: Dawud ibn Ali narrated to us, saying: "We were with Ibn al-A'rabi, when a man came to him and said: 'What is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]?' He said: 'He is upon His Throne as He informed us.' The man said: 'O Abu Abd Allah! Its meaning is only *istawla*.' He said: 'Be silent! One does not say *istawla* over a thing unless there is an opponent in it, and whichever of the two overcomes, it is said he *istawla*. Allah, the Exalted, has no opponent, and He is upon His Throne as He informed us.'" Then he said: "*Al-istila'* is after overcoming, as al-Nabigha said:

*"Except for one like you, or one whom you outrun, / Outrunning the horse when it has taken the lead over the course."*

(The poem is quoted as it stands.)

Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn al-Nadr, who said: "Ibn al-A'rabi was our neighbor, and his nights were the finest of nights. He mentioned to us that Ibn Abi Du'ad asked him: 'Do you know in the language *istawa* with the meaning of *istawla*?' He said: 'I do not know it!'" In another narration: "Ibn Abi Du'ad wanted me to search for him, in some of the Arabic dialects and their meanings, [for a case where] ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] means *istawla*. I said to him: 'By Allah, this does not occur, and I have not found it.'" Ibn al-A'rabi, Abu Abd Allah, was the linguist of his age, as al-Dhahabi said.

Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari said in his book he named *al-Ibana fi Usul al-Diyana*, which his followers mention is the last book he composed, and on which they rely in defending him against those who criticize him:

**Chapter**
**On clarifying the statement of the People of Truth and the Sunnah**

If someone says: "You have denied the views of the Mu'tazila, the Qadariyya, the Jahmiyya, the Harurriyya, the Rafida, and the Murji'a, so tell us the view you hold," it is said to him: "Our view is adherence to the Book of our Lord, the Sunnah of our Prophet, what has been related from the Companions, the Successors, and the imams of hadith. We hold fast to that, and we follow what Abu Abd Allah Ahmad ibn Hanbal used to say, may Allah make his face radiant, raise his rank, and magnify his reward. We speak in accordance with him, and those who oppose his statement are opposed, because he is the excellent imam and the complete leader, through whom Allah made the truth clear, pushed back misguidance, suppressed the innovations of the innovators, and the deviation of the deviators."

Then he said under the heading "On *istiwa'* over the Throne": If someone says, "What do you say about *istiwa'*?" it is said to him: "We say that Allah is established upon His Throne as He said: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. And Allah said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10]. And He said: ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾ [An-Nisa': 158] (p-2712). And He said: ﴿He arranges the affair from the heaven to the earth; then it ascends to Him﴾ [As-Sajda: 5]. And He related of Pharaoh: ﴿Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways﴾ [Ghafir: 36], ﴿the ways of the heavens, that I may look at the God of Moses, though I think him a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 37]. Moses was accused of lying in his saying that Allah is above the heavens. And He said: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven, that He will cause the earth to swallow you?﴾ [Al-Mulk: 16]. Above the heavens is the Throne, so when the Throne was above the heavens, He said: ﴿He who is in the heaven﴾ [Al-Mulk: 16], because He is established upon the Throne which is above the heavens. Everything that is high is called 'heaven,' and the Throne is the highest of the heavens. When He said, 'He who is in the heaven,' He did not mean all of the heaven, but He meant the Throne, which is the highest of the heavens. Do you not see that Allah mentioned the heavens and said: ﴿and made the moon therein a light﴾ [Nuh: 16]? He did not mean that the moon fills them, and that it is in all of them together. We have seen all the Muslims raising their hands toward the sky when they supplicate, because Allah is upon the Throne which is above the heavens. Had it not been that Allah is upon the Throne, they would not have raised their hands toward the Throne, just as they do not lower them toward the earth when they supplicate."

Then he said:

**Chapter**
Some of the Mu'tazila, the Jahmiyya, and the Harurriyya have said that the meaning of His saying ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5] is that He seized dominion, ruled, and subdued, and that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is in every place. (p-2713) They denied that Allah is upon His Throne, as the People of Truth say, and they interpreted *istiwa'* as "power" (*al-qudra*). If this were as they stated, there would be no difference between the Throne and the seventh earth, because Allah is capable of all things. Allah is capable of the earth, of the latrines, and of everything in the world. So if Allah were established upon the Throne in the sense of *istila'*, and He, the Mighty and Majestic, has dominion over all things, He would be established upon the Throne, upon the earth, upon the heaven, and upon the latrines and filth, since He is capable of things and has dominion over them. And since He is capable of all things, and no Muslim has permitted saying that Allah is established upon the latrines and the privies, it cannot be that *istiwa'* over the Throne means *istila'*, which is general to all things. It must be that the meaning of *istiwa'* is specific to the Throne and not all things. He cited proofs from the Qur'an, the hadith, the consensus (*ijma'*), and reason. End of his words.

I say: The latter statement of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari is taken from the book *Radd al-Imam Ahmad 'ala al-Jahmiyya*, where he said in the book mentioned:

"Among the things the misguided Jahmiyya denied is that Allah, glory be to Him, is above the Throne. We said: Why do you deny that? Allah, glory be to Him, is above the Throne, and Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5], and He said: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne, the Most Merciful; so ask about Him one who is informed﴾ [Al-Furqan: 59]. They said: 'He is beneath the seventh earth just as He is upon the Throne, so He is upon the Throne, in the heavens, in the earth, and in every place. No place is empty of Him, and He is not in one place rather than another.' And they recited verses from the Qur'an: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ [Al-An'am: 3]. We said: Muslims know many places in which there is nothing of the greatness of (p-2714) Allah. They said: 'Which place?' We said: 'Your bowels, the bellies of pigs, the latrines, and the filthy places: there is nothing of the greatness of the Lord, glory be to Him, in them.' He has informed us that He is in the heaven, so He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Are you secure from He who is in the heaven, that He will cause the earth to swallow you?﴾ [Al-Mulk: 16], to the end of the verse. He said: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10]. He said: ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth, and those who are with Him﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 19]. He said: ﴿Indeed, I will take you and raise you to Me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 55]. He said: ﴿Rather, Allah raised him to Himself﴾ [An-Nisa': 158]. He said: ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾ [An-Nahl: 50]. He said: ﴿The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 4]. He said: ﴿He is the Subduer over His servants, and He is the Wise, the All-Aware﴾ [Al-An'am: 18]. So this is Allah informing that He is in the heaven, and we find everything below to be blameworthy. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾ [An-Nisa': 145]. ﴿And those who disbelieved will say: Our Lord, show us those who misled us of the jinn and mankind; we will put them beneath our feet so that they will be among the lowest﴾ [Fussilat: 29]. And we said to them: Do you not know that Iblis had his place, (p-2715) and the devils had their place? Allah does not gather Himself with Iblis. Rather, the meaning of His saying, blessed and exalted, ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and in the earth﴾ [Al-An'am: 3], is that He is the God of those in the heavens and the God of those in the earth, and He is upon the Throne! His knowledge has encompassed what is below the Throne; no place is empty of Allah's knowledge, and Allah's knowledge is not in one place rather than another. That is His saying: ﴿So that you may know that Allah is over all things competent, and that Allah has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [At-Talaq: 12]."

He said: Among the considerations on this matter: if a man holds a cup of clear glass with something in it, his sight encompasses the cup without him being inside the cup. So God, glory be to Him, and to Him belongs the most exalted likeness, encompasses all His creation without being within anything of His creation. Another example: if a man builds a house with all its amenities, then shuts its door and leaves it, the son of Adam is not unaware of how many rooms are in his house and how spacious each room is, without the owner of the house being inside it. So God, glory be to Him, and to Him belongs the most exalted likeness, encompasses everything He has created, and knows how it is and what it is, without being within anything He has created.

Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Among the interpretations the Jahmiyya (the followers of Jahm ibn Safwan) gave of God's words, ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7], up to His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7], they said: Allah, mighty and majestic, is with us and among us. We said: Why have you cut off the report from its beginning? God says: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth? There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7], meaning that Allah is the fourth of them by His knowledge, ﴿nor of five but that He is the sixth of them, nor of fewer than that or more but that He is with them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7], by His knowledge of them. He opens the report by His knowledge and closes it by His knowledge. End of quotation.

(p-2716) Then Imam Ahmad said at the end of his aforementioned book: We said to the Jahmiyya: You claim that Allah is in every place, that no place is free of Him. We said to them: Tell us about the words of Allah, may His praise be exalted: ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. Why did He manifest Himself, if He is in it according to your claim? If He were in it, as you claim, He would not have manifested Himself to anything. Rather, Allah, exalted, is above the Throne, and He manifested Himself to something He was not in, and the mountain saw something it had never seen before that.

We said to the Jahmiyya: Is Allah light? They said: He is entirely light. We said: Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿And the earth shines with the light of its Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 69]. So He, may His praise be exalted, has informed that He has light. We said: Tell us, since you claim that Allah is in every place and He is light, why does a dark house not illuminate with the light in which He is, if you claim that Allah is in every place? And what is the matter with the lamp, that when it is brought into a dark house it gives light? At that point, their lie against Allah became clear.

May Allah have mercy on the one who understands from Allah and turns back from the opinion that contradicts the Book and the Sunnah, who adopts the view of the scholars, which is the view of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and who abandons the religion of Satan and the religion of Jahm and his followers. End of quotation.

The Imam, the memorizer Ibn Abd al-Barr, said in his book (al-Tamhid), in explanation of the hadith: "Our Lord descends (p-2717) every night..." the hadith, the following text: This hadith is established through transmission, with a sound chain, and the people of hadith do not differ over its authenticity. In it is evidence that Allah, exalted, is in the heaven, above the Throne, above the seven heavens, as the community has said. It is their proof against the Mu'tazila and the Jahmiyya in their statement: "Allah is in every place, and not above the Throne." The evidence for the correctness of what the people of truth have said on this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]. Then he cited a number of verses on this and said: All these verses are clear in refuting the statement of the Mu'tazila. As for their claim of metaphor in "istiwa'" (establishment), and their interpretation of "istawa" as "istawla" (to seize dominion), there is no meaning to it, because it is not apparent in the language. The meaning of "istila'" in the language is overpowering, and Allah, exalted, is not overpowered by anyone, and He is the One, the Eternal Refuge.

It is necessary that speech be taken according to its literal meaning, until the Ummah agrees that a metaphorical meaning was intended, since there is no way to follow what has been sent down to us from our Lord, exalted is He, except in this way. The speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, is only interpreted according to its most well-known and apparent aspects, so long as nothing prevents this that requires submission.

If claiming metaphor were permitted for every claimant, no act of worship would be established. Allah is too exalted to address except in what the Arabs understand, according to their customary modes of address, in what its meaning is correct for the listeners. And "istiwa'" is known and understood in the language: it is elevation and rising above a thing, and settling and being firmly established upon it.

Abu Ubayda said, regarding the words ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]: he said: "'alā" (rose above). He said: The Arabs say: "I istawaytu (I mounted/settled) above the riding animal," and "I istawaytu above the house." Another said: "istawā" means "istaqarra" (settled), and he cited the words of Allah, exalted: ﴿And when he reached his maturity and istawā﴾ [al-Qasas: 14], meaning his youth ended and he became settled, so there was no further increase in his youth.

Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Istiwa' is settling in height. With this Allah, exalted, addressed us in His Book, saying: (p-2718) ﴿That you may sit firmly upon its backs, then remember the favor of your Lord when you are seated upon them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 13]. He, exalted, also said: ﴿And it settled (istawat) upon al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44]. And He, exalted, said: ﴿And when you and those with you are settled (istawaytum) upon the ship﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28]. And the poet said:

They led them to water in a barren desert,
while the Yemeni star had risen and settled (istawā).

This cannot be interpreted by anyone as "istawla," because the star does not seize dominion. And al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, who was trustworthy, reliable, and eminent in the knowledge of religion and language, mentioned, saying: al-Khalil told me, and that is enough with al-Khalil, saying: I went to Abu Rabi'a al-A'rabi, who was among the most knowledgeable people I had seen. He was on a roof. We greeted him, and he returned the greeting and said: "Istawu" (rise up). We remained bewildered and did not know what he had said. A bedouin beside him said to us: He has commanded you to ascend. Al-Khalil said: It is from the words of Allah: ﴿Then He istawā toward the heaven﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. So we climbed up to him.

He said: As for those who clung to a hadith narrated by Abdullah ibn Dawud al-Wasiti, (p-2719) from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Samad, from Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, regarding the words ﴿The Most Merciful is established upon the Throne﴾ [Ta-Ha: 5]: he said: He seized dominion over all His creation, so there is no place free of Him. 

The answer is: This is a munkar (rejected) hadith attributed to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and its transmitters are unknown or weak. As for Abdullah ibn Dawud al-Wasiti and Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid, both are weak. Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Samad is unknown and not recognized. Moreover, they do not accept solitary reports (akhbar al-ahad). How then can it be permissible for them to argue with a hadith like this, if they had understanding and were fair? Have they not heard Allah, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿And Pharaoh said: O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the means﴾ [Ghafir: 36], ﴿the means of the heavens, so that I may look at the God of Moses, though I think he is a liar﴾ [Ghafir: 37]? This indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, used to say: "My God is in the heaven," while Pharaoh thought him a liar. The poet said:

Glory be to Him whom creation cannot measure in His true measure,
He who is above the Throne, the One, the Unique.
A King over the Throne of the heaven, the Guardian,
before His might the faces bow and prostrate.

This poetry belongs to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, and in it he says, describing the angels:

And their prostrating one does not raise his head for ages,
he exalts a Lord above him and glorifies Him.

He said: If they argue with the words of Allah, exalted: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], and with His words: ﴿And He is Allah in the heavens and on the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 3], and with His words: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7]... (p-2720) and they claim that Allah, glory be to Him, is in every place in His essence and His self, blessed is His majesty, it is said: There is no disagreement between us and you and between the rest of the Ummah that He is not in the earth in His essence, below the heaven. Therefore it is obligatory to take these verses according to the correct, agreed-upon meaning, which is that He is a God worshipped in the heaven by its inhabitants, and a God worshipped on the earth by its inhabitants. So too have the people of knowledge of tafsir (exegesis) said.

The apparent meaning of this revelation testifies that He is above the Throne, so the dispute on this falls away. The happiest of people with it is the one whom the apparent meaning supports. As for His words in the other verse: ﴿And on the earth a God﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 84], consensus and agreement have clarified that what is meant is that He is worshipped by the inhabitants of the earth. So reflect on this, for it is decisive.

Also among the proof that He, mighty and majestic, is above the Throne above the seven heavens is that all the monotheists, both Arabs and non-Arabs, when a matter distresses them or a calamity befalls them, raise their faces toward the heaven, and lift their hands pointing toward the heaven, seeking help from Allah their Lord, blessed and exalted. This is more famous and better known among the elite and the common people than that it needs more than a mention.

Because it is an instinctive reaction, no one has disagreed with them about it, nor has any Muslim denied it to them. And the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the slave girl whose master wished to free her, (p-2721) if she was a believer: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ tested her by saying to her: "Where is Allah?" She pointed to the heaven. Then he said to her: "Who am I?" She said: You are the Messenger of Allah. He said: "Free her, for she is a believer." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was satisfied from her with her raising her head toward the heaven, and that sufficed him from anything else.

He said: As for their argument with His words, exalted is He: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7], there is no proof for them in the apparent meaning of this verse, because the scholars among the Companions and the Successors, from whom interpretation of the Qur'an was transmitted, said the interpretation of this verse is: He is above the Throne, and His knowledge is in every place. No one who is cited as an authority has opposed them in this.

Sunayd reported from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, regarding the words of Allah, exalted: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them﴾ [al-Mujadila: 7]: he said: He is above His Throne, and His knowledge is with them wherever they are.

He said: And it has reached me from Sufyan al-Thawri something similar. Sunayd said: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us from Asim ibn Bahdala, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Allah is above the Throne, and His knowledge is in every place; nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him.

Then he cited through the route of Yazid ibn Harun, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Asim ibn Bahdala, from Zirr, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The distance between the heaven and the earth is a five-hundred-year journey, and the distance between each heaven and the next is five hundred years, and the distance between the seventh heaven and the Kursi (Footstool) is a five-hundred-year journey, and the distance between the Kursi and the water is a five-hundred-year journey, (p-2722) and the Throne is upon the water, and Allah is above the Throne, and He knows your deeds. He mentioned this statement, or something close to it, in the book (al-Istidhkar).

Shaykh al-Islam Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him, said in (al-Risala al-Madaniyya): When Allah describes Himself with an attribute, or His Messenger ﷺ describes Him with it, or the believers describe Him with it, those whose guidance and understanding the Muslims agree upon, then turning it away from its apparent meaning that befits His majesty, glory be to Him, and from its understood reality to a hidden meaning that contradicts the apparent meaning, and to a metaphor that contradicts the reality, requires four things:

The first of them: that this word is used in a metaphorical sense, because the Book, the Sunnah and the speech of the early generations came in the Arabic tongue, and it is not permissible that what is meant by it be contrary to the Arabic language, or contrary to all languages. Thus that metaphorical meaning must be one that the word is intended to convey, otherwise every falsifier could interpret any word with any meaning that abrogates it, even if it has no basis in the language.

**Second:** There must be a indication that requires diverting the wording from its literal (*haqiqa*) to its figurative (*majaz*) meaning. Otherwise, if a term is used with one meaning in its literal sense and with another in its figurative sense, it is not permissible to interpret it figuratively without an indication that requires diverting it, by the consensus of the rational. Whoever claims that it must be diverted from the literal sense needs a decisive proof, rational or textual, that requires the diversion. And if one claims that the diversion from the literal sense is apparent, then a proof that favours the figurative interpretation is still needed.

**Third:** That diverting indication must be free from a contrary indication. Otherwise, if a Qur'anic or faith-based proof stands showing that the literal meaning is intended, abandoning it is prohibited. If that proof is not considered in opposition to its counterpart, and it is apparent, then preference (*tarjih*) is still required.

**Fourth:** When the Messenger (ﷺ) spoke a statement and intended by it the opposite of its apparent meaning and its literal sense, he must clarify to the community that he did not intend its literal sense but its figurative sense, whether he specified it or not. This is especially so in a knowledge-based discourse, in which what is required from them is belief and knowledge, not the action of the limbs. Indeed, He (glorified be He) made the Qur'an a light, a guidance, a clarification for mankind, and a cure for what is in the breasts, and He sent the Messenger (p-2723) to clarify for people what was revealed to them, and so that he might judge between people concerning what they differed about, and so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers. Then this unlettered Arab Messenger was sent with the most eloquent of languages and the clearest of tongues and expressions. Then the community who took from him were the deepest of people in knowledge, the most sincere to the community, and the clearest of them in the Sunnah. It is therefore not permissible that he and they speak a statement intending by it the opposite of its apparent meaning unless he has established an indication that prevents taking it in its apparent sense. This indication is either rational and manifest, such as His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [An-Naml: 23], for everyone knows by his reason that the meaning is: she has been given of the kind of thing that such things are given. Likewise His saying: ﴿the Creator of all things﴾ [Az-Zumar: 62], where the listener understands that the Creator is not included in this generality. Or it is a manifest textual indication, such as the indications in the Book and the Sunnah that restrict some apparent meanings.

(p-2724) It is not permissible that He direct them to a hidden indication that only individuals among people can deduce, whether it is textual or rational. For when He speaks a statement that conveys a meaning, and repeats it many times, and addresses all creatures with it, among whom are the intelligent and the dull, the jurist and the non-jurist, and He has obligated them to contemplate that address, understand it, reflect upon it, and believe its implication, then obligated them not to intend by this address any of its apparent meaning, because there is a hidden indication that individuals among people deduce, indicating that He did not intend its apparent sense, that would be deception or confusion, and would be the opposite of clarification and the opposite of guidance. It would resemble riddles and enigmas more than guidance and clarity. How much more so when the indication of that address upon its apparent sense is stronger by many degrees than the indication of that hidden proof that the apparent is not intended; how much more so when that hidden thing is a doubt that has no reality? End of quote.

**Second:** Many think that affirming elevation (*'uluw*) and settling (*istiwa'*) entails affirming embodiment (*tajsim*), and many of the traditionists have been accused of this. Among those who made this accusation is al-Jalal al-Dawani in his commentary on al-'Adudiyya's creed, where he said, may Allah pardon him: Most of the anthropomorphists (*mujassima*) are the literalists (*zahiriyya*) who follow the apparent meaning of the Book and the Sunnah, and most of them are the traditionists. Ibn Taymiyya Abu al-'Abbas and his companions have a great inclination to affirm a direction, and an exaggeration in criticising its negation. I saw in some of his works that there is no difference, by the immediate judgement of reason, between saying: He is non-existent, and saying: I sought Him in all places and did not find Him. He attributed the deniers to nullification (*ta'til*). This is despite his high standing in the rational and transmitted sciences, as one who examines his writings will attest.

The summary of some people's words in some places is that the Law came with specifying Him, exalted be He, with the direction of "above," just as He specified the Ka'ba by being the House of Allah, and for this reason one turns toward it in supplication.

It is not hidden that there is no danger at all in this degree. But some of the later people of hadith did not accept this statement, and denied that "above" is the direction of supplication. Rather, he said: The direction of supplication is Himself, just as the Ka'ba itself is the direction of prayer. He explicitly stated that He is literally the direction of Allah, exalted be He, without any figurative usage. End of al-Dawani's words.

(p-2725) Several scholars responded to him:

Among them: Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani in his gloss on it called *Majla al-Ma'ani*. He said: Ibn Taymiyya is not one who affirms embodiment, for he explicitly stated that Allah, exalted be He, is not a body, in a treatise in which he discussed the hadith of descent.

He said in another treatise: Whoever says that Allah, exalted be He, is like the body of a human, or that Allah, exalted be He, resembles any of the created things, has slandered Allah, glorified be He. Rather, he holds, according to the way of the Salaf, that Allah, exalted be He, is literally above the Throne, with the negation of the implications, and he reported the consensus of the Salaf on it. He stated this in the *al-Risala al-Qadariyya*. End of quote.

Among them: Wali Allah al-Dihlawi, may his secret be sanctified. He said in his book *Hujjat Allah al-Baligha*: These meddlers have overpowered the people of hadith, calling them anthropomorphists and likeners, and said: They are those who hide behind *al-Balkafa*. It has become clear to me, very clearly, that this overpowering is nothing, and that they are wrong in their statement both in transmission and in understanding, and erring in their slander of the imams of guidance. End.

Among them: Shihab al-Din al-Alusi, the exegete. He wrote on al-Dawani's statement the following text: Far be it from Allah that he (meaning Ibn Taymiyya) should be among the anthropomorphists; rather he is the most free of people from them. Yes, he says the affirmation of above, and that is the way of the Salaf, and it is far removed from embodiment. Jalal al-Din and his like are the most ignorant of people regarding the hadiths and the statements of the righteous Salaf, as is not hidden from the knowledgeable and fair. His son transmitted this from him in *Muhakamat al-Ahmadayn*.

I say: Whoever accuses such an imam of embodiment has lied and did not know it. However, his excuse is that he did not search for the gems of his speech in his fatwas, in which he clarified the truth and illuminated the way of the Salaf entirely. Here is a fragment from his pearls. He said, may Allah have mercy on him, in some of his fatwas:

The principle in this matter is that everything established in the Book of Allah, exalted be He, or the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ) must be affirmed, such as the elevation of the Lord, His settling upon His Throne, and the like. As for the innovated terms (p-2726) of negation and affirmation, such as the saying of one who says: He is in a direction, or He is not in a direction, He is delimited (*mutahayyiz*) or He is not delimited, and the like of terms about which people disputed, and none of them has a text, neither from the Messenger (ﷺ), nor from the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) and those who followed them in goodness, nor from the imams of the Muslims, none of them said that Allah, exalted be He, is in a direction, nor said He is not in a direction, nor said He is delimited, nor said He is not delimited, nor even said He is a body or substance, nor said He is not a body or substance. These terms are not stated in the Book, nor in the Sunnah, nor in consensus, and those who utter them may intend a correct meaning. If they intend a correct meaning that agrees with the Book and the Sunnah, that is accepted from them; and if they intend a false meaning that contradicts the Book and the Sunnah, that meaning is rejected from them. So when one says: Allah, exalted be He, is in a direction, it is said to him: What do you mean by that? Do you mean that He, glorified be He, is in an existent direction that confines Him and encompasses Him, such as being within the heavens? Or do you mean by "direction" a non-existent matter, namely that there is nothing of the created things above the world?

If you mean the existent direction, and you make Allah confined within the created things, this is false. If you mean by the non-existent direction and you mean Allah alone above the created things, separate from them, this is true, and it does not mean that any of the created things confined Him, or encompassed Him, or was above Him; rather He is exalted above them, encompassing them.
