Allah, exalted be He, has said: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾ [Az-Zumar: 67], the verse. It is established in the Sahih from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, mighty and majestic, grasps the earth on the Day of Resurrection and folds the heavens (p-2727) in His right hand, then shakes them and says: I am the King, where are the kings of the earth?" And Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: The seven heavens and the seven earths and what is in them and what is between them, in the hand of the Most Merciful, are not but like a mustard seed in the hand of one of you.

In another hadith, He will throw them as children throw a ball. So whoever has all created things in relation to His grasp, exalted be He, and to this contempt and insignificance, how could they encompass Him and confine Him? And whoever says that Allah, exalted be He, is not in a direction, it is said to him: What do you mean by that? If he means by it that there is no Lord worshipped above the heavens, nor a god upon a Throne, and our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) was not caused to ascend to Allah, exalted be He, and hands are not raised to Allah, exalted be He, in supplication, and hearts do not turn toward Him, then this is Pharaonic, a denier and rejecter of the Lord of the worlds. If he believes that he affirms Him, then he is ignorant and self-contradictory in his speech. From here entered the people of indwelling (*hulul*) and unification (*ittihad*), and they said: Allah, exalted be He, is in His essence in every place, and the existence of created things is the existence of the Creator. But if he says: By my statement "not in a direction" I mean that created things do not encompass Him, then he is correct in this meaning.

Likewise, whoever says that Allah, exalted be He, is delimited or says He is not delimited: if he means by "delimited" that created things contain Him and encompass Him, he is wrong; and if he means by it separate from created things, distinct from them, high above them, he is right. Whoever says "not delimited," if he means created things do not contain Him, he is right; and if he means He is not separate from them, but is neither inside them nor outside them, he is wrong. People in this matter are of three categories: the people of indwelling and unification, the people of negation and denial, and the people of faith, monotheism and the Sunnah.

The people of indwelling say: He is in His essence in every place, and they may say unification and oneness, saying: The existence of created things is the existence of the Creator.

As for the people of negation and denial, they say: He is neither inside the world nor outside it, nor separate from it, (p-2728) and this is the statement of the speculative Jahmiyya who nullify (*mu'attila*), just as the first is the statement of the worshippers among the Jahmiyya. The speculative Jahmiyya do not shrink from anything, and the devotional Jahmiyya worship everything, and their statements return to nullification and denial, which is the statement of Pharaoh.

It is known that Allah, exalted be He, existed before He created the heavens and the earth, then He created them. Either He entered into them, and this is a false indwelling; or they entered into Him, and this is even more false; or Allah, glorified be He, is separate from them, not having entered into them, nor they into Him, and this is the statement of the people of truth, monotheism and the Sunnah.

The people of denial and nullification have doubts in this matter with which they oppose the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic, the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), what the Salaf of the Community and its imams agreed upon, what Allah, exalted be He, instilled in His servants, and what sound rational proofs indicate. All these proofs agree that Allah, exalted be He, is above His creation, high above it. Allah, exalted be He, instilled this in the old women, the Bedouins and the children, as in the Book, just as He instilled in them acknowledgement of the Creator, exalted be He.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 54 (part 5 of 8):

The Prophet (ﷺ) said in the authentic hadith: "Every child is born upon the fitrah (natural disposition). Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you see any mutilation in it?" Then Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "Recite if you wish: ﴿The nature (fitrah) of Allah upon which He created mankind. There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾ [al-Rum: 30]." This is the meaning of the saying of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (may Allah have mercy on him): "Hold to the religion of the Bedouins and the children in the kuttab (Qur'anic school). Hold to what Allah the Exalted has created them upon, for Allah, glory be to Him, created His servants upon the truth. The Messengers were sent to complete the fitrah and confirm it, not to transform and change the fitrah."

As for the enemies of the Messengers, such as the Jahmiyyah (followers of Jahm ibn Safwan) of the Pharaonic type and their like, they seek to change the fitrah of Allah the Exalted and His religion. They present doubts to people in ambiguous words, which most people do not understand the intent of, and it is not fitting for them to be answered. I have explained their views at length in other places. The root of their misguidance is their speaking with general (mujmal) terms that have no basis in the Book of Allah the Exalted, nor in the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and that none of the Imams of the Muslims ever uttered, such as the terms "mutahayyiz" (occupying a space), "jism" (body), "jihah" (direction), and the like. Whoever knows the reality of their doubts should clarify them, and whoever does not know about this should turn away from their speech and accept nothing except what the Book and the Sunnah have brought, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when you see those who engage in [denigration of] Our verses, turn away from them until they engage in a conversation other than it﴾ [al-An'am: 68].

Whoever speaks about Allah the Exalted, His names and His attributes, in a way that contradicts the Book and the Sunnah, is among those who engage in vain discourse regarding the verses of Allah the Exalted. Many of these people attribute to the Imams of the Muslims what they did not say. Many of them have read books of kalam (scholastic theology) that contain doubts which misled them, and they did not find guidance to their refutation. They find in those books that if Allah the Exalted were above the creation, it would necessitate corporeality (tajsim), spatial occupation (tahayyuz), and direction (jihah). They do not know the realities of these terms, nor what their authors intended by them. The mention of the term "jism" (body) in the names and attributes of Allah the Exalted is an innovation (bid'ah) that neither the Book nor the Sunnah has spoken of, and none of the early generations (salaf) of the Ummah or its Imams said it. None of them said: "Allah the Exalted is a jism," nor "Allah the Exalted is not a jism," nor "Allah the Exalted is a jawhar (substance)," nor "Allah the Exalted is not a jawhar."

The term "jism" is a general (mujmal) term. Its meaning in the language is the body. Whoever says that Allah the Exalted is like the body of a human is a fabricator against Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Indeed, whoever says that Allah the Exalted resembles anything of His creation is a fabricator against Allah and astray. Whoever says that Allah the Exalted is not a jism, and intends by that that He does not resemble any of the creatures, then the meaning is correct, although the term is an innovation. As for whoever says that Allah the Exalted is not a jism and intends by that that He will not be seen in the Hereafter, or that He did not speak the Arabic Qur'an, but that the Arabic Qur'an is created, or is the composition of Jibril (peace be upon him), or something similar, then he is a fabricator against Allah the Exalted in what he negates from Him. This is the root of the misguidance of the Jahmiyyah from among the Mu'tazilah and those who agree with them in their doctrine. They display tanzih (declaring Allah free of imperfections) to people, but the reality of their speech is ta'til (negation of the attributes). They say: "We do not attribute a body to Allah; rather we say Allah is not a body," and by this they intend the negation of the reality of His names and attributes.

[The text continues:] He, glory be to Him, is described with the attributes of perfection, free from every deficiency and defect. For this reason, the doctrine of the salaf of the Ummah and its Imams is that they describe Allah the Exalted with what He described Himself with, and with what His Messenger (ﷺ) described Him with, without distortion (tahrif), negation (ta'til), modality (takyif), or likening (tamthil). They affirm what He affirmed for Himself of names and attributes, and they declare Him free of what He declared Himself free of, namely resemblance to created things. Affirmation without likening, and declaring free without negation. He, may His majesty be exalted, said: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11] is a refutation of the mumaththilah (those who liken Allah to creation), and His saying ﴿and He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ [al-Shura: 11] is a refutation of the mu'attilah (those who negate the attributes). End of the summarized quotation.

He (may Allah be pleased with him) also said, in an answer to a question submitted to him, the text of which is: "Is istiwa' (settling/establishment) a literal reality (haqiqah) or a figurative meaning (majaz)?" The summarized text of his answer is:

The discussion of istiwa' and nuzul (descent) is like the discussion of all the attributes with which He described Himself in His Book and upon the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ). Allah the Exalted named Himself with names and described Himself with attributes, so the discussion regarding some of these attributes is like the discussion regarding others. The doctrine of the salaf of the Ummah and its Imams is that we describe Allah the Exalted with what He described Himself with and what His Messenger (ﷺ) described Him with, without distortion, negation, modality, or likening. It is not permissible to negate the attributes of Allah the Exalted with which He described Himself, nor is it permissible to liken them to the attributes of created beings.

It is known by necessity from the religion of Islam that it is not permissible to apply absolute negation to what Allah the Exalted affirmed for Himself of the Most Beautiful Names and attributes. Rather, this is a denial of the Creator and a likening of Him to non-existent things. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: "The People of the Sunnah agree on affirming all the attributes that occur in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, believing in them, and understanding them according to their literal reality and not as figurative meanings, because they do not negate any of them, nor do they find in them a limited attribute." But the people of innovation, among the Jahmiyyah, the Mu'tazilah, and the Khawarij, deny them and do not take them according to their literal reality. They claim that whoever affirms them is a mushabbih (one who likens Allah to creation). In the view of those who affirm them, they are negators of the One who is worshipped, not affirmers. The truth lies in what the speakers of the truth have said, from what the Book and the Sunnah have expressed, and they are the Imams of the community (jama'ah). This is what Ibn Abd al-Barr related.

Whoever denies that any of these names and attributes is a literal reality has only denied out of ignorance of the meaning of "haqiqah," or out of disbelief and ta'til of what the Lord of the Worlds deserves. He may think that applying these terms implies that the created being resembles the Creator, so it is said to him: this is false. Allah exists in reality, the servant exists in reality, Allah has a true essence (dhat), and the servant has an essence in reality, but His essence is not like the essences of created things. Likewise, He has knowledge, hearing, and sight in reality, and the servant has hearing, sight, and knowledge in reality, but His knowledge, hearing, and sight are not like the knowledge, hearing, and sight of the servant. Allah has speech in reality, but the speech of the Creator is not like the speech of created beings. Allah settled upon His Throne in reality, and the servant settles upon a ship in reality, but the istiwa' of the Creator is not like the istiwa' of the created. Allah does not depend on anything and does not need anything; rather He is free of need of everything. Allah the Exalted carries the Throne and its bearers by His power, and ﴿He holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease﴾ [Fatir: 41]. Whoever thinks that the meaning of the statement of the Imams ("Allah is literally established upon His Throne") necessitates that His istiwa' is like the istiwa' of the servant upon a ship or livestock, it would necessarily follow that their statement "Allah has literal knowledge, literal hearing, literal sight, and literal speech" necessitates that His knowledge, hearing, sight, and speech are like the knowledge, hearing, sight, and speech of created beings. Whoever thinks that literal reality only applies to the created attribute of the servant and not to the attribute of the Creator is in the utmost ignorance. The attribute of Allah is more perfect, complete, and more deserving of these Most Beautiful Names. There is no proportion between the attribute of the servant and the attribute of the Lord, just as there is no proportion between His essence and the essence of the servant.

How can the servant be deserving of the Most Beautiful Names in reality, while the Lord deserves them only figuratively? It is known that every perfection that comes to be in a created being is from the Creator, glory be to Him and exalted, and to Him belongs the highest likeness (al-mathal al-a'la). Every perfection found in a created being, the Creator is more deserving of it, and every deficiency from which a created being is declared free, the Truth is more deserving of being declared free from it. For this reason, to Allah belongs the highest likeness. He is not measured by His creation, nor is He likened to them, nor are examples struck for Him. He and the created being do not share a likeness or an analogy. The doctrine of the People of the Sunnah and the Jama'ah is the affirmation of attributes for Allah, blessed and exalted. Rather, the attributes of perfection are necessarily inherent in His essence. It is impossible for His essence to exist without the necessary attributes of perfection; indeed, it is impossible for any essence to exist free of all attributes. All of this is explained at length in other places. So when one says: the existence of Allah, the essence of Allah, the knowledge of Allah, the power of Allah, the hearing of Allah, the sight of Allah, the speech of Allah, the mercy of Allah, the anger of Allah, the istiwa' of Allah, the nuzul of Allah, the love of Allah, and the like, all these names are literal realities for Allah the Exalted, without anything of created things entering into them, and without anything of created things resembling Him in them.

When one says: the existence of the servant and his essence, his quiddity (mahiyyah) and his knowledge, his power, his hearing and his sight, his speech, his istiwa' and his descent, this is a literal reality for the servant specific to him, without his attributes resembling the attributes of Allah the Exalted. Moreover, Allah informed that in Paradise there are foods, drinks, garments, spouses, and dwellings which He mentioned in His Book, as He mentioned that in it there are milk, honey, wine, meat, silk, gold, silver, maidens, and palaces, and other things.

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in the Hereafter except the names." Those realities that are in Paradise are not like these realities that are in this world, although they resemble them in some respects. The name encompasses both of them as literal realities. It is known that the Creator is further removed from resembling the created, and the created from resembling the Creator. How then could it be imagined that what Allah the Exalted affirmed of His names and attributes resembles His creatures, and that it would be said: this is not a literal reality? Who is more deserving of these Most Beautiful Names and Lofty Attributes than the Lord of the heavens and the earth, when their separation from created things is greater than the separation of any created thing from any other created thing?

The ignorant person goes astray by saying: the Arabs only coined the word istiwa' for the settling of a human upon a couch or a ship, or the settling of the Ark upon al-Judi, or something similar to the settling of some created things. This is like one who says: they only coined the words hearing, sight, and speech for what has an organ of eyeballs and eyelids, ears and earlobes, lips and a tongue, and they only coined the words knowledge, mercy, and will for what has a lump of flesh and a heart. All of this is ignorance on his part. The Arabs only coined for the human what they attributed to him. When they say the hearing of the servant, his sight, his speech, his knowledge, his will, and his mercy, which are specific to him, this encompasses the specific characteristics of the servant. When it is said the hearing of Allah, His sight, His speech, His knowledge, His will, and His mercy, this encompasses what is specific to the Lord, and nothing of the specific characteristics of created beings enters into it. Likewise, when it is said the istiwa' of the Lord, this istiwa' attributed to Allah is like the knowledge, hearing, and sight attributed to Allah. It is not permissible for it to encompass anything of the specific characteristics of created beings.

These ignorant people, at the beginning of their understanding, liken the attributes of the Creator to the attributes of the created, then they negate that and render it void. So they understand from it nothing except what is specific to the created, and they negate its meaning. Thus they deny what the Lord deserves of His specific characteristics and attributes, and they distort the names of Allah the Exalted and His signs, and they depart from rational analogy and from the legislated text. Thus there remains in their hands neither clear reason nor authentic transmission.

Then it is necessary for them to affirm some of the names and attributes that the people of affirmation (ahl al-ithbat) affirm. So when they affirm some and negate others, it is said to them: What is the difference between what you have affirmed and what you have negated? Why is this to be taken literally, while that is not to be taken literally? They have no answer at all, and their ignorance and error, both by revelation (shar') and by reason ('aql), become evident.

The parallels to this are numerous. Whoever thinks that if the names of God Most High and the names of His attributes are taken literally, it necessarily follows that He resembles created beings, and that His attributes are like their attributes, is among the most ignorant of people. The beginning of his speech is sophistry (sophistry, safsata) and its end is heresy (zandaqa), because it entails the negation of all of God's names and attributes, and this is the utmost of zandaqa and atheism (ilhad).

And if one distinguishes between one attribute and another, while they are equal in the grounds for being literal or metaphorical, he is inconsistent in his statement, incoherent in his position, and resembles one who believes in part of the Book and disbelieves in part.

When the discerning and virtuous person reflects on these matters, it becomes clear to him that the position of the Salaf and the Imams is in the utmost uprightness, soundness, correctness and consistency, that it is what sound reason (al-ma'qul al-sarih) and authentic transmission (al-manqul al-sahih) require, and that whoever opposes it, along with the contradiction in his varying statements by which whoever is turned away is turned away, is outside the requirement of reason and revelation, opposed to the natural disposition (fitra) and the Shari'a. May God complete His blessing upon us and upon all our brothers among the Muslim believers, and gather for us and for them the good of this world and the Hereafter. End of quotation.

Benefit
On the source of this ta'til (denial of attributes)

He (may God be pleased with him) also explained, in another fatwa of his on the attributes, the origin of this ta'til. He said, may God be pleased with him:

Then the root of this doctrine is taken from the students of the Jews, the polytheists, and the misguided Sabians. The first person known to have said this doctrine, I mean that God is not literally above the Throne, and that (istawa) means (istawla) and similar, was Ja'd ibn Dirham, and Jahm ibn Safwan took it from him and spread it, so the doctrine of the Jahmiyya is attributed to him. Ja'd took his doctrine from Aban ibn Sam'an, and Aban took it from Talut, the nephew of Labid ibn A'sam, and Talut took it from Labid ibn A'sam the Jewish sorcerer who bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ).

This Ja'd, it is said, was from the people of Harran, and among them were many Sabians and philosophers, remnants of the people of the religion of Nimrod the Canaanites, about whose sorcery some later authors wrote, and they worshipped the stars and built temples for them. Their doctrine regarding the Lord is that He has only negative or relational attributes, or a combination of both. They are the people to whom Abraham the Friend (ﷺ) was sent. So Ja'd took it from the Sabian philosophers. Jahm also took it, as Imam Ahmad and others mention, from the Samaniyya, some philosophers of India, who deny all knowledge except sensory perception. Thus the chains of Jahm trace back to the Jews, the Sabians and the polytheists.

The misguided philosophers are either from the Sabians or from the polytheists. Then, when the Roman books were translated around the beginning of the second century, the trial increased, along with what Satan cast into the hearts of the misguided, starting from the same kind of thing he cast into the hearts of their like.

When it was around the beginning of the second century, this doctrine, which the Salaf used to call the doctrine of the Jahmiyya, spread because of Bishr ibn Ghiyath al-Marisi and his circle. The statements of the Imams, such as Malik (may God be pleased with him), Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna, Abu Yusuf and al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq, al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, Bishr al-Hafi and others, about this Bishr al-Marisi are numerous in condemning him and declaring him misguided. And these interpretations (ta'wilat) found today in people's hands, like most of the interpretations mentioned by Abu Bakr ibn Furak in the book (al-Ta'wilat), and mentioned by Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn 'Umar al-Razi in his book he named (Ta'sis al-Taqdis), and found in much of the speech of others besides these, such as Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, 'Abd al-Jabbar ibn Ahmad al-Hamdani, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri, Ibn 'Aqil, Abu Hamid al-Ghazali and others, are exactly the same interpretations that Bishr al-Marisi mentioned in his book. Although there may be found in the speech of some of these a refutation and rejection of interpretation, and they have good statements on various matters, that only shows that the very essence of their interpretations is the essence of al-Marisi's interpretations. We know this from the book (al-Radd) written by Uthman ibn Sa'id al-Darimi, one of the famous Imams in the time of al-Bukhari, who wrote a book named (Naqd Uthman ibn Sa'id 'ala al-Kadhib al-'Anid fima iftara 'ala Allah fi al-Tawhid), in which he related these very interpretations from Bishr al-Marisi, in words implying that al-Marisi was more firmly grounded in them and more knowledgeable in reason and transmission than those later authors who received them from his direction. Then Uthman ibn Sa'id refuted them with words which, when an intelligent and perceptive reader studies them, he will know the reality of what the Salaf held, and it becomes clear to him the evident strength of their path and the weakness of the argument of those who opposed them.

Then, when he sees the Imams, the Imams of guidance, have unanimously condemned the Marisiyya, and most of them declared them unbelievers or misguided, and he knows that this doctrine circulating among these later authors is the doctrine of al-Marisi, the guidance becomes clear to him, for whomever God wills to guide. There is no power and no strength except with God.

He (may God be pleased with him) then said:

The doctrine of the Salaf lies between ta'til (denial) and tamthil (likening). They do not liken God's attributes to the attributes of His creation, just as they do not liken His essence to the essence of His creation, nor do they negate what He described Himself with, or what His Messenger described Him with. So they do not deny His Most Beautiful Names and His Highest Attributes, nor do they distort the words from their places, nor do they deviate concerning God's names and His signs.

Each of the two groups, the deniers and the likeners, combines ta'til and tamthil. As for the deniers, they understood from God's names and attributes only what is suitable for created beings, then they set about negating those understandings. So they combined tamthil and ta'til: they likened first and then denied, and this is a likening on their part of the understood meaning of His names and attributes to the understood meaning of the names and attributes of His creatures, and a denial of what He, glory be to Him, deserves of names and attributes befitting God, glory be to Him and exalted.

For when someone says: If God were above the Throne, it would necessarily follow that He is either larger than the Throne, or smaller, or equal to it, and all of that is impossible, and similar speech, he has not understood from God being upon the Throne anything but what is established for any body, upon any body. And this necessary consequence follows from this understanding. But an istiwa' (settling) that befits the majesty of God and is specific to Him does not entail any of these three consequences, just as they apply to all bodies. This is like the words of the one who likens: If the world has a Maker, then He is either a substance or an accident, since no existent is conceived other than these two; or his saying: If He is settled upon the Throne, then He is like a man's settling upon a bed or a ship, since istiwa' is only known in this way. Both of them likened, and both denied the reality of what God described Himself with. The first is distinguished by denying every named meaning of true istiwa', and the second is distinguished by affirming an istiwa' that is one of the particularities of created beings. The decisive position is that held by the middle community (al-umma al-wasat): that God is settled upon His Throne in a manner befitting His majesty and specific to Him. Just as He is described as knowing everything, powerful over everything, hearing and seeing, and similar, and it is not permissible to affirm for His knowledge and power the accidental properties that belong to the knowledge and power of created beings, so likewise He, glory be to Him, is above the Throne, and we do not affirm for His aboveness the particular features of the aboveness of a created being over a created being and its necessary consequences.

Know that there is nothing in sound reason, nor in clear transmission, that requires opposing the Salafi way at all. But this place does not have room for answering the doubts that come against the truth. Whoever has a doubt in his heart and wishes to resolve it, that is easy and simple. End of his words.

Whoever's intellect encompasses these gems will know the innocence of the Salaf from what they were accused of, namely anthropomorphism (tajsim). In these precious benefits there is what will satisfy the one who stops at them, in their length.

Third: the word 'arsh (Throne) is used with several meanings: a couch (sarir), as in the verse ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾ [al-Naml: 23]; and kingdom, as one says "their throne was destroyed"; and the roof of a house, as in the verse ﴿and it is fallen down upon its roofs﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]; and a hadith: "like a lamp hung from the 'arsh"; or a building, as in ﴿and what they were building (ya'rishun)﴾ [al-A'raf: 137], meaning they build; and from this comes 'arish, which is what one shades under. The 'arsh attributed to God Most High is not to be limited (la yuhadd).

Al-Qamus says: The 'arsh, the 'arsh of God Most High, is not to be bounded. End.

Al-Raghib said: The Throne of God, mighty and majestic, is something human beings do not know except by its name in reality, and for this reason no hadith describing it is authentic, and everything transmitted about that is not among the sound narrations.

Al-Bayhaqi said in the book (al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat): The sayings of the people of tafsir are that the 'arsh is a couch, and that it is an embodied body which God created, and commanded His angels to carry it, and made them worship by glorifying it and circumambulating it, just as He created on earth a House and commanded the children of Adam to circumambulate it and face it in prayer. Most of the verses indicate the soundness of what they held, and the reports and narrations transmitted about its meaning are evidence for the soundness of that. End.

Al-Hafiz al-Dhahabi said in the book (al-'Uluw): Know that God, mighty and majestic, has informed us, and He is the most truthful of speakers, that the throne of Bilqis is a mighty throne: ﴿And she has a mighty throne﴾ [al-Naml: 23], then He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿God, there is no god but He, Lord of the Mighty Throne﴾ [al-Naml: 26]. So her throne was mighty in relation to her, and we do not now know in full detail its features, its measure, or its reality. Then he said: So what is to be supposed about what God, exalted, has prepared of couches and palaces in Paradise for His servants? What then is to be supposed about the mighty Throne which the Most High, the Mighty, has taken for Himself, in its height and vastness, its legs and its reality, its carriers surrounding it, its beauty, its splendour and its value? Listen and understand what is said, and take refuge in belief in the unseen, for the report is not like direct observation. The Qur'an is filled with mention of the Throne, and so are the narrations, in ways that make it impossible for the intended meaning to be 'kingdom'. So leave off obstinacy and disputation, for disputation about the Qur'an is disbelief. We believe in God, and we testify that we are Muslims. There is no god but God, the Forbearing, the Generous. There is no god but God, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but God, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Noble Throne. All praise is due to God, Lord of the worlds. End of al-Dhahabi's words, may God Most High have mercy on him.

Fourth: Shaykh Taqi al-Din ibn Taymiyya, may mercy and good pleasure be upon him, was asked about the Throne: is it a sphere or not? If it is a sphere, and God is beyond it, encompassing it and separate from it, what is the benefit of the servant turning towards God, glory be to Him, at the time of supplication and worship, so that he intends the height above rather than anything else, since then there is no difference between intending the direction of height and the other directions that surround the supplicant? Yet we find in our hearts an intention seeking height, not turning right or left. So inform us about this necessity which we find in our hearts, and with which we were created.

He, may God have mercy on him, answered with his words:

Someone might say: no evidence on which one can rely has established that the Throne is one of the spherical, rotating orbs (*aflak*, sing. *falak*). Rather, it was mentioned by a group of later scholars who studied astronomy (*'ilm al-hay'a*). They saw that the orbs are nine, and that the ninth, which is the Atlas (*al-Atlas*), encompasses them and moves them with the eastward motion, although each orbit has its own motion. Then they heard in the reports of the prophets the mention of the Throne of God, the Most High, His Footstool (*Kursi*), and the seven heavens. They said, by way of conjecture, that the Throne is the ninth orbit, because they believed that there is nothing beyond it, either absolutely or at least no created thing beyond it. Then some of them saw that it is what moves all the orbits, so they made it the origin of events. Some of them called it the Spirit or the Soul. Some of them made it the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). Some people claimed that they knew this through unveiling (*kashf*), but that is not correct. Rather, they took it from these philosophers, as the authors of the *Epistles of the Brethren of Purity* (*Rasa'il Ikhwan al-Safa'*) did.

The reports indicate that the Throne is separate from the other created things and that it was before the heavens and the earth. It is established in the Sahih of al-Bukhari that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God existed and there was nothing other than Him, and His Throne was upon the water, and He wrote in the Reminder (*al-Dhikr*) everything, and He created the heavens and the earth," and that He has legs (*qawa'im*) [for the Throne]. This is as in the hadith of Abu Sa'id: "Then I found Moses holding onto one of the legs of the Throne."

Whoever argued that it is dome-shaped (*muqabbab*) relied on what Abu Dawud related from the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace: "God, the Exalted, is upon His Throne, and His Throne is above His heavens, and His heavens are above His earth, like this," and he gestured with his fingers like a dome (*qubba*). This does not indicate that it is one of the orbs, nor that it is rotating like that. However, the word "dome" entails a curvature from above, not from all sides, unless there is a separate evidence. The word "orb" (*falak*) is used as evidence for rotation in general, as Ibn 'Abbas said regarding "each in an orbit" (Qur'an 21:33): "in a spindle-whorl like the whorl of a spindle." As for the word "dome," it does not address this meaning, neither by negation nor by affirmation, but it does indicate curvature from above.

Know that the Throne, whether it is this ninth orbit, or a body encompassing it, or whether it is above it from the direction of the surface of the earth, encompassing it, or whether something other than that is said about it, it must be known that the upper and lower worlds, in relation to the Creator, the Exalted, are extremely small, as He, the Exalted, said: "They did not measure God with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate" (Qur'an 39:67).

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "God, Blessed and Exalted, will seize the earth on the Day of Resurrection, and will fold the heaven in His right hand, then He will say: I am the King. Where are the kings of the earth?" And in the two Sahihs, on the authority of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, from him, upon him be prayers and peace, that he said: "God, Mighty and Majestic, will fold up the heavens on the Day of Resurrection, then He will take them in His right hand, then He will say: I am the King, where are the tyrants, where are the arrogant? Then He will fold up the earths with His left hand, then He will say: I am the King, where are the tyrants, where are the arrogant?" In another wording: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) swayed to his right and to his left, until I saw the pulpit moving from beneath him, something [moving]."

In another narration he said: "He recited on the pulpit: 'While the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection' (Qur'an 39:67), to the end of the verse," and he said: "[The earth] is folded in His palm; He tosses it as a boy tosses a ball." So in these hadiths and others, whose authenticity is agreed upon, there is what shows that the heavens and the earth and what is between them, in relation to His greatness, Mighty and Majestic, are smaller than to be [anything but] like a small thing in the hand of one of us, until He spreads them out as a ball is spread out.

Then he said in the answer: What God has described of Himself and His names through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ), we name as He named it, and we do not burden ourselves with knowing what is other than that. So we do not deny what He described, nor do we burden ourselves with knowing what He did not describe. Since this is so, He is able to seize them and spread them out like a ball. In that there is an encompassing of them that is not hidden, and if He wishes He does not do so. In any case, He is separate from them, not in contact with them. It is known that one of us, and to God belongs the highest likeness, if he has a mustard seed, if he wishes he seizes it, so his grip encompasses it, and if he wishes he does not seize it but places it beneath him, he is in both states separate from it. Whether one supposes that the Throne encompasses the creatures, like the encompassing of a ball of what is in it, or it is said that it is above them and does not encompass them, like the surface of the earth on which we stand in relation to its interior, and like the dome in relation to what is beneath it, or other than that, in any case the Throne is above the creatures, the Creator, Glory be to Him, is above it, and the servant in his turning towards Him, Mighty and Majestic, intends the height, not the depth.

The completion of this discussion is that it may be said: it is either the case that the Throne is spherical like the orbs and encompasses them, or that it is above them and not spherical.

If it is the first, then it is known, by the agreement of those who know this, that the orbs are round and spherical, that the upper direction is the direction of the encompassing, which is the bounded, and that the lower direction is the center. The orbs have only two directions: upward and downward. As for the six directions, they belong to the animal, for it has six sides: it faces one direction, so it is in front of it; it turns its back on another, so it is behind it; one direction is opposite its left, one direction is opposite its right, one direction is opposite its head, and one direction is opposite its feet. These directions have no inherent necessary attribute in themselves, but are according to relation and reference. So the right of one thing is the left of another, and above one thing is below another. But the directions of up and down for the orbs do not change. The encompassing is upward and the center is downward, although the surface of the earth, which God, the Exalted, placed for the people and fixed with mountains, is where the humans, the animals, and others are.

As for the other side of it, the sea encompasses it, and there is no one of the children of Adam or those who follow them there. If one supposes that there is someone there, he would be on the surface of the earth, and those in this direction would not be beneath those in that direction, nor those in this one beneath those in that one. Just as the orbs encompass the center, and neither side of the orb is beneath the other, nor is the northern pole beneath the southern, nor the reverse. Although the northern is what is visible to us according to the distance of people from the equator, so whatever its distance from the equator is, say thirty degrees, the elevation of the pole for him is (p-2744) thirty degrees, and this is what is called the latitude of the place. Just as the sides of the earth that encompass it, and the sides of the rotating orb, are not above one another nor below one another, so likewise whoever is on the earth is not said to be beneath those [on the other side]. This is only an imagination that a person imagines, and it is a relative "below." It is like an ant walking under a ceiling: the ceiling is above it, even if its feet are touching it. Likewise, one who is hung upside down is beneath the sky, even if his feet are next to the sky. Likewise, a person may imagine, when he is on one side of the earth or the orb, that the other side is beneath him. This is a matter about which no two people disagree who hold that the orbs are rotating. This is as much the view of the people of astronomy and calculation, it is what the scholars of the Muslims hold, as Abu al-Husayn al-Mannawi, Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm, Abu al-Faraj ibn al-Jawzi, and others have mentioned. It is what is taken from the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and others. Whoever thinks that the one who is on one side of the orb has beneath him the one on the other side of the orb in reality, is, in their view, a person who imagines.

When this is the case, if it is supposed that the Throne is rotating and encompasses the creatures, then it is their highest point and their ceiling, and it is above them absolutely. So a person does not turn toward it, or toward what is above it, except from above.

Whoever turns toward the eighth or ninth orb, for example, not from the direction of above, is ignorant by the agreement of the intelligent. How then about turning toward the Throne or toward what is above it! The most that could be is that it has a round shape, and God, the Exalted, encompasses all the creatures with an encompassing that befits His majesty, for the seven heavens and the earth in His hand are smaller than a chickpea in the hand of one of us. As for the saying of the one who says: "If it is spherical, and God is behind it, encompassing and separate from it, what is the benefit of turning toward the upper direction rather than the lower, and yet we find in our hearts the intention of height?" It is said: this only arose from the imagination that half of the orb would be beneath the earth and beneath what is on the surface of the earth, of humans and animals, and this is an error. For if the orb were beneath the earth from one direction, it would be beneath it from every direction, and it would follow that the orb is beneath the earth absolutely. This is an inversion of realities, for the orb is above the earth absolutely. The people of astronomy say: If the earth were pierced toward the side of our feet, and a heavy thing like a stone or the like were dropped into the hole, it would reach the center, so that if another stone were dropped from that side, both would meet at the center, which is the middle point of the sphere of the earth. If it were supposed that two people met at the center instead of the stone, their feet would meet, and neither of them would be beneath the other, rather both would be above the center, and both would be beneath the orb.

If someone's object is above the orb, he does not seek it except from the upper direction, because his object from that direction is closer. For if it were supposed that a man or an angel ascends to the heaven, his ascent would be from the side of his head, and no intelligent person would say that he pierces the earth and then ascends from that side, or goes right or left and then ascends. If a man wanted to address the moon, he would not address it except from the upper direction, even though it rises and sets. How then about what is above everything, which does not set nor disappear, Glory be to Him and Exalted is He.

Just as the movement of a stone seeks its center by the shortest path, which is the straight line, so the volitional seeking that stands in the hearts of the servants, how would it deviate from the straight path?

**A section on the hadith of the lowering (*al-Idla'*)**

[Al-Qasimi] went on to say:

The hadith of the lowering (*hadith al-Idla'*), which Abu Hurayra and Abu Dhar related, has been transmitted by al-Tirmidhi and others from the hadith of al-Hasan on the authority of Abu Hurayra, and it is *munqati'* (disconnected), for al-Hasan did not hear from Abu Hurayra. But the hadith of Abu Dhar, which is marfu' (traced to the Prophet), strengthens it. If it is established, its meaning is consistent with this. For his saying (ﷺ): "If one of you were to lower a rope, it would descend upon God," is only a supposed hypothesis, meaning: if the lowering took place, it would fall upon Him. But it is not possible for anyone to lower anything to God, Mighty and Majestic, because He is high in His essence, and when something is lowered toward the direction of the earth, it stops at the center. The intended purpose is to show the encompassing of the Creator, Glory be to Him, just as He showed that He seizes the heavens, folds up the earth, and similar things in which there is a demonstration of His encompassing, Exalted is He. For this reason, he recited at the end of the hadith:

(p-2747) This is all on the assumption that it is authentic. When al-Tirmidhi transmitted it, he said: "Some of the scholars interpreted it to mean that He descended to the knowledge of God." Some of the Hulūliyya (those who hold that God indwells creation) and the Ittiḥādiyya (those who hold that God is one with creation) suppose that it contains what supports their false claim, namely that He, glory be to Him, dwells in His essence in every place, or that His existence is the existence of places, and similar notions. Likewise, interpreting it as "knowledge" is not sound. Rather, even if it is established, what is meant is encompassment. We speak only of what we know, and what we do not know we refrain from. God Most High has created people with an innate disposition to turn toward the direction of height when they supplicate, and God Most High said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. Thus the Sharia came with worship and supplication in accordance with this innate nature.

It is established in the two Sahihs that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you stands to pray, let him not spit in front of his face, for God Most High is before his face, nor to his right, for there is an angel on his right; let him spit to his left or under his foot." In another narration, he permitted spitting into one's garment. And in the well-known hadith of Abu Razin (p-2748), when the Prophet (ﷺ) informed them that no one would be left alone with his Lord, Abu Razin said to him: "How can it accommodate us, O Messenger of God, when He is One and we are many?" He said: "I will tell you of a similar matter among the signs of God Most High: this moon is one of the signs of God Most High, and all of you see it alone, so God is greatest."

In the two Sahihs: "Let people stop raising their gaze in prayer, or their gaze will not return to them."

The scholars agreed that a worshipper raising his gaze to the sky during prayer is forbidden. Muhammad ibn Sirin related that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to raise his gaze to the sky during prayer, until there was revealed: ﴿Those who are humble in their prayer﴾ [al-Muminun: 2], after which his gaze did not go beyond the place of his prostration.

This is among the things the Sharia brought to perfect the innate nature, because the supplicant who is commanded to humility should not look toward the side of the One he is calling upon. This is in contrast to the Jahmiyya, who make no distinction between the Throne and the bottom of the sea. God Most High said: ﴿We have seen the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ [al-Baqara: 144], etc. Then he explained the interpretation of: "The Black Stone is the right hand of God on earth; whoever shakes hands with it and kisses it, it is as if he shook hands with God Most High and kissed His right hand." He said: "They thought that this and similar things need interpretation, and this is a delusion, for if this wording were established from the Prophet (ﷺ), it would be explicit that the Stone is not one of His attributes, and restricting it to the earth indicates that it is not His hand absolutely, so the hand is not literal. And his saying: 'it is as if he shook hands with God Most High' ... etc., is explicit that the one who shakes hands is not shaking hands with Him, Most High, because the likened is not the likened-to."

He continued: All of this is on the assumption that the Throne is spherical. But if it is assumed that it is not spherical in shape, rather that He is above the world from the direction that is the surface of the earth, and that He is above the spheres, just as the surface of the earth, which is laid out for people, is above the spherical half of the earth, or other such measures by which the Throne is supposed to be above everything else, then in every case one does not turn toward God Most High except toward height, while He is on His Throne, separate from His creation. Based on what we have mentioned, none of the impermissible or contradictory consequences follow. This removes every doubt arising from a corrupt belief, namely the supposition that if the Throne is spherical, and God Most High is above it as His essence requires (glory be to Him above resemblance to created beings), then (according to the claimant) He must be spherical, and then one believes that since He is spherical, it is valid to turn toward whatever is spherical, such as the ninth sphere, from all directions. This is an error. The claim that the Throne is spherical does not permit supposing that it resembles the spheres in their shapes, measures, or attributes. Rather, it has become clear that He, glory be to Him, is far greater and more exalted than that created things should be, in His sight, smaller than a chickpea in the hand of one of us. If a chickpea is, for example, in a person's hand or under it or the like, would any rational person imagine, when he perceives the person's height over it and his encompassing it, that the person is like the sphere? God Most High, and to Him belongs the highest likeness, is far greater than to be thought of in that way. Only those who have not measured God with His due measure suppose this, while the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand, glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate. If He is not spherical, the matter is clear from what has preceded, and by this the answer to the question becomes evident from multiple aspects. God Most High knows best.

(p-2750) We have elaborated on this topic because it is among the foundations of religious creed and the most important matters of monotheistic doctrine. Disputes of opinions have multiplied in it and clashes of desires have occurred. The majority of the interpreting theologians have not produced anything that adheres to the hearts of the intelligent; rather they strove to bring forth far-fetched explanations which the innate nature of God rejects with the utmost refusal. Thus the souls of the verifying partisans of the Sunna remained inclined to the creed of the righteous predecessors (al-Salaf al-Salih), for their Imams held the belief that we have explained, so do not be among the doubters. And praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds.

His saying Most High: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, that is: He covers it with it, meaning that God Most High brings the night over the day, so it covers and clothes it until it takes away its light, and the atmosphere becomes dark after it had been bright.

Al-Shihab said: He permitted considering "the night and the day covered" as a metaphor, by making the covering of the place of the day and its darkening equivalent to the covering of the day itself, as if it wrapped it in a wrapping, or he likened the concealment of each of them by the onset of the other to the covering of clothing for the one who wears it. End quote.

He did not mention the reverse, either because it is known, or because the wording allows it. For this reason it was read as: "The day covers the night" with the night in the accusative and the day in the nominative: ﴿seeking it swiftly﴾, that is: it follows it quickly, as one who pursues it, with nothing separating them.

Al-Razi said: God, glory be to Him, described this motion as swift because the succession of night and day occurs only through the motion of the greatest sphere, and that motion is the most rapid of motions and the most perfect in intensity. Even the researchers into the conditions of existents said: if a person is running at full intense speed, in the time it takes him to lift his foot and set it down, the greatest sphere moves three thousand miles. Since this is so, that motion is at the utmost degree of intensity and speed. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿seeking it swiftly﴾. ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars subjected by His command﴾, that is, made subservient to what is intended for them, of rising and setting, moving and returning, by His decree and His direction.

Al-Shihab said: He called them "command" by way of comparison, since He made these things, because they are subject to His management and direction as He wills, as if they were commanded and obedient to His command; and it is valid to take it in its apparent sense. End quote.

(p-2751) That is, the command is speech, so God Most High commanded these bodies to move continuously, with constant motion, until the end of the world and the ruin of this world. It has been read ("and the sun") and what follows it in the accusative, as conjoined to "the heavens," and "subjected" in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Ibn 'Amir read them all in the nominative, as a beginning, with the predicate: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belong creation and command﴾, that is, He is the One who created all things, and He is the One who directs them according to the excellence of His will. He interpreted "command" as decree and judgment.

Two notes:

First: Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna derived from this meaning that the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, is not created. He said: God Most High distinguished between creation and command, so whoever combines them has disbelieved. He means that whoever makes the command, which is His speech, part of what He created, has disbelieved, because a created thing does not subsist in a created thing like itself. Thus in al-Lubab. In al-Iklil it is said: Ibn 'Uyayna used it as evidence that the Qur'an is uncreated; Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted this. For "command" is speech, and He has conjoined it to "creation," which requires that it be other than it, since conjunction requires difference. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi preceded him in this inference. End quote.

Second: In al-Lubab it is said: The verse contains evidence that there is no creator except God, Mighty and Majestic, by the restriction derived from fronting the adverbial phrase. Thus it is a refutation of those who say that the sun, the moon, and the stars have influences upon this world.

﴿Blessed is God, Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, He is sanctified, exalted, high, and magnified. In al-Taj it is said: Abu al-'Abbas was asked about the interpretation of ﴿Blessed is God﴾, and he said: "He is exalted." End quote.

When God Most High mentioned the proofs indicating perfect power and wisdom, so that they would single Him out for divinity, He commanded them to supplicate to Him alone, humbly and sincerely, and so He, glory be to Him, said:

(p-2752)

The commentary on His words, the Exalted:

[55] ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾

﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret.﴾ "Humbly" is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: while being in a state of humility and secrecy. Taḍarru' is on the pattern taf'ul, derived from al-ḍarāʿa, which means abasement. Khufyah, with either a damma or a kasra on the kh, is a verbal noun of khafiya, in the sense of ikhtafā, meaning to hide oneself and conceal oneself. He only commanded supplication together with these two states because the purpose of supplication is that the servant witness his need, his helplessness and his poverty before his Lord, who possesses overwhelming power and vast mercy. When this is achieved, it is necessary to protect it from ostentation (riyāʾ), and that is done through concealment, as a means of reaching sincerity (ikhlāṣ).

Benefits:

In this verse is the legitimacy of supplication, under its two stated conditions.

Al-Suyūṭī said in al-Iklīl: Among humility is raising the hands in supplication, and this is recommended. Al-Bazzār has related from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ raised his hands at ʿArafa, supplicating, and the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ said: 'This is supplication with complete devotion.' Then the camel moved, and he opened one of his hands, took it, while he was still raising the other." End of quotation.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī: "The people raised their voices in supplication, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'O people! Be gentle with yourselves, for you do not call upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed, the One you call upon is All-Hearing, Near.'" The hadith continues.

ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Mubārak said, from Mubārak ibn Faḍāla, from al-Ḥasan, who said: "A man would gather the Qur'an and people would not notice it; a man would acquire much jurisprudence and people would not notice it; a man would pray a long prayer in his house while visitors were with him, and they would not notice it. We have indeed known people for whom there was no deed on earth that they were able to do in secret which would ever become public. The Muslims would strive in supplication, and no voice of theirs would be heard, except a whisper between them and their Lord. That is because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret﴾. And that is because Allah mentioned a righteous servant whose action He approved, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]."

Ibn Jurayj said: Raising the voice, shouting and yelling in supplication is disliked, and humility and submissiveness are commanded.

Al-Nāṣir said in al-Intiṣāf: It suffices as proof that concealment is required in supplication that it is joined with humility in the verse. Neglecting it is like neglecting humble submission to Allah in supplication. A supplication without humility or reverence yields little benefit, and likewise a supplication not accompanied by secrecy and dignity. You see many people of your time relying on shouting and yelling in supplication, especially in congregational mosques, until the noise grows great and intense, the ears are deafened and stunned, and the supplicant sways the people, not knowing that he has combined two innovations: raising the voice in supplication, and doing so in the mosque. Perhaps the common people are moved at that time by a tenderness that is not produced when the voice is lowered, and when the dignified manner and the established Sunnah transmitted through reports are observed. But this is nothing more than a tenderness resembling the passing softness of women and children, not coming from the core of the heart, for if it were from a true root, it would be fuller, more complete and purer when the Sunnah is followed in supplication and in lowering the voice. How much falsehood is mixed with truth to the minds of many creatures! O Allah, show us the truth as truth and grant us to follow it, and show us falsehood as falsehood and grant us to avoid it. End of quotation.

It has been related by the memorizer (ḥāfiẓ) Abū al-Shaykh in al-Thawāb, from Anas, traced to the Prophet: "A supplication in secret equals seventy supplications in public."

His words, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ That is: He does not love the supplication of those who exceed what they were commanded in every matter. This includes transgression by abandoning the two mentioned matters, humility and concealment, as a primary inclusion.

Al-Suyūṭī said in al-Iklīl: The verse indicates the disliking of transgression in supplication. Zayd ibn Aslam interpreted it as loud speech; Abū Mijlaz as asking for the ranks of the prophets; and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr as supplicating against a believer in secret. Ibn Abī Ḥātim related this. It is not hidden that all of this is included in transgression.

Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd related that: Saʿd heard his son supplicating, saying: "O Allah, I ask You for Paradise, its bliss and its brocade, and similar things, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire, its chains and its shackles." He said: "You have asked Allah for much good, and sought refuge in Allah from much evil. Indeed I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'There will come a people who will transgress in supplication.'" In another wording: "They will transgress in purification and supplication." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾ to the end of the verse. It is sufficient for you to say: "O Allah, I ask You for Paradise and whatever brings me near to it of speech or deed, and I seek refuge in You from the Fire and whatever brings me near to it of speech or deed."

Imam Aḥmad and Abū Dāwūd also related that ʿAbdullāh ibn Mughaffal heard his son saying: "O Allah, I ask You for the white palace on the right side of Paradise when I enter it." He said: "My son, ask Allah for Paradise and seek refuge in Him from the Fire, for I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'There will be a people who transgress in supplication and purification.'"

(p-2755)Discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[56] ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation. And call upon Him in fear and aspiration. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.ﴩ

﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation.﴾ Abu Muslim said: That is, do not corrupt it after Allah has reformed it, by creating it in the best of orders, sending the messengers, clarifying the way, and nullifying disbelief.

Abu Hayyan said: This is a prohibition against bringing about corruption on the earth and introducing its reality into existence in all its kinds, including the corruption of souls, wealth, lineages, intellects, and religions.

The meaning of ﴿after its reformation﴾ is: after Allah has made its creation good, in the manner suited to the benefits of creatures and the welfare of those who are accountable. End of quote.

﴿And call upon Him in fear and aspiration.﴾ That is, [being] those possessing fear of the grievous punishment, in view of the deficiency of your deeds, and aspiration for what is with Him of abundant reward, in view of the vastness of His mercy and the abundance of His grace and beneficence. ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾ That is, His mercy is prepared for the doers of good, those who follow His commands and abstain from His prohibitions, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things, so I will prescribe it for those who fear Me﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], and so on.

Subtleties:

The first: In al-Lubab he said: If you say: At the beginning of the verse He said, ﴿Call upon your Lord in humility and secrecy﴾ [al-A'raf: 55], and here He says ﴿and call upon Him﴾, and this is the conjoining of a thing with itself, so what is the benefit of that?

I say: The benefit is that what is meant by His saying ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 55] is: let the supplication be accompanied (p-2756) by humility and submissiveness; and His saying ﴿and call upon Him in fear and aspiration﴾ indicates that the benefit of supplication is one of these two matters. Thus the first verse explains a condition for the validity of supplication, and the second verse explains the benefit of supplication. It has also been said: its meaning is: be combining within yourselves, in all your deeds, between fear and hope, and do not presume that you have fulfilled Allah's right in worship and supplication even if you have striven in both.

The second: In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah﴾ and so on, there is a preference of hope over fear, because the believer is between hope and fear, but when he sees the vastness of His mercy and its precedence, hope prevails over him. In it there is also an alert to that by which one reaches acceptance, which is goodness in speech and action.

Matar al-Warraq said: Demand the fulfillment of Allah's promise by obeying Him, for He has decreed that His mercy is near to the doers of good.

The third: The masculine form of (qarib, "near"): because (al-rahma, "mercy") is in the sense of (al-rahim, "womb"), or because it is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning: a near matter; or by analogy with (fa'il), which has the sense of (maf'ul); or because it is a verbal noun like (al-naqid, "the cry") and (al-sahil, "the neighing"); or to distinguish between "near" in terms of kinship and "near" in other respects, for one says: "She is near to me [qarība]" only in kinship, while for place and other things both forms are permissible; or because it acquires masculinity from the genitive noun, just as the annexed noun acquires femininity from the noun it is annexed to. They have extended the explanation of its masculine form to fifteen aspects.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earth, and that He is the Disposer, the Judge, the Governor, the Subjugator, and guided to supplicating Him because He is capable of whatever He wills, He drew attention to the fact that He is the Provider, and that He will restore the dead on the Day of Resurrection, so He, glorified is He, said:

(p-2757)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 57:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[57] ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy, until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water therewith and bring forth therewith fruits of all kinds. Thus do We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember.﴾

"﴿And it is He who sends the winds as glad tidings before His mercy﴾" i.e., before His mercy, which is the rain. The Sabā (east wind) stirs up the clouds, the Shamāl (north wind) gathers them, the Janūb (south wind) milks them, and the Dabūr (west wind) scatters them. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired and spreads His mercy﴾ [al-Shura: 28], and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of glad tidings﴾ [al-Rum: 46]. Al-Tha'alabi said: "The bearers of glad tidings are those that bring the clouds and the rain."

Note:

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is read *nushuran* with a ḍammah on both the nūn and the shīn, and it is a plural. For its singular there are two possibilities. The first is *nashūr*, like *ṣabūr* and *ṣubur*. On this reading, *fa'ūl* may be in the sense of *fā'il*, i.e., "it spreads the earth." It may also be in the sense of *maf'ūl*, like *rakūb* in the sense of *markūb*, i.e., "spread out after being folded," or "revived," from your saying: God revived the dead, so he is *munsharun*. It may also be the plural of *nāshir*, like *bāzil* and *buzl*. It is read with a ḍammah on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn, as a lightening of the ḍammah. It is read *nashran* with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn, being the verbal noun of *nashara* after folding, or from your saying: God revived the dead, so he came to life (*nushira*). Its accusative case is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning "spreading," or "possessing spreading," just as you say: "He came running" (*rakḍan*), meaning "running." End.

It is also read *bushran* with a ḍammah on both the bā' and the shīn, the plural of *bashīr*, like *qalīb* and *qulub*. It is read the same way except with a sukūn on the shīn as a lightening. It is read *bushrā*, like *ḥublā*, meaning "possessing glad tidings." It is read *bashran* with a fatḥah on the bā' and a sukūn on the shīn, being the verbal noun of *bashshartuhu* (pronounced with lightening), i.e., when you give him good news. End.

﴿Until, when they carry heavy clouds﴾ i.e., they bear them, ﴿heavy clouds﴾ i.e., because of the great quantity of water in them. ﴿We drive them﴾ i.e., the clouds. Al-Shihab said: *al-sahab* is a collective noun whose singular is distinguished by the tā' marker, like *tamr* and *tamrah*. It may be masculine or feminine, its adjective may be singular, and it may be plural; the lexicographers call it a plural, so both considerations are observed regarding its adjective and its pronoun. End. That is: We sent it, even though its nature is to descend, ﴿to a dead land﴾ i.e., for its sake and its benefit, or for its revival or for its watering. "Dead" (*mayyit*) is read both with and without the shaddah.

﴿And We send down water therewith﴾ i.e., the pronoun (in *bihi*) refers to the land. ﴿And bring forth therewith fruits of all kinds﴾ i.e., of differing kinds, even though their water is one. What is meant by "all fruits" are those customary in every land, which emerge in the manner in which God has established the custom and arranged it.

The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the water or to the land. ﴿Thus﴾ i.e., in the likeness of that bringing forth, ﴿do We bring forth the dead﴾ i.e., We revive them after they have become dust on the Day of Resurrection. God, glorified and exalted, sends down water from the sky, and it rains upon the earth for forty days, and bodies grow from it in their graves, just as grain grows in the earth. ﴿Perhaps you will remember﴾ i.e., We have only described this illustration so that you may remember, from the conditions of the fruits which were returned to their state after their destruction, the conditions of the Hereafter, so that you may know that whoever is capable of that is capable of this without doubt.

Note:

Among the rulings of the verse, as al-Jashami said: it indicates the greatness of His blessings upon us through rain; it indicates the proof for the resurrection of the dead through the revival of the earth by plants; and it indicates that He intends from all of this that we remember. It also indicates that He established the custom of bringing forth plants by water, though He is capable of bringing them forth without water; He arranged the custom in ways which we witness, for a kind of benefit in religion and in worldly life.

Among them: when one sees good land being cultivated while salt-marsh land is not, and that these are adjacent plots, one knows the corruption of blind imitation, and that one must investigate the truth until one holds it as belief. Among them: when one sows and knows the necessity of protecting it from things that nullify it, one knows the necessity of protecting righteous deeds from things that cause them to fail.

The explanation of His words, exalted is He:

[58] ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord; and that which is corrupt, its vegetation comes forth only meagerly. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾

﴿And the good land﴾, that is, the land noble in its soil, ﴿its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord﴾, that is, its vegetation comes forth abundant, good, and greatly beneficial, by His will and facilitation. ﴿And that which is corrupt﴾ — that is, like the ḥarrah (volcanic land), which is land covered with black stones, and like the sabakhah (with a kasra on the bāʾ), which is land containing salt. ﴿Comes forth only﴾ — that is, its vegetation ﴿meagerly﴾, that is, scanty and of no benefit. It is said: "ʿaṭāʾun nakid" (a gift that is nakid), meaning scant, with no good in it; and likewise "rajulun nakid" (a man who is nakid). A poet said:

*Give what you have given, pleasantly; there is no good in the one who is cursed (al-mankūd) and the one who is nakid.*

And another said:

*Do not fulfill the promise if you promise, and if you give, you have given a paltry and nakid thing.*

Note:

Ibn ʿAbbās said regarding the verse: this is a parable God struck for the believer and the disbeliever.

Qatadah said: The believer hears the Book of God, retains it with his intellect, and benefits from it, like the good land which the rain reaches and which then produces vegetation; the disbeliever is the opposite of that. This is as in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Abū Mūsā, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The likeness of the guidance and knowledge with which God has sent me is like abundant rain which fell upon land; part of it was pure, which absorbed the water and produced grass and abundant herbage; and part of it was barren, which held the water so that God benefited people by it, and they drank, gave drink, and cultivated; and it fell upon another portion which was only smooth ground that holds no water and produces no grass. That is the likeness of one who comprehends the religion of God and is benefited by what God has sent me with, so he knows and teaches; and the likeness of one who does not raise his head to that and does not accept the guidance of God with which I have been sent."

Curiosity:

Abū al-Baqāʾ said: It is read ﴿yakhruju nabātuhu﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, a ḍammah on the rāʾ, and the nabāt in the nominative. It is also read thus, except with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, in the passive voice (mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu). It is read with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the rāʾ and the nabāt in the accusative, meaning: "God brings forth" or "the water." Then he said: ﴿nakidan﴾ is read with a fatḥah on the nūn and a kasrah on the kāf, and it is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative). It is read with both of them fatḥah, as a maṣdar (verbal noun), meaning: possessing nakid. It is read with a fatḥah on the nūn and a sukūn on the kāf, and it is also a maṣdar, a dialectal form. And it is read "yukhriju" with a ḍammah on the yāʾ and a kasrah on the rāʾ, with nakidan as its object.

﴿Thus do We vary the signs﴾, that is, We make clear the aspects of the proofs, repeat them and reiterate them, ﴿for a people who give thanks﴾. That is: just as We have struck this parable, so We make clear the signs that indicate tawḥīd and faith, sign after sign and proof after proof, for a people who give thanks to God, exalted is He, for His blessing upon them with guidance and for keeping them away from the path of error. He singled out the grateful for mention only because they are the ones who benefited from hearing the Qur'an.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[59] ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a great day."﴾

﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people﴾ Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned at the beginning of the surah the story of Adam and what is connected with it of the signs of His power and the wondrous aspects of His creation, which point to His oneness and lordship, and established the decisive proof of the truth of resurrection after death, He followed that with the stories of the prophets, upon them be prayer and peace, and what befell them with their nations.

Al-Razi said: In this there are benefits:

(p-2761) The first: an alert that people's turning away from accepting these proofs and clear signs is not peculiar to the people of the Prophet ﷺ. Rather, this blameworthy habit existed among all the earlier nations, and a calamity, when it is widespread, becomes lighter. So the mention of their stories and the recounting of their persistence and obstinacy serves as consolation to the Prophet ﷺ and lightens that burden on his heart.

The second: that He, exalted is He, relates in these stories that the outcome of those deniers was curse in this world and loss in the Hereafter, while the outcome of the upholders of truth was dominion in this world and felicity in the Hereafter. This strengthens the hearts of the upholders of truth and breaks the hearts of the falsifiers.

The third: an alert that He, exalted is He, although He gives these falsifiers respite, does not neglect them, but takes vengeance upon them in the most perfect manner.

The fourth: a clarification that these stories are evidence of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, because he was unlettered, did not read a book, and did not study under a teacher.

So when he mentions these stories in the manner they occurred, without distortion or error, this shows that he learned them only through revelation from Allah, exalted is He.

Noah, upon him be peace, is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalakh, son of Akhnukh, son of Yarid, son of Mahla'il, son of Qaynan, son of Anush, son of Shith, son of Adam, upon him be peace. This is how Ibn Ishaq and a number of the imams traced his lineage, and its origin is from the Torah.

The meaning of (We sent) is "We dispatched," and he was the first prophet Allah sent after Idris. So says al-Lubab. Idris is Akhnukh according to what they claim.

Ibn Kathir said: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: No prophet suffered from his people such harm as Noah did, except a prophet who was killed. Yazid al-Raqashi said: He was named Noah only because of how much he wailed (naha) over himself. End of quote.

In this there is a point of scrutiny, for what he mentioned would be valid only if Noah were a nickname alongside another name for him, and the word were Arabic, owing to the suitability of derivation. But since it is his original name and the word is not Arabic, it does not hold. In the book (Ta'wil al-Asma' al-Waqi'a fi al-Kutub al-Salifa) it is stated that Noah means "rest" or "consolation," so verify this.

(p-2762) Before the mission of Noah, upon him be peace, there were people who knew Allah and worshipped Him, especially within the family of Shith, upon him be peace. Then the offspring of Shith also became corrupt, mixed with the wicked, the earth was filled with their crimes, they deviated from the straight path, and they began to worship idols and images. So Allah, exalted is He, sent Noah, upon him be peace, to guide them to the path of righteousness.

Ibn Kathir said: Abdullah ibn Abbas and a number of scholars of tafsir said: The first time idols were worshipped was when some righteous people died, and their people built places of worship over their graves and fashioned their images within them, so that they would remember their condition and worship and emulate them. When time passed, they made bodies in the likeness of those images, and when time stretched on, they worshipped those idols and named them after those righteous people: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghuth, Ya'uq, and Nasr. When the matter grew severe, Allah, glorified is He, to whom belong praise and grace, sent His messenger Noah, and he commanded them to worship Allah alone, with no partner. ﴿So he said, "O my people"﴾ That is, those whose right it is to share in My perfections. ﴿Worship Allah; you have no deity﴾ That is, none deserving of worship in existence ﴿other than Him﴾.
