It is read with the three vowels: the nominative is an adjective of "deity," taking into account its position, which is nominative as a subject or agent; the genitive follows the wording; and the accusative is in exception. The rule of (ghayr) is the rule of the noun following (illa), meaning: you have no deity except Him.

﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾ That is, if you abandon worshipping Him or worship other than Him. ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾ It is the Day of Resurrection, when you meet Allah while associating others with Him, or the day the punishment descends upon them, which is the flood.

Describing the day as (great) clarifies the greatness of what occurs in it and completes the warning.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask: what is the position of the two sentences after His words "worship Allah"? I say: The first is an explanation of the reason He alone deserves worship, and the second is an explanation of what motivates worshipping Him, because it is He whose punishment is feared, not what they used to worship besides Allah.

(p-2763)

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, may He be exalted:

[60] ﴿The chiefs of his people said: "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾

﴿The chiefs of his people said﴾ — that is, the nobles, or the group, or those possessing rank and assembly.

﴿Indeed, we see you﴾ — that is, [we see you] commanding [us] to worship Allah and to abandon the worship of others, and warning of punishment for abandoning the worship of Allah and for worshipping others.

﴿in manifest error﴾ — that is, [you are] going astray from the path of truth and correctness, because it contradicts what we found our fathers upon.

Ibn Kathir said: "Such is the state of the wicked: they only see the righteous to be in error, as in His words: ﴿And when they see them, they say, 'Indeed, these are surely astray.'﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 32] and ﴿Those who disbelieved said to those who believed, "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it. And since they have not been guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient lie.'"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11], and other verses like these."

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[61] ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no misguidance in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no misguidance in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ " .

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[62] ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I give you sincere counsel, and I know from Allah what you do not know.﴾

﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord﴾ "That is, what has been revealed to me over long periods of time, or in various meanings: commands and prohibitions, admonitions and warnings, glad tidings and threats. It is also possible that he means the messages sent to him and to the prophets before him, from the scrolls of his forefather Idris (Enoch). This is the reason for using the plural (al-risalat). Otherwise, the message of each prophet is one, and it is a verbal noun (masdar), and the original rule is that it should not be pluralized, so it was pluralized for the reason mentioned."

(p-2764) ﴿And I give you sincere counsel﴾ "I intend your welfare with sincerity." ﴿And I know from Allah what you do not know﴾ "That is, from the unseen matters that are known only through revelation (wahy), things of which you have no knowledge. Or it means: I know of His overwhelming power and the severity of His seizing of His enemies, and that His punishment cannot be averted from the guilty people, which you do not know."

Ibn Kathir said: "This is the mark of the Messenger: that he be an eloquent conveyer, a sincere advisor, and one who knows Allah, such that none of Allah's creation can attain these qualities. As is related in Sahih Muslim, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions on the Day of 'Arafah, when they were at their most numerous and their greatest in total: 'O people! You will be asked about me, so what will you say?' They said, 'We testify that you have conveyed, fulfilled, and given sincere counsel.' Then he began raising his finger toward the sky and lowering it toward them, saying: 'O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness.'"

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 63:

(p-2765) The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[63] ﴿Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, so that he may warn you and that you may fear God, and that perhaps you may receive mercy?﴾

﴿Do you wonder that a reminder [dhikr] has come to you﴾ — i.e., an admonition — ﴿from your Lord through a man from among you, so that he may warn you﴾ — i.e., of the punishment if you do not believe — ﴿and that you may fear God﴾ — i.e., that God-consciousness (taqwa, which is fear arising from the warning) may come to be found among you — ﴿and that perhaps you may receive mercy﴾ — i.e., that you may be shown mercy through taqwa, if it is found in you.

The discussion of the Lord's words:

[64] ﴿So they denied him, and We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people.﴾

﴿So they denied him⁠﴾ — meaning: they persisted in denying him despite the long period of his stay among them, and only a few believed with him from among them. ﴿And We saved him and those with him in the ship, and We drowned those who denied Our signs. Indeed, they were a blind people⁠﴾ — meaning: blind to the truth. They did not perceive the truth, nor were they illumined by the light of revelation, which is like the sun, nor by the manifest signs, nor by the sign of the flood that would drown them after his warning them of it, in response to their denial. Blindness (ʿamā) is the loss of the sight of the eyes and the sight of the heart. It is said: ʿamiya, so he is aʿmā and ʿammin, as in the Qamus (the lexicon al-Qamus al-Muhit).

As for the matter of Noah, peace be upon him: when his people turned away from faith, persisted in disobedience and the worship of idols, and their affair became prolonged for him, he complained of them to God Most High. God revealed to him that ﴿none of your people will believe except those who have already believed⁠﴾ [Hud: 36], and they were a small group. At that, he invoked against them, saying: ﴿And Noah said, "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers an inhabitant⁠﴾ [Nuh: 26]. God revealed to him that he should build the ship, and his people began to mock him, saying: "O Noah! You have become a carpenter after being a prophet!" He said: ﴿If you mock us, then indeed we mock you as you mock⁠﴾ [Hud: 38]. ﴿So you will come to know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment⁠﴾ [Hud: 39]. When he finished building the ship, God Most High commanded him to carry in it two of every kind, a pair of each of the kinds of animals, so that their offspring would not be cut off, and He gathered them to him from every direction. When he saw the water gushing from the oven, which was the sign between him and God Most High at the beginning of the flood, he boarded the ship, he and those who believed with him, and he carried two of every kind. God Most High commanded the sky to pour down rain, and the earth to burst forth with springs. The water rose in this flood above the peaks of the mountains, and every living thing on the earth of the animal kind perished; none remained alive except the people of the ship.

In the Torah: the rains poured down for forty days and nights without ceasing, until the waters covered the face of the earth and rose fifteen cubits above the lofty mountains, and every living creature perished by the flood. Then God sent a violent wind, the rains ceased, and the waters receded little by little. Noah remained a full year inside the ship, and upon his exit from it he built an altar for offerings, in thanks to God Most High. Mankind multiplied from the three sons of Noah: Shem, Ham and Japheth. Shem settled the lands of Asia, Ham dwelt in the regions of Africa, and Japheth inhabited the European lands. And God knows best.

Admonition:

al-Jushami said: In these verses there are several benefits, among them: Noah first called them to monotheism (tawhid). A messenger, even if he carries the laws (shara'i'), has no way to explain the laws except after knowledge of monotheism, and because they would not benefit from them except after holding monotheism, so he began with it. All the messengers began with monotheism and then with the laws, and for this reason most of the arguments of our Prophet, peace be upon him, in Mecca concerned monotheism. End.

Ibn Kathir said: God Most High has shown in this story that He avenged His allies upon their enemies, and saved His messenger and the believers, and destroyed their enemies, the disbelievers, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We shall surely help Our messengers⁠﴾ [Ghafir: 51], and this is God's custom with His servants, in this world and the Hereafter, that the final outcome belongs to the righteous, and victory and dominance are theirs, just as He destroyed the people of Noah by drowning and saved Noah and his believing companions.

Malik related from Zayd ibn Aslam: The people of Noah had become so numerous that the plain and the mountain were crowded with them. And ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: God did not punish the people of Noah except when the earth was full of them, and there is no patch of earth but that it has an owner and possessor.

And the Most High's saying:

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[65] ﴿And to ʿĀd [We sent] their brother Hūd. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?"﴾

﴿And to ʿĀd﴾ is connected to an implied verb that is conjoined to His words ﴿We sent﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 59] in the account of Noah. That is: and We sent to ʿĀd, a tribe that worshipped idols, and who were endowed with physical stature and strength, subduing people by the excellence of their power.

Al-Shihāb said: "ʿĀd" is the name of their father, by which the tribe or clan was named, so it may be inflected or left uninflected, like Thamūd, as Sībawayh mentioned.

Al-Layth said: The first ʿĀd are the people of ʿĀd son of ʿAwṣ... [the text reads: ʿĀd son of ʿĀdiyā son of Sām son of Noah], whom Allah destroyed.

Zuhayr said:

"And He destroyed Luqmān son of ʿĀd and ʿĀdiyā."

As for the later ʿĀd, they are the Banū Tamīm, who dwell in the sands of ʿĀlij.

In the Kitāb al-Ansāb: ʿĀd is the son of ʿAwṣ son of Iram son of Sām son of Noah. He worshipped the moon. It is said that he saw, from his loins and the offspring of his offspring, four thousand, and that he married a thousand concubines. Their lands were Iram, mentioned in the Qur'an, which extended from ʿUmān to Ḥaḍramawt. Among his descendants was Shaddād son of ʿĀd, the lord of the city mentioned, as stated in Tāj al-ʿArūs.

Ibn ʿArafa said: The people of ʿĀd had their dwellings in the sand, and it is al-Aḥqāf.

Ibn Isḥāq said: al-Aḥqāf is sand lying between ʿUmān and Ḥaḍramawt.

As for His words, Exalted Is He, ﴿their brother Hūd﴾: that is, their brother in lineage, since he was one of them, according to the genealogists. It was also said: all people are brothers in lineage, since they are the offspring of Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ, so the meaning is "one of them" and "one among them," (p-2769) as one says, "O brother of the Arabs," addressing one of them. He was sent from among them because they would understand his speech better than the speech of others, and would know better his truthfulness, his trustworthiness, and the nobility of his origin, and would be more inclined to follow him.

Al-Shihāb said: It is well known that Hūd was an Arab, while the apparent sense of Sībawayh's words is that he was non-Arab (aʿjamī), and what has been said supports this: "The first of the Arabs was Yaʿrub." End.

Hūd, according to what Ibn Isḥāq said, is the son of Shālikh son of Arfakhshad son of Sām son of Noah. Other than this is also said, and Allah knows best.

Ibn Isḥāq narrated from ʿĀmir ibn Wāthila, who said: I heard ʿAlī say to a man from Ḥaḍramawt: "Have you seen a reddish sand-hill mixed with red clay, with many arak and sidr trees, in such-and-such a region of the land of Ḥaḍramawt?" He said: "Yes, O Commander of the Faithful! By Allah, you describe it as one who has seen it!" He said: "No, but I have been told about it." The Ḥaḍramī said: "And what is its matter, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "In it is the grave of Hūd, peace be upon him." (Ibn Jarīr narrated it.)

Ibn Kathīr said: In this there is the benefit that their dwellings were in Yemen, and that Hūd, peace be upon him, was buried there. He also said: They used to shelter among pillars in the open country, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with ʿĀd, Iram of the pillars, the likes of which were not created in the lands?﴾ [al-Fajr: 6–8]. This was because of their great might and strength, as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿As for ʿĀd, they were arrogant in the land without right and said, "Who is greater than us in strength?" Did they not see that Allah, who created them, is greater than them in strength? And they were deniers of Our signs﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 15]. Therefore Hūd, peace be upon him, called them to worship Allah alone, with no partner, and to obey Him and fear Him, as Allah, the Exalted, said.

﴿He said﴾: that is, Hūd. ﴿O my people﴾: that is, those whose duty it is to be like me. ﴿Worship Allah﴾: that is, Him alone. ﴿You have no deity other than Him. Will you not then fear Him?﴾: that is, will you not fear His punishment?

(p-2770)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 66:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[66] ﴿The chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: Indeed, we see you in folly, and indeed we think you are among the liars.﴾

"﴿The chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: Indeed, we see you in folly﴾" That is: in lightness of intellect and feebleness of reason, in that you abandon the religion of your people for another religion. He made "folly" a container (ẓarf) by way of metaphor; they meant that he is firmly established in it, not separated from it. "﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾" That is: in your claim to prophethood, since they considered it far-fetched that God would send anyone from among the people of the earth to them.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[67] ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾

﴿He said: "O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ That is: to you, to set right the affairs of your two lives (nash'atayn).

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[68] ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you.﴾

"﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord, and I am a sincere and trustworthy adviser to you.﴾" That is: a sincere adviser to you in what I command you concerning the worship of Him alone, exalted is He, and trustworthy in conveying the message, I do not lie in it.

﴿أوَعَجِبْتُمْ أنْ جاءَكم ذِكْرٌ مِن رَبِّكم عَلى رَجُلٍ مِنكم لِيُنْذِرَكم﴾ Do you wonder that a reminder from your Lord has come to you through a man from among you, to warn you? (p-٢٧٧١) That is, "the days of Allah" and "His meeting": do not wonder at it, and praise Allah for this. ﴿واذْكُرُوا إذْ جَعَلَكم خُلَفاءَ مِن بَعْدِ قَوْمِ نُوحٍ﴾ And remember when He made you successors after the people of Noah. That is, you succeeded them in their dwellings, or in the land, by making you rulers after them. It is said that Shaddad ibn 'Ad was among those who ruled the inhabited earth, from the sands of 'Alij to the shores of Shihr 'Oman, so they said. ﴿وزادَكم في الخَلْقِ بَسْطَةً﴾ And He increased you in stature and build. That is, in height and strength. ﴿فاذْكُرُوا آلاءَ اللَّهِ﴾ So remember the bounties of Allah. That is, in your succession, in the vastness of your bodies, and in what else of His gifts there is, so that you single Him out for worship. ﴿لَعَلَّكم تُفْلِحُونَ﴾ That you may prosper. That is, that you may attain success.

Two Notes:

The first: al-Zamakhshari said: In the response of the prophets, peace be upon them, to those who attributed to them error and foolishness, with what they answered them of speech issuing from forbearance and forgiveness, and leaving aside retaliation with what they said to them, despite their knowledge that their opponents were the most misguided and foolish of people, is a fine manner and a great character. And Allah's relating of this is a teaching to His servants on how they should address the foolish, and how they should overlook them and pass by them, despite what they do. End of quote.

al-Qadi added: In this there is perfect sincere advice and compassion, humbling of the self, and good disputation. He said: Thus should every advisor be. End of quote.

The second: One should not rely on what some historians who are fond of transmitting strange reports say, without subjecting them to the scale of examination and criticism, of exaggeration regarding the height of the people of 'Ad and the enormity of their bodies, and that the tallest of them was one hundred cubits and the shortest sixty cubits. For no rational or transmitted proof supports that, and it is an illusion.

As for His saying, exalted is His majesty, addressing the people of 'Ad: ﴿وزادَكم في الخَلْقِ بَسْطَةً﴾, it does not indicate what they intended; it only indicates the greatness of their bodies, their strength and their might. This is among the ordinary matters, for nations are not equal in the massiveness, height and strength of their bodies, but they differ, though by a modest degree.

Among what indicates that the bodies of those who came before us were like our bodies, and did not differ from them by a great difference, are the enduring dwellings of the people of Thamud, the people of Salih, and their manifest remains. Similar to it, indeed even more deluded, is what they transmit describing 'Awj ibn 'Unuq, the giant, king of Bisan, that he would hold back the clouds and drink from them because of his height, and would take the fish from the depths of the sea and roast it by the sun's eye, raising it to it. Yet the sun is a star with no temperament of heat or cold; its heat comes only from the reflection of its rays upon the surface of the earth and the air, so its heat is intense on the earth, and the heat diminishes in what rises above it by the measure of the height.

Al-Allamah Ibn Khaldun denied all of that in the Muqaddimah of his History, and made clear that what introduced the illusion among people regarding the height of the ancients is what they see of some of their bodily remains and their great edifices, such as the pyramids of Egypt and the Iwan of Kisra, so they imagine for their builders bodies commensurate with that.

The fact is that the greatness of these edifices and remains among a nation arises from the greatness of its essence, the expansion of its realms, the might of its power, the growth of its wealth, and its employment of experts in the art of hauling heavy loads, for that can carry what human powers are unable to bear even a tenth of. He also denied what they transmit of the story of the Garden of 'Ad, that it was a great city whose palaces were of gold and whose pillars were of emerald and ruby, containing all kinds of trees and flowing rivers, and that it was built over three hundred years in the deserts of Aden, built by Shaddad ibn 'Ad when he heard the description of Paradise; and that when its construction was complete, Allah sent upon its people a cry, and they all perished; and that its name is (Iram of the pillars), and that it is the one referred to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ألَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ فَعَلَ رَبُّكَ بِعادٍ﴾ Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad? ﴿إرَمَ ذاتِ العِمادِ﴾ Iram of the pillars, ﴿الَّتِي لَمْ يُخْلَقْ مِثْلُها في البِلادِ﴾ the like of which was not created in the lands. [al-Fajr: 6-8]. They claim that it has never ceased to exist in the land of Yemen, but has only been veiled from sight. Since that has not been related from the Truthful, Trustworthy one, we do not rely upon it, nor do we give heed to it. Most of those who are fond of transmitting such fabricated strange reports are historians who rely on the reports of the Children of Israel and follow them without proof or evidence. And Allah is the Guide to the straight path. So did one of the verifiers state.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed of the rebellion and insolence of 'Ad and their denial of Hud, peace be upon him, saying, glorified is He:

(p-٢٧٧٣)

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[70] ﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾

﴿They said: "Have you come to us so that we worship Allah alone"﴾ — i.e., so that we single Him out for worship. ﴿"and abandon what our fathers used to worship? Then bring us what you threaten us with"﴾ — i.e., of the punishment indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Will you not then be wary [of Allah]?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]. ﴿"if you are among the truthful"﴾ — i.e., in reporting the descent of the punishment.

"Concerning the interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:

[71] ﴿He said: Uncleanness and wrath have already fallen upon you from your Lord. Do you dispute with me about names which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority? So wait; indeed I am with you among those who wait.﴾

"﴿He said: Uncleanness (rijs) has already fallen upon you from your Lord﴾ — that is, punishment. Rijs and rijz have the same meaning, to the extent that it is said that one of them is a substitute for the other, like al-Asad and al-Azd. The original sense of the word is agitation (al-idtirab). It is said: 'The sky trembled (rajasat al-sama'): it thundered intensely and was in labour,' and 'they are in a rijsa (confusion) of their affair,' meaning in a state of mixing and confusion. Then it became widespread in the sense of punishment because of the agitation of the one who is struck by it.

Some of them claimed that using rijs in the sense of punishment is metaphorical (majaz), saying: 'Because it is literally (haqiqa) used for a filthy thing, so it was borrowed for their recompense.' The apparent usage of the language is that it is literal. The reason for expressing with the past tense what will happen is that the anticipated is treated as though it has already occurred, as in: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. ﴿And wrath﴾ — that is, indignation, because you associated with Him one who is in the utmost deficiency, while He is at the peak of His perfections, which is divinity. ﴿Do you dispute with me about names which you and your fathers have named﴾ — that is, about things which are nothing but names, with no named realities beneath them, (p-2774) because you call them gods, while the meaning of divinity in them is absent and its existence is impossible. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They worship besides Him nothing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 42] — thus in al-Kashshaf.

Al-Shihab said: He made 'names' an expression for the false idols, as one says of what does not befit something: 'it is merely a name,' so the meaning is: 'Do you dispute with me about named entities for which there are names that do not befit them,' and thus the blame is directed at naming devoid of meaning. The pronoun in that case refers to 'names,' which is the first object of 'named,' and the second is 'gods.' Had it been reversed, it would entail an istikhdam (a figure of speech in which one word carries two meanings). End of quote.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾ — that is, no proof or evidence for this naming. This is because the one truly deserving of worship is none other than the One who brought all into existence. Had they deserved it, that would be by His appointment, either through sending down a revelation or establishing a proof, and both are impossible. Thus the falsity of what they hold is established.

Al-Jushami said: The verse indicates the corruption of blind imitation, since He blamed them for following the way of their fathers. It also indicates that knowledge is acquired, and it indicates the falsity of every doctrine for which there is no proof. His saying ﴿Do you dispute with me﴾ indicates that the one in the wrong is blameworthy in his disputation, and it is obligatory for him to reflect in order to know the truth. End of quote.

Al-Qadi said: He, Exalted is He, made clear that the ultimate of their argument and their basis is that the idols are called gods without any evidence establishing the reality of what is named, and the attribution of this designation to one whose words are not regarded, to display the extreme of their ignorance and the excess of their dullness.

﴿So wait﴾ — that is, for the descent of the punishment which you demanded by your saying ﴿then bring us what you threaten us with﴾ [al-A'raf: 70], because he has made the truth clear while you persist in obstinacy. ﴿Indeed I am with you among those who wait﴾ — that is, for what will befall you.

Al-Mahayimi said: Their expected thing came in such a way that by the ordinary course no one would escape it, and it was made to be of the kind of the wind that precedes rains, because of their disbelief in the winds of mercy (al-irsal)."

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[72] ﴿So We saved him and those with him by a mercy from Us, and We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs, and they were not believers.﴾

﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾: that is, those who believed in him, through a departure from the normal course of events. ﴿by a mercy from Us﴾: so as to show Our mercy toward them in the Hereafter. ﴿And We cut off the last remnant of those who denied Our signs﴾: that is, We uprooted them completely.

Al-Shihab (al-Alusi) said: "Cutting off the last remnant (qat' al-dabir) is a metaphor for complete annihilation, to the point of destroying all of them. This is because the usual pattern of a calamity, when it strikes one part of a people, is that it passes over others. When a thing's root is extended, it is taken in its entirety. Al-dabir means al-akhir (the last one)." ﴿And they were not believers﴾ is coordinated with "denied" and is included with it under the same grammatical construction (ḥukm al-ṣilah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you ask: what is the benefit of denying belief to them in His words, ﴿and they were not believers﴾, alongside affirming that they denied the signs of God? I say: it is an allusion to those among them who believed, such as Mardath ibn Sa'd, and those who were saved with Hud, peace be upon him. It is as if He said: 'We cut off the last remnant of those among them who denied, and they were not like those among them who believed,' to indicate that the destruction was specific to the deniers, and God saved the believers." End of quote.

Al-Tibi said: "That is, when the believer hears that destruction was specific to the deniers, and knows that the cause of salvation is faith alone, his desire for it increases and its worth grows in his eyes." End of quote.

Ibn Kathir said: "God, glorified is He, has described their destruction in other places of the Qur'an as being that He sent against them the barren wind: ﴿It left nothing it came upon without making it like powdered remains﴾ [al-Dhariyat 51:42], as He said in another verse: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a screaming, violent wind﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:6], ﴿which He imposed upon them for seven nights and eight days in succession, so you would see the people lying in it prostrate as if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:7], ﴿so do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:8]. When they rebelled and transgressed, God destroyed them with a violent wind. It would lift a man from among them and carry him into the air, then turn him over onto the top of his head, and his skull would be torn off until it was separated from his body."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "The dwellings of 'Ad and their people, when God sent Hud to them, were al-Ahqaf (the sand dunes), between 'Oman and Hadramawt, and all of Yemen." He said: "Al-Ahqaf is sand."

Yet, along with that, they had spread throughout the whole earth and subdued its people by the excess of their strength, which God had given them. They were worshippers of idols they worshipped besides God: an idol called (Sada), an idol called (Samud), and an idol called (al-Haba'). So God sent to them Hud, who was among the most noble of them in lineage and the best of them in position. He commanded them to affirm the oneness of God, not to associate anyone with Him as a god, and to refrain from wronging people. He did not command them, as is reported, and God knows best, to do anything other than this. But they refused and denied him, and said: ﴿Who is mightier than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 41:15].

A group of them followed him, a small number who concealed their faith. Among those who believed in him and affirmed him was a man of 'Ad called (Mardath ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr), who used to conceal his faith. When they transgressed against God, blessed and exalted is He, denied their prophet, spread corruption throughout the land, acted tyrannically, and built on every high place a landmark in vain, without benefit, Hud addressed them and said: ﴿Do you build on every high place a monument, playing?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:128], ﴿and make for yourselves fortresses that perhaps you will abide forever?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:129], ﴿and when you strike, you strike as tyrants﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:130], ﴿so fear God and obey me﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:131].

﴿They said, "O Hud, you have brought us no clear evidence, and we will not abandon our gods on your word, nor will we believe in you."﴾ [Hud 11:53] ﴿We only say that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾ [Hud 11:54] That is: what you have brought us is nothing but madness that has afflicted you through some of these gods of ours which you disparage. ﴿He said, "I call God to witness, and you bear witness that I am free of what you associate﴾ [Hud 11:54] ﴿with Him. So scheme against me all together, then give me no respite."﴾ [Hud 11:55] up to His words: ﴿on a straight path.﴾ [Hud 11:56]

When they did that, God withheld the rain from the sky for three years, as they claim, until the drought exhausted them.

When calamity or hardship befell the people in that time and they sought relief from God, their supplication to God was at His Sacred House in Makkah, Muslim and polytheist alike. Many diverse people of different religions would gather in Makkah, and all of them held Makkah in honor, knowing its sanctity and its status with God.

Ibn Ishaq said: "The House in that time was known in its place, and the Sacred Precinct was standing, as they relate. The people of Makkah at that time were the 'Amaliq. They were named 'Amaliq because their forefather was ('Amliq ibn Lawadh ibn Sam ibn Nuh). The chief of the 'Amaliq at that time in Makkah, as they claim, was a man called Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr. His father was still alive in that time, but he had grown old, and his son led his people. Leadership and nobility among the 'Amaliq, as they claim, belonged to the people of that House."

The mother of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr was Kaladah, daughter of al-Khaybari, a man of 'Ad. When the rain failed from 'Ad and they were afflicted, they said: "Send from among you a delegation to Makkah, and let them ask for rain for you, for you have perished!" They sent Qayl ibn 'Anz, Laqim ibn Hazzal ibn Hazil, 'Atil ibn Sadd ibn 'Ad the Elder, Mardath ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr, who was a Muslim concealing his Islam, and Julhumah ibn al-Khaybari, the maternal uncle of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, his mother's brother.

Then they sent Luqman ibn 'Ad ibn Fulan ibn Fulan ibn Sadd ibn 'Ad the Elder. Each of these men set out with a band of his people, until the number of the delegation reached seventy men. When they arrived in Makkah, they stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, who was on the outskirts of Makkah, outside the Sacred Precinct. He lodged them and honored them, for they were his maternal uncles and his in-laws.

When the delegation of 'Ad stayed with Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, they remained with him for a month drinking wine, while the two singing-girls of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, al-Jaradatan, sang to them. Their journey had taken a month and their stay was a month.

When Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr saw how long they remained, and that their people had sent them to seek refuge with them from the calamity that had befallen them, it grieved him. He said: "My maternal uncles and in-laws are dying! And these are staying with me, my guests lodging with me! By God, I do not know what to do with them. I am ashamed to order them to leave for what they were sent for, lest they think I am weary of their stay with me, while those behind them among their people have perished from hardship and thirst!" Or as he said.

He complained of their situation to his two singing-girls, the two al-Jaradatan. They said: "Compose a poem for us to sing to them, without them knowing who said it; perhaps that will move them!"

Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, when they had urged him to this, said:

Ah, O Qayl, woe to you! Arise and call out, perhaps God will make a cloud for us to rise up,
Which will water the land of 'Ad, for 'Ad ∗∗∗ has become unable to speak clearly,
From the severe thirst, for we do not hope ∗∗∗ through it for the old man nor the boy,
And their women were once in goodness ∗∗∗ but now their women have become childless,
And the wild beasts come to them openly ∗∗∗ and do not fear the arrows of the 'Adi,
And you are here, in what you desire ∗∗∗ of your day and your night in full,
So may your delegation be disgraced, a delegation of a people ∗∗∗ who were not greeted with peace and salutation.

When Mu'awiyah had said that poem, the two al-Jaradatan sang it to them. When the people heard what the two sang, some of them said to others: "O people, your people only sent you to seek refuge with you from this calamity that has befallen them, and you have delayed too long for them! Enter this Sacred Precinct and ask for rain for your people!"

Mardath ibn Sa'd ibn 'Ufayr said to them: "By God, you will not be watered by your supplication, but if you obey your prophet and turn to him in repentance, you will be watered!" At that, he openly declared his Islam. Julhumah ibn al-Khaybari, the maternal uncle of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr, when he heard his words and realized that he had followed the religion of Hud and believed in him, said:

O Abu Sa'd, you are of a noble tribe ∗∗∗ of people of honor, and your mother is from Thamud.
Indeed we will not obey you as long as we live ∗∗∗ and we will not do what you desire.
Do you command us to abandon the religion of Rifd ∗∗∗ and Ramal and the family of Sadd and al-'Ubud?
And to abandon the religion of noble forefathers ∗∗∗ who had sound judgment, and to follow the religion of Hud?

Then he said to Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr and his father Bakr: "Hold back Mardath ibn Sa'd from us, so that he does not go with us to Makkah, for he has followed the religion of Hud and abandoned our religion!"

Then they set out for Makkah to ask for rain for 'Ad. When they turned toward Makkah, Mardath ibn Sa'd left the dwelling of Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr and caught up with them there, before they had asked God for anything for which they had set out. When he reached them, he stood up and prayed to God in Makkah, while the delegation of 'Ad was gathered there praying. He said: "O God, give me my request alone, and do not include me in anything for which the delegation of 'Ad calls upon You."

Qayl ibn 'Anz was the head of the delegation of 'Ad.

The delegation of 'Ad said: "O God, give Qayl what he asks of You, and make our request join his request."

Luqman ibn 'Ad, who was the chief of 'Ad, had stayed behind from the delegation of 'Ad when they prayed.

When they had finished their prayer, he stood and said: "O God, I have come to You alone with my need, so give me my request." Qayl ibn 'Anz, when he prayed, said: "O our God, if Hud is truthful, then water us, for we have perished." So God created for them three clouds: white, red, and black. Then a caller called out to him from the cloud: "O Qayl! Choose for yourself and your people from these clouds." He said: "I choose the black cloud, for it is the most abundant in water." A caller called out: "You have chosen a pulverized ash, that leaves nothing of the family of 'Ad alive, neither parent nor child that it does not reduce to dust, except the family of al-Luwadhiyyah, the guided ones." The family of al-Luwadhiyyah were the descendants of Laqim ibn Hazzal ibn Hazilah ibn Bakr. They were residents of Makkah with their maternal uncles, and they had not been with 'Ad in their land, so they are the later 'Ad, and whoever was among their descendants who remained of 'Ad.

God drove the black cloud, as they relate, which Qayl ibn 'Anz had chosen, with what it contained of vengeance, toward 'Ad, until it emerged upon them from a valley called (al-Mughith).

When they saw it, they rejoiced at it and said: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain.﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:24] God says: ﴿Rather, it is what you were hastening: a wind in which is a painful punishment,﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:24] ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord.﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:25] That is, everything it was commanded to destroy.

The first to perceive what was in it and to know that it was a wind, as they relate, was a woman of 'Ad called (Mahdad). When she became certain of what was in it, she screamed and then fainted. When she recovered, they said: "What did you see, O Mahdad?" She said: "I saw a wind in which were things like shooting sparks of fire, and before it were men leading it!"

God imposed it upon them ﴿for seven nights and eight days in succession﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:7], as God said, and "ḥusum" means continuous. It left no one of 'Ad alive without destroying them. Hud withdrew, as I have been told, along with those believers who were with him, into an enclosure, so that the wind did not touch him or those with him, except what softened their skins and pleased their souls.

It passed over 'Ad lifting them between heaven and earth, and it struck them with stones. The delegation of 'Ad left Makkah until they passed by Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr and his father, and they stayed with him.

While they were with him, a man came riding a camel of his on a moonlit night, on the third evening after the calamity of 'Ad. He informed them of the news. They said to him: "Where did you leave Hud and his companions?" He said: "I left them on the seashore."

They seemed to doubt what he had told them, so Hazilah, daughter of Bakr, said: "He speaks truly, by the Lord of the Ka'bah!"

Ibn Kathir said: "This is a strange narrative, containing many benefits. God, exalted is He, has said: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and We saved them from a severe punishment.﴾ [Hud 11:58]

[p. 2776] [p. 2777] [p. 2778] [p. 2779] [p. 2780] [p. 2781]

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Wa'il, from al-Harith al-Bakri, who said: "I set out to complain about al-Ala' ibn al-Hadrami to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I passed by al-Rabadhah, and there I found an old woman from the Banu Tamim who had been left stranded there. She said to me: 'O servant of Allah! I have a need with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Will you convey me to him?' So I carried her and came to Madinah. There, the mosque was packed with its people, and a black banner was fluttering, and Bilal was girded with a sword before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I asked: 'What is the matter with the people?' They said: 'He intends to send 'Amr ibn al-'As on a mission.' So I sat down. He (ﷺ) entered his dwelling, or said his tent, and I asked permission to see him. He permitted me, so I entered, greeted him, and he said: 'Was there any matter between you and Tamim?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'The upper hand over them was ours, and I passed by an old woman from the Banu Tamim who had been left stranded, and she asked me to carry her to you, and here she is at the door.' He permitted her, and she entered. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah! If you see fit to make a barrier between us and Tamim, then make it al-Dahna.' The old woman became angry and rose up quickly, and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Then where will you go, when you are forced to [go to] your harmer?' He said: I said: 'My example is that of the one who said: (a she-goat carried its own death). I carried this one, and I did not realize that she would be an adversary to me. I seek refuge in Allah and His Messenger from being like the envoy of 'Ad!' He said: 'Go on, and what was the envoy of 'Ad?' — and he knew the story better than I did, but he wanted him to recount it. I said: 'The 'Ad suffered drought, so they sent an envoy of theirs called Qayl. He passed by Mu'awiyah ibn Bakr and stayed with him for a month, being given wine to drink, and two slave girls named al-Jaradatan sang to him. When the month had passed, he went out to the mountains of Tihamah and called out: "O Allah, You know that I did not come to a sick person to treat him, nor to a captive to ransom him. O Allah, give drink to 'Ad as You used to give them drink!" Then dark clouds passed over him, and he was called from among them: "Choose." He pointed to a black cloud among them, and he was called from it: "Take it as ashes, scattering, leaving none of 'Ad alive."' He said: 'It did not reach me that there was sent upon them of the wind except the amount that flows through this ring of mine, until they perished.' Abu Wa'il said: 'And he spoke truly.' He said: 'So whenever the men and women of them sent an envoy, they would say: "Do not be like the envoy of 'Ad."'" Thus did Imam Ahmad narrate it in the Musnad, and al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir also narrated it.

And His Exalted saying:

The Explanation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[73] ﴿And to Thamud [We sent] their brother Salih. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. This is the she-camel of Allah, as a sign for you, so leave her to eat in the earth of Allah, and do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you."﴾

﴿And to Thamud﴾ "That is: And We sent [to] Thamud, who were another tribe of the Arabs, named after their forefather Thamud ibn Amir ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh, and he was the brother of Jadis ibn Abir. Likewise the tribe of Tasm; all of these were tribes of the original Arabs (al-'Arab al-'Aribah), before Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil), upon him be peace."

Thamud came after 'Ad, and their dwellings were well known between the Hijaz and the Levant, as far as Wadi al-Qura and its surroundings. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by their dwellings in the year nine [AH] while going to Tabuk, as related by Ibn Kathir.

Thamud is pronounced like sabur, and its tha' may be vocalized with a damma; it has also been read thus. It has also been read with and without tanwin. As for the second reading (without tanwin), it is because it is the name of a tribe, so it combines definiteness (al-'alamiyyah) and feminine gender (al-ta'nith). As for the first (with tanwin), it is because it is the name of a group of people, or because, since its name was the name of the forefather or of a small amount of water, it was treated as diptote-free (masruf), since it is a masculine proper noun, or it is a common noun (ism jins); so after the transfer (naql), its original status was retained. Thus [it is stated] in (al-'Inayah).

﴿Akhahum Salihan﴾ "He, according to what the scholars of tafsir and genealogy have said, is: the son of Ubayd ibn Asaf ibn Masih ibn Ubayd ibn Hadhir ibn Thamud. ﴿He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him."﴾ He called them, upon him be peace, to what all the Messengers call to, which is the worship of Allah alone, with no partner. As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger except that We revealed to him that there is no deity except Me, so worship Me﴾ [al-Anbiya': 25], and He said: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah and avoid the taghut"﴾ [al-Nahl: 36]. ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾ That is, a manifest proof indicating the truth of my prophethood. ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, as a sign for you﴾ That is, He created her as a proof and a sign of my messengership. He attributed her to Himself as an honour and distinction, like (the House of Allah), or because no one else owns her, Exalted is He, or because she is a proof against them: if they guard her and let her graze and drink freely, they will be preserved, but if they betray her they will be destroyed. Therefore He said: ﴿So leave her to eat in the earth of Allah﴾ that is, the earth which none other than Him owns, the pasture. ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾ That is: do not strike her, do not drive her away, and do not trouble her with any kind of harm, even if your animals are harmed by her, out of honour for the sign of Allah. ﴿Lest a painful punishment seize you﴾ That is: in both abodes, for your audacity against the signs of Allah.

"The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[74] ﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad and settled you in the land, taking for yourselves palaces in its plains and carving out the mountains as houses. So remember the bounties of God, and do not commit abuse in the land, spreading corruption.﴾

"﴿And remember when He made you successors after 'Ad﴾ Al-Shihab said: He did not say 'successors of 'Ad,' indicating that there was a long period of time between them. ﴿And settled you in the land﴾" That is, He lodged you in the land of al-Hijr. The mabā'ah (ماءة, dwelling place) is the abode. ﴿Taking for yourselves palaces from its plains﴾" That is, you build palaces in its plains to dwell in during the days of summer. So "min" (مِن, "from") is in the sense of "fi" (فِي, "in"), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9]. Or it is the "ibtida'iyyah" (inceptive "min," meaning "from"), or the "tab'idiyyah" (partitive "min," meaning "some of"), that is: you make the palaces from a material taken from the plain (sahl), which is clay. The sahl is the opposite of the hazn (rough, rocky ground), which is the place of stones and mountains. ﴿And carving out the mountains as houses﴾, that is, so that you may dwell in them during the days of winter. As for al-Jibal (الجِبالَ, "the mountains"), it is either a second object (maf'ul thani) by implying the meaning of "ittakhadha" (to take) in "nahata" (to carve), or it is in the accusative by removing the preposition, as in the other verse. And naht (carving) is well known in every hard rock, and its present tense has a kasra on the ha' (taḥḥatu, yanḥitu... i.e., tanḥitūna). Al-Hasan read it with a fatha because of a guttural letter. And it was read tanhātūna with ishbā' (vowel lengthening), like yanbā', as Al-Shihab reported.

The Discussion of Ishba' (Vowel Lengthening) in the Middle of a Word

I say: By this reading, the occurrence of ishba' in the middle of a word in the language is established. Its parallel is (yanbā', "flows"), mentioned above, which comes from the words of 'Antarah:

"It flows from the nape of a furious, swift she-camel,"

that is: the sweat flows from behind the ear of a furious she-camel, so he lengthened the fatha to complete the metre, and an alif was produced from its lengthening.

Its parallel is our saying (āmīn, "amen"), and the original is (amīn), and the fatha was lengthened, so an alif was produced from its lengthening, as said by al-Zawzani.

Its parallel is (istakāna, "he submitted"), on the view that it is of the form ifta'ala from (sukūn, "stillness"), so the alif was added for the lengthening of the fatha, as in the Sharh al-Shafiyah.

And from it is ('aqrāb, "scorpion"). In Taj al-'Arus it is said: he heard 'aqrab as a generic noun. He said:

"I seek refuge in God from the scorpions, the tail-raising ones with knotted tails."

He said: According to the grammarians of morphology, the alif in ('aqrāb) is for ishba', because the pattern fa'lāl with a fatha does not exist. End of quote.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾, that is, His blessings upon you, so that you may direct them to the purpose for which He created them.

﴿And do not commit abuse in the land, spreading corruption﴾ through sins and the worship of other than Him, exalted is He."

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 75:**

**The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:**

[75] ﴿The eminent ones of his people who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed, to those among them who believed: "Do you know that Salih is sent from his Lord?" They said: "Indeed, we are believers in that with which he has been sent."﴾

﴿The eminent ones who were arrogant﴾ — meaning: arrogant toward belief after the sign of the she-camel and the sincere admonitions had become manifest. ﴿from his people, to those who were oppressed﴾ — meaning: the leaders of the disbelievers oppressed them and humiliated them, since they had no arrogance that would prevent them from submitting. ﴿to those among them who believed﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "those who were oppressed," with the preposition repeated. If the pronoun refers to "his people," it is a complete substitute (badal al-kull), which indicates that their oppression was restricted to the believers. If it is a partial substitute (badal al-ba'd), and the pronoun refers to "those who were oppressed," then it indicates that the oppressed included both believers and disbelievers.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The first is the correct view, since there is no reason to direct the address first to all the oppressed, together with the fact that the reply is to the believers among them, and because the oppression was specific to the believers. That is, they said to the believers whom they had oppressed and despised: ﴿Do you know﴾ — meaning, from the sign of the she-camel and the sincere admonitions ﴿that Salih is sent from his Lord﴾ — to you, to worship Him alone, with no partner.

(p-٢٧٨٧) They said this in a spirit of mockery and derision, because they knew that the believers knew this. For this reason the believers did not answer them according to the apparent requirement; rather they deviated from it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They said: "Indeed, we are believers in that with which he has been sent."﴾ They turned away from the answer that matched their question, which would have been to say "Yes" or "Indeed, he is sent from Him, exalted is He," hastening toward establishing the truth and displaying the steadfast, continuous belief that the nominal sentence indicates. It also draws attention to the fact that the matter of his being sent is so evident that one should not ask about it; what is truly worthy of being asked about is belief in it. This was conveyed by Abu al-Su'ud.

This is of the wise mode of address (al-uslub al-hakim), which is responding to the questioner and the addressee with something other than what they expect, in order to draw attention to the fact that this is what should be asked about.

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[76] ﴿The arrogant ones among his people said: "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed in."﴾

"﴿The arrogant ones among his people said: Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which you have believed in.﴾" They did not say, "Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which he was sent," in order to show their opposition to them and to reject their statement.

Al-Qasimi said, citing al-Intisaf: "If they had matched the two statements, the requirement of matching would have been for them to say, 'Indeed, we are disbelievers in that with which he was sent.' But they refused this, out of caution against what its outward form implies, namely their affirmation of his messengership while they were denying it. Something like this may occur as mockery, as Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:27], thereby affirming his being sent in mockery. But this is not a place for mockery, for the purpose is to inform each of the two groups, the believers and the deniers, about its own state. Therefore the disbelievers kept their statement free of any hint of belief in the messengership, out of caution for disbelief and extremism in persistence." End of quotation. For this reason they also denied the sign of the she-camel and called him a liar regarding the punishment that would befall them for harming it, as the Most High said:

(p-2788)

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[77] ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel, and they defied the command of their Lord, and they said, "O Salih, bring us what you have threatened us with, if you are indeed one of the messengers."﴾

﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾: that is, they slaughtered her. *Al-'uqr* means a wound, and a mark like a cut on the legs of a horse or camel. It is said: *'aqarahu* *bil-sayf* (he hamstrung him with the sword), *ya'qiruhu* with a kasra, and *'aqqarahu ta'qiran*, meaning he cut its legs with the sword while it was standing.

Al-Azhari said: *al-'uqr* among the Arabs is cutting the hamstring of a camel. Then they use *al-nahr* (slaughter) to mean *'uqr*, because the one who slaughters camels hamstrings them and then slaughters them.

In *Lisan al-'Arab*: "'Aqara the she-camel and 'aqqaraha" means that he did this to her until she fell, so that he could slaughter her while she was under his control, that is, so that she would not bolt during the slaughter.

In a hadith: "There is no *'uqr* in Islam."

Ibn al-Athir said: They used to hamstring camels at the graves of the dead, that is, they would slaughter them, saying that the occupant of the grave used to slaughter for guests during his lifetime, so we repay him with the like of his deed after his death. Thus (it is stated) in *Taj al-'Arus*.

The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, because it was done with their consent, even though only some of them actually did it. It is said of a large tribe: "You did such-and-such," though only one of them did it. Thus (it is stated) in *al-Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari).

Abu al-Su'ud said: In this there is such an emphasis on the gravity of the matter and its horror that its harm reached everyone, which is clear.

﴿And they defied the command of their Lord﴾: that is, they waxed arrogant against obeying it, and it is His command to worship Him alone, or [it refers to] the warning against harming the she-camel. And they increased in mockery: ﴿and they said, "O Salih, bring us what you have threatened us with"﴾, that is, the punishment for hamstringing the she-camel. The imperative here is for urgency, because they believed that this could not happen. Therefore they said: ﴿if you are indeed one of the messengers﴾, that is, for indeed God helps His messengers against their enemies.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 78:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[78] ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homeland.﴾

﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾ "That is: the cry from which violent quaking resulted, in place of the sound of the she-camel when she was hamstrung, and in place of her convulsion at the departure of the soul." ﴿And they became in their abode﴾ "in their lands or their dwellings" ﴿prostrate﴾ "That is: fallen on their faces, lifeless, not moving, dead, in place of the death and fall of the she-camel." The cry and the quaking are among the effects of the sent wind, which had been a mercy and turned into a punishment.

**Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 79 (part 1 of 2):**

On the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[79] ﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you, but you do not like advisors."﴾

﴿So he turned away﴾: that is, Salih turned away from them. ﴿from them and said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the message of my Lord"﴾, which includes the warning of punishment from Him. ﴿and advised you﴾: I commanded you to every good and forbade you from every evil. ﴿but you do not like advisors﴾: that is, from among the messengers, prophets and scholars, because they oppose your desires.

It is apparent that Salih, peace be upon him, was witnessing what befell them, and that he turned away from them after seeing them lying prostrate, turning away grieved and regretful over what he had missed of their faith, sorrowing for them in his words ﴿O my people﴾, etc. This is as stated in al-Kashshaf. Or he addressed them in the manner of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the people of the well of Badr when he said: "Indeed we have found what our Lord promised us to be true; have you found what your Lord promised to be true?" as narrated by al-Bukhari. This was not out of sorrow, but to inform them of Allah's victory for him and the realization of his message, increasing their grief and rebuke, for the living are no more able to hear them, but they cannot speak, as in the Sahih. It is also permissible to take his saying ﴿So he turned away﴾ as conjoined with His saying ﴿Then the earthquake seized them﴾ [al-A'raf: 78], so the address to them would be at the time they were on the verge of destruction, not after it. Then he, peace be upon him, turned away from them as one departing from them, disavowing their persistence when he saw the signs of the descent of the punishment. The first is the more apparent, due to the evident sequential meaning of the fa' (then), and Allah knows best.

**Notes**

**First:** Here we cite what the historians and genealogists have narrated in expounding the story of Thamud, for its place in admonition and lesson, in detail. Otherwise, it is clear that what the Noble Revelation has summarized has no further extent in that matter, and what it has been silent about from those stories, there is no need to pursue it, since it cannot be known with certainty. Except for increasing admonition and strengthening the lesson. For this reason it is authentically reported from him (ﷺ) that he said: "Narrate from the Children of Israel, and there is no harm."

The summary of what they narrated about Thamud is that when 'Ad was destroyed, Thamud settled their lands and succeeded them on the earth, and they were in ease and comfort of life. They became arrogant towards Allah, spread corruption on the earth, and worshipped idols. So Allah, exalted is He, sent to them Salih, peace be upon him. They were an Arab people, and Salih was of the middle of them in lineage. He called them to worship Allah alone, and none followed him except a few weak ones among them. He warned and admonished them, so they asked him for a sign, and proposed to him that he bring forth for them a pregnant she-camel from a solid rock, which they specified themselves. That rock was isolated in a part of the mountain, called al-Ka'ibah. So Salih took from them covenants and pledges: if Allah answered their request, they would certainly believe in Him and follow him. When they gave him their covenants and pledges on that, Salih, peace be upon him, went to his prayer and called upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, so that rock moved, **[p. 2791]** then split open, and out came a she-camel, pregnant and with a fully formed fetus, its young moving between its sides, just as they had asked. At that, their chief Jund'a ibn 'Amr ibn Labid believed, and al-Khabbab, the owner of their idols, and Rabab ibn Sa'mar ibn Jalmas. Jund'a ibn 'Amr had a paternal cousin, Shihab ibn Khalifah ibn Mahallah ibn Labid ibn Jawas, who was among the nobles and excellent men of Thamud. He wished to embrace Islam also, but that group forbade him, and he obeyed them. A man from the believers of Thamud, called Mihwash ibn 'Anmah ibn al-Zamil, may Allah have mercy on him, said concerning that:

*A band from the family of 'Amr had called Shihab to the religion of the Prophet,*
*the mighty one of all Thamud together, so he resolved to respond, and had he responded,*
*Salih would have become mighty among us, and they would not have exchanged their leader for a tail-tuft.*
*But the deviators from the family of Hijr turned away after their guidance, like flies.*

The she-camel and her young remained among them, after she had given birth, for a period. She would drink from their well one day, and leave it to them one day. On her day of drinking they would milk her, and fill whatever vessels and containers they wished. As He said in another verse: ﴿And inform them that the water is shared between them, each portion attended﴾ [al-Qamar: 28]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿This is a she-camel; for her is a drink, and for you is a drink of a known day﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 155]. She used to graze in some of those valleys, coming from one direction and departing from another, so that she would have room, because she used to drink her fill of water. She was, as it is mentioned, a huge creature and a splendid sight. When she passed by their livestock, they would shy away from her. When this lasted long for them, and their denial of the Prophet Salih, peace be upon him, intensified, they resolved to kill her so that they could monopolize the water every day. It is said that they all agreed on killing her. Qatadah said: "It reached me that the one who killed her went around to all of them, [to ask] whether they were content with killing her, even the women behind their curtains." Ibn Kathir said: "I say, this is the apparent meaning, due to His saying: ﴿So they denied him and hamstrung her, so their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them﴾ [al-Shams: 14]. **[p. 2792]** And He said: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her thereby﴾ [al-Isra': 59]. And He said: ﴿Then they hamstrung the she-camel﴾ [al-A'raf: 77]. So He attributed that to the whole tribe, which indicates the consent of all of them to that, and Allah knows best."

Imam Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir and others among the scholars of tafsir mentioned that the cause of her killing was that a woman from Thamud called 'Unaizah bint Ghanm ibn Mijlaz, kunyah Umm Ghanm, of the Banu 'Ubayd ibn al-Mahl, brother of Rumail ibn al-Mahl, was the wife of Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr. She was an old, aged woman, and had beautiful daughters, and she owned wealth of camels, cattle and sheep.

And another woman called Sadduf bint al-Muhayya ibn Dahr ibn al-Muhayya, the chief of the Banu 'Ubayd and the owner of their idols in earlier times. The valley was called "Wadi al-Muhayya," that is, al-Muhayya the Greater, grandfather of al-Muhayya the Lesser, father of Sadduf.

Sadduf was among the most beautiful of people, and she was rich, possessing wealth of camels, sheep and cattle. These two women were among the fiercest enemies of Salih in Thamud and the greatest in disbelief towards him. The two would scheme that the she-camel be hamstrung, despite their disbelief in him, because she harmed their livestock.

Sadduf was under the protection of a maternal cousin of hers called Sunthum ibn Harawah ibn Sa'd ibn al-Ghitrif, of the Banu Halas. He embraced Islam and his Islam was good. Sadduf had entrusted her wealth to him, and he spent it on those who had embraced Islam with him from the companions of Salih, until the wealth dwindled.

**[p. 2793]** Sadduf learned of his conversion to Islam, so she reproached him for that. He declared his religion to her, and invited her to Allah and to Islam, but she refused him and plotted against him. She took his sons and daughters from him and hid them among the Banu 'Ubayd, the clan from which she came.

Sunthum, her husband, was of the Banu Hulayl, and was her maternal cousin. He said to her: "Return my children to me." She said: "Not until I make you judge with me before the Banu San'an ibn 'Ubayd or the Banu Jund'a ibn 'Ubayd." Sunthum said to her: "Rather, I will make you judge with me before the Banu Mirdas ibn 'Ubayd," because the Banu Mirdas ibn 'Ubayd had hastened into Islam while the others had lagged behind.

She said: "I will not judge with you except before the one I have named to you."

The Banu Mirdas said: "By Allah, you will surely give him his son, willingly or unwillingly."

When she saw that, she gave them to him.

Then Sadduf and 'Unaizah conspired to hamstring the she-camel because of the misfortune that had befallen them. Sadduf summoned a man of Thamud called al-Hubab to hamstring the she-camel, and offered him herself in exchange if he did it, but he refused her. So she summoned a paternal cousin of hers called Mus'addi' ibn Muhrij ibn al-Muhayya, and made herself his reward on condition that he hamstring the she-camel. She was among the most beautiful of people, and wealthy with much property, so he agreed to that.

'Unaizah bint Ghanm summoned Qidar ibn Salif ibn Jund'a, a man from the people of Qurh.

Qidar was a red, blue-eyed, short man. They claimed that he was the product of an illicit union, from a man called Sihyad, and that he was not the son of his father Salif, to whom he was ascribed. Yet he was born on Salif's bed, and he was called after him and ascribed to him.

She said: "I will give you whichever of my daughters you wish, on condition that you hamstring the she-camel."

**[p. 2794]** 'Unaizah was a noble woman among the women of Thamud, and her husband Dhu'ab ibn 'Amr was among the nobles of the men of Thamud. Qidar was mighty and invincible among his people.

So Qidar ibn Salif and Mus'addi' ibn Muhrij set out, and they incited the deviants of Thamud. Seven men followed the two of them, so they became nine men.

One of those who followed them was a man called Huwayl ibn Muballigh, the maternal uncle of Qidar ibn Salif, a brother of his mother through both father and mother. He was mighty among the people of Hijr. Also Da'ir ibn Ghanm ibn Da'ir, who was of the Banu Khalawah ibn al-Mahl. And Da'b ibn Muhrij, the brother of Mus'addi' ibn Muhrij. And five whose names have not been preserved for us.

They lay in wait for the she-camel when she came away from the water. Qidar had hidden himself at the base of a tree on her path, and Mus'addi' had hidden at the base of another. She passed by Mus'addi', and he shot her with an arrow, which lodged in the muscle of her leg. Then 'Unaizah, Umm Ghanm, came out and commanded her daughter, who was among the most beautiful of people in face. She unveiled her to Qidar and showed him her, then she urged him on, so he struck the she-camel with the sword and cut her hamstring. She fell, and cried out a single cry, warning her young one. Then he thrust into her chest and slaughtered her.

Her young one ran until it came to a towering mountain, then came to a rock at the top of the mountain, frightened, and sought refuge in it. The name of the mountain, as they claim, was Sinw.

Then Salih came to them, and when he saw the she-camel had been hamstrung, he said: "You have violated the sanctity of Allah. So rejoice in the punishment of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, and His vengeance."

Four men of the nine who hamstrung the she-camel followed the young one, among them Mus'addi' ibn Muhrij. Mus'addi' shot it with an arrow, which pierced its heart. Then he dragged it by its leg and brought it down, and they threw its meat in with the meat of its mother.

When Salih said to them, "Rejoice in the punishment of Allah and His vengeance," they said to him, mocking him: "When is that, O Salih? **[p. 2795]** And what is the sign of that?" They used to name the days among themselves: Sunday was "Awwal," Monday was "Ahwan," Tuesday was "Wabar," Wednesday was "Jubar," Thursday was "Mu'min," Friday was "al-'Urubah," and Saturday was "Shiyar." They had hamstrung the she-camel on Wednesday. Salih said to them when they said that to him: "You will awake on the morning of Mu'min, meaning Thursday, with your faces yellowed. Then you will awake on the day of al-'Urubah, meaning Friday, with your faces reddened. Then you will awake on the day of Shiyar, meaning Saturday, with your faces blackened. Then the punishment will overtake you on the day of Awwal, meaning Sunday."

When Salih said that to them, the nine who had hamstrung the she-camel said: "Come, let us kill Salih. If he is truthful, we will have hastened him before us; and if he is lying, we will have sent him to join his she-camel."

So they came to him at night to ambush him in his household, but the angels struck them with stones. When they were slow in returning to their companions, they came to the dwelling of Salih and found them crushed, smashed with stones. They said to Salih: "You killed them!" Then they intended to attack him. But his tribe stood between him and them, wearing their weapons, and said to them: "By Allah, you shall never kill him, for he promised you that the punishment would descend upon you within three days. If he is truthful, you will only increase your Lord's wrath against you; and if he is lying, you will be relieved of what you desire!"

So they turned away from them that night, and the group whom the angels struck with stones were the nine whom Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in the Qur'an with His saying: ﴿And there were in the city nine men who spread corruption in the land and did not amend﴾ [al-Naml: 48], up to His saying: ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who know﴾ [al-Naml: 52].

Then, on the morning after that night in which they had left Salih, their faces were yellowed. They became certain of the punishment and knew that Salih had told them the truth, so they sought him in order to kill him. Salih fled from them until he took refuge with a clan of Thamud called (Banu Ghanm). He alighted upon their chief, a man among them called Nufayl, who was known by the kunya Abu Hudb, and he was a polytheist. He concealed him, and they could not reach him.

Then they went to the companions of Salih and tortured them so that they would point them to him. A man from among Salih's companions called (Maydu' ibn Haram) said: "O Prophet of God, they are torturing us so that we will point them to you. Shall we point them to you?" He said: "Yes." So (Maydu' ibn Haram) pointed them to him. When they learned the place where Salih was, they came to Abu Hudb and spoke to him, and he said to them: "Salih is with me, and you have no way to him." So they turned away from him and left him, and what God had sent down upon them of His punishment occupied them away from him. Some of them informed others of what they saw in their faces on the morning of Thursday, for their faces had become yellowed. Then they awoke on Friday with their faces reddened, then they awoke on Saturday with their faces blackened. Until, when the night of Sunday came, Salih went out from among them, together with those who had embraced Islam with him, toward Syria, and he alighted at Ramla in Palestine. One of his companions called (Maydu' ibn Haram) remained behind and alighted at Qurh, which is Wadi al-Qura, and between Qurh and al-Hijr there are eighteen miles. He alighted upon their chief, a man called (Amr ibn Ghanm), who had eaten from the meat of the she-camel and had not taken part in slaying it. Maydu' ibn Haram said to him: "O Amr ibn Ghanm, leave this town, for Salih said: whoever remains in it perishes, and whoever leaves it is saved."

Amr said: "I did not take part in hamstringing her, nor did I approve of what was done to her." When the morning of Sunday came, the Blast seized them, and none of them, small or great, survived except a paralysed girl called (al-Zuraya'a), who was (al-Kalba, the daughter of al-Silq). She was an unbeliever, intensely hostile to Salih. God freed her legs after she had witnessed the entire punishment, so she went out as swiftly as anything has ever been seen to move, until she came to the people of Qurh and informed them of what she had witnessed of the punishment and what had befallen Thamud. Then she asked for water and was given it, and when she drank, she died.

Second: al-Razi said: Some of the heretics claimed that the wordings of the revelation in narrating this event differ, namely al-Rajfa, al-Taghiya and al-Sayha. The answer is what Abu Muslim said: al-Taghiya is a name for everything that exceeds its limit, whether it is an animal or not, and the ha' was attached to it for emphasis. Muslims call a tyrannical king "al-taghiya" and "al-taghut." God the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, verily man becomes insolent﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6] ﴿when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [al-'Alaq: 7]. It is said: taghā, tughyān, and he is ṭāghin and ṭāghiya. God the Exalted said: ﴿Thamud denied by their rebellion﴾ [al-Shams: 11], and He said of non-animate things: ﴿Indeed when the water rose high﴾ [al-Haqqa: 11], meaning it overpowered and exceeded its limit.

As for al-Rajfa, it is the earthquake, a movement outside the usual. So it is not far-fetched to apply the name al-Taghiya to it. As for al-Sayha, the usual case is that an earthquake is not separated from a great, terrifying cry. As for al-Sa'iqa, the usual case is that it is the earthquake, and likewise al-Zajra, as God the Exalted said: ﴿It will be but one single shout﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 13] ﴿and behold, they will be upon the surface of the earth﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 14]. Thus what that group claimed is refuted.

Third: the scholars of tafsir said: No one of the offspring of Thamud remained except Salih, peace be upon him, and those who followed him, may God be pleased with them, except that a man called Abu Righal, who, when the vengeance fell upon his people, was then residing in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram), so nothing befell him. Then when he went out on some day to al-Hill, a stone came down upon him from the sky and killed him.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Jabir, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr, he said: 'Do not ask for signs, for the people of Salih asked for them. She-camel would come to drink from this path and go out from this path, but they rebelled against the command of their Lord and hamstrung her. She used to drink their water one day, and they would drink her milk one day, until they hamstrung her. So a Cry seized them, and God destroyed everyone beneath the surface of the sky among them, except one man who was in the Sacred Precinct of God.' They said: 'Who is he, O Messenger of God?' He said: 'Abu Righal.' When he came out of the Sacred Precinct, what had befallen his people befell him."

Ibn Kathir said: This hadith is not found in any of the Six Books, but it is according to the conditions of Muslim.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar: Isma'il ibn Umayya informed me that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by the grave of Abu Righal and said: "Do you know who this is?" They said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "This is the grave of Abu Righal, a man of Thamud, who was in the Sacred Precinct of God, and the Sacred Precinct of God protected him from the punishment of God. When he went out, what had befallen his people befell him, and he was buried here, and a golden branch was buried with him." Then the people dismounted, rushed upon it with their swords, searched for him, and extracted the branch. Abu Righal is the ancestor of the Thaqif who used to live in al-Ta'if, as has been related with a marfu' chain to the Prophet (ﷺ), recorded by Abu Dawud and others.

Fourth: We mentioned earlier that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by the dwellings of Thamud, now known as the Mada'in Salih, while he was going to the expedition of Tabuk, in the ninth year, and he commanded his companions to enter them weeping and fearful lest what befell their people befall them, and he forbade them to drink from their water.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) alighted with the people during the year of Tabuk; he alighted with them at al-Hijr, by the houses of Thamud. The people drew water from the wells from which Thamud used to drink, and they kneaded dough with it and set cooking pots with meat. The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them, so they poured out the pots and fed the dough to the camels. Then he set off with them until he alighted with them at the well from which the she-camel used to drink, and he forbade them to enter upon the people who were punished, and said: 'I fear that what befell them may befall you, so do not enter upon them.'"

Ahmad, al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Ibn Umar, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by al-Hijr, he said: 'Do not enter upon these punished people unless you are weeping; if you are not weeping, do not enter upon them, lest what befell them befall you.' Then he covered his head and hastened his pace until he had passed the valley."

In al-Bukhari, it is related that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hijr during the expedition of Tabuk, he commanded them not to drink from its wells or draw water from them. They said: "We have kneaded dough with it and drawn water." So the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded them to throw away that dough and pour out that water.

Fifth: Ibn Kathir said: Some exegetes mention that every prophet whose nation was destroyed would go and stay in the Sacred Precinct, the Haram of Makkah, and God knows best.

Imam Ahmad said: Waki' narrated to us, Zam'a ibn Salih narrated to us, from Salama ibn Wahram, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) passed by the valley of 'Usfan during his pilgrimage, he said: 'O Abu Bakr! What valley is this?' He said: 'This is the valley of 'Usfan.' He said: 'Hud and Salih passed by it on red she-camels, whose nose-ropes were of palm fibre, their waist-wrappers were of woollen cloaks, and their mantles were of striped cloth, chanting the talbiya, performing pilgrimage to the Ancient House.'" Ibn Kathir said: This hadith is gharib from this route; none of them recorded it.

And His, the Exalted's, saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 80:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[80] ﴿And Lot, when he said to his people, "Do you commit an abomination such as no one in the worlds has preceded you in?"﴾

﴿And Lot﴾: It is in the accusative, governed by a suppressed verb coordinated with what preceded it, i.e., "And We sent Lot." His name is non-Arabic, and its meaning in Arabic is (rolled up) or (bitter), as in the interpretation of the names in the Torah and the Gospel. He is, according to what the scholars of genealogy and exegesis have said, Ibn Haran ibn Tarih, and it is said Azar, and he is the nephew of Ibrahim al-Khalil, peace be upon them both. He had believed along with Ibrahim, peace be upon them both, and migrated with him to Syria, (p-2800) and they settled in the land of the Canaanites, of Palestine, which is the Holy Land.
