Then a dispute arose between their herdsmen, so Lot moved away to the valley of the Jordan and settled in the city of Sodom. So God sent him to its people and to the villages around it. He began calling them to God, Exalted is He, and commanding them to what is right, and forbidding them from the sins and abominations they were committing, which they had invented, and which no one among the worlds, of the children of Adam, had preceded them in, other than them, namely intercourse with males.

Ibn Kathir said: This is something the children of Adam had not practised or become accustomed to, and it did not occur to their minds, until the people of Sodom, may the curses of God be upon them, did it.

Amr ibn Dinar said: No male mounted a male until the people of Lot.

And al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik, the Umayyad caliph, builder of the Mosque of Damascus, said: Had God, Mighty and Majestic, not related to us the story of the people of Lot, I would not have thought that a male could rise above a male.

Then He, Exalted is He, made clear Lot's denunciation of them by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿when he said to his people, "Do you commit the abomination"﴾, i.e., the act that is extremely ugly. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿such as no one in the worlds has preceded you in﴾, i.e., no one before you knew it. The particle "bi" (with) is for transitivity, from your saying "sabaqtuhu bil-kurah" (I preceded him with the ball) when you struck it before him. And from this is His saying ﷺ: "Ukkasha has preceded you with it." Thus in (al-Kashshaf).

Abu al-Su'ud said: The clause is resumed, brought to emphasise the denunciation and to intensify the reproach and rebuke, for committing ugliness is ugly, and inventing it is uglier. So God first denounced for them the committing of the abomination, then rebuked them for being the first to do it, then resumed explaining that abomination in emphasis of the earlier denunciation and in intensification of the reproach, with His saying, Exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[81] ﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire instead of women. Rather, you are a people who transgress.﴾

﴿Indeed, you approach men﴾ — i.e., those whom Allah created to approach women, not for men to approach them. It was recited with two clear hamzas, and with softening of the second, without elongation and also with elongation. The addition of (inna, indeed) and (the lam, the emphatic lam) conveys stronger reproach and rebuke, as if such a thing could not conceivably proceed from anyone. The choice of the word (men) rather than (boys), (beardless youths) and the like is for the sake of intensifying the reproach. "Ta'tūna" (you approach) is from (atā al-mar'ah), when he has intercourse with her. So said al-Zamakhshari.

In Taj al-'Arus: "Ata al-fāḥishah" means he engaged in it. Coming (ityān) is used as a euphemism for sexual intercourse, and it is one of the most elegant euphemisms. A man who is approached (ma'tiyy) is one who is approached in it. From this is the saying of one of the later (muwallad) poets:

"He approaches and is approached; he denies neither this nor that, just as the eye of the needle [admits both the thread and the...]"

End of quotation.

His words, may He be exalted, ﴿with desire﴾ — (shahwatan) is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning for the sake of desiring, i.e., there is no motive driving you to it except mere appetite without any other incentive. There is no greater blame than this, because it describes them as beastly, and that they have no motive from the side of reason whatsoever, such as seeking offspring or the like. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning desiring, following appetite, not heeding decency. Thus in (al-Kashshāf). ﴿Instead of women﴾ — i.e., transgressing beyond the women who were created for that purpose. Abu al-Su'ud said: It is also permissible that what is intended by His words ﴿with desire﴾ is denunciation of them and rebuke for their desiring that vile, detestable act, as His words ﴿instead of women﴾ indicate, i.e., going beyond the women who are the objects of desire, as His words, may He be exalted, ﴿They are purer for you﴾ [Hud: 78] indicate. ﴿Rather, you are a people who transgress﴾ — a turning away from denunciation to informing them of the state that necessitates committing abominations and calls to following appetites. Namely, they are a people whose habit is excess and transgressing limits in everything; therefore they exceeded in the matter of satisfying appetite, until they went beyond the customary to the non-customary. Similar is His words: ﴿Rather, you are a people who exceed bounds﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 166]. Thus in (al-Kashshāf).

**On the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[82] ﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure."﴾

﴿And the answer of his people was﴾ — that is, the arrogant ones, in response to his counsel. ﴿Only that they said, "Expel them"﴾ — that is, Lut and the believers with him. ﴿From your town﴾ — that is, your land.

Al-Zamakhshari said: This means that they did not answer him with anything that would be a reply to what Lut, peace be upon him, had spoken to them, namely his denunciation of the abomination and his magnifying of its gravity, and his branding them with the mark of extravagance (*israf*), which is the root of all evil. Rather, they brought up something else that had no connection to his speech and his counsel: the command to expel him and those believers with him from their town, out of impatience with them and with what they heard of his admonition and advice. Their words, ﴿Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾, were mockery of them and of their purity from the abominations, and boasting of the filth they were engaged in, just as the rogues among the debauched say to some of the pious when they admonish them: "Keep this ascetic away from us, and give us rest from this ascetic who renounces the world."

Ibn Kathir said: Mujahid said: "They keep themselves pure from the anuses of men and the anuses of women." The same was narrated from Ibn Abbas.

Al-Suyuti said in *al-Iklil*: From this it is derived as evidence for the prohibition of anal intercourse with women, on the basis that a companion's interpretation (*tafsir*) carries the ruling of a *marfu'* report (one traced back to the Prophet, ﷺ).

Ibn al-Qayyim, however, preferred that it has the ruling of a *mawquf* report (one that stops at a companion, not traced to the Prophet, ﷺ).

The matter was discussed comprehensively earlier, in His words, ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 223], so refer back to it.

**A note:**

Imam Shams al-Din Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his book *I'lam al-Lahfan* (*Ighathat al-Lahfan*): Allah, glory be to Him, has branded polytheism, fornication, and sodomy with filth and impurity in His Book, rather than all other sins, even though other sins may include these. What occurs in the Qur'an is His words, ﴿O you who believe, the polytheists are only impure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28], and His words concerning the people of Lut (sodomites): ﴿And Lut—We gave him judgment and knowledge and saved him from the town that used to commit the abominations. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Anbiya': 74]. And the people of Lut said: ﴿Expel the family of Lut from your town. Indeed, they are people who keep themselves pure﴾ [al-Naml: 56]. Thus they acknowledged, along with their polytheism and disbelief, that they themselves were the vile and the impure, and that Lut and his family were purified from that by their avoidance of it.

He, exalted is He, said concerning fornicators: ﴿Evil women are for evil men, and evil men are for evil women﴾ [al-Nur: 26]. As for the impurity of polytheism, it is of two kinds: a severe impurity and a light impurity. The severe impurity is major polytheism, which Allah, mighty and majestic, will not forgive, for Allah, mighty and majestic, does not forgive that He be associated with. The light impurity is minor polytheism, such as slight showing-off (*riya'*), affectation toward created beings, swearing by other than Allah, and fearing or hoping in them.

Then he said: The impurity of fornication and sodomy is more severe than other impurities, in that it corrupts the heart and greatly weakens its monotheism. For this reason, those most afflicted with this impurity are those who are most polytheistic. Whenever polytheism predominates in the servant, this impurity and these abominations become more numerous in him, and whenever his sincerity is greater, he is further from them, as He, exalted is He, said concerning Joseph the truthful, peace be upon him: ﴿Thus, that We might avert from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our sincere servants﴾ [Yusuf: 24]. For the passion for forbidden forms is a kind of worship of them—indeed, it is among the highest kinds of worship—especially when it takes control of the heart and becomes entrenched in it, and becomes *tatayyum* (infatuation), and *tatayyum* means worship. The lover becomes a worshipper of his beloved. Often his love, his remembrance of the beloved, his longing for him, his striving for his pleasure, and his preference of what the beloved loves over the love and remembrance of Allah and striving for His pleasure, come to dominate him. Indeed, often that completely removes Allah from the lover's heart, and he becomes attached to a beloved among the forms (of creation), as is observed. Then the beloved becomes his god besides Allah, mighty and majestic. He prefers the beloved's pleasure and love over Allah's pleasure and love, draws near to the beloved in ways he does not draw near to Allah, spends for the beloved's pleasure what he does not spend for Allah's pleasure, and avoids the beloved's displeasure in ways he does not avoid Allah's displeasure. Thus the beloved becomes more beloved to him than his Lord, in love, submission, humility, hearing, and obedience. For this reason, passion and polytheism are mutually linked. Allah, glory be to Him, related passion of the polytheists of the people of Lut and of the wife of the Aziz, who at that time was a polytheist. Whenever the polytheism of the servant grows strong, he is afflicted with passion for forms, and whenever his monotheism grows strong, that is turned away from him.

The fornicator and the sodomite—the full pleasure of their lust occurs only with passion, and their companion is never free of it. It is only that it moves him from place to place; his passion does not remain confined to one place but is divided among many arrows, and each beloved has a share of his idolatry and worship. There is no sin more corrupting to the heart and to religion than these two abominations. They have a special property in distancing the heart from Allah, for they are among the greatest of the vile things. When the heart is dyed with them, it becomes distant from the One who is pure, and nothing ascends to Him except the pure. Whenever it grows more vile, it grows further from Allah. For this reason, the Messiah said, as narrated by Imam Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*: "The idlers will not be among the wise, and fornicators will not enter the kingdom of heaven." Since this is the condition of fornication, it was paired with polytheism in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicating woman or a polytheist, and the fornicating woman is not married except by a fornicator or a polytheist, and that has been made unlawful for the believers﴾ [al-Nur: 3].

Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The point is that Allah, glory be to Him, named adulterous women and men "vile" (*khabithin* and *khabithat*). The category of this act has been prescribed purification for, even if it is lawful (within marriage), and He named its doer *junub* (in a state of major ritual impurity), because of its distancing him from reciting the Qur'an, from prayer, and from the mosques, and He forbade him all of that until he purifies himself with water.

Likewise, when it is unlawful, it distances the heart from Allah, the Exalted, and from the Last Abode. Indeed, it stands between him and faith, until he produces a complete purity through repentance and a purity of his body with water.

The saying of the people of Lut, ﴿Expel them from your town, indeed they are people who keep themselves pure﴾, is of the same kind as His words, glory be to Him, concerning the People of the Trench: ﴿They did not hold it against them except that they believed in Allah, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ [al-Buruj: 8]. And His words, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you resent us except that we believed in Allah and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 59]. Likewise the polytheist resents the monotheist his devotion to monotheism and that it is not mixed with association. Likewise the innovator resents the Sunni his devotion to following the Messenger and that he has not mixed it with the opinions of men or anything that opposes it.

So the patience of the monotheist who follows the Messenger, in the face of what the people of polytheism and innovation resent in him, is better and more beneficial for him, and easier for him, than his patience in the face of what Allah and His Messenger resent of conforming to the people of polytheism and innovation:

*If there is no escape from patience, then be patient for the truth; that patience is one whose outcome is praised.*

End.

(Ends here.)

And when the people of Lut resolved to expel him and banish him and those with him from among them, Allah, the Exalted, brought him out safely, and destroyed them in their land, humiliated and disgraced, as He indicated with His words, glory be to Him:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 83:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[83] ﴿So We saved him and his family, except his wife; she was of those who remained behind.﴾

﴿So We saved him and his family﴾ "That is, and whoever is specially attached to him of his kin, or of the believers, because of their goodness." Ibn Kathir said: None of them believed in him except his household alone, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers. But We found not therein any but one house of Muslims.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 35-36]

﴿except his wife﴾ "That is, We did not save her because of her wickedness." Ibn Kathir said: She did not believe in him; rather she was upon the religion of her people, colluding with them and informing them of whichever guests came to him, by signals between her and them. For this reason, when Lut, peace be upon him, was commanded to set out by night with his family, he was commanded not to inform her and not to bring her out of the city. Some say instead that she followed them, and when the punishment came she turned around, and what befell them befell her.

The more evident view is that she did not leave the city, and Lut did not inform her; rather she remained with them. For this reason He said here, ﴿except his wife﴾. ﴿She was of those who remained behind﴾ "That is, of those who lingered in their dwellings, that is, remained and were destroyed." It was also said: "of those who were destroyed." This is an explanation by way of what necessarily follows. The masculine form is used for the sake of predominance, and to show that she deserved what those who commit the abomination deserve.

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[84] ﴿And We rained upon them a rain, so look at how was the end of the criminals.﴾

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾: That is, We sent down upon them a strange kind of rain, unfamiliar and unusual. It is explained by His words: ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾ [al-Hijr: 74], that is, clay that had turned into stone.

Al-Mahayimi said: Because they disbelieved in the rain of the revealed laws, which gives life by sustaining the progeny and other things, it turned against them in the form of punishment.

(p-2806) I read in the Arabized Torah that the two angels who came to Lot, peace be upon him, informed him and gave him good news of the destruction of his people. They said to him: "Bring out of this place whoever you have here, from your sons-in-law, your sons, your daughters, and all who belong to you, for we have been sent by the Lord to destroy this city."

When it was the time of the rising of dawn, the two angels urged Lot to take his wife and his two daughters. Then they took hold of their hands, all of them, and brought them outside the city, and said: "None of you should look back behind him, and escape to the mountain." When the sun rose, the Lord rained down from heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah brimstone and fire, and overturned those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and the growth of the land. His wife looked back behind her, and she became a pillar of salt. Abraham rose early in the morning from his land and looked toward the direction of Sodom and Gomorrah, and behold, the smoke of the land was rising like the smoke of a furnace. End of quotation.

I read in the prophecy of Ezekiel, peace be upon him, in the sixteenth chapter, in the explanation of the sin of Sodom, the following text:

"Pride, fullness of bread, and abundance of idleness were in Sodom and her daughters; they did not strengthen the hand of the poor and the needy, and they were haughty and committed abomination before Me, so I removed them as you have seen." End of quotation.

The place of those cities has become a sea of bitter water which has remained to this day, and it is known as the Dead Sea, or the Lake of Lot. The land next to it is barren and produces nothing.

Al-Qasimi said, citing "Murshid al-Talibin": The Sea of Lot is the Sea of Sodom, and it is also called the Dead Sea. It is a salt pool in Palestine, fifty miles long and ten miles wide, and it is about 1,250 feet lower than the Mediterranean Sea. Its location is at the place where Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim were. End of quotation.

His words: ﴿so look at how was the end of the criminals﴾ mean: These people committed crimes by disbelief and by doing indecent acts; look at how We destroyed them.

The "looking" here is for wonder at their condition and as a warning against their deeds, for whoever is overcome by the vice of debauchery is restrained by it from success in soul and body, and it brings him to the places of destruction and perdition, as a recompense for what the following of desires has earned for them.

(p-2807) Admonition on the definition of the sodomite:

Know that the Sunnah has come with the killing of whoever commits sodomy with a male, even if he is unmarried, and likewise the passive partner if he is willing, based on the hadith of Ibn Abbas, in the collections of Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lot, kill the one who does it and the one it is done to." Ibn Hajar said: Its narrators are trustworthy, except that there is disagreement about it.

Ibn Majah and al-Hakim also reported from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, raised to the Prophet ﷺ: "Kill the one who does it and the one it is done to, whether they are married or not." Its chain is weak.

Ibn al-Tilla' said in his book "al-Ahkam": It is not established from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he stoned anyone for sodomy, nor that he ruled on it. But it is established from him that he said: "Kill the one who does it and the one it is done to," which Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurairah related from him. End of quotation.

Al-Bayhaqi reported from Ali that he stoned a sodomite.

Al-Bayhaqi also reported from Abu Bakr that he gathered the people concerning a man who was being used as women are used, and he asked the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it. Among the strictest in statement that day was Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: (p-2808) "This is a sin which no nation of the nations has committed except one nation, which Allah dealt with as you know. We see that he should be burned with fire." So the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ agreed that he should be burned with fire, and Abu Bakr wrote to Khalid ibn al-Walid that he should be burned with fire.

Abu Dawud reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, from Ibn Abbas, concerning a virgin who is seized for sodomy: he is to be stoned.

Al-Bayhaqi also reported from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about the punishment of the sodomite, and he said: One looks at the highest building in the village, and he is thrown from it head first, then he is followed with stones.

Al-Mundhiri said: Abu Bakr and Ali burned sodomites with fire, and so did Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik.

In summary: Since it is established that its prescribed punishment is killing, the scholars continued to differ over its method, whether by burning, throwing down, or otherwise.

Some verifying scholars said: If sodomy can be included under the general evidence for fornication, then it is particularized by what is reported about killing for every doer, whether married or not. If it is not included under the evidence for fornication, then its specific evidence suffices and is conclusive. End of quotation.

Imam al-Jashmi al-Yamani said: If there had been a known prescribed punishment for sodomy, it would not have been hidden from the Companions, to the extent that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, consulted them about it when Khalid ibn al-Walid wrote to him.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Zad al-Ma'ad": It is not established from him ﷺ that he ruled on sodomy with anything, because the Arabs did not know this, and it was not brought before him ﷺ. But it is established from him that he said: "Kill the one who does it and the one it is done to," related by the authors of the four Sunan, and its chain is sound. Al-Tirmidhi said: It is a good hadith. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq ruled by it and wrote with it to Khalid after consulting the Companions, and Ali, may Allah honour his face, was the strictest of them in this. (p-2809)

Ibn al-Qassar and our shaykh said: The Companions agreed on killing him, and they only differed over the manner of killing him. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq said: He is thrown from a height. Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: A wall is demolished upon him. Ibn Abbas said: They are both killed with stones. So this is an agreement among them on killing him, even though they differed over its manner.

This agrees with his ruling ﷺ concerning one who has intercourse with a forbidden female relative, because intercourse in both cases is never permitted to the one who does it. For this reason, he combined them in the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, for it is related from him ﷺ that he said: "Whoever you find doing the deed of the people of Lot, kill him."

It is also related from him: "Whoever has intercourse with a close relative, kill him." And in his hadith also, with a chain: "Whoever has intercourse with an animal, kill him and kill the animal with him."

This ruling is in accordance with the ruling of the Lawgiver, for the more forbidden things are, the more severe their punishment becomes, and intercourse with one who is never permitted is greater in crime than intercourse with one who is permitted in some circumstances, so its prescribed punishment is more severe.

Ahmad, in one of the two reports from him, stated explicitly that the ruling for one who has intercourse with an animal is the same as the ruling for sodomy, so he is killed in every case, or his punishment is the punishment for the fornicator.

The early scholars differed on this. Al-Hasan said: Its punishment is the punishment for the fornicator. Abu Salamah said: He is killed in every case. Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: He receives discretionary punishment (ta'zir). This is the view taken by al-Shafi'i, Malik, Abu Hanifah, and Ahmad in one report, for Ibn Abbas issued a ruling to that effect, and he is the narrator of the hadith. End of quotation.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar criticized, in his takhrij of the hadiths of "al-Hidayah", the claim of consensus of the Companions on killing the sodomite, based on the report of al-Bayhaqi: that Abu Bakr gathered the Companions and asked them, and the strictest in statement among them was Ali, who said: "We see that he should be burned with fire," and their opinion agreed on that. Ibn Hajar said: I say: It is very weak, and even if it were authentic, it would be conclusive evidence. End of quotation.

It is clear that the punishments of killing are the greatest of the prescribed punishments (hudud), so they are not to be imposed except on definitive proofs from the Book, or a mutawatir Sunnah (a Sunnah transmitted by so many chains that its authenticity is certain), or a consensus (ijma'), or a hadith whose chain and text are sound and whose indication is definitive.

Therefore the judge must exert his utmost effort in this matter, to safeguard his religion. And Allah knows best.

(p-2810)

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Midian, their brother Shu'ayb. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him. There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord. So give full measure and weight, and do not deprive the people of their due, and do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation. That is best for you, if you are believers."﴾

﴿And to Midian, their brother Shu'ayb﴾: meaning, "And We sent to them." Ibn Ishaq said: they were descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, and Shu'ayb was the son of Mikayil ibn Yashjur ibn Madyan.

Ibn Kathir said: "Madyan" refers both to the tribe and to the town near Ma'an on the road to the Hijaz, and they were the People of al-Aykah.

﴿He said, "O my people﴾: meaning, those whose perfection in religion and worldly life he desired. ﴿Worship Allah; you have no deity other than Him﴾: and this is the call of all the messengers, as we have mentioned before. ﴿There has certainly come to you clear evidence from your Lord﴾: meaning, that by which the truth is distinguished from falsehood, namely his call and his guidance. For this reason some said: by "clear evidence" is meant the coming of Shu'ayb, and that he had no sign except prophethood. Whoever interprets "clear evidence" as proof, demonstration and a tangible miracle does so on the basis that a prophet who calls to a law (shar') that requires its acceptance must have a proof by which his truthfulness is known, and that is nothing but a miracle. He said: the miracle of Shu'ayb is not mentioned in the Qur'an, and not all the signs of the prophets are mentioned in the Qur'an. It is not hidden that, by their usage, "clear evidence" is more general than "miracle." Thus whoever has his error removed by a doubt-dispelling argument, and has the proof of the truth to which he is called made manifest to him, has indeed received clear evidence, because the true reality of clear evidence is everything that makes the truth clear. So keep this in mind.

Al-Jashami said: they differed. It was said: it is not permissible for a prophet to be sent except with a law (shar'), according to Abu Hashim. And it was said: it is permissible for him to call to what is known by reason, according to Abu Ali. End of quotation.

(p-2811) These verses indicate that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, called them to monotheism (tawhid) and to the laws (shara'i') in accordance with the customary practice of the messengers. Among them is His saying: ﴿So give full measure and weight﴾: meaning, complete them for the people by giving them their rights. ﴿And do not deprive the people of their due﴾: meaning, do not diminish their rights, and do not betray the people in their wealth by taking it in the manner of deprivation (bakhs), which is the reduction of measure and weight, secretly and by deception, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1] down to His saying: ﴿to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6].

It is said: "bakhasahu haqqahu" means he reduced it for him and wronged him in it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: they used to deprive the people of everything in their transactions, or they were tax-collectors who did not leave anything without levying a toll on it. Zuhayr said:

Is there in every market of Iraq a levy, and on everything a man sells a dirham's toll?

Al-Qadi said: he said ﴿their due﴾ in a general sense, as an alert that they used to deprive the great and the small, the little and the much. End of quotation.

The prohibition of diminution entails the command to give what is due. It was said: the benefit of explicitly mentioning what is forbidden is to make clear its ugliness.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Zayd, concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not deprive﴾, the verse, that he said: meaning, do not name a price for them and then give them something other than that. The verse indicates that giving full measure and weight is obligatory according to what is customary in the manner of measuring and weighing. ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth﴾: meaning, by disbelief and wrongdoing. ﴿After its reformation﴾: meaning, after the prophets and their righteous followers, who act by their laws, had reformed its affairs and its people by establishing measure, weight, prescribed limits and rulings. ﴿That﴾: a reference to acting upon what they were commanded and forbidden. ﴿Is best for you﴾: in the present, because of people's regard for you due to the goodness of your reputation, and in the future. ﴿If you are believers﴾: meaning, if you affirm my words.

(p-2812)

The discussion of the words of His Most High:

[86] ﴿And do not sit at every path, threatening and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, and seeking to make it crooked. And remember when you were few and He multiplied you. And observe how was the end of the corrupters.﴾

"﴿And do not sit at every path, threatening﴾ is a prohibition against cutting off the path in the physical sense. That is: do not sit on every road where strangers pass, striking them, frightening them, taking their garments, and threatening them with death if they do not give you their wealth.

Mujahid said: "They were tax-collectors" (narrated by Abu al-Shaykh), and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated similarly from al-Suddi.

And from Ibn 'Abbas and others: that is, they threatened the believers who came to Shu'ayb so that they would follow him.

Ibn Kathir said: "The first is more apparent, because He said ﴿at every path﴾," and the path is the road. The second is His saying: ﴿and barring from the way of Allah those who believe in Him, and seeking to make it crooked﴾, that is: you turn away from the religion of Allah and His obedience those who believe in Shu'ayb, and you seek to make it crooked by casting doubts and describing it with what diminishes it in order to alter it. ﴿And remember when you were few and He multiplied you﴾ in number and provision, so be thankful for the blessing of Allah upon you in that. ﴿And observe how was the end of the corrupters﴾, that is: of the past nations and the earlier generations, and what befell them of punishment and retribution due to their audacity against the disobedience of Allah and their denial of His messengers."

The Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[87] ﴿And if there is a group among you who believe in that with which I have been sent, and a group who do not believe, then be patient until Allah judges between us. And He is the best of judges.﴾

"﴿And if there is a group among you who believe in that with which I have been sent, and a group who do not believe﴾ meaning: and if you differ concerning my message, becoming two factions, a believing one and a disbelieving one. ﴿Then be patient until Allah judges between us﴾ (p-2813) i.e., between the two groups, by granting victory to the righteous over the falsifiers. So this is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers.

Al-Shihab said: The address in ﴿be patient﴾ is to the believers, but it may also be to both groups, i.e., let the believers be patient over the harm of the disbelievers, and the disbelievers be patient over what grieves them from their belief. Or it is to the disbelievers, i.e., wait, so that you may see Allah's judgment between us and you. ﴿And He is the best of judges﴾" because He is exalted above injustice in His judgment; so He will grant the final outcome to the God-fearing and destruction upon the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 88:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[88] ﴿The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said, "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you from our city, or you will return to our religion (millah)." He said, "Even though we are unwilling?"﴾

﴿The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said﴾ [al-A'raf: 75], that is, "from faith," ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you from our city, or you will return"﴾, that is, to abandoning the claim of prophethood and acknowledging it, entering ﴿into our religion﴾, that is, the religion (millah) of the polytheists.

Al-Jashami said: The millah is the religious system (diyanah) that a great group agrees to act upon. Its origin lies in the repetition of a matter, from their saying: "a well-trodden path (tariq mimill and milil)," when its travel has been repeated until it became marked out. From it comes al-malal (tedium): the repetition of something upon the self until one becomes weary of it. End of quotation.

﴿He said﴾, that is, Shu'ayb: ﴿"Even though we are unwilling?"﴾, that is: "Will you compel us to that, even though we are unwilling of it?" Moreover, there is no benefit in compulsion, because if your religion is true, we would not be submitting to it through compulsion, and if it is false, we would not be characterized by it through compulsion, since in reality belief is an attribute of the heart, and your compulsion does not reach it. And how could we not be averse to it, when it entails the utmost ugliness and wrongdoing?

(p-2814)

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[89] ﴿We would be inventing a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has delivered us from it. It is not for us to return to it, unless Allah, our Lord, wills it. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In Allah we have put our trust. Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of those who decide.﴾

﴿We would be inventing a lie against Allah﴾: that is, we would be fabricating falsehood against Him by ascribing to Him a partner. ﴿If we returned﴾: to abandoning the claim to prophethood and affirming it, so that we would enter ﴿your religion﴾, which holds that He has a partner. ﴿After Allah has delivered us from it﴾: He showed us that this is like being rescued from the Fire.

﴿It is not for us﴾: that is, it is not befitting for us ﴿to return﴾: that is, from the claim to prophethood and affirming it, so that we would become ﴿in it﴾. ﴿Unless Allah, our Lord, wills it﴾: that is, the One who nurtures us by what He knows of our readiness, because ﴿our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾. That is, He knows the readiness of each one at every time. But ﴿in Allah we have put our trust﴾: that is, that He would protect us from arriving at it. ﴿Our Lord﴾: if they intended to compel us to it or to expel us from our town. ﴿Decide between us and our people in truth﴾, so that You overcome them for our sake. ﴿For You are the best of those who decide﴾: that is, the best of judges. So do not let the wrongdoers prevail over the wronged, however numerous they are, when they seek Your decision.

Notes:

First: Know that the apparent meaning of His saying, ﴿or you will certainly return to our religion﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], and His saying, ﴿after Allah has delivered us from it﴾, indicates that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was upon their religion before his mission. It is known that the prophets are protected from major sins, let alone from polytheism.

In (al-Mawaqif wa Sharhuha) [the Mawaqif of al-Iji and its commentary]: the community has agreed on the prophets' protection from disbelief both before prophethood and after it. However, the Azariqa, a sect of the Kharijites, permitted sin for them, and since every sin is disbelief in their view, it followed that they permitted disbelief. The Shi'a permitted the outward display of disbelief out of dissimulation (taqiyya) when fearing destruction, and to avoid casting oneself into ruin. The same is found in (Sharh al-Tajrid) [the commentary on al-Tajrid].

Since the community's consensus on what has been mentioned is established, the scholars have several interpretations of this verse:

Among them: the return that is the opposite of leaving is the return to abandoning the claim to prophethood and affirming it.

The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: let there be among you the leaving of our town, or the return to abandoning the claim to prophethood and affirming it, entering into our religion. This interpretation is the one al-Mahayimi restricted himself to, and we followed him in it along with the explanation of the rest of the verse.

Among them: the return mentioned is to what one has left, which is the town. The prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause as in the previous one, meaning: let there be among you the leaving of our town or the return to it, being within our religion. The verb ʿāda is followed by fī (in), as though the religion were for them like a container enclosing them.

Among them: this statement was made according to their assumption that he had been in their religion, because of his silence before the mission about denouncing them.

Among them: it was said by their leaders as deception toward the people and to give the impression that he was upon their religion. What came from Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was in the manner of mushakala (matching in form).

Among them: "la-ta'ūdunna" means "la-taṣīrunna" (you will become), since ʿāda often occurs in the sense of ṣāra (became), and then it works like kāna (was), and does not require a return to a previous state. Rather, the opposite is the case: it denotes the transition from a previous state to a new state, like ṣāra.

It is as though they said, and Allah knows best: "We will certainly expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you, from our town, or you will become disbelievers like us."

Al-Razi said: The Arabs say: "Something disliked has returned to me from so-and-so," meaning: something disliked has come to me from him for the first time. The poet said:

*If the days were kind to me for a period,*
*then sins have returned to them [i.e., have come to be theirs].*

He meant: sins have become theirs, and he did not mean that sins were theirs before the kindness. End of quote.

From this is the hadith of Mu'adh. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Have you become a fitnah-causer, O Mu'adh?" meaning: have you become.

From this is the hadith of Khuzayma: "The cutting-tool has become a mujarnthim" [a term for a hardened, branded thing], meaning: it has become.

In the hadith of Ka'b: "I wish this milk would turn into tar," meaning: would become. It was asked of him: "Why is that?" He said: "Quraysh followed the tails of camels and abandoned the congregations."

Al-Shihab said: However, it has been said that this does not fit His saying, ﴿after Allah has delivered us from it﴾. Unless it is said that there is taghlib (predominance of the plural form) in it, or it is said: deliverance does not necessarily have to come after falling into what is disliked. Do you not see His saying, ﴿So We delivered him and his family﴾ [al-A'raf: 83] and similar verses?

Among them: the verb ʿāda is used in the sense of starting something anew. This was verified by al-Raghib, al-Jarbardi, and others.

They cited the poet's saying:

*And the head has become like thaghām [white plant] on me.*

The meaning of the verse is: "you will certainly enter into our religion." And His saying ﴿if we return﴾ means: if we enter. So says (Taj al-'Arus) [the Taj al-'Arus of al-Zabidi].

Among them: keeping the form of ʿawd (return) on its literal meaning, given that it requires the return of the one returning to a state he was in before, as one says ʿāda lahu (it returned to him) after he had turned away from it. However, the statement is in the mode of taghlib. Al-Zamakhshari said: When they said, ﴿O Shu'ayb, we will certainly expel you and those who believe with you﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], they conjoined those among them who had entered faith after their disbelief with his pronoun. They said, ﴿you will certainly return﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], and so they gave precedence to the group over the individual, making them all returners, applying the statement according to the rule of taghlib.

Upon this, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) gave his answer, saying: ﴿We would be inventing a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has delivered us from it﴾. He meant the return of his people, but he included himself in their number, although he was innocent of that, applying his statement according to the rule of taghlib. End of quote.

Among them: what al-Nasir said in (al-Intisaf): he accepts the usage of ʿawd in the sense of returning to a previous matter, and he answers this with a response similar to the answer to His saying: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut; they bring them out of light into darkness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 257].

Bringing out requires a prior entering into that from which one is brought out. We know that the believer who grew up in faith never entered the darkness of disbelief at all, nor was he in it. Likewise the original disbeliever never entered the light of faith at all, nor was he in it. But since faith and disbelief are among the voluntary acts, which Allah created the servant able to perform, each of them being within his reach if he wills it, He expressed the believer's capacity for disbelief, and then his turning away from it to faith, as bringing out from darkness into light, as a grace from Allah toward him and a kindness to him. And the reverse is the case regarding the disbeliever.

A similar consideration has passed at His saying: ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased error in exchange for guidance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16]. This is metaphor in which the cause is expressed by its effect. The benefit of choosing it in these places is to affirm the capacity and volition, to establish Allah's proof over His servants. And Allah knows best. End of quote.

Second: Regarding His saying, ﴿unless Allah, our Lord, wills it﴾, the reference back to Allah, exalted is He, is correct.

Al-Wahidi said: What the people of knowledge and the Sunna hold regarding this verse is that Shu'ayb and his companions said: "We would not return to your religion after we have come to know that it is misguidance that brings entry into the Fire, unless He wills our destruction. Our affairs are returned to Allah and are not outside His grip; He makes happy whom He wills with obedience, and makes wretched whom He wills with disobedience." This is a submission from Shu'ayb and his people to the will of Allah.

The prophets and the great ones have never stopped fearing the consequence and the reversal of affairs. Do you not see the words of the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]? Our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) often said: "O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "It is not for us to return to it, unless it has already preceded in Allah's knowledge and will that we would return to it." Confirmation of this is His saying: ﴿Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, meaning that He, exalted is He, knows what will be before it comes to be, and what will be. He, exalted is He, was knowing from eternity of all things. So the happy one is he who is made happy in Allah's knowledge, and the wretched one is he who is made wretched in Allah's knowledge.

Al-Nasir said in (al-Intisaf): The placement of His saying, ﴿Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, is an acknowledgment of the limitation in knowing the outcome and of insight into hidden matters. The return to disbelief is possible within Allah's power that it should occur from the servant. If it occurs, it is by Allah's power and will, which are hidden from His creation. So vigilance remains and fear is necessary.

A parallel is the saying of Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him, unless my Lord wills something. My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. Will you not remember?﴾ [al-An'am: 80]. When he referred the matter to the will, which is hidden, he glorified Allah, exalted is He, by His sole possession of the knowledge of the unseen. And Allah knows best. End of quote.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The meaning of ﴿It is not for us﴾ and so on is: it is not valid for us to return to it in any state or at any time, unless Allah wills, that is, unless Allah wills it in a state, or at a time, for our return to it. And that is something that hardly could happen, as His saying indicates: ﴿our Lord﴾. The mention of His lordship over them indicates the impossibility that He would will their apostasy definitively. Likewise His saying, ﴿after Allah has delivered us from it﴾: His delivering them from it is one of the indications that He does not will their return to it.

It has also been said that its meaning is: unless Allah wills our abandonment (khidhlan), indicating that disbelief is by His will, exalted is He. In any case, the purpose of this is not to show that return to it is within the realm of possibility and a real risk, based on His will being such, but rather to show the impossibility of its occurrence, as though it were said: "It was not for us to return to it, unless Allah, our Lord, willed it, and that is far-fetched," by the evidence of the aforementioned factors that prevent His will for it. End of quote.

It is not hidden that the conveying of this impossibility is in terms of what actually is and what the station of prophethood requires. But if the station of fear and dread is considered, which is among the highest stations of the elect, then what we mentioned first is more subtle and more worthy of acceptance.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Tariq al-Hijratayn) [The Path of the Two Migrations]: Allah, glorified is He, has praised His nearest servants for fearing Him. Regarding His prophets, after praising them and commending them, He said: ﴿They used to hasten to good deeds and call upon Us in hope and fear﴾ [al-Anbiya': 90]. So raghab is hope, and rahab is fear and dread.

And about His angels, whom He has granted security from His punishment, He said: ﴿They fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded﴾ [al-Nahl: 50]. In the Sahih, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am the most knowledgeable of you about Allah, and the most fearful of Him." In another wording: "I am the most fearful of you toward Allah, and the most knowing of you regarding what I should guard against." And he (ﷺ) used to pray with a sound in his chest like the boiling of a cauldron, from weeping. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Only those among His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fatir: 28]. So the more knowledgeable the servant is of Allah, the more fearful of Him he is. End of quote.

Third: Al-Farra' said: The people of Oman call the judge "al-Fatih" (the one who opens) and "al-Fattah" (the great opener), because he opens the places of truth. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "I did not know the meaning of His saying, ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾, until I heard the daughter of Dhu Yazan say to her husband: 'Come, let me fath you,' meaning: let me judge between us."

Al-Shihab said: Fath, in the sense of judgment, is a dialect of Himyar or of Murad, and al-futaha, with a dammah, among them means judgment. Or it is a metaphor meaning: reveal and clarify our matter, until what is between us and them is uncovered, and the true is distinguished from the false. From this is "fath al-mushkil," meaning clarifying and resolving a difficulty, likened to opening a door and removing the locks, until one reaches what is behind it.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[90] ﴿And the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: "If you follow Shu'ayb, then indeed you will be losers."﴾

"﴿And the chiefs of those among his people who disbelieved said: If you follow Shu'ayb⦆" That is: in what he commands you and forbids you. "﴿Then indeed you will be losers⦆" That is, ignorant and cheated, since you would be exchanging his misguidance for your guidance, or because of the loss of what you gain from defrauding in measure and weight.

﴿فَأخَذَتْهُمُ الرَّجْفَةُ﴾ "That is, the severe earthquake."

Ibn Kathir said: Here God informs us that the quake (al-Rajfah) seized them, just as they had shaken Shu'ayb and his companions and threatened them with expulsion. He mentioned this in Surat Hud, saying: ﴿When Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, and the Cry seized those who did wrong.﴾ [Hud: 94]. The connection there, God knows best, is that they mocked him when they said: ﴿Does your prayer command you...﴾ [Hud: 87], so the Cry came and silenced them.

God said in ash-Shu'ara: ﴿But they denied him, and the punishment of the Day of the Shade seized them. Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 189]. This was only because they had said to him, in the course of the story: ﴿So make fragments of the sky fall upon us﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 187], and so He informed that the punishment of the Day of the Shade afflicted them. All of this came upon them together: the punishment of the Day of the Shade, which was a cloud that overshadowed them, containing sparks of fire, flame, and a tremendous blaze; then a Cry came upon them from the sky, and a violent quaking from the earth beneath them. Their souls departed, their spirits left them, and their bodies went still.

﴿فَأصْبَحُوا في دارِهِمْ﴾ "That is, their city." ﴿جاثِمِينَ﴾ "That is, fallen dead, lifeless, who gained nothing from the capital of their wealth or its surplus."

The discussion of the words of God, the Exalted:

[92] ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—it was as if they had never dwelt there. Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers.﴾

"﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb—it was as if they had never dwelt there﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining their being afflicted as a consequence of their saying: ﴿We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believe with you, from our town﴾ [al-A'raf: 88], and their punishment in return for it.

The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the subject, and its predicate is the clause ﴿it was as if they had never dwelt there﴾, meaning: they were utterly uprooted, and became as though, when the punishment struck them, they had never lived in their dwellings from which they had wished to expel the Messenger and his companions.

Then God, the Exalted, said, in response to their earlier speech: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb, they were the losers﴾, in religion and in worldly life, not those who affirmed him and followed him, as they claimed.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is another resumptive clause explaining their being afflicted with the punishment for their last statement. The repetition of the relative pronoun and its clause as they are is for the sake of emphasis and to indicate that what was mentioned in the clause of the relative is what necessitated the two punishments; that is, those who denied him, peace be upon him, were punished for their last saying, so they became the losers, not those who followed him. By this restriction he dispensed with explicitly stating his deliverance, peace and blessings be upon him, as occurred in Surah Hud in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him﴾ [Hud: 58].

And al-Zamakhshari said: In this resumption and beginning, and this repetition, there is exaggeration in refuting the statement of the chiefs to their followers, a belittling of their opinion, mockery of their advice to their people, and magnification of what befell them.

In (al-'Inayah) it is stated: It is a habit of the Arabs to use resumption without conjunction in blame and rebuke, so they say: "Your brother who plundered our wealth, your brother who exposed our secrets." End.

And the words of God, the Exalted:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[93] ﴿So he turned away from them and said, "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you, but how can I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾

﴿So he turned away from them﴾ — i.e., he turned away from interceding for them and from grieving over them. ﴿And said﴾ — i.e., in making his excuse: ﴿O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord﴾ — i.e., the commands and prohibitions. ﴿And advised you﴾ — i.e., I warned you of the punishment of Allah, and called you to repentance and to belief, which brings the benefit of both abodes and protects you from losing them both, but you disbelieved. ﴿But how can I grieve﴾ — i.e., I would grieve with severe grief ﴿over a disbelieving people﴾ — i.e., disbelievers in Allah, should they perish, let alone that I should occupy myself with interceding for them. That is to say, he does not grieve over them, because they are not deserving of grief.

Note:

Al-Jashami (al-Jashami) said: Among the rulings of the verse is that it indicates that the people of Shu'ayb were destroyed by a punishment of total annihilation when they did not accept the advice of their prophet. Thus it indicates the obligation of accepting sincere advice in religion. It also indicates that it is not permissible to grieve over the destruction of disbelievers and wrongdoers; rather, it is obligatory to praise Allah and thank Him, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So the last remnant of the people who did wrong was cut off. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [al-An'am: 45]

A subtle point:

They mentioned that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, is called the "orator of the prophets" (khatib al-anbiya') for the eloquence of his expression and the forcefulness of his admonition. The origin of this is what Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned Shu'ayb, he would say: 'That is the orator of the prophets, for the goodness of his dialogue with his people.'"

Al-muraja'ah (the dialogue/exchange) is a form of mufa'alah derived from al-ruju' (returning), and it is used metaphorically for mutual discourse. It is said: rajaʿahu al-qawl (he exchanged words with him). What the Prophet (ﷺ) meant is what is mentioned in this surah, as is known upon reflection on it. Thus in (al-Inayah).

Then He, exalted is He, pointed, in summary, to the conditions of the rest of the nations with their prophets, following the detailed explanation of the nations mentioned, and so He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion of the words of His, the Exalted, saying:

[94] ﴿And We did not send a prophet to any town without seizing its people with adversity and hardship, that they might humble themselves﴾

"﴿And We did not send a prophet to any town﴾" meaning: its people denied him. "﴿Except that We seized its people﴾" meaning: before total destruction. "﴿With adversity﴾" meaning: severity of poverty. "﴿And hardship﴾" meaning: sickness, because of their arrogance toward following their prophet and their obstinacy against him. "﴿That they might humble themselves﴾" meaning: so that they would humble themselves and submit, and cast off the cloaks of pride and self-importance, and thus believe.

**The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:**

[95] ﴿Then We replaced the bad state with good, until they multiplied, and said: "Hardship and ease have touched our forefathers too." So We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive.﴾

﴿Then We replaced the bad state with good﴾: That is, instead of the trials they had been in, such as hardship and sickness, We gave them abundance and health. ﴿Until they multiplied﴾: that is, they increased and grew in their persons and their wealth, from their saying: "the plants multiplied (ʿafā al-nabāt)," and "the fat and the wool multiplied (ʿafā al-shaḥm wa-l-wabar)," when they increased. From this is His ﷺ saying: "Let the beards grow (wa-aʿfū al-liḥā)."

﴿And said: "Hardship and ease have touched our forefathers too"﴾: That is, their blessings made them insolent and arrogant, and in ingratitude for them they said: "This is the custom of the age; it alternates among people between hardship and ease. Our forefathers likewise experienced such things and endured them in their religion, so we are like them and follow their example. This is not a trial from God to His servants, confirming the promise of the messengers." Thus they increased in disbelief after the verbal and practical warnings. The meaning is: God, exalted is He, tested them with the bad state so that they would turn back to Him, but they did not do so. Then He tested them with the good state so that they would give thanks, but they did not do so. When neither this nor that benefited them, nothing remained but that He should seize them with punishment, and He did so, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿So We seized them suddenly while they did not perceive﴾, that is: We seized them with the most severe and dreadful seizing, which is seizing them unexpectedly, without any awareness on their part and without any thought of an adversity crossing their minds. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until, when they rejoiced in what they had been given, We seized them suddenly﴾ [al-Anʿām: 44], and so on. In a hadith: "The sudden death is a relief for the believer and a grip of regret for the wicked." It was narrated by Imam Aḥmad and al-Bayhaqī from ʿĀʾisha, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

**Caution (tanbīh):**

The belief that the alternation of hardship and ease is merely the custom of the age, without any cause that brings them about or any wisdom in them, is among the beliefs of the disbelievers.

Ibn Kathīr said: The believer is one who perceives what God has tested him with of hardship and ease: he gives thanks to God for ease and is patient in hardship. Therefore it has come in a hadith: "A trial will not cease to befall the believer until he leaves it pure of his sins. The hypocrite is like the donkey, which does not know why its family tied it up nor why they let it loose," or as he said.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs: "How wonderful is the affair of the believer! All of his affairs are good, and this is so for no one but the believer: if ease touches him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; and if hardship touches him, he is patient, and that is good for him."

And His saying, exalted is He:

(p-2825)

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[96] ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth. But they denied, so We seized them for what they had been earning.﴾

﴿And if the people of the towns﴾ — i.e., the towns that were destroyed. ﴿Had believed﴾ — i.e., in God and their messengers. ﴿And been mindful﴾ — i.e., of disbelief and sins. ﴿We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ — i.e., We would have expanded good for them and made it easy for them from every direction, in place of the various kinds of punishment that befell them, some of which came from the heaven and some from the earth. In ﴿fataḥnā﴾ ("We would have opened"), there is a subsidiary metaphor (isti'ara taba'iyya), since the facilitating of blessings for them is likened to the opening of doors in the ease of reaching them. Alternatively, it is a metonymy (majaz mursal), since it entails facilitation, which is what is meant. Or what is meant by ﴿blessings of the heaven﴾ is rain, and by ﴿blessings of the earth﴾ is plants and fruits. ﴿But they denied﴾ — i.e., the messengers. ﴿So We seized them﴾ — i.e., We punished them ﴿for what they had been earning﴾ — of disbelief and sins.

Admonition:

The verse indicates the scarcity of belief among the people of the towns to whom messengers were sent, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then why was there not a town that believed so that its faith benefited it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world and let them enjoy for a time﴾ [Yunus: 98]. That is: no town as a whole believed except the people of Jonah, and they believed only after they had witnessed the punishment, as He, exalted is He, said of them: ﴿So they believed, and We let them enjoy for a time﴾ [al-Saffat: 148].

And His saying, exalted is He:

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[97] ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾

﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾ — i.e., the towns mentioned — ﴿that Our punishment will come upon them﴾ — i.e., Our torment and retribution — ﴿by night﴾ — i.e., at night, at a time of nighttime attack — ﴿while they are asleep﴾ — i.e., in a state of complete heedlessness.

(p-2826) The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[98] ﴿Or did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would not come upon them by night while they were sleeping?﴾

"﴿Or did the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment would come upon them in the forenoon while they were at play?﴾ That is: they were plunging into falsehood and amusing themselves out of extreme heedlessness."

Discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[99] ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah? None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are losers.﴾

﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ "And it is His seizing the servant from where he does not expect." ﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are losers.﴾ That is: no one feels secure that Allah, exalted is He, will seize the servant from where he does not perceive, despite how much he has seen of Allah seizing the servants from where they do not expect, except the people who have lost their intellects and squandered the fitrah of Allah upon which He created mankind, namely the near readiness derived from reflection upon the signs. Thus they became losers of their humanity, rather, lower than the beasts. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of Allah?﴾ is a repetition of the rebuke in His saying ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure?﴾ [al-A'raf: 97], for the sake of increasing the affirmation.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The sensible person must be in fear of the plan of Allah, like the warrior who fears his enemy's ambush, night raid, and surprise attack. It is reported from al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym that his daughter said: "Why do I see people sleeping while I do not see you sleeping?" He said: "O my daughter, your father fears the night raid," intending His saying ﴿that His punishment should come upon them by night while they are sleeping﴾ [al-A'raf: 97]. End of quotation.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: The believer performs acts of obedience while he is apprehensive, fearful and afraid, whereas the wicked person commits sins while he feels secure.

Note:

Feeling secure from the plan of Allah is a major sin according to the Shafi'is, and it is persisting in sins, relying on the pardon of Allah, as in Jam' al-Jawami'.

(p-2827) The Hanafis said: It is disbelief, like despair, based on His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of Allah except the disbelieving people﴾ [Yusuf: 87] ﴿None feels secure from the plan of Allah except the people who are losers.﴾

The Shafi'is cited the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "Among the major sins is feeling secure from the plan of Allah." What has been reported that it is disbelief is understood as a matter of severe emphasis, as stated in al-Inayah.

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bazzar narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "he ﷺ was asked: 'What are the major sins?' He said: 'Associating partners with Allah, despair of the mercy of Allah, and feeling secure from the plan of Allah.'" Some of them said: What is more likely is that it is a statement of a Companion (mawquf).

Ibn Hajar said: That it is the greatest of the major sins was stated by Ibn Mas'ud, as narrated from him by 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabarani.

Kamal ibn Abi Sharif said: Their conjoining of despair and feeling secure with "associating partners with Allah" in the hadith, which is understood as absolute disbelief, clearly indicates that they are other than disbelief.

He also said: What the Shafi'is mean by it being a major sin is that whoever is overcome by hope to such an extent that he enters the definition of one who feels secure from the plan, just as whoever deems the pardon of his sins far-fetched due to their magnitude enters the definition of the despairing person. As for whoever's sense of security is based on the belief that there is no plan, just as whoever's despair is based on denying the vastness of mercy for his sins, then each of these two is to be considered a disbeliever according to the Shafi'is too, and the Qur'anic text is understood accordingly. End of quotation.

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[100] ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the earth after its former people that, if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins, and seal their hearts so that they hear not?﴾

﴿Has it not become clear﴾: i.e., it becomes evident (yatabayyanu). ﴿to those who inherit the earth after its former people﴾: i.e., those who were seized (by punishment) in the past (al-ma'khudhin).

(p-2828) ﴿That if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins﴾: i.e., as We afflicted those before them, destroying the inheritors just as We destroyed those who were inherited from. ﴿And seal their hearts so that they hear not﴾: i.e., We set a seal upon them, so they accept neither admonition nor faith.

Abu al-Baqa' said: It is read as (yahdi) with the letter ya', and its subject is (an law nasha'). Here (an) is a lightened form of the heavy (an), meaning: "Has it not been made clear to them by their knowledge of Our will?" It is also read with the letter nun. And (an law nasha') is its object. It was said: the subject of (yahdi) is a pronoun referring to the name of God, Exalted. End of quote.

This is supported by the reading with nun. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to what is understood from what precedes it, i.e., "Has it not made clear what happened to the earlier nations?" The construction of (yahdi) with the preposition lam is because it carries the meaning of (yubayyinu), either by way of metaphor or by way of implicit meaning (tadmin).

Al-Shihab said: It was given the meaning of (yubayyinu), although (hada) takes an object directly and also with lam and with ila, because that usage applies to the second object, not the first, as here; so this is a different usage. It was also said: you may take the lam as additional, as in His saying ﴿radifa lakum﴾ [An-Naml: 72]. The intended meaning of (alladhina) is the people of Makkah and those around it, as transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both. End of quote.

And His Exalted saying:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:

[101] ﴿Those were the cities; We relate to you some of their news. Their messengers did come to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus does Allah seal the hearts of the disbelievers.﴾

﴿Those were the cities﴾ — i.e., the ones mentioned, namely the peoples of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Lot, and the people of Shuʿayb. ﴿We relate to you some of their news﴾ — which shows that they were called to account for their sins because they persisted in them after being warned.

(p-2829) Then He explained, may He be exalted, that He had left them without excuse by making the truth clear to them through proofs upon the tongues of the messengers, in His words: ﴿Their messengers did come to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe﴾ — at the time the messengers came with clear signs and decisive evidences — ﴿in what they had denied before﴾ — i.e., because of their denial of the truth at the very first time it came to them, for they had accustomed themselves to denial, so the signs did not benefit them, and the two states became equal for them, like His words: ﴿And what will make you realize that when they come they will not believe?﴾ [al-Anʿam: 109] and ﴿We turn their hearts and their sight away, just as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-Anʿam: 110], and so on. For this reason He said: ﴿Thus does Allah seal the hearts of the disbelievers﴾ — i.e., of those mentioned and others — so the signs and warnings hardly affect them, because He knew that they choose to remain steadfast in disbelief.

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[102] ﴿And We did not find most of them to have any covenant. And indeed, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient.﴾

"﴿And We did not find most of them to have any covenant﴾ — i.e., any fulfillment of a covenant — ﴿And indeed, We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾." That is: departing from obedience, transgressing. Therefore We seized them.

Al-Zamakhshari said: The pronoun ("them") refers to "the people" in general, meaning: We did not find for most of the people any covenant. That is, most people broke the covenant of God and His pledge concerning faith and piety. The verse is a parenthetical statement (i'tiraD).

It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the nations mentioned earlier, and that they, when they made a covenant with God in time of harm and fear, saying, "If You deliver us, we will surely believe," and then He delivered them, they broke their word.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, may He be exalted:

[103] ﴿Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wronged themselves by them. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾

﴿Then after them We sent﴾ "i.e., the messengers mentioned earlier, namely Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb, or the nations described after their destruction. ﴿Moses with Our signs﴾" These were the staff, the white hand, the years of drought, the loss of crops, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs and the blood, as will be detailed later. ﴿To Pharaoh﴾" He was the king of Egypt in the time of Moses. ﴿And his chiefs﴾" i.e., his people. ﴿But they wronged themselves by them﴾" i.e., they disbelieved in them. He applied the word "wrong" (zulm) in the sense of "disbelief" (kufr) in its construction with the preposition bi, although zulm is transitive by itself, because the two belong to the same category. Compare ﴿Indeed, associating partners with God is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13]. Alternatively, it means disbelief figuratively or by implicit meaning (tadmin), i.e., they disbelieved in them, placing disbelief in a place other than its proper place, which is faith, since they were given the signs so that they would necessitate belief in what he brought. They reversed this, disbelieving, and so they put the thing in other than its proper place. Or the bi is causal (sababiyyah), and its object is omitted, i.e., they wronged themselves because of them, by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment. Or they wronged people by barring them from belief in them. What is meant is their persistence in disbelief in them until they suffered the punishment they suffered, as His saying indicates: ﴿So see how was the end of the corrupters﴾, i.e., since they corrupted the creatures' beliefs, God corrupted their kingdom for them, gave it to their enemies, and drowned them all, before the eyes of Moses and his people.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[104] ﴿And Moses said, "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾

"﴿And Moses said, 'O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds.'﴾" That is: the One who sent me to you is the Creator and Lord of everything.

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿Worthy it is of me that I should not say of Allah except the truth. I have come to you with clear evidence from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel.﴾ (7:105)

﴿Worthy it is of me that I should not say of Allah except the truth﴾: "i.e., I am deserving of that and fit for it, given what you know of my condition." The preposition "bi" (ب, "with/by") and "ʿalā" (على, "on/upon") are interchangeable. It is said: "ramaytu bi-l-qawsi" and "ramaytu ʿalā l-qawsi" (I shot with the bow / I shot on the bow), and "jāʾa ʿalā ḥālin ḥasanatin" and "jāʾa bi-ḥālin ḥasanatin" (he came in a good state). Ubayy (may Allah be pleased with him) read it as "ḥaqīqun bi-an lā aqūla" (worthy of [bi-] not saying).

﴿I have come to you with clear evidence from your Lord﴾: "i.e., a sign from Him that bears witness, by necessity, to my truthfulness in what I have brought you."

﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾: It is narrated that Allah the Exalted commanded him to come to Pharaoh and say to him: "Our God has commanded us to travel three days into the wilderness, offer sacrifices to Him and worship Him." Allah the Exalted knew that Pharaoh would not let them go, but He willed to display His signs through the hand of Moses and to destroy his enemy. When Moses came to Pharaoh and spoke to him about sending his people with him, Pharaoh rejected the Lord's command to him and said: "Why do you distract the people from their work?" They were forced to labour for Pharaoh in making bricks, and he ordered that their labour be increased, by having them gather the straw themselves, after they had previously been given it by Pharaoh.

Then Pharaoh asked Moses for a sign, as Allah the Exalted said:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He:

[106] ﴿He said, "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful."﴾

" ﴿He said, "If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful."﴾

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[107] ﴿So he threw his staff, and behold, it was a serpent, plainly visible.﴾

﴿So he threw his staff﴾ — "which was inanimate matter." ﴿And behold, it was﴾ — i.e., without any concealment or the treatment of any means. ﴿A serpent﴾ — i.e., a large, terrifying snake, upon which life overflowed, to show the great outpouring of life at his hands. ﴿Plainly visible﴾ — i.e., manifest, not imagined.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[108] ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white to the onlookers.﴾

﴿And he drew out his hand﴾ — i.e., he took his hand out of his garment (dir', "coat" or "shirt of mail") after he had put it into it. ﴿And behold, it was white to the onlookers﴾ — i.e., white with an extraordinary, luminous whiteness that departs from the usual, so that the spectators gathered around it in amazement at its condition. This indicates that he manifests upon his hands rules (shara'i', "laws") whose spiritual lights overcome the sensible lights, and by which life is strengthened through God.

The Interpretation of His Words, the Exalted:

[109] "The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, 'Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer.'"

"The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said" — that is, the nobles who dislike another's superiority over them, in repelling these manifest signs from the minds of the creatures. "Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer" — that is, adept in it.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[110] ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?﴾

﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ — i.e., out of the land of Egypt, by his sorcery, so that he may take possession of it. ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ — i.e., what do you counsel regarding his matter? This is either part of the continued report of the words of the chiefs (al-mala'), or a new statement from the words of Pharaoh, its implied form being: "So he said: What do you advise?" And the saying of Exalted God confirms this, as follows:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 111:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[111] ﴿They said, "Put them off, [both] him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers,﴾

﴿They said, "Put them off, [both] him and his brother"﴾ — i.e., postpone their matter and dismiss them from you, until you see your opinion regarding them and consider their affair, so that you will not be attributed to clear injustice.

Abu Mansur said: The command to delay indicates that another command had preceded it from him, namely the intention to kill him (Musa). So they said, "Delay him, so that his condition may become clear to the people."

The origin of "arjih" is "arji'hu," as it has been recited thus, from (arja'a, to postpone). ﴿And send into the cities﴾ — i.e., the cities of the Sa'id (Upper Egypt) from the regions of Egypt, ﴿gatherers﴾ — i.e., those who will gather for you the magicians and assemble them.

(p-2833)

Commentary on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[112] ﴿They will bring you every skilled sorcerer.﴾

﴿They will bring you every sorcerer﴾ — it is also read "sahhar" (ﷺ-less, intensive form: "sahhār") — ﴿skilled﴾, i.e., proficient in the art of magic, so that they may oppose Moses with the like of the clear signs that he showed them.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: This verse indicates the great magnitude of Moses' miracle, and it indicates the ignorance of Pharaoh and his people, in that they did not know that turning the staff into a moving serpent is something no one can do except God Almighty, so they attributed it to sorcery. It also indicates that it is the custom of people that whoever sees a great matter wants to oppose it; therefore Pharaoh summoned the sorcerers. This shows that if the Arabs had been able to produce the like of the Qur'an, they would have opposed it.

It also indicates that the way with miracles is to oppose them by bringing the like of them; for this reason God Almighty said in the Qur'an: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾ [Yunus: 38]. For this reason Pharaoh and his people did not resort to anything other than opposition and the casting of doubts. It also indicates that they denied his affair out of concern for their kingdom and wealth; for this reason they said ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land﴾ [al-A'raf: 110]. This shows that among the strongest motives for abandoning religion is the preservation of leadership, wealth and status, as is the custom of people in this age. End of quotation.

Then Pharaoh's agents hurried, and they gathered them, as God Almighty said:
