The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[113] ﴿And the magicians came to Pharaoh; they said, "Indeed, is there a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾

" ﴿And the magicians came to Pharaoh; they said, "Indeed, is there a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[114] ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾

"﴿He said, 'Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.'﴾" And when they had secured a pledge from Pharaoh.

(p-2834)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 115:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[115] ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw or we will be the ones who throw."﴾

﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw or we will be the ones who throw."﴾ That is, "who throw first," as in the other verse. It was said: they gave Moses the choice to show boldness, and they did not mind whether he went first or last.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Their giving him the choice is a fine courtesy, which they observed with him, as people of crafts do when they meet, like debaters before they engage in disputation, and wrestlers before they grip one another for the contest.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 116:

The explanation of His saying, exalted is He:

[116] ﴿He said, "Throw down." And when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people and frightened them, and they produced a great magic.﴾

﴿He said﴾ — i.e., Musa said to them, ﴿Throw down﴾ — i.e., what you are about to throw. He permitted them to go first out of contempt for their station, indifference toward them, and confidence in the divine support he had been granted, and that a miracle would never be overcome by magic ever. ﴿And when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ — i.e., they made them imagine what was not in reality. ﴿And frightened them﴾ — i.e., they terrified and alarmed them by what they did of magic, as in the other verse: ﴿Then behold, their ropes and their staffs, by their magic, seemed to him to be moving⁠—﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66] ﴿So Musa felt within himself a fear﴾ [Ta-Ha: 67] ﴿We said, "Fear not; indeed, you are the superior"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 68]. ﴿And they produced a great magic﴾ — i.e., in the domain of magic, or in the eyes of whoever saw it, for each of them threw down his staff, and the staffs became serpents.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: The verses indicate that the people brought forth what was within their capacity of deception, and the age was an age of magic, and the predominant concern among them was occupation with it. So Musa, peace be upon him, came with something of the same kind as what they were engaged in, (p-2835) something no one could achieve, so that they would know that it was a miracle and not magic. Thus it is fitting that miracles be of the kind that is common among the people, while its like is impossible for them. Medicine was predominant in the time of Isa, so he brought the raising of the dead and the healing of the blind and the leper, and that is not within the capacity of any physician. In the time of our Prophet, peace be upon him, eloquence, sermons and poetry were predominant, so the Qur'an came and challenged them with it. And it indicates that by tricks they made the ropes and staffs move until they gave the impression that they were alive; but when the origin of what they did was discovered and known, and its like was within the power of everyone who practices their craft, it was known to be sleight of hand. For this reason miracle and sleight of hand differ: the origin of sleight of hand can be identified, its like can be produced, and its matter is concealed, unlike the miracle.

Then he said: It also indicates Pharaoh's acknowledgment of humiliation and weakness, in that he sought their help and their trade to repel a harm. End.

The discourse concerning the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[117] ﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsely fabricating.﴾

﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up﴾ — i.e., it devours — ﴿what they were falsely fabricating﴾ — i.e., what they cast down and make appear to be true, while it is false.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, exalted is He:

[118] ﴿So the truth was established, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾

﴿So the truth was established﴾ — i.e., the miraculous nature (al-i'jaz) was confirmed. ﴿And what they had been doing was nullified﴾ — i.e., the sorcery, since it was rendered void by the miracle (al-i'jaz).

The discussion of His saying, Exalted is He:

[119] ﴿So they were overcome there, and they returned humbled.﴾

﴿So they were overcome there﴾: i.e., at the place of the appointment where the people of Egypt gathered on his summons, expecting the sorcerers to prevail. ﴿And they returned﴾: i.e., they went back, ﴿humbled﴾: i.e., disgraced.

(p-2836)

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[120] ﴿And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate.﴾

"﴿And the sorcerers were thrown down prostrate.﴾"

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[121] ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,"﴾

"﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,"﴾"

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[122] ﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾

"﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾. Al-Jashami (al-Jushami) said: The verse indicates that the sorcerers recognized that the matter of the staff is not of the same kind as sorcery, so they believed immediately. It also indicates that by those signs they reasoned their way to monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood (nubuwwah), and therefore they acknowledged both of them."

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[123] ﴿Pharaoh said: "You believed in him before I gave you permission. Indeed, this is a scheme that you have plotted in the city, to drive out its people from it. But you will come to know."﴾

"﴿Pharaoh said: You believed in him before I gave you permission. Indeed, this﴾" i.e., the thing you have done, "﴿is a scheme﴾" i.e., a stratagem, "﴿that you have plotted﴾" i.e., that you and Musa have devised, "﴿in the city﴾" i.e., in Egypt, before the departure at the appointed time, "﴿to drive out its people from it. But you will come to know﴾" is a threat which he stated in summary and then detailed with his saying:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 124:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[124] ﴿Surely I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all.﴾

"﴿Surely I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides﴾, i.e., from every side, a limb different from the other, (p-2837) like the hand from one side and the foot from the other."

Al-Shihab said: "﴿On opposite sides﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning differing (mukhtalifah). It has also been said that 'min' is causal (ta'liliyyah), related to the verb, meaning because of your opposition, but this is far-fetched."

"﴿Then I will crucify you all﴾, i.e., to disgrace you, and to make an example (tankil) of your likes."

The exposition on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[125] ﴿They said: Indeed we are to our Lord returning.﴾

"﴿They said: Indeed we are to our Lord returning.﴾ That is: so we do not care about what you threaten us with, for He is the One who brings us near to those in whom we have believed, and so He will give us life with a life better than the worldly life."

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[126] ﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims.﴾

"﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us﴾" meaning: you find no fault in us except our belief in the signs of God. That is, what you find fault with and deny is in fact the greatest of our virtues, for it is the best of deeds and the highest of excellent qualities, so we will not turn away from it seeking your approval. "﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾" meaning: pour upon us abundant patience so that we may stand firm in Your religion. "﴿And cause us to die as Muslims﴾" meaning: steadfast upon Islam.

**The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:**

[127] ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and abandon you and your gods?" He said, "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and indeed we are dominant over them."﴾

﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said﴾: that is, out of fear that the creation would turn against them when they saw that the magicians had openly embraced Islam and were not deterred by the threats. ﴿Will you leave﴾: that is, will you let go ﴿Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land﴾: that is, in the land of your kingdom by turning people away from you. ﴿And abandon you and your gods﴾: "gods" is the plural of "ilah" (deity), meaning the worshipped one. The Egyptians had many gods, among them one called Osiris. They believed that his spirit resided in a bull called Apis, so they worshipped it too. They also worshipped many animals and worshipped darkness. They worshipped Baal-Zebub, the idol of Aqrun, whose function they believed was to drive away flies.

In short, they surpassed all others in misguidance. They prostrated to the sun, the moon, the stars, human figures, and animals, even to insects and the smallest creeping creatures of the earth. Thus some careful scholars have related about them.

Al-Shahrastani mentioned in *al-Milal wa al-Nihal* (*The Sects and the Creeds*) that Pharaoh was at first on the creed of the Sabians (al-Ṣābi'a), then he deviated from that and claimed lordship for himself, seeing in himself the power to command and to employ others. End of quotation.

The creed of the Sabians has already been explained in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, so reflect on it.

Some have said: the word "gods" (ālihah) is a technical term among the Hebrews, meaning the judges and rulers who judge by the command of God. If it is taken in this sense here, it is not far-fetched, and the meaning would be: "and abandon you and your judges and those in authority over you." The purpose of mentioning them together with him would be to magnify the matter, to inflame Pharaoh's heart against Moses, and to stir up his anger. Several scholars have stated that words from non-Arabic languages occur in the Qur'an, as al-Suyuti transmitted in the thirty-eighth type of his *al-Itqan* (*Perfection in the Sciences of the Qur'an*). End of quotation. However, the more evident view is the one we presented first.

﴿He said, "We will kill﴾: it was read with light and with intensive pronunciation of the letters. ﴿Their sons﴾: the male newborns. ﴿And spare﴾: that is, let live. ﴿Their women﴾: that is, for servitude. ﴿And indeed we are dominant over them﴾: that is, with superiority and power over them. So they did that to them, and the Children of Israel complained.

(p-2839)

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[128] ﴿Moses said to his people, "Seek help in God and be patient. Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants. And the good outcome is for the righteous.}﴾

"﴿Moses said to his people, 'Seek help in God and be patient.'﴾ That is, against their harm. ﴿Indeed, the earth belongs to God; He gives it as inheritance﴾ That is, He grants it ﴿to whomever He wills of His servants. And the good outcome is for the righteous.﴾" That is, victory and triumph are for the righteous over their enemy.

God, exalted is He, had promised Moses that He would drive the Egyptians out of their land, destroy them, and deliver his people from the torment of Pharaoh's household inflicted upon them.

A note:

Al-Jamshi said: The verses indicate that when Pharaoh's people were unable to prevail against Moses through the signs, they turned to inciting Pharaoh against Moses, and led him to believe that leaving him alone would bring corruption to the land; and at that point he threatened him. This is among the strongest proofs of Moses' prophethood, for the killing of the bearer of a miracle does not discredit his miracle. For this reason our teachers said: when the Arabs turned away from opposing the Qur'an, whose challenge would have nullified the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), to fighting, which does not achieve that, this showed their incapacity. Such is the condition of every misguided innovator: when proof fails him, he turns to threats and intimidation. It also indicates that when one fears oppressors, it is obligatory to take refuge in God, exalted is He, to seek His help, and to be patient. There is no refuge except in these two: namely, devoting oneself to God, exalted is He, by seeking aid in repelling harm, and His gentleness toward one in patience. It also indicates that the praiseworthy outcome is attained through taqwa (God-consciousness), which is guarding against the major sins and transgressions. End of quote.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[129] ﴿They said, "We were harmed before you came to us and after you have come to us." He said, "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and then He will observe how you will act."﴾

﴿They said﴾: that is, the people of Musa (Moses). ﴿"We were harmed before you came to us and after you have come to us"﴾: that is, they inflicted upon us humiliation and degradation both before your mission (ba'tha) and after it.

Then Musa explicitly stated to them the good news that he had previously alluded to. ﴿He said, "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy"﴾: that is, Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his soldiers. ﴿"and make you successors in the land, and then He will observe how you will act"﴾: that is, He will see what deeds you do, good and bad, and your gratitude for the blessing and your ingratitude for it, so that He may recompense you according to what is found in you.

Then Allah, exalted is He, clarified what befell Pharaoh and his people of hardship when they refused to answer Musa and to send the Children of Israel with him, by His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[130] ﴿And We had certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of crops, that they might take heed.﴾

"﴿And We had certainly seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾, that is, with barrenness and dearth, ﴿and shortage of fruits, that they might take heed﴾", that is, that they might be admonished and turn back from their disbelief to the command of Musa. This is because hardship softens the hearts and inclines one to humble supplication to Allah, exalted is He.

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates that hardship and adversity may be a means of grace (lutf) and of righteousness in religion; for this reason He said, ﴿that they might take heed﴾. End quote.

Then Allah, exalted is He, clarified that, despite those trials and calamities upon them, they only increased in rebellion and disbelief, so He said, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 131:

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[131] ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is due to us." And if an evil afflicted them, they would attribute it to omens from Moses and those with him. Unquestionably, their omen is with Allah, but most of them do not know.﴾

﴿But when good came to them﴾ — i.e., health and abundance. ﴿they said, "This is due to us"﴾ — i.e., on account of us and our deserving it, and they did not see that it was from the favor of Allah upon them, so that they would thank Him for His bounty. ﴿And if an evil afflicted them﴾ — i.e., hardship. ﴿they would attribute it to omens from Moses and those with him﴾ — i.e., they would consider it an ill omen (yatashā'amū). Its origin is (yataṭayyarū), meaning that they would say: "This is because of their ill omen." ﴿Unquestionably, their omen is with Allah﴾ — i.e., their hardship, and what came upon them of decree and destiny is with Allah, not with anyone else, i.e., from Him, exalted is He. ﴿but most of them do not know﴾ — i.e., that what afflicted them is from Allah, exalted is He, which is why they say what they say, as He related about them. Then the Exalted informed of the severity of the rebellion of Pharaoh and his people and their haughtiness, through His saying, glorified is He:

The discussion of the words of God, the Exalted:

[132] ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will never believe you."﴾

"﴿And they said, 'Whatever sign you bring us to bewitch us with, we will never believe you'﴾" — i.e., we will not affirm the message as true.

Commentary on the Words of God Most High:

[133] ﴿So We sent upon them the flood, and the locusts, and the lice, and the frogs, and the blood, as distinct signs; but they waxed arrogant, and they were a guilty people.﴾

﴿So We sent upon them the flood﴾ — that is, upon the family of Pharaoh. As for the people of Moses, God showed them kindness, so no harm from the flood or anything else touched them or their dwellings.

The flood (ṭūfān), linguistically, is a heavy rain, and it is applied to any calamity that surrounds a person and encompasses him. The flood covered the desert, destroyed its herbage, and broke its trees; thunder, lightning and the fires of thunderbolts followed one another over the whole land of Egypt. ﴿And the locusts﴾ — they consumed all the herbage and fruit of the land of Egypt that the flood had left, so that nothing remained of fruit or greenness on the trees, nor any herbage in the desert. ﴿And the lice﴾ — they spread over the land of Egypt and were upon the people and the animals. It is, with a dammah and a shaddah, like (sukkar), the small gnats, or a small thing with a red wing, or small creatures of the kind of ticks, or the wingless locust, which is the small locust.

Abu al-Baqa' said: (al-qummal) is read with shaddah and with lightening (takhfīf), with a fatḥah on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. It was said: they are two dialects. And it was said: they are the well-known louse found in clothing and the like, and the shaddah form is used for lice in food. End of quote.

Ibn Sayyidah rejected the view that what is meant is human lice, and al-Majd followed him in this in al-Qāmūs. ﴿And the frogs﴾ — they rose up from the rivers, canals and pools and covered the land of Egypt. ﴿And the blood﴾ — all the waters of Egypt became thick blood, the fish in them died, the rivers became foul, and the Egyptians could not drink any of them. ﴿As distinct signs﴾ — that is, clear, such that no intelligent person would doubt that they are signs of God Most High and His retribution, or separate, some following others. (Āyāt, "signs," is a ḥāl, a circumstantial accusative, of the objects mentioned before.) ﴿But they waxed arrogant﴾ — that is, they were arrogant toward faith, so they did not believe Moses and did not send the Children of Israel with him. ﴿And they were a guilty people﴾ — that is, disobedient and disbelieving.

Al-Jushamī said: The verse indicates the obstinacy of the people, their persistence in disbelief and their ignorance, since in every sign he brought they pledged, upon his truthfulness and the establishment of the covenant, that they would not believe in it. This is not the habit of one whose aim is the truth. It also indicates the blame of one who sees the signs and does not reflect upon them, and it indicates the obligation of contemplating the signs. End of quote.

[134] When the punishment fell upon them, they said, "O Moses, pray to your Lord for us, by what He has covenanted with you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe in you and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you."

﴿ولَمّا وقَعَ عَلَيْهِمُ الرِّجْزُ﴾ "That is, the distinct punishment descended upon them." ﴿قالُوا يا مُوسى ادْعُ لَنا رَبَّكَ بِما عَهِدَ عِنْدَكَ﴾ "That is, by His covenant with you, which is prophethood. Here (ما) is a masdariyyah (a particle that turns the following clause into a verbal noun)."

Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji) said: "Prophethood was called a covenant (ʿahd) because God pledged to honour the prophets with it, and they pledged to Him to bear its burdens. Or because it has rights that must be preserved, just as covenants are preserved. Or because it is like a covenant and a decree from God, Exalted is He." End of quote.

﴿لَئِنْ كَشَفْتَ عَنّا الرِّجْزَ لَنُؤْمِنَنَّ لَكَ ولَنُرْسِلَنَّ مَعَكَ بَنِي إسْرائِيلَ﴾ "That is, those whom you were sent to seek, so that they may worship their Lord, Exalted is He."

(p-2843)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 135:

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[135] ﴿So when We removed from them the punishment until a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾

"﴿So when We removed from them the punishment until a term which they were to reach﴾ meaning: until the time that was set for them, which was the time of their destruction by drowning in the sea. ﴿Behold, they broke their word﴾" i.e., they violated the covenant they had undertaken, and did not fulfil it. For Pharaoh, whenever a calamity from those mentioned earlier befell Egypt, would call upon Moses and ask him to intercede with God, exalted is He, to remove it, and would promise him that if it were removed he would release his people to worship Him, exalted is He. But once it was removed, he would break what he had promised and his heart would harden. And when they did not heed what they had witnessed of the earlier signs, the decisive punishment came upon them, as God, exalted is He, said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 136:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[136] ﴿So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾

"﴿So We took retribution from them and drowned them in the sea﴾, i.e., the sea (al-bahr), ﴿because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, i.e., their drowning was due to their denial of the signs of God Almighty and their turning away from them, their failure to reflect upon them, and their indifference to them. It has been narrated that Pharaoh, after he saw what he saw of the lordly plagues upon Egypt, permitted Moses and his people to leave Egypt so that they might establish the worship of God Almighty wherever they wished. The Children of Israel set out hastily by night, and they travelled with everything they had of sheep, cattle and livestock, from 'Ayn Shams to "Sukkot," and they took the route of the desert of the Red Sea. When Pharaoh heard of their departure, he regretted what he had done in releasing them from his service, so he gathered his army and his war chariots, pursued them and overtook them, for they had already reached the shore of the Red Sea. At that moment the Israelites were afraid and began to complain against Moses. He said to them: "Do not fear, for God is with us." Then God Almighty commanded Moses, and he stretched out his hand over the Red Sea, and its water split, and a wide path appeared within it. God sent a strong east wind, and the bed of the sea dried up, so the Israelites crossed through it, with the water on their right and left. Pharaoh and his soldiers followed them and entered into the middle of the sea. Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, by God's permission, and its water returned swiftly, covering Pharaoh, his soldiers and his chariots, and they all drowned. Then their corpses floated on the surface of the water and were cast up onto the shore, and the Israelites saw them with their own eyes. This is a summary of what has been narrated here.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates that He destroyed them after removing the pretext through the signs. It indicates that what befell them was a punishment and a recompense for their deeds. It indicates the ugliness of objecting to the signs of God. It indicates the obligation of reflection (al-nazar). And it indicates that breaking the covenant and turning away were their deeds, and therefore He punished them for both. End of quotation.

The Discussion on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[137] ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land which We had blessed, and the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience, and We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and building, and what they had been raising up.﴾

﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed﴾ "means: by enslavement and the killing of their sons. Describing them in this way shows the complete kindness of God Most High toward them and His great beneficence to them, in raising them from the depths of humiliation to the height of honor. ﴿the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ "means: the Holy Land, its eastern and western regions, which the Children of Israel came to possess after the Pharaohs and the Amalekites, and they disposed of its expanses as they wished. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿which We had blessed﴾ "mean: with fertility and abundance of provision. ﴿And the good word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel﴾ means: it came to pass and remained in effect for them, and it is His promise to them of victory and establishment. ﴿because of their patience﴾ "means: because of their patience under the hardships which they endured from Pharaoh and his people.

al-Zamakhshari (may God have mercy on him) said: It is sufficient to exhort one to patience, and it indicates that whoever meets trial with impatience, God leaves him to it, while whoever meets it with patience and waiting for victory, God guarantees him relief.

It is reported from al-Hasan (al-Basri): "I am amazed at the one who becomes light-headed, how he becomes light-headed, when he has heard the saying of God Most High," and he recited the verse. The meaning of "became light-headed" (خَفَّ) is that he was thrown into turmoil by anxiety and lacked patience, and he did not have the steadfastness of those of firm resolve.

﴿And We destroyed﴾ "means: We ruined and annihilated. ﴿what Pharaoh had been making﴾ "and ﴿his people﴾ means: what they had been working at and building of structures and the construction of palaces. ﴿and what they had been raising up﴾ "(with the ra' read with kasra or with damma), meaning: of gardens, or what they raised of lofty buildings toward the sky, like the tower of Haman. This is as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And We wished to bestow favor upon those who had been oppressed in the land, and to make them leaders and to make them the inheritors﴾ [al-Qasas: 5] ﴿and to establish them in the land, and to show Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts what they had been fearing from them﴾ [al-Qasas: 6]. And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind﴾ [al-Dukhan: 25] ﴿and crops and a noble station﴾ [al-Dukhan: 26] ﴿and luxury in which they had been delighting﴾ [al-Dukhan: 27] ﴿Thus, and We caused other people to inherit them﴾ [al-Dukhan: 28].

al-Zamakhshari said: This is the last of what God related of the account of Pharaoh and the Copts, and of their denial of the signs of God, their wrongdoing and their disobedience. Then He followed it with the relating of the account of the Children of Israel, and what they produced after their deliverance from the dominion of Pharaoh and his enslavement, and their witnessing of the great signs, and their crossing of the sea, of worshipping the calf, and of seeking to see God openly, and other kinds of disbelief and disobedience, so that one may know the state of man, and that he is as He described him: ﴿Indeed, man is a great wrongdoer, a great disbeliever﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], ignorant and ungrateful, except for the one whom God protects: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ [Saba': 13]. And in order to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for what he was shown of the Children of Israel in Medina, God Most High said:

(p-2846)

The discussion of the words of His Exalted saying:

[138] ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoting themselves to their idols. They said, "O Moses, make for us a god just as they have gods." He said, "Indeed you are a people who are ignorant."﴾

"﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾" — that is, the sea in which He drowned their enemies. It is the Sea of Qulzum (Bahr al-Qulzum), like Qunfudh; a town that was in the east of Egypt, near Mount Tur, and it was attributed to it because it lies on its shore. The town is known today as Suez. As for one who claims that the sea is the Nile of Egypt, he has erred, as is mentioned in (al-'Inayah).

"﴿They came upon a people devoting themselves﴾" — it is read with a ḍammah and with a kasrah on the kāf (ya'kufūna and ya'kifūna). "﴿to their idols﴾" — that is, they persist in worshipping them and remain constantly attached to them. "﴿They said, 'O Moses, make for us a god﴾" — that is, an idol upon which we may devote ourselves. "﴿just as they have gods﴾" — that is, idols to which they devote themselves. "﴿He said, 'Indeed you are a people who are ignorant﴾" — that is, of the matter of divinity (al-ulūhiyyah) and its greatness, and that it is not deserved except by Allah alone.

Al-Baghawi (may Allah have mercy on him) said: That was not a doubt on the part of the Children of Israel concerning the oneness of Allah the Exalted; rather its meaning was: "Make for us something that we may magnify, and draw near to Allah the Exalted by magnifying it." They thought that this did not harm their religion, and that was due to the severity of their ignorance. End.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[139] ﴿Indeed, these — what they are in is destroyed, and worthless is what they have been doing.﴾

﴿Indeed, these﴾ — meaning the worshippers of those images. ﴿What they are in is destroyed﴾ — i.e., doomed to perish. ﴿What they are in﴾ — i.e., of polytheism. ﴿And worthless is what they have been doing﴾ — i.e., the worship of idols, and even if their intention in that was drawing near to Allah, Exalted is He, it is pure disbelief.

Al-Razi said: All the Prophets, peace be upon them, agreed that the worship of other than Allah, Exalted is He, is disbelief, whether one believes that other to be a god of the world, or believes that worshipping it is a drawing near to Allah, Exalted is He. This is because worship (ʿibadah) is the utmost extent of glorification, so it is not befitting except for one from whom comes the utmost bounty, and that is by creating the body, life, desire, power, intellect, and creating the things from which benefit is derived.

And none is capable of these things except Allah, Exalted is He, so worship is only befitting for Him. End of quote.

And on the authority of Abu Waqid al-Laythi, may Allah be pleased with him: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for the Battle of Hunayn, he passed by a tree of the polytheists upon which they would hang their weapons, called Dhat Anwat. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Make for us a Dhat Anwat just as they have a Dhat Anwat.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Subhan Allah! This is just as the people of Musa said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138]. By Him in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those before you.'" Recorded by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir and others.

Imam Abu Bakr al-Turtushi al-Maliki said: "Look, may Allah have mercy on you, wherever you find a lote tree or a tree that people visit, venerate, and hope for healing and cure through it, and drive nails and rags into it, that is Dhat Anwat, so cut it down."

Al-Hafiz Abu Shamah al-Shafi'i al-Dimashqi said in the book al-Bida' wal-Hawadith: "The affliction has become widespread through Satan's adornment for the common people of decorating walls and pillars. They do this and maintain it, while neglecting the obligations and Sunnah practices of Allah, and they think they are drawing near to Allah by it. Then they go further, until the importance of those places becomes great in their hearts, so they venerate them, hope for cure for their sick, fulfilment of their needs, and make vows to them, whether they be springs, trees, walls, or stones." Then he described a particular tree, saying: "How similar it is to Dhat Anwat mentioned in the hadith."

Ibn Waddah narrated in his book, saying: I heard Isa ibn Yunus say: "Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered the tree under which the Prophet (ﷺ) had received the pledge to be cut down, so it was cut down, because the people had been going and praying beneath it, and he feared for them the trial (fitnah)." For this discussion there is an important continuation in Ighathat al-Lahfan by Ibn al-Qayyim, so refer to it.

[140] "He said, 'Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has preferred you over the worlds?'"

Said [﴿قالَ﴾]: "That is, Musa, reminding his people of the blessings of Allah the Exalted upon them, which necessitate that they single out Allah the Exalted for worship." [﴿أغَيْرَ اللَّهِ أبْغِيكم إلَهًا﴾]: "That is, shall I seek for you a deity to be worshipped?" One says "abghahu al-shay'" meaning "he sought it for him," like "baghahu iyyahu" (he sought it for him), which takes two objects directly and is not of the category of elision and conveyance (al-hadhf wa-al-iysal). In a hadith: "Get me some stones with which I may cleanse myself" (ibghini), with a hamza of cutting and of joining. The poet said:

"How often I hope, from one with wealth and kinship, that he will seek good for you, and he is not one who acts."

The interrogation in the verse is for denial, wonder, and rebuke: [﴿وهُوَ فَضَّلَكم عَلى العالَمِينَ﴾]: "That is, while the state is that He the Exalted has favored you with blessings He did not give to others."

The discussion of His saying, exalted is He:

[141] ﴿And (remember) when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and letting your women live. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾

﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ — i.e., from Pharaoh and his people. ﴿who were afflicting you with the worst torment﴾ — i.e., they imposed it upon you, or they put it in charge of you. It is said: "sāmahu al-amr yasūmuhu," meaning he burdened him with it, compelled him to it, and obliged him to it; or he assigned it to him. ﴿slaughtering your sons and letting your women live. In that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾ — i.e., He delivered you from it alone, without anyone's intercession.

A note:

al-Jashami said: The verse indicates that the destruction of enemies is a blessing from Allah which must be met with gratitude. It also indicates that trials concerning children and family are on the same footing as trials concerning oneself, and it follows the same rule. End of quotation.

(p-2849)

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[142] ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights, and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Moses said to his brother Aaron, "Take my place among my people, and act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾

"﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights, and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights.﴾

It is narrated that when the Children of Israel left Egypt, they camped in the wilderness of Mount Sinai (Ṭūr Sīnāʾ), and the period of their departure until they camped was a month and a half. When they camped facing the mountain, Moses ascended to it, and he heard His speech, exalted is He, and His commands and His injunctions. Then Moses descended to his people and informed them of what they had been commanded. They began to see upon the mountain a cloud, a sound of thunder, and lightning. Then God, exalted is He, commanded Moses to ascend the mountain so that He might give him the laws which He had written for his people. So Moses ascended the mountain, and it was covered with cloud, and Moses entered into the midst of the cloud and remained on the mountain for forty days, neither eating nor drinking, owing to the spiritual strength with which he was supported and the holy manifestations. In the course of that period he was given the tablets upon which their laws were written. When he returned to his people, there were dazzling rays of light upon his face, so they feared to draw near to him, and he placed a veil (burqaʿ) over his face. Thus, whenever he ascended the mountain for private communion (munājāh), he lifted it, and whenever he came to them, he put it down. And God knows best.

﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron﴾ "i.e., when he set out for private communion, ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ "i.e., be my successor among them ﴿and act rightly, and do not follow the way of the corrupters﴾ "i.e., do not follow those who pursue corruption, and do not obey those who call you to it.

Note:

Al-Jashami (al-Jishamī) said: The verse indicates that he appointed Aaron as his deputy upon his departure, since he saw that they were more obedient to him and more receptive to him. Moses's addresses to Aaron and Aaron's replies to him, such as His saying, ﴿Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 93], and Aaron's saying, ﴿Do not seize me by my beard﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 94], and ﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice over me﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 150], all of this points to Moses having a particular kind of authority (wilāyah), even though the two shared in prophethood.

The apparent meaning is that he appointed him as deputy until he returned, since that is what is understood by appointing a deputy during an absence. It also shows that it is permissible for one to forbid someone from a thing which one knows he will not do, and to command him to a thing which one knows he will do, as an admonition to him, a lesson for others, and as reinforcement and a benefit for all. End of quotation.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[143] ﴿When Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said: "My Lord, show me (Yourself) that I may look upon You." He said: "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me." So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust, and Musa fell down unconscious. And when he recovered, he said: "Glory be to You! I have turned to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers."﴾

"﴿When Musa came at Our appointed time﴾" means: he arrived at the mountain at the time We had set and determined for him. "﴿and his Lord spoke to him﴾" means: He addressed him without an intermediary angel. "﴿He said: 'My Lord, show me (Yourself) that I may look upon You.' He said: 'You will not see Me, but look at the mountain. If it remains firm in its place, then you will see Me.'﴾" means: you will not be able to bear seeing Me, because this human frame in this worldly state has no capacity for that, since it is not prepared for it. Rather, what is greater in bulk and stronger and firmer in creation, namely the mountain, cannot withstand it but crumbles. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: "﴿But look at the mountain﴾," that is, which is stronger than you. "﴿If it remains firm﴾" means: if it stays in its place when I manifest Myself to it, and does not tremble. "﴿Then you will see Me﴾" means: you will be able to endure My sight when I manifest Myself to you; otherwise there is no capacity for it. In this there is such gentle treatment of Musa, such honouring of him, and such condescension of the Holy Presence that is not hidden.

"﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾" means: He appeared to it and became clear. This is what al-Zajjaj said. "﴿He made it﴾" that is, the manifestation "﴿crumble to dust﴾" that is, pulverised, so it did not remain in its place. Thereby God drew attention to the fact that the mountain, despite its strength and solidity, does not remain firm; so the human being, with the weakness of his frame, is all the more unable to remain firm. In this there is consolation for the heart of Musa, that what prevents disclosure is compassion for him. As for the claim that what prevents it is the impossibility of seeing, there is no indication of this in the Qur'an.

"﴿And Musa fell down﴾" means: he fell. "﴿unconscious﴾" means: he was overcome and senseless from the terror of what he saw. "﴿And when he recovered, he said: 'Glory be to You! I have turned to You in repentance﴾" means: from presuming to ask You to be seen. "﴿and I am the first of the believers﴾" means: [I believe] that no one can remain firm to see You in this worldly state.

Al-Nisaf said: Musa, peace be upon him, glorified God only because it became clear to him that knowledge had already preceded that the vision would not occur in this world. God, exalted is He, is sanctified above the occurrence of what is contrary to His knowledge, and above any change in His true report and truthful word. So when it became clear that what he sought was contrary to what was known, he glorified God and sanctified His knowledge and His report from any change.

As for repentance in the case of the prophets, it does not necessarily imply that it is from a sin, because their exalted station requires them to be pure and free from everything that might lower them. There is no doubt that refraining from asking to see [God] until permission was given was more perfect. It has been transmitted: "The misdeeds of those brought near are the good deeds of the righteous."

Warning:

The theologians (mutakallimun) said: The verse indicates the permissibility of seeing Him, exalted is He, from two aspects.

The first: Musa's request, peace be upon him, to see Him indicates that it is possible, because a sane person, let alone a Prophet (ﷺ), does not seek the impossible. Nor is there any room for saying that Musa, peace be upon him, was ignorant of the impossibility, for one who is ignorant of what is not permissible for God is not fit for prophethood, since the purpose of prophethood is to guide people to correct beliefs and righteous deeds. There is no doubt about the prophethood of Musa, peace be upon him, and that he was one of the Messengers of firm resolve (ulu al-azm).

The second: God, exalted is He, made the vision conditional upon the mountain remaining firm, and that is something possible in itself, and what is conditional upon the possible is itself possible. This is because the meaning of a conditional is the report that the conditioned thing will occur when the condition occurs, and the impossible does not hold under any of the possible scenarios.

As for the claim of the Mu'tazila (a theological school that denied the vision of God) that seeing is a metaphor for necessary knowledge, the meaning of His words "﴿Show me﴾" would be: make me know You with necessary knowledge, which goes against the apparent sense. For the verb "look" (nazar) when followed by "ila" (to) is explicit in referring to visual sight, so it is not to be abandoned on the basis of possibility. Moreover, seeking necessary knowledge is not reasonable for one who addresses and converses with Him. Likewise their claim that Musa, peace be upon him, asked for it on behalf of his people, when they said: "﴿We will not believe you until we see God openly﴾" [al-Baqarah: 55], so that they might know its impossibility. This is contrary to the apparent sense and is a forced reading that removes the beauty of the composition, and the wording of the verse rejects it. The occurrence of the vision of God, exalted is He, in the Hereafter is established by the Book and the Sunnah. As for the Book, it is by His saying: "﴿Faces that day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾" [al-Qiyamah: 22-23]. As for the Sunnah, its narrations cannot be counted. But when someone is afflicted with the disease of obstinacy against a clear truth, it becomes hard to persuade him, however strong the proof and however great the argument.

Al-Nisaf (Fath al-Bayan) said: The vision of Him, exalted is He, in the Hereafter is established by numerous successive reports (mutawatir), to an extent that is not hidden from one who knows the pure Sunnah. Debate and evasion on such a matter bring no benefit. The path of truth is clear. But adherence to a school of thought in which a person was raised, and upon which he found his father and the people of his land, together with a failure to reflect on what is truly required of servants by this pure Shari'ah, leads to fanaticism. The fanatic, though his eyesight is sound, has a blind insight, and his ear is deaf to hearing the truth. He rejects the truth while thinking that he rejects nothing but falsehood, and he supposes that what he was raised upon is the truth, out of heedlessness and ignorance of the correct reasoning God has made obligatory upon him, and of receiving what the Book and the Sunnah brought with submission and acceptance. How few are the fair-minded after the emergence of these schools in both principles and branches of law, for the door of truth has become barred by them, and the path of fairness has become difficult. The matter belongs to God, glory be to Him, and guidance is from Him:

"A man refuses anything but following his desire, though the path of truth is clear to him."

End of quotation.

This is an allusion to the Mu'tazila, and at their head al-Zamakhshari. He, may God pardon him, later moved on to ridiculing the People of the Sunnah with what he recited:

"A group who named their desire a sunnah, and a group who are donkeys, by my life, hobbled."

"They likened Him to His creation and feared the disgrace of the people, so they concealed themselves behind 'bila kayf' (without how)."

"Bilkafa" is a coined term, like "basmala": it means their saying "bila kayf."

Al-Nisaf said: Were it not for the precedent set by Hassan ibn Thabit al-Ansari, companion and poet of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who defended him, and whom the Holy Spirit supported, we would have said to these self-styled "Adliyya" (Justice-theorists) and "Najiyun" (the Saved): peace. But just as Hassan defended the Messenger of God (ﷺ) against his enemies, so we defend the companions of the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) against their enemies, and we say:

"A group disbelieved in the vision of their Lord, though it is truly true, and God's promise will not fail."

"They named themselves 'Adliyya.' We say: Indeed, they 'equalized' (adalu) others with their Lord, so folly is enough for them."

"They named themselves 'the Saved.' No indeed! They, if they are not in the Fire, are on its brink."

Abu Hayyan replied to him:

"You have likened the ignorance of the community of Ahmad and the people of insight to the hobbled donkeys."

"Loss is upon you. Look fairly at the verse of al-A'raf, for it is the fair one."

"Did Musa come with an ignorance that he brought, and did your shaykhs come with what they brought without knowledge?"

"Indeed, faces will look toward Him; this is what the Book came with, yet you said: 'This is folly!'"

"The Book has spoken, while you speak according to your desire, so desire has cast you into the destroying abysses."

Al-Allama al-Jarbardi said:

"How strange, a people who are wrongdoers, who conceal themselves behind justice, though by my life they have no true knowledge."

"There has come to them from where they do not perceive it the denial of the Essence of God together with the negation of the attributes."

Al-Subki, in his Tabaqat, in the biography of al-Jarbardi, cited several poems and fragments in refutation of him. Then God, exalted is He, mentioned that He addressed Musa by choosing him, in His saying, glory be to Him:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 144:

(p-2854) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[144] ﴿He said, "O Moses, I have chosen you over the people by My messages and by My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the grateful."﴾

"﴿He said, 'O Moses, I have chosen you over the people'﴾ meaning: I have selected you over the people of your time, and preferred you over them." "﴿by My messages and by My speech﴾ meaning: and by My speaking to you." "﴿So take what I have given you﴾ meaning: what I have bestowed upon you of the nobility of prophethood and of intimate conversation." "﴿and be among the grateful﴾ meaning: for this blessing."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 145:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[145] ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything. So take it with strength, and enjoin your people to take the best of it. I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient.﴾

"﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets of everything an admonition and a detailed explanation of everything﴾" of the lawful and the unlawful. "﴿So take it with strength﴾" i.e., with determination to act upon what is in it. "﴿And enjoin your people to take the best of it﴾" i.e., what they were commanded, rather than what they were forbidden. "﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾" and it is the land that they were promised, from Palestine. They did not receive it until after forty years from their departure from Egypt and their remaining in the wilderness. When Musa, peace be upon him, died, Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun) succeeded him, and he fought the nations and the kings who were living in the land of Canaan, and conquered their lands, and they became a possession for the Children of Israel.

Note:

Al-Jishumi said: The verse indicates that His speech is created (ḥudūth kalāmihi), because His saying "﴿I have chosen you﴾" [al-A'raf: 144], i.e., I have singled you out with it, and if it were eternal, Musa and others would be equal, and singling out would not be valid. And His saying "﴿And We wrote﴾" indicates that He gave him the Torah written on the tablets at the appointed time, so that it would be preserved, and so that those present would convey it to those who were absent, so that knowledge of it would occur to them necessarily. It also indicates that the Torah contains laws and everything that is needed. And His saying "﴿with strength﴾" indicates that the servant is capable of the act before the act, and that he acts by power. End.

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[146] ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth without right. And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it. And if they see the way of right guidance, they will not adopt it as a way; but if they see the way of error, they will adopt it as a way. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾

"﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant upon the earth﴾ That is, I will prevent the understanding of the proofs and evidences that indicate My greatness, My law and My rulings from the hearts of the arrogant, who are arrogant toward people and reject My obedience. Just as they were arrogant, Allah humbles them through ignorance, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We turn their hearts and their sights, just as they did not believe in it the first time﴾ [al-An'am: 110], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ [al-Saff: 5].

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿without right﴾, it is either attached to the verb, meaning they are arrogant with what is not right, which is their false religion, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its subject, meaning they are arrogant while not being in the right." ﴿And if they see every sign﴾ That is, every proof among the signs and proofs sent down to them. ﴿they will not believe in it﴾ out of arrogance toward it. ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance﴾ meaning the path of truth, guidance and uprightness, clear and manifest, ﴿they will not adopt it as a way﴾ because it is contrary to their desires. ﴿And if they see the way of error﴾ that is, the going astray from the truth and destruction, ﴿they will adopt it as a way﴾ meaning a path toward which they incline. ﴿That﴾ refers to the turning away from the signs, or to their adopting error as a way. ﴿That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾ meaning: they were negligent, not reflecting upon them and not taking admonition from them, or they were heedless of what would befall them from the punishment of the messengers.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 147:

Then He explained the threat against the deniers, saying:

(p-2856) The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[147] ﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, their deeds have become worthless. Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾

"﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾ — i.e., the Resurrection, which is the second return. It was called al-akhirah (the Hereafter) because it comes after the worldly life (al-dunya)."

"﴿Their deeds have become worthless﴾ — i.e., they became void, so they produced no benefit. What is meant is the recompense for their deeds, because 'habita' (to become worthless) is applicable only to what is awaited, not to what has already passed. This is like His saying, ﴿that they may be shown their deeds﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 6]."

"﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ — i.e., they are recompensed only for the fruit of their deeds, namely disbelief and sins."

Note of caution:

Some scholars held that His saying, ﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 146], etc., is an address to the people of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that it is connected to what preceded of their stories, namely ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 100], etc.

The mention of the story of Musa and Fir'awn is for taking admonition.

Al-Ka'bi and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: this statement completes what Allah promised Musa, peace be upon him, concerning the destruction of his enemies. The meaning of "turning them away" is their destruction, so that they will not be able to prevent Musa from conveying it, nor be able to prevent the believers from believing in it. This is similar to His saying: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message. And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. So Allah, exalted is He, willed to prevent the enemies of Musa, peace be upon him, from harming him, and to prevent him from carrying out what was required of him in conveying prophethood and messengership. End of quotation. And Allah knows best.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[148] ﴿And the people of Moses took, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body having a lowing sound. Did they not see that it does not speak to them or guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.﴾

"﴿And the people of Moses took, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body having a lowing sound.﴾" Exalted is He informs about the misguidance of those among the Children of Israel who went astray in worshipping the calf that the Samiri had made for them from the ornaments of the Copts, which they had borrowed from them. He fashioned for them a calf, a body without a soul in it, and he contrived to introduce wind into it until it produced a lowing sound, that is, a sound like the sound of a cow. He attributed the sound to it only because it was the place where the wind entered its hollow. This happened on their part after Moses had gone to the appointed time of his Lord, exalted is He, and God, exalted is He, informed him of this while he was on the mountain, where He says, relating from Himself, the Noble: ﴿Indeed We have tried your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85].

Subtleties:

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say: why was it said "and the people of Moses took a calf," when the one who took it was the Samiri? I say: in this there are two aspects.

The first: that the act is attributed to them, because a man among them handled it and it was found among them, as one says: "The Banu Tamim said such-and-such and did such-and-such," while the speaker and the doer are one person. And because they were desirous of taking it and content with it, so it is as if they had all agreed upon it.

The second: that what is meant is: they took it as a god and worshipped it. If you say: why did He say "from their ornaments," when the ornaments were not theirs, but were borrowed items in their hands? I say: attribution may be made on the slightest connection, and their being in their hands as loans is sufficient connection. Moreover, they came to own them after the destroyed ones, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit them﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 59]. End.

Al-Nasafi said: In this is evidence that whoever swears not to enter the house of so-and-so, and enters a house he has borrowed, breaks his oath; and that seizing the wealth of the disbelievers causes their ownership of it to cease. End.

Al-Huliyy, with a damma on the ha' and a shadda, is the plural of (hal'y), with a fatha then a sukun, like (thady) and (thudiyy), and it is a name for that with which one beautifies oneself, of gold and silver.

(p-2858) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them or guide them to a way?﴾ is a rebuke for the extremity of their misguidance and their neglect of reflection. The meaning: Did they not see, when they took it as a god, that it has no power to speak, nor to guide to a path, as ordinary humans do? It is an inanimate thing that neither benefits nor harms, so how could it be a god?

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They took it﴾ is a repetition to emphasise the blame, meaning: they took it as a god and worshipped it. ﴿And they were wrongdoers﴾ meaning: placing things in other than their proper places. The clause is either resumptive (isti'nafiyya), or an concluding parenthetical addition (i'tiradh tadhyiliyy) informing that this was their custom and habit before that, so this should not be denied of them. Or it is circumstantial (haliyya), meaning: they took it in this settled state that was theirs.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates the validity of argument in religion, and that He, exalted is He, guided them, in refuting the taking of the calf as a god, by pointing out that it does not speak or guide. He mentioned speech because the lowing is a sound in which trickery is exhausted, whereas trickery is not exhausted in speech. It also indicates that removing doubts in religion is obligatory, as God, exalted is He, removed them. It indicates that the people were ignorant, not knowing the reality of things, which is why they worshipped the calf. It indicates that those ornaments were owned by the Children of Israel, which is why He said "from their ornaments." If it is established that they had borrowed them, this indicates the cessation of their ownership and the transfer of ownership to the Children of Israel, as the property of the people of war is taken. And it indicates that the taking was their act.

"﴿And when they regretted, and saw that they had gone astray, they said: 'If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.'﴾"

[149] ﴿And when they were overcome with remorse and saw that they had indeed gone astray, they said, "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾

"﴿And when they were overcome with remorse﴾ i.e., they regretted worshipping the calf. "﴿And saw﴾ i.e., they knew and became certain. "﴿That they had indeed gone astray﴾ i.e., away from the truth and guidance. "﴿They said, 'If our Lord does not have mercy on us﴾ i.e., by accepting our repentance. "﴿And forgive us﴾ i.e., what we committed of worshipping the calf. "﴿We will surely be among the losers﴾ i.e., through punishment; that is, among those who lost their deeds and their lives."

(p-2859) A NOTE OF REFINEMENT:

It is said of one who regrets what he has done, al-Hasir ('alā mā faraṭa minhu), and "qad sufiṭa fī yadihi" and "ūsqiṭa" (both with a dammah), as al-Zajjaj said.

Al-Farra' said: It is said "suqiṭa fī yadihi" and "ūsqiṭa," from regret, and "suqiṭa" is more common and more eloquent.

Abu 'Amr rejected "ūsqiṭa" with the alif, while al-Akhfash permitted it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is the way of one whose regret and grief are intense to bite his hand out of distress, so that his hand becomes "maswūṭan fīhā" (fallen into it), because his mouth has fallen into it.

Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is that regret fell into their hands, i.e., into their hearts and souls, just as it is said, "a disliked thing occurred in his hand," although it is impossible for it to be in the hand, as a comparison of what occurs in the heart and soul to what occurs in the hand and is seen with the eye. End of quotation.

Al-Farisi said: That is, they struck their palms upon their palms out of regret. If this is correct, then it is from "al-suqūṭ" (falling).

In (al-'Ubab): This is a construction that was not heard of before the Qur'an, nor did the Arabs know it. Its original meaning is the descent of a thing from high to low and its falling to the ground. Then it was extended, so that an error in speech is called "saqata," because they likened it to what one has no need for and so it falls away. The hand is mentioned because regret arises in the heart, and its effect appears in the hand, as in His saying, ﴿So he began to turn over his palms over what he had spent﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. Also because the hand is the greatest limb, so what it did not directly do is sometimes attributed to it, as in His saying, ﴿That is for what your hands have sent forth﴾ [al-Hajj: 10]. End of quotation.

Based on this, "suqiṭa" would be from "al-siqāt," which is frequent error, as the poet said:

"How could they hope for my faltering after whiteness has overtaken my head and baldness has spread?"

It has also been said: It is customary for one who regrets to lower his head and rest it on his hand, leaning on it, and at times (p-2860) he places it beneath his chin, with half of his face in a position such that if his hand were removed he would fall upon his face. So the hand becomes "maswūṭan fīhā," because the falling is firmly settled in it. His saying "﴿was overcome with remorse in their hands﴾" would then mean "fell upon their hands," as in His saying, ﴿And I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71], i.e., upon them. Some counted "suqiṭa" among the verbs that do not inflect, like "ni'ma" and "bi'sa." It has been read as "saqata" in the active voice, meaning the regret or the biting or the losing, and all of this is an image. It has been read as "ūsqiṭa" in the fourth form, passive, and this is a dialect transmitted by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj, as we have mentioned.

Then Allah (exalted be He) explains what happened to Musa, peace be upon him, after his return from the appointed time (al-miqat), since He had informed him of the trial of his people. So He, glorified be He, said:

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted be He:

[150] ﴿When Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me. Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward him. (Harun) said: "Son of my mother, the people deemed me weak and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies rejoice over me, and do not place me with the wrongdoing people."﴾

"﴿When Musa returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾": that is, extremely angry at his people because of their worship of the calf, and sorrowful over what he had missed of conversing with his Lord. "﴿He said: Evil is what you have done in my absence after me﴾": that is, evil is what you did after me, or what you did in my place, when you became my successors (khulafa'i) after me. The address may be either to the worshippers of the calf, namely al-Samiri and his followers, or to the leaders of the Children of Israel, namely Harun, peace be upon him, and the believers with him. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. On the first interpretation, the meaning is: evil is what you did in my absence, since you did not prevent the worship of other than Allah, exalted be He.

So said al-Razi.

"﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾": that is, His promised appointment of forty (nights), which He had promised me, and you did not wait for its completion. They had been slow to see him come down from the mountain, so they conspired to make an idol to worship and to rally around. They did so, and began to sing, dance, eat, drink and play around it, saying: "This is the god who brought us out of Egypt," (we seek refuge in Allah).

Abu Muslim said: its meaning is "you outpaced the command of Allah, and worshipped what He had not commanded you."

"﴿And he threw down the Tablets﴾": that is, he cast them down from intense anger and extreme distress before them, so they broke. They were tablets of stone on which the laws and divine commandments were written. He, peace be upon him, threw them only because of the overwhelming astonishment that overcame him on seeing them devoted to the calf. When he came down from the mountain and approached their encampment, and saw the calf and their dancing around it, his anger flared up, so he threw them out of zeal for Allah and protectiveness for His religion. He was, in himself, hot-tempered and of intense anger, while Harun was gentler in manner, and for this reason he was beloved to his people.

Note:

al-Suyuti said in (al-Iklil): Ibn Taymiyya used His saying, exalted be He, ﴿And he threw down the Tablets﴾ as evidence that whoever throws a book to the ground in his hand while angry is not blamed. End of quotation. And it is evident.

"﴿And he seized his brother by the head﴾": that is, by his hair, "﴿dragging him toward him﴾", supposing that he had fallen short in forbidding them, as He said in the other verse: ﴿He said: O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray? That you did not follow me? Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92–93] ﴿He said: O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94].

Here He said: ﴿"Son of my mother"﴾ is read with a fatḥa and with a kasra. Its origin is yā ibna ummī ("O son of my mother"), lightened by dropping the vocative particle and the yā, and he mentioned the mother in order to soften him toward him. His saying ﴿The people deemed me weak and nearly killed me﴾ is a clarification to remove the suspicion of shortcoming on his part. The meaning is: I exerted my full effort in restraining them, until they overpowered and weakened me, and they came close to killing me. "﴿So do not let the enemies rejoice over me﴾": that is, by harming me. Shamatah (rejoicing at another's misfortune) is the joy of enemies at what befalls a person. "﴿And do not place me with the wrongdoing people﴾": that is, by punishing me, counting me among them, or do not consider me one of them, given my innocence and absence of shortcoming.

al-Jushami said: this verse shows that enjoining good may lapse when there is fear for one's self, and in a situation where it is known that it will not benefit; for this reason Harun said ﴿They deemed me weak﴾. It also shows that anger and grief over the innovator (mubtadi') is praiseworthy in religion. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 151:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[151] ﴿He said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

"﴿He said﴾: that is, Musa, peace be upon him, humbly beseeching his Lord, seeking to draw down His mercy and seeking refuge in His forgiveness from His wrath. The requirement of the situation for this is clear: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾

Al-Zamakhshari said: When his brother apologized to him and mentioned to him the gloating of the enemies, he said, ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my brother﴾ in order to satisfy his brother and to show to the people who gloat that he is pleased with him, so that their gloating would not be complete. He sought forgiveness for himself for what had transpired from him toward his brother, and for his brother for what he may have fallen short in regarding the good conduct of the succession, and he asked that they not be separated from His mercy, and that it continue to encompass them both in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 152:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[152] ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [for worship] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the worldly life. And thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾

"﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [for worship] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the worldly life. And thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾" That is, whoever invents an innovation (bid'ah), for the humiliation of innovation and opposition to the Message is upon his shoulders. As al-Hasan al-Basri said: "The humiliation of innovation is upon their shoulders, even if mules trot with them and thoroughbred horses prance with them."

And thus Ayyub narrated from Abu Qilabah al-Jarmi that he recited this verse, ﴿And thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, and said: "By Allah, it applies to every fabricator until the Day of Resurrection." And Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said: "Every possessor of an innovation is humiliated." Then, exalted is He, alerted His servants and guided them to the fact that He accepts repentance from any sin whatsoever, even disbelief, by His saying:

(p-2863)

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[153] ﴿And those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed — indeed, your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

"﴿And those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them﴾" — to Allah. "﴿And believed﴾" — i.e., they made their faith sincere. "﴿Indeed, your Lord, after them, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾" — i.e., One who effaces their sins and bestows upon them the Garden.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 154:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[154] ﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.﴾

"﴿And when it subsided﴾, i.e., it calmed down. "﴿from Moses, the anger, he took up the tablets﴾, i.e., those that he had thrown down out of the intensity of anger, so they broke. "﴿And in their inscription﴾, i.e., in what was copied from them, meaning written. Nuskhah is an form (fu'lah) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like khutbah. "﴿was guidance and mercy﴾ through the divine laws and commandments, which guide to what contains good and righteousness. "﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾, i.e., who stand in awe."

Two subtle points:

The first: Abu al-Su'ud said: In this noble construction, namely His saying, exalted is He, "﴿And when the anger subsided from Moses﴾," there is eloquence and emphasis, by treating the anger, which impels him to what proceeded from him of deed and speech, as if it were a commander who orders that, and who incites him to domineering and severity, and by expressing its calming with "subsiding" – what a thing, which is not hidden. End.

Its origin is from al-Zamakhshari, where he said: This is a metaphor, as if the anger was inciting him to what he did, saying to him: "Say to your people such and such, throw down the tablets, and drag your brother's head towards you," but he left off speaking accordingly and ceased the incitement. Every person of sound nature and correct taste has not found this expression pleasing nor eloquent except for this reason; and because it is of the branches of eloquence. Otherwise, what of the reading of Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, "﴿And when the anger calmed down from Moses﴾," where the soul does not find in it any of that agitation and a portion of that awe? End.

By "metaphor" he means that it is a metaphor in the implicit form, where he likened anger to a commanding and forbidding person, and attributed to it silence by imagination.

Some grammarians of Arabic counted the verse among the inverted (maqlub) constructions, i.e., of the pattern of reversing a literal statement into a figurative one, and the original was supposedly: "and when Moses fell silent from the anger," as in "the nail tore the garment."

In al-Intisaf it is said: The verified view is that it is not of this type, and that this inversion is more noble and more eloquent, because of the eloquent meaning it contains, namely that the anger had taken firm hold of Moses, to the extent that it was as if it directed his commands. A beautiful nuance like this is not found in "the nail tore the garment." End.

It has been read as "sakana", "sakkata" and "askata", i.e., Allah silenced him, or his brother silenced him by his apology to him.

The second: The lam in "﴿for those who﴾" is connected to an omitted element, as a descriptive of "mercy", i.e., existing for them. Or it is the lam of purpose, i.e., guidance and mercy for their sake. The lam in "﴿their Lord﴾" serves to strengthen the action of the verb that comes after it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you can interpret dreams﴾ [Yusuf: 43]. Or it is also the lam of cause, and the object is omitted, i.e., they fear sins for the sake of their Lord, not for show and reputation – as Abu al-Su'ud stated.

**The explanation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[155] ﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. When the earthquake seized them, he said, "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? This is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of forgivers."﴾

﴿And Moses chose from his people seventy men for Our appointed time. When the earthquake seized them, he said, "My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too. Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?"﴾

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated that when Moses, peace be upon him, returned to his people and saw what they were engaged in, namely the worship of the calf, and said to his brother and to al-Samiri what he said, and burned the calf and scattered it into the sea, he chose seventy men from the Children of Israel, the best of them, the best of them. He said: "Go to God, repent to Him for what you have done, and ask Him to accept the repentance of those you have left behind you of your people. Fast and purify yourselves, and purify your garments." He set out with them toward Mount Sinai for an appointed time that his Lord had set for him, and he would not come to it except with His permission and knowledge. The seventy said to him, as is reported to me, when they had done what he had commanded them and went out with him to meet their Lord: "Moses, ask on our behalf that we may hear the speech of our Lord." He said: "I will do so." When Moses drew near the mountain, a column of cloud descended upon it until it covered the entire mountain, and Moses drew near and entered into it, and said to the people: "Come near." Whenever God spoke to Moses, a bright light appeared on Moses' forehead, which no one among the sons of Adam could look upon, so he placed a veil between himself and them. The people drew near until, when they entered the cloud, they fell prostrate, and they heard Him speaking to Moses, commanding him and forbidding him: "Do this, do not do that." When He had finished what He wished to say to him, and the cloud lifted from Moses, he came to them. They said to Moses: ﴿"We will not believe you until we see God plainly"; so the thunderbolt seized you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:55]. This was the thunderbolt by which violent shaking occurs, and they all died. Moses stood pleading with his Lord, calling upon Him, beseeching Him, and saying: ﴿"My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too"﴾, [and saying that] they had acted foolishly; "Will You destroy those behind me of the Children of Israel?"

In the narration of al-Suddi: Moses stood weeping and saying, "O Lord! What shall I say to the Children of Israel when I meet them, after You have destroyed their best? ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You could have destroyed them before, and me too.﴾"

Ibn Ishaq said: "You chose from among them seventy men, the best, the best. I am returning to them, and no man from among them is with me. What then will they believe me or trust me concerning this after this?" According to this interpretation, the meaning is: "If You had willed, You could have destroyed them before our departure, and the Children of Israel would have witnessed that and would not have accused me."

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "If You had willed, You could have caused them to die before You tested them with what made the earthquake obligatory for them." End of quotation.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (*Ighathat al-Lahfan*), after quoting the words of those we have mentioned: "All of these have circled around the intended meaning. What appears to me, and God knows best His intent and the intent of His Prophet, is that this is an appeal by Moses, peace be upon him, to his Lord, and a means of seeking nearness to Him through His pardon of them before, when their people worshipped the calf and they did not object to them. Moses is saying: 'They have already committed what calls for their destruction, yet Your pardon and forgiveness embraced them and You did not destroy them. So let them be embraced today as they were embraced before.' This is like a servant whose master seized him for a crime, and he says: 'If You had willed, You could have seized me before this for something greater than this crime, but Your pardon embraced me first, so let it embrace me today.'"

Then the Prophet of God said: ﴿"Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?"﴾ Ibn al-Anbari and others said: This is an interrogative in the sense of denial, meaning: "You are not doing that." The foolish ones here are the worshippers of the calf.

Al-Farra' said: Moses thought they had been destroyed because their people had taken the calf, so he said: ﴿"Would You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?"﴾ Their destruction was only due to their saying ﴿"Show us God plainly"﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:153]. End of quotation.

The view that this is an interrogative of appeal was preceded by al-Mubarrad.

**Note:**
