*Al-Lubab* said: Most of the narrations say that they died because of that earthquake, and then they were revived.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: That earthquake was not death. Rather, when the people saw that appearance, the trembling seized them, they were agitated and shook, until their joints nearly separated. When Moses saw that, he had compassion for them and feared death for them, and the loss of them was hard upon him, for they had been his supporters in goodness, listening to him and obeying him. At that moment Moses called upon Him, wept, and pleaded with his Lord. God then removed that earthquake from them, and they were reassured and heard the speech of God. And God knows best.

﴿This is only Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will﴾: that is, the trial into which the foolish fell is nothing but Your testing, Your examination of Your servants. You tested them and examined them, so the whole matter belongs to You and is in Your hand. None can remove it but You, just as none tested or examined with it but You. So we seek refuge in You from You, and we flee to You from You. That is, the matter is only Your matter and the judgment belongs only to You; whatever You will, it happens. You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will.

Al-Wahidi said: This verse is among the clear proofs against the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination), against whom no excuse can stand. ﴿"You are our Protector"﴾, that is, the one who manages our affairs and sustains them, ﴿"so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of forgivers."﴾

**On the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:**

[156] ﴿And prescribe for us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter; indeed, we have turned back to You. He said, "My punishment - I afflict with it whom I will; but My mercy encompasses all things. So I will decree it for those who fear Me and give zakah and those who believe in Our verses."﴾

"﴿And prescribe for us in this world a good﴾: that is, establish for us in it a good quality, such as well-being, a good life, and success in obedience." "﴿And in the Hereafter﴾: that is, also a good, which is the good reward and Paradise." "﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾: that is, we have repented to You. It is said: *hada ilayhi yahudu* (haada ilayhi yahuudu), when one returns and repents, so he is *ha'id* (a penitent)." Some of them said:

*"O rider of sin, turn back, turn back, and prostrate, as if you were a hoopoe (hudhud)."*

Another said:

*"Indeed, I am a man who has turned back from what I have committed."*

Abu al-Baqa' said: The well-known reading is with a *damma* on the *ha'*, from *hada yahudu* when he repented. It has also been read with a *kasra*, from *hada yahidu*, when he moved or was moved, meaning: "We have moved our souls toward You." On both readings, the phrase admits both the active and passive forms: "we inclined," or "others inclined us"; or "we moved ourselves," or "others moved us." This is because the form is the same and the meaning is sound, even though the implied construction differs.

"﴿He said﴾: this is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*), occurring as an answer to a question that the discourse leads to, as if it were said: 'What did the Exalted say in response to the supplication of Musa?' So it is said: He said, "﴿My punishment - I afflict with it whom I will﴾": that is, His chastisement of the disobedient. "﴿But My mercy encompasses all things﴾: mercy is applied to compassion, forgiveness, kindness, and Paradise (p-2868), as He, Exalted, said: ﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾ [al-Insan: 31]. Perhaps it is this that is intended here, as indicated by its contrast with the punishment mentioned before, just as He paired the verse we mentioned with His saying: ﴿And for the wrongdoers He has prepared a painful punishment﴾ [al-Insan: 31]. And God knows best."

"﴿So I will decree it﴾: that is, this mercy." "﴿For those who fear Me﴾: that is, [those who guard against] disbelief, polytheism, and grave immoralities." "﴿And give zakah﴾: that is, they give the zakah of their wealth." "﴿And those who believe in Our verses﴾: that is, in Our Book and Our Messenger." "﴿Believe﴾: that is, they affirm (as true)."

**Note (tanbih):**

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates the goodness of asking for the blessings of this world, just as asking for the blessings of the Hereafter is good. It also indicates that it is obligatory for the one who supplicates to accompany his supplication with repentance and sincerity; for this reason they said, ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾. It also indicates that the Exalted bestows blessings upon both the righteous and the wicked, but singles out the believer for reward; that is why [the verse] makes a distinction. Whoever reflects upon this question and answer will recognize the great place of this clarification, for he (peace be upon him) asked for the blessings of this world and of religion immediately after the earthquake (*rajfah*). So the answer was that punishment in particular strikes whoever deserves it, whereas blessings, insofar as they belong to the matters of this world, encompass everything to which enjoyment applies; and whatever belongs to the matters of the Hereafter is written for those who possess its described qualities.

It also indicates that mercy is not attained merely by faith, which is assent (*tasdiq*), until acts of obedience are joined to it; this refutes the view of the Murji'a (a sect that deferred judgment on the place of deeds in faith).

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[157] ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written in what they have of the Torah and the Gospel. He enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the foul things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honor him, support him, and follow the light that was sent down with him, they are the successful.﴾

"﴿Those who﴾" is a substitute (badal al-kull, substitution of the whole) for the first relative clause, or it is in the accusative as an expression of praise, or in the nominative with an implied subject, meaning "I mean those who" or "they are those who."

"﴿Follow the Messenger﴾" means the one sent to the creatures to perfect them.

"﴿The Prophet﴾" means the one informed with the most perfect beliefs, deeds, morals, states, and stations, by way of revelation.

"﴿The unlettered﴾" means the one who did not acquire knowledge from any human being.

"﴿Whom they find written﴾" means by his name (Muhammad and Ahmad) and his attributes.

"﴿With them﴾" is added for the sake of further affirmation, and to show that his matter, upon him be prayers and peace, is present with them and never absent from them at all.

"﴿In the Torah and the Gospel﴾." "﴿He enjoins on them what is right﴾" means faith in God, His oneness, the laws, and noble morals, because the soundness of all of that is known either by reason or by revelation.

"﴿And forbids them what is wrong﴾" means disbelief, polytheism, sins, and bad morals, because reason and revelation reject them.

"﴿And makes lawful for them the good things﴾" means those that had been made unlawful for them because of their disobediences.

"﴿And makes unlawful for them the foul things﴾" means those they used to consume, such as swine, carrion, and blood. This concerns the category of food.

"﴿And relieves them of their burden﴾" means the matter that weighs heavily on them of arduous obligations.

"﴿And the shackles that were upon them﴾": the plural of ghull (shackle), with a damma on the ghayn, which is what is placed on the neck or hand of iron. It is used figuratively for the constricting conditions and the severe covenants, meaning that he lightens for them what they were charged with of these. This concerns the category of acts of worship.

"﴿So those who believe in him﴾" means in the unlettered Prophet, who is Muhammad (ﷺ). "﴿And honor him﴾" means they exalt him and show him reverence. "﴿And support him﴾" means against his enemies in religion, so they repel them from him. "﴿And follow the light that was sent down with him﴾" is the Qur'an, so they make lawful its lawful and unlawful its unlawful.

It may be objected: the Qur'an was sent down with Gabriel, so what is the meaning of "sent down with him"? The answer is that what is meant is that it was sent down with his prophethood, because his being made a prophet was accompanied by the Qur'an and joined with it. It is also permissible to attach it to "they followed," meaning: they followed the Qur'an that was sent down together with following the Prophet and acting by his sunnah, and by what he commanded and forbade. Thus it is a command to act by the Book and the Sunnah. Or it is a circumstantial clause, meaning: they followed the Qur'an as he followed it, accompanying him in following it. In describing the Qur'an as "light," there is an indication that it is manifest in itself by its inimitability, and that it makes other things manifest, namely the rulings, in keeping with the connection with following.

"﴿Those are the successful﴾" means those who attain mercy and are saved from punishment.

(p-2870)

Remarks:

The first: It appears from the context of the verse that His words, exalted is He, "﴿He said: My punishment…﴾" [al-A'raf: 156] etc., are an answer to Moses, peace be upon him. That is because he had asked forgiveness for all his people, and that good things of this world and the Hereafter be written for them. So he was answered, first, that this does not come about for all his people, pious or wicked, because of what had preceded in His, glorified is He, decree that He punishes whomever He wills among the wicked, out of wisdom and justice from Him. For this reason al-Hasan and Zayd ibn Ali read here "for whoever has done evil" (li-man asa'a), a past-tense verb from "evil-doing" (al-isa'ah). Implied in this is that what befell his people of the earthquake was from His punishment, exalted is He, which He willed to strike them with because of their deeds. Second, that the writing of the two good things is deserved only by the God-fearing, those who give charity, and those who believe in the signs, who follow the unlettered Prophet. Whoever remains steadfast in these conditions, that is written for him. One should not say, on this basis, "How could they follow him when they did not reach his time?" Because we say: following is more general than following in actuality, and that is by believing in him in general, as the two Books indicated to those whose death preceded the time of his mission; and following in fact is for those who lived to the time of his mission. In this there is good news to Moses about the Prophet (ﷺ), an introduction to his status and an informing of his status, that the writing of mercy is conditional on following him.

Accordingly, His words, exalted is He, "﴿Those who follow﴾" are a substitute for the first relative clause, a substitution of the whole, or in the accusative as praise, or in the nominative with an implied subject, meaning: "I mean those who," or "they are those who."

Some have said: the answer of Moses ends at His words, exalted is He, "﴿And those who believe in Our signs﴾" [al-A'raf: 156], and what follows is a new statement. It is as if He, exalted is He, informed Moses that He is one who has punishment, with which He strikes whom He wills, as He struck the people of the earthquake; and that He is one of wide mercy, which is written for the God-fearing, those who give charity, and those who believe in the signs. That is: "Command your people to be among the group that is shown mercy by walking in this described manner." Then, He, exalted is He, began a fresh announcement about those who follow the unlettered Prophet, that they are indeed the successful. Accordingly, His words, exalted is He, "﴿Those who follow﴾" are a subject whose predicate is "﴿those are the successful﴾," and the story is a sequel following the affair of the Children of Israel, that when they follow the unlettered Prophet, they will be the successful.

(p-2871)

Some have allowed that His words, exalted is He, "﴿He said: My punishment…﴾" [al-A'raf: 156] are an extemporaneous address to the Prophet (ﷺ), intended to inform the People of the Book contemporary with him, (ﷺ), that if they follow him, believe in him, and confirm him, His wide mercy will be due to them, and otherwise they cannot be safe from being struck by His vengeance, as happened to their predecessors. In all of that there is a great deal of honoring the status of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of his God-fearing followers, which is not hidden.

The second: Mercy (rahmah) is used for tenderness, forgiveness, and kindness; this is what is mentioned in the lexicon. In my view, in the Noble Qur'an it may be used for Paradise, as He, exalted is He, said: "﴿He admits whom He wills into His mercy﴾" [al-Insan: 31], based on the contrast with His words "﴿and the wrongdoers, for them He has prepared a painful punishment﴾" [al-Insan: 31]. So perhaps the mercy in His words, exalted is He, here, "﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾" [al-A'raf: 156], means Paradise, based on its being contrasted with punishment before it. And God knows best.

Abu Mansur said: There is no one, Muslim or disbeliever, except that upon him are traces of His mercy in this world. By it they make their living, bond with one another, and show affection, and in it they turn about. But it is for believers specifically in the Hereafter; the disbeliever has no share in it. That is His words: "﴿So I will write it for those who fear﴾" [al-A'raf: 156], that is, the disobedience of God and opposition to Him. "﴿And who give the zakat﴾" [al-A'raf: 156], like His words, exalted is He: "﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of God which He brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision? Say: they are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely, on the Day of Resurrection﴾" [al-A'raf: 32]. He made the good things of this world and its bounties shared between the Muslim and the disbeliever, but purely for those who believed on the Day of Resurrection, the disbeliever having no share in them. Accordingly, His mercy reaches everyone in this world, but it is for those who believed and guarded themselves against polytheism specifically in the Hereafter. His words, and God knows best, "﴿And write for us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter﴾" [al-A'raf: 156] may mean that they asked for mercy, so He said: "I will write it for those who fear the disobediences of God and His opposition." End of quotation.

(p-2872)

The third: He singled out zakat for mention, although it enters into piety before it, because of its loftiness and nobility, for it is the sign of guidance; and because it was harder for them, so He mentioned it lest they neglect it.

The fourth: That he (ﷺ) neither wrote nor read is a established and well-known matter. Did this proceed from him in the writing of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah, as the apparent sense of the well-known hadith indicates, or did he not write, and it was only ascribed to him figuratively, or did it proceed from him as a miracle? See the detailed discussion in Fath al-Bari (the Lord of Creation's Victory, a commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari, by Ibn Hajar).

The word "unlettered" (ummi) is a relative adjective referring to the nation of the Arabs, because most of them were like that, as in the hadith: "Indeed we are an unlettered nation; we neither write nor calculate." As for its being ascribed to Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Cities, i.e., Mecca), it is because its people were like that; or to "his mother," as if he was in the state in which his mother bore him. It has been said: it is ascribed to "the mother" (al-umm), with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "intention," because he is the intended one; and the damma on the hamza is a change of the relative form. This is supported by the recitation of Ya'qub (a variant reading, qira'ah) "al-ummiyy" with a fatha on the hamza, though it may also be a change of the relative form. God, exalted is He, described him with it only to draw attention to the fact that his perfect knowledge together with his condition is one of his miracles. So it is praise for him and an elevation of his rank, because it is a miracle for him, as al-Busayri said:

"Your knowledge of the unlettered is enough as a miracle."

Just as the attribute of pride is praiseworthy for God and blameworthy for anyone else, so says al-Inayah (a commentary on al-Hidayah by al-Babarti).

The fifth: In His words, exalted is He, "﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾" there is an indication to the glad tidings of the prophets, peace be upon them, concerning his prophethood (ﷺ).

Al-Mawardi said in A'lam al-Nubuwwah (Signs of Prophethood), in the fifteenth chapter, on the glad tidings of the prophets concerning his prophethood, upon him be prayers and peace:

(p-2873)

God, exalted is He, has a support for His commands and an independence from His prohibitions. It is as if the prophets of God, exalted is He, were helped to establish prophethood by what they put forward of its glad tidings, and what they manifest of its signs and rites, so that the earlier one is a bearer of good news and a warner, and the later one a confirmer and helper. Thus obedience of creatures endures through them, and the continuity of the truth is ordered through them.

The glad tidings of the earlier prophets concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) have indeed preceded, being a proof against their nations and a miracle indicating his truthfulness to others, through what God, exalted is He, made him aware of of His unseen, so that it would be a support for the Messenger and an incitement to acceptance. Among them is one who named him by his name, among them one who mentioned him by his attribute, among them one who ascribed him to his people, among them one who attributed him to his land, among them one who singled him out by his deeds, and among them one who distinguished him by his manifestation and spread. God, exalted is He, has realized all of these in him, until he became clear after possibility and certain after doubt. Then al-Mawardi went on to list the glad tidings from the texts of their books.

In Izhar al-Haqq (The Manifestation of the Truth, by Rahmatullah al-Kayranawi) there came the following: "The announcements made concerning Muhammad (ﷺ) are still numerous, despite the distortions that have occurred in these books. Whoever first knows the method of the earlier prophet's announcement of the later prophet, as you have come to know in the second matter, meaning in his words, then looks a second time with an eye of fairness at these announcements, and compares them with the announcements that the Evangelists transmitted concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, will be certain that the Muhammadan announcements are of the utmost strength."

There came in Minyat al-Adhkiya' fi Qisas al-Anbiya' (The Wish of the Intelligent in the Stories of the Prophets) the following: "Our Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, was given good news of by the earlier prophets, and they bore witness to the truthfulness of his prophethood, and described him with a description that removed every possibility, for they explicitly stated his name, his land, his kind, his appearance, his stages, and his marks. However, the People of the Book deleted his name, meaning from their latest copies; but that did not benefit them, because the attributes on which historians of every kind and creed agreed remain, and they are more evident in indicating the one named than the name is, since two may share a name, but it is impossible for two to share all attributes.

But those who have been at it for not a long time have begun to distort some of the attributes, so that their truthfulness regarding the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, would be remote. So you find that every later copy differs from what preceded it in some places, a difference not hidden from the intelligent person, nor what it was intended (p-2874) by it. It has only served them to strengthen the doubt upon them, since copies have spread through printing, and comparison between them has become easy. Here we present a fragment of the glad tidings they hold:"

Among them: in chapter 16 of the Book of Genesis, concerning Hagar, it reads thus:

11. The angel of the LORD said to her, "Behold, you are with child, and you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, because the LORD has given heed to your affliction."

12. "He shall be a wild man; his hand shall be against every man and every man's hand against him, and he shall dwell over against all his brothers."

This is a glad tidings (bisharah) of Muhammad (ﷺ), not of his forefather Ishmael, because Ishmael (ʿalayhi al-salam) did not have his hand above the hand of all, nor was the hand of all extended toward him in particular. Rather, the Torah states that Ishmael and his mother Hagar were driven out of their homeland under compulsion. Ishmael did not inherit together with Isaac, and kingship and prophethood were among the children of Isaac. The children of Ishmael were in the thirsty deserts, and it was not heard that nations submitted to them, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sent. Then kings submitted to him, nations humbled themselves before him, and his hand and the hands of the children of Ishmael rose above every hand, and the hand of everyone became subject to them. Thus the mention of Ishmael was intended to refer to his descendant.

Just as in many places of the Torah, Jacob is mentioned while the intended reference is to the children of Jacob. Among these is His saying in the Fifth Book: "O Israel! Will you not fear the LORD your God, and walk in His ways, and serve Him?" This is an address to the children of Israel by the name of their father. Likewise His saying to the people of Moses: "Hear, O Israel, then keep and do, that the LORD your God may bless you and you may multiply and prosper." Its parallels are many.

Thus it becomes clear that the name of the father may be mentioned while the son is intended, by way of metaphor (majaz), through the indication of the context (qarinat al-hal); otherwise, the Almighty's report would be false.

Among them: in chapter 33 of the Book of Deuteronomy it reads thus:
1. "And this is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death."
(p-2875) 2. "He said: The LORD came from Sinai, and rose from Seir upon them; He shone forth from Mount Paran, and He came with ten thousands of holy ones from the south, from His mountain slopes, and at His right hand was a fiery law for them."

There is no ambiguity that the coming of Allah, exalted and high, from Sinai is an expression for His sending down the Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai. So say the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab), and the matter is thus. Therefore his shining forth from Seir must be an expression for His sending down the Gospel to Jesus. Jesus lived in the land of Galilee, at Seir, in a village called Nazareth, and the name "Christians" (al-Nasara) is derived from it.

His rising up from the mountains of Paran is an expression for His sending down the Qur'an to Muhammad on Mount Paran. Paran is Mecca, and the People of the Book do not dispute this with us. In chapter 21 of the Book of Genesis, concerning the situation of Ishmael (ʿalayhi al-salam), it reads thus:
20. "And God was with the lad, and he grew up; he lived in the wilderness and became an expert with the bow."
21. "He lived in the wilderness of Paran, and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt."

There is no doubt that Ishmael's dwelling was in Mecca, that he died there, and that he was buried there. This glad tidings is explicit concerning our Prophet (ﷺ), manifest and not hidden except from one who does not know the moon. Which prophet appeared in Mecca after Moses other than Muhammad, whose religion spread to the east and west of the earth, as the manifest rising described in the glad tidings requires?

Among them: in chapter 18 of the Book of Deuteronomy it reads thus:
17. "And the LORD said to me, 'They have rightly said all that they have spoken.'"
18. "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and will put my words in his mouth, and he shall speak to them all that I command him."
19. "And whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him."

This glad tidings concerning our Prophet (ﷺ) is certain, because he is of the offspring of Ishmael, and the offspring of Ishmael are called brothers of the children of Abraham, as evidenced by what is mentioned in the Torah concerning Ishmael, that he would dwell over against his brothers. The custom of the revealed books has been to call cousins, even those of distant kinship, "brothers," just as the Qur'an calls Hud and Salih "brothers" of ʿAd and Thamud, though they are far removed as cousins.

And as it is said in the Book of Numbers in chapter 20:
14. "And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom: 'Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the hardship that has befallen us.'" (though they are cousins at a far remove).

This testimony is not concerning any of the prophets of the children of Israel. Otherwise it would have said, "I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among them or from themselves," as the Most High said, reporting the supplication of Abraham (ʿalayhi al-salam) for the offspring of Ishmael: ﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129]. And as He said in addressing the children of Ishmael: ﴿There has certainly come to you a messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128].

As for what the Jews claim, that the intended one is Joshua, the successor of Moses, it is false for several reasons:
1. The one promised is from among the brothers of the children of Israel, not from the children of Israel themselves, whereas Joshua was from the children of Israel themselves.
2. Joshua was not like Moses (ʿalayhi al-salam), as stated at the end of the Book of Deuteronomy (chapter 34).
10. "And there has not arisen since then a prophet in Israel like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face." And because Moses (ʿalayhi al-salam) was the bearer of a Book and a new law comprising commands and prohibitions, whereas Joshua was not so; rather he was commanded to follow the law of Moses.
3. Joshua (ʿalayhi al-salam) was present there, and he was referred to by an explicit expression before this, in the first chapter of this book.
38. "Joshua the son of Nun, who stands before you, he shall enter there; encourage him, for he shall cause Israel to inherit it."

Then what need is there for symbol and allusion after this explicit statement? And what justification is there for introducing "sawfa" (will), which indicates the future, upon an act that has already occurred?

(p-2877) As for what the Christians claim, that the intended one is Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam), this too is false for several reasons:
1. He is from the children of Israel, whereas the one promised here is from other than them.
2. Moses gave glad tidings of a prophet like himself, while they claim that Jesus is God and deny that he was a prophet sent. Otherwise the sender and the sent would be united, which is inconceivable. Moreover, the resemblance of Moses to our Prophet, upon both of them be blessings and peace, is stronger than his resemblance to Jesus, since they share several matters:
 1. Both had parents and wives, unlike Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam).
 2. Both were commanded to wage jihad, unlike Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam). In this glad tidings, He has indicated by His saying:
 19. "And it shall be that whoever will not listen to my words that he shall speak in my name, I myself will require it of him,"
 that this prophet is commanded to wage jihad against whoever disbelieves in what came from Allah, and to take vengeance upon him with his keen sword. The Christians claim that the vengeance here means the otherworldly punishment of those who deny him, and this is an error, because that is not specific to this prophet; rather, everyone who denies what any prophet brought will be avenged upon in the Hereafter, so there is no meaning in singling out this prophet for mention in that case.
 3. Both their laws comprise the prescribed penalties (hudud), retaliation (qisas), discretionary punishment (taʿzir), and the obligation of the ritual bath (ghusl) upon the one in major impurity, the menstruating woman, and the woman in postnatal bleeding, and the obligation of purity at the time of worship. None of these exists in the law of Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam), according to what the Christians say. Similar examples are many. In this glad tidings there is also an indication that this prophet is unlettered and cannot read, where He said ("he shall listen to my words that he shall speak in my name"). By this you know the secret of describing him with that in the words of the Most High: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered﴾, the verse with which we are concerned.

Among them: in chapter 14 of the Gospel of John it reads thus: "If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will pray the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you."

This is a glad tidings from the Messiah (ʿalayhi al-salam) that Allah, exalted, will send to people (p-2878) one who will stand in his place, act as deputy in conveying his message and governing his creation, and whose law will remain perpetual forever. And is this anyone other than Muhammad (ﷺ)? "The Father" here means the Lord and the God, because that is the terminology of the two Books (the Torah and the Gospel) (Ahl al-Kitabayn).

By calling himself "the Spirit of truth," Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam) indicated that truth, before his mission, would be like a corpse without movement or revival, and that when he is sent, it will be as a spirit to it, so truth will then rise, standing upon the earth.

There is no doubt that he (upon him be blessings and peace) is the one through whom Allah revived the truth after Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam), after it had been effaced and no soul remained in it. Then he said: "But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." There is no doubt that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the one who knew all things of realities, clarified what was hidden of subtleties, and reminded the community of Jesus of what they had forgotten of his sayings, which contained that he was a servant of the servants of Allah, Exalted, whom He drew near through the message and chose, and that he called to nothing but the worship of Allah, His unity, His transcendence and His glorification. His saying "in my name" means "with prophethood."

Then he explained to them the reason for informing them of it before it came, saying: "And now I have told you before it comes to pass, so that when it does come to pass, you may believe."

In chapter 15 of the aforementioned Gospel: "But when the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."

And in chapter 16 of it: "But I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment: concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no longer; concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged. I have many more things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you. All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you."

Whoever considers these expressions carefully (p-2879), and notes what they contain of meaning and allusion, will be certain that the Paraclete is Muhammad (ﷺ). For he is the one who appeared after Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam), who bore witness to Jesus' prophethood and messengership, who glorified him and cleared him of what the Christians fabricated against him concerning the claim of divinity, and of what the Jews fabricated against him concerning being a sorcerer and a liar, and against his mother concerning her chastity being impugned, while she was pure of garment and innocent of accusation. He is the one who reproached the world, especially the Jews, for their sins, especially the sin of disbelief in Jesus (ʿalayhi al-salam) and the slander against his pure and virgin mother. He is the trustworthy and truthful one who knew all the realities, and he is the one who revealed of the secrets what minds could not bear before his coming. He is the one who "does not speak from desire; it is only a revelation revealed, taught to him by one mighty in power."

The scholar Ibn Qutaybah interpreted "the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father" as meaning that it issues forth with the revealed speech of Allah, and he cited in evidence the words of the Most High: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. What is meant here is the Noble Qur'an, because it is what bears witness to the Messiah's prophethood and purity from what was fabricated against him, and that he is the Spirit of Allah, His Word, His chosen one and His messenger, just as the disciples who were with him bore witness and were guided by his guidance. No testimony of any book other than the Qur'an has been established for this, so it is determined that it is the one intended.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 157 (part 3 of 3):

In the words of Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿It is better for you that I depart, for if I do not depart, the Paraclete will not come to you﴾, is an indication that our Prophet (ﷺ) is the most excellent.

The word "Faraqlit" (Paraclete) is of Greek origin. It has been said that its origin is "Barakali Tos," meaning the comforter, the helper, the trustee, or the intercessor. It has also been said that it is "Biraklutos," which would be close in meaning to Muhammad and Ahmad. It is known that the Messiah (peace be upon him) spoke the Hebrew tongue, the language of his people, and did not speak Greek, for he was a Hebrew, the son of a Hebrew woman, raised among his Hebrew people. Therefore the transmission of his sayings in these Gospels is a transmission by meaning. So the preference of those Christians who favored the view that the original of "Faraqlit" is the first form is a preference without a preponderant reason, and the difference between the two wordings is very slight, and the Greek letters are similar.

Whatever its origin, the inference is sound, because the word, in all its meanings, applies clearly to the Prophet (ﷺ), a clarity that is hidden only from the contentious.

This good tidings was the cause of the conversion to Islam of the virtuous ʿAbd Allah al-Turjuman, as he explained in his book (Tuhfat al-Adib fi al-Radd ʿala Ahl al-Salib, "The Gift of the Man of Letters in Refuting the People of the Cross").

Moreover, the Christians later discarded the Gospels that explicitly mention the name Muhammad, because they were a bone stuck in the throats of their desires, such as the Gospel of (Barnabas), in which there is an explicit statement, "until Muhammad, the Messenger of God, comes," as transmitted by (Izhar al-Haqq).

If their condition in their translations, regarding the title of their God and the title of his vicegerent, is what is known, then how can the correct preservation of the word "Muhammad or Ahmad" be expected from them? Yet the sword of truth is sharper, and the arrows of the right target pierce deeper, so there are among the explicit descriptions and the sound indications what leaves no pause for the perplexed.

Furthermore, their books contain many good tidings, which a number of scholars have addressed, exceeding twenty in number.

Al-Mawardi said: "Perhaps what has not reached us of them is more." We have limited ourselves to what we have presented, seeking brevity and ease of reference to the rest, such as (A'lam al-Nubuwwa by al-Mawardi) and (Izhar al-Haqq) and others.

The author of (Izhar al-Haqq), Shaykh Rahmat Allah, may God have mercy on him, said: Among the scholars of the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam in the first century, those who testified to the existence of Muhammadan good tidings in the books of the two Covenants include ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, the two sons of Saʿya, Benjamin, Mukhayriq, Kaʿb al-Ahbar, and other scholars of the Jews; and like Bahira, Nestor the Abyssinian, Dughatir, who was the Roman bishop who embraced Islam at the hand of Dihya al-Kalbi at the time of the Message, whom they killed; and al-Jarud, al-Najashi, the Sus, and the monks who came with Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and others of the scholars of the Christians.

Heraclius, Emperor of the Romans, Muqawqis, ruler of Egypt, Ibn Suriya, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, and others, have acknowledged the validity of his prophethood and the universality of his message, but envy led them to wretchedness and they did not embrace Islam.

When the Christians of Najran came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and he disputed with them concerning the matter of Isa (peace be upon him) and they disputed with him, he invited them to mutual cursing (mubahala) by the command of the Exalted, but they turned back on their heels, fearing the ill consequences of its outcome. They were like the people of Pharaoh, who had believed in them: ﴿And their souls were convinced of them, out of injustice and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14].

Sixth: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿He commands them with what is right﴾ may be a new sentence, and may be an explanation of ﴿written﴾, meaning, of what is written.

Seventh: "the good things" is more general than the good things in food, such as fats, and likewise the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham.

And among the good things in terms of the ruling of the Shari'a is like trade, and whatever earnings are free from unlawful gain; and likewise "the bad things" are what is considered repulsive, such as blood, carrion, the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God, or what is bad in ruling, such as usury, bribery, and other unlawful earnings.

It has been said: the intention of what is good or bad in ruling is unlikely, because its meaning then would be what the Shari'a has ruled as lawful, or ruled as forbidden, so the statement returns to saying that He makes lawful what He rules as lawful and forbids what He rules as forbidden, and there is no benefit in it. They replied that it does have a benefit, and what a benefit! Because its meaning is that lawfulness and unlawfulness are by the ruling of the Shari'a, not by reason and opinion.

Eighth: In the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and He relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ is an indication that he (ﷺ) came with ease and tolerance, as the hadith has been related through various chains from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "I was sent with the upright, tolerant monotheism." And he (ﷺ) said to his two governors, Mu'adh and Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, when he sent them to Yemen: "Give good tidings and do not repel, make things easy and do not make them difficult, cooperate and do not differ."

We have previously mentioned that "the burden and the shackles" is a metaphor for the arduous matters that were in their laws. Among them is the prohibition of cooking a kid in its mother's milk. Among them is the system of festivals which they celebrate to God during the year, namely the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Harvest, and the Feast of Booths, and likewise the feast of every Sabbath, in which no least work is done.

Likewise the Sabbath of the farmer: every seventh year is a Sabbath for the land, in which it is not sown, and the vine is not pruned, but the lands are left fallow, and the produce of the vines is food for the poor of their people and the beasts of the field. Among them: whoever strikes his father or his mother, or insults them, or rebels against them and disobeys them, is put to death as a prescribed penalty. Likewise whoever works on the Sabbath day is put to death; whoever has a jinn or a familiar spirit is stoned to death; whoever marries a young woman and claims he did not find her to be a virgin, then his lie is proven, both of them are put to death; if a woman grasps the private part of a man, her hand is cut off; if an ox gores a man or a woman and the gored one dies, the ox is stoned and its flesh is not eaten; and whoever lies with a menstruating woman, both are cut off from their people; and whoever divorces his wife, and she then marries another, and he divorces her or she is widowed, it is not lawful for her first husband to take her back; and other burdens, some of which were mentioned at the end of Surat al-Baqara, so refer to it.

Ninth: al-Jushami said: The verse indicates that his law (ﷺ) is the easiest of laws, and that he removed from his community every burden that was in the earlier nations, and that is a great blessing upon this community.

It also indicates the obligation of honouring the Messenger, and supporting him through jihad, and aiding him by supporting his religion, and every matter that leads to weakening what is connected with that, because all of that falls under support. This is not restricted to his time; all of that is binding until the end of the obligation. Perhaps jihad through explanation, presenting proof, writing books on it, and resolving the doubts of opponents, in many circumstances exceeds jihad by the sword, and for this reason we have said: "the ranks of scholars in this are the greatest ranks." End.

Tenth: The allamah al-Biqa'i said: When the verses were interlinked and the account of Musa (peace be upon him) grew long, with the description of his great virtues and his mighty merits, and that may have caused some souls to think that he was the highest of the messengers in rank and the greatest in station, the Exalted ordered these verses in this manner, in this way, which shows the highest of them in ranks and the most pure of them in merits, He who granted His mercy to whoever believes in Him among His creation in strength or in deed.

He, glory be to Him, placed this within the account of the Children of Israel, for the sake of giving it attention and hastening it, along with what will be mentioned, which makes clear its excellence and clarifies its perfection, through his story with his people, at the beginning of his mission, its middle, and its end, in Surat al-Anfal and all of Bara'a.

Then al-Biqa'i said: When what the Exalted arranged during these stories of the jewels of the attributes of this noble Prophet was complete, He urged belief in him, obligatorily, in a manner from which it is known that he is the Messenger of God to every responsible person, whether of an earlier or later time, and He commanded him, glory be to Him, to state explicitly what had been alluded to, and to declare what covenant He had taken from the messengers concerning him, to confirm the universality of his message and the comprehensiveness of his call. So the Exalted said:

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on Surah 7, verse 158:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[158] ﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all, of He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet, who believes in God and His words, and follow him that you may be guided."﴾

"﴿Say, O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you all﴾," meaning: entirely. "﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death﴾" are descriptive epithets of the Name of Majesty (Allah), meaning: the One who sent me is the Creator of everything, its Lord and its Sovereign, in whose hand is the dominion, the giving of life, and the causing of death. The verse is explicit in the generality of his mission to both the red and the black, and to both the Arab and the non-Arab.

In a hadith: "I have been given five things that no prophet before me was given, and I say this not out of boasting: I have been sent to all people, the red and the black; I have been supported with awe for a distance of a month's journey; spoils of war have been made lawful for me, which were not lawful for anyone before me; the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification; and I have been given intercession, and I have deferred it for my community, so it is for those who do not associate anything with God."

Imam Ahmad narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas (p-2884) as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet). He also narrated it from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed I have been given five things tonight that no one before me was given. As for me, I have been sent to all people, entirely, whereas whoever came before me was sent only to his own people. I have been supported against the enemy with awe, so that if between me and them there were a distance of a month's journey, they would be filled with terror of it. Spoils of war have been made lawful for me, and I eat them, whereas those before me used to regard eating them as a grave matter; they would burn them. The earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification, so wherever prayer overtakes me, I perform ablution with dust (tayammum) and pray, whereas those before me used to regard this as a grave matter; they only prayed in their houses of worship and churches. And the fifth, what a fifth it is! It was said to me: "Ask," for every prophet has asked. So I deferred my request until the Day of Resurrection, and it is for you, and for whoever testifies that there is no deity except God.'"

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said: "Their chains of narration are good and strong."

Imam Ahmad narrated a report with a similar meaning from Ibn 'Umar and Abu Musa, and it is established in the two Sahihs (the two authentic collections of Bukhari and Muslim) from Jabir.

Muslim recorded from Abu Musa, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'By the One in whose hand is my soul! No one from this community hears of me, whether Jew or Christian, and then does not believe in me, except that he will enter the Fire.'"

﴿So believe in God and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet﴾, meaning: the one who has been given tidings of what guides all creatures, despite being unlettered. Describing him with this serves to confirm his affair and to establish that he is the one described in the two Scriptures. "﴿Who believes in God and His words﴾", meaning: what was revealed to him and to the messengers before him, of their books and their revelation. "﴿And follow him that you may be guided﴾."

(p-2885)

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 159:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[159] ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it they act justly.﴾

"﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth﴾ That is: steadfast and firm in certainty, guiding people by the word of truth, directing them to uprightness, and showing them the right way." ﴿And by it they act justly﴾: and by the truth they judge justly among them, and they do not deviate. The verse was brought to repel what might be suggested by restricting the bestowal of mercy, piety and faith to the followers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), namely that the predecessors of the people of Moses (peace be upon him) were deprived of every good, and to make clear that not all of them were as their conditions have been described. It was said that they are those who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), but this is rejected by the fact that their mention has already passed in what preceded. Related by Abu al-Su'ud.

This verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among the People of the Book is a upright community who recite the verses of Allah in the hours of the night while they prostrate﴾ [Al 'Imran: 113], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbly submissive to Allah. They do not exchange the verses of Allah for a small price. Those will have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is swift in account.﴾ [Al 'Imran: 199]

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[160] ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations. And We revealed to Moses, when his people asked him for water: "Strike the rock with your staff." And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quails: "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

"﴿And We divided them﴾" means the people of Moses. "﴿Into twelve tribes﴾" means We made them into divisions (qit'an), that is, groups (firaq), and distinguished some of them from others. The asbat (tribes, sing. sibt) are the descendants of a son's offspring (awlad al-walad). They were twelve tribes, descended from twelve sons of Ya'qub (Jacob), upon him be peace [p. 2886]. "﴿Nations﴾" means great and numerous communities of a dense count. "﴿And We revealed to Moses when his people asked him for water﴾" means in the wilderness (al-tih). "﴿That strike with your staff the rock﴾," so he struck it. "﴿And there gushed forth﴾" means there burst forth. "﴿From it twelve springs﴾" according to the number of the tribes. "﴿Every people knew﴾" means every tribe among them. "﴿Its drinking place﴾." "﴿And We shaded them with clouds﴾" in the wilderness from the heat of the sun. "﴿And We sent down upon them manna and quails. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. They did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves﴾" in that they made deserved for themselves the lasting punishment.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying:

[161] ﴿And when it was said to them: "Dwell in this town, and eat from it wherever you wish, and say: 'Ḥiṭṭah' (remove the burden), and enter the gate prostrating. We will forgive you your sins and will increase the good-doers."﴾

"﴿And when it was said to them: Dwell in this town﴾ meaning Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). The speaker was Musa (Moses), peace be upon him, who called them to enter Bayt al-Maqdis, or Yusha' (Joshua), for he called them after the death of Musa to campaign against Bayt al-Maqdis." "﴿And eat from it wherever you wish, and say: Ḥiṭṭah﴾ meaning, say: 'Remove from us our sins.' It was said: they were commanded with a word which, when they said it, their burdens would be removed from them." "﴿And enter the gate﴾ meaning the gate of the town." "﴿Prostrating﴾ meaning bowing down or humbled. They were commanded to enter it with humility, and that was a condition for the acceptance of their deed." "﴿We will forgive you your sins; We will increase the good-doers.﴾"

The commentary on His words, exalted is He:

[162] ﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon them a plague (rijz) from the sky because they used to do wrong.﴾

"﴿So those who did wrong among them substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon them a plague (rijz)﴾ (p. 2887) i.e., a punishment, "﴿from the sky because they used to do wrong.﴾" The explanation of all of this has already been given in Surat al-Baqarah, sufficiently so that it need not be repeated.

The discussion of His words, exalted is He:

[163] ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and did not come to them on the day they did not observe the Sabbath. Thus We tested them for what they used to defy.﴾

" ﴿And ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and did not come to them on the day they did not observe the Sabbath. Thus We tested them for what they used to defy.﴾ This context elaborates on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And you have already known those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 65]

So His words ﴿And ask them﴾ are coordinated with ﴿Remember﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 110], which is implied by His words ﴿And when it was said﴾ [al-A'raf: 161]. That is, "And ask the Jews contemporary with you," as a question of rebuke and confirmation, concerning their ancient disbelief and their transgression of the bounds of God, and as an informing that this is among their knowledge which is not known except through a Book or revelation. So when someone who has not read their Book informs them of it, it is known that it comes from revelation.

Ibn Kathir said: That is, "Ask these Jews in your presence about the story of their forefathers who opposed the command of God, so that His retribution overtook them for their deed, their transgression, and their scheming in opposition," and warn these people against concealing your description which they find in their books, lest there befall them what befell their brethren and predecessors.

This town is Ayla, between Madyan and al-Tur. It was said that it is Matna, between Madyan and Aynuna.

The meaning of its being ﴿by the sea﴾ is that it was near it, sitting on its shore.

(p-2888) His words, exalted is He: ﴿when they transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾ mean they exceeded God's limit regarding it, which was their hunting on the Sabbath day, while they had been forbidden from it. Indeed, the covenants and solemn pledges had been taken from them that they would preserve the Sabbaths from any work.

Al-hitan means fish, and the Arabs most often use al-hut in the sense of a single fish.

﴿Shurra'an﴾ is the plural of shari', from (sharaʿa) meaning "approached." It is said: "So-and-so approached us (sharaʿa ʿalayna)" when he drew near to us and came close to us; and "I approached so-and-so in his house, and I saw him doing such-and-such." It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿their fish﴾, meaning: they come to them on their Sabbath day visibly upon the surface of the water, near the shore. And on the day they do not observe the Sabbath, they do not come to them at all until the next Sabbath.

﴿yasbituna﴾ has been read as a triliteral form and as a derived form from (asbata), both in the active and in the passive voice, with the meaning: they do not enter upon the Sabbath, and it is not turned upon them.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We tested them﴾ mean: like that wondrous, dreadful trial, We test them by making the fish appear to them on the surface of the water on the day when hunting it was forbidden to them, and hiding it from them on the day when hunting it was lawful for them. That is, We deal with them as one who tests them, because of their defiance, so their transgression becomes evident, and they deserve to be called to account.

Then Allah (exalted is He) showed their persistence in transgression and their refusal to desist from it, after admonitions and warnings, through His words:

The discussion on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[164] ﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" They said, "As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾

"﴿And when a community among them said﴾ i.e., a group of their righteous ones, who were debating with a faction of those who persisted in admonishing them" "﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy﴾ i.e., will cut off and cleanse the earth of them:" "﴿or punish with a severe punishment﴾ i.e., rather, He will punish them with a severe punishment, for mere destruction may still be accompanied by kindness, whereas severe punishment is the crushing blow." "﴿They said﴾ i.e., the preachers," "﴿As an excuse before your Lord﴾ i.e., we admonish them as an excuse before Him, exalted is He, so that we will not be attributed with neglect in fulfilling His command to forbid evil." It was also read with the nominative (raf'), i.e., "our admonition is an excuse" (ma'dhiratun). "﴿And perhaps they will fear Him﴾ i.e., and in hope that they will fear Him, repent, and thereby be saved from destruction."

"The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[165] ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong with a severe punishment, because they used to defiantly disobey.﴾

"﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ meaning: when they abandoned what their righteous ones had admonished them with, abandoning it as one forgetting a thing, and turned away from it completely, such that not a single thought of those admonitions came to their minds at all. ﴿We saved those who forbade evil, and We seized those who did wrong﴾ meaning, those who committed the wrong." ﴿with a severe punishment﴾ meaning: severe in weight and in meaning. ﴿because they used to defiantly disobey﴾ by committing the wrong."

The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[166] ﴿So when they persisted in defiance of what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾

"﴿When they persisted in defiance of what they had been forbidden﴾" means: they became arrogant and refused to give up what they had been forbidden. "﴿We said to them, 'Be apes, despised and driven away'﴾" means: abased, humiliated, distanced from people.

Al-Zajjaj said: They were commanded to become so by a word that was heard.

Others said: The intended command is the creational (takwini) command, not the verbal (taklifi) command, since it is not within their capacity to be commanded to do it.

In the verse there is an imaginative metaphor (isti'arah takhyiliyyah): the effect of His power on what He wills, without any delay, without any effort or use of an instrument, is likened to the command of a ruler obeyed by his subject in the accomplishment of what is commanded, without delay. So (al-'Inayah) says.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that God first punished them with a severe punishment, and after that they persisted, so He transformed them. It is also possible that the second verse is a confirmation and elaboration of what precedes it.

Remarks:

First: Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates that they were obligated to the prohibition of hunting on the Sabbath, that the obligation was made stricter upon them by its manifestation on that day, and that they opposed God's command; this much the apparent meaning requires. If it is asked: Was the appearance of the fish on the Sabbath alone, and not on other days, a miracle? We say: Scholars differed on this. It was said: It was a miracle for the prophet of that time, because it does not happen for fish to come to the rivers in great numbers on one day and not appear on the rest of the days; if that is so, then God must have strengthened the fishes' impulses on the Sabbath so that they appeared, and turned them away on the other days so that they did not appear, and so it was a miracle. It was also said: Their custom had been to refrain from hunting on the Sabbath, so the fish, knowing this, grew numerous on that day in accordance with their custom, just as animals become accustomed to many things. End.

Many narrations have been transmitted concerning their transgression on the Sabbath:

Among them: They devised ways to catch the fish on it by setting snares and pools before the Sabbath, so that when the fish came on the Sabbath in their usual abundance, they were caught in those snares and could not escape during that day; then when night came, they took them after the Sabbath had ended.

Among them: They used to take them on the Sabbath in fact, but ate them on other days. Satan then made it appear to them that the prohibition concerned only eating them on that day, not hunting them. A group among them forbade them from this and said: "We do not see you rising until God rises upon you with a sinking, or a hurling, or some of His punishment." When they rose in the morning, they found that the transformation had befallen them, and behold, they were apes. (Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir.) There are other narrations as well.

It is related from Mujahid that their hearts were transformed, not their bodies, and God knows best.

Second: This story has been cited as evidence for the prohibition of legal stratagems (hiyal).

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Ighathat al-Lahfan): Among the snares of Satan with which he tried to harm Islam and its people are stratagems, deceit and trickery, which involve making lawful what God has forbidden, dropping what He has made obligatory, and opposing His command and prohibition. These belong to false opinion, which the Salaf agreed to censure. For opinion is of two kinds: an opinion that agrees with the texts and is attested by soundness and consideration, which is what the Salaf took into account and acted upon; and an opinion that contradicts the texts and is attested by nullity and invalidity, which is what they condemned and denounced.

Likewise stratagems are of two kinds: one by which one arrives at doing what God has commanded and abandoning what He has forbidden, and at escaping the unlawful, and at freeing the rightful from the unjust who prevents him, and freeing the oppressed from the hand of the aggressive oppressor; this kind is praiseworthy, and its doer and teacher are rewarded. And another kind which involves dropping obligations, making lawful what is forbidden, turning the oppressed into the oppressor and the oppressor into the oppressed, and turning truth into falsehood and falsehood into truth; this is what the Salaf agreed to condemn, and they cried out against its people from every corner of the earth.

Then he cited the many aspects of its prohibition and invalidity.

In the sixth of them he said:

God, exalted is He, informed about the people of the Sabbath among the Jews that they were transformed into apes because they devised ways to make lawful what God had forbidden them of hunting, by setting nets on Friday and, when the prey fell into them, taking it on Sunday. Some of the imams said: In this there is a great deterrent for whoever engages in stratagems against the legal prohibitions, from among those who are dressed in the knowledge of jurisprudence while not being a jurist; for the jurist is one who fears God by guarding His limits, glorifying His sanctities, and standing before them, not one who devises ways to make lawful His prohibitions and to drop His obligations.

It is known that they did not make this lawful out of denial of Moses, peace be upon him, or disbelief in the Torah; rather it was making lawful by interpretation, and a stratagem whose outward appearance is that of fulfilling, while its inward reality is transgression. For this reason, God knows best, they were transformed into apes, because the form of the ape bears a resemblance to the form of man, and in its attributes there is a resemblance to them, yet it differs from man in its definition and reality. When those transgressors abrogated the religion of God in such a way that they held only to what resembles religion in some of its outward aspects, and not its reality, God transformed them into apes resembling them in some of their outward features, and not in reality, as a fitting recompense.

(p-2892) Then he related in the tenth of them, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Do not commit what the Jews committed, and make lawful the sanctities of God by the slightest stratagems."

Third: The verses indicate that the people of this town became three groups: a group that committed the forbidden and devised stratagems to catch fish on the Sabbath, as we have explained; a group that forbade that and separated itself from them; and a group that remained silent, neither doing nor forbidding, but said to the group that forbade: "Why do you admonish these people, when you know that they have perished and deserved punishment from God, so there is no benefit in your forbidding them?" The forbidding group answered them: "We do it as an excuse before our Lord, and in order that we may fulfil what was taken from us regarding enjoining good and forbidding evil."

Then God, exalted is He, stated explicitly the deliverance of those who forbade and the destruction of the wrongdoers.

Ibn Kathir said: He was silent about the silent ones, because the recompense is of the same kind as the deed; they do not deserve praise so as to be praised, nor did they commit a grave sin so as to be blamed. Yet the imams differed concerning them: were they among the perished or among the saved? There are two opinions. It is narrated that Ibn ʿAbbas had withheld judgment concerning them, then came to hold that they were saved, when his servant ʿIkrimah said to him: "Do you not see that they disliked what those people were doing and opposed them, and said: 'Why do you admonish a people whom God is going to destroy?'" So he clothed him with a robe.

Fourth: The saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear God."﴾ [al-A'raf: 164] indicates that forbidding evil does not lapse even if the one who forbids knows there is no benefit in it, since it is not a condition of it that compliance be achieved; and even if there were nothing in it but the performance of a great pillar of the religion, zeal for the limits of God, and an apology to Him, exalted is He, this would suffice as benefit when its neglect is strictly censured.

When God, exalted is He, mentioned some of the evil qualities of the Jews, He followed it with the statement that He had decreed for them humiliation and abasement until the Day of Resurrection, so He, glorified is He, said:

(p-2893)

The commentary on His saying, exalted is He:

[167] ﴿And [remember] when your Lord declared that He would surely send against them, until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them the worst torment. Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment, and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

"﴿And when your Lord declared﴾, meaning ādhana (proclaimed), (as tawaʿada means awʿada, to threaten), from al-īdhān in the sense of al-iʿlām (informing). It is treated like the verb of an oath, as in ʿalima Allāh (Allah knows) and shahida Allāh (Allah bears witness). For this reason it is followed by what follows an oath, which is His saying: ﴿He would surely send against them﴾, meaning: and when your Lord decreed and ordained that He would surely impose upon the Jews ﴿until the Day of Resurrection, those who would inflict upon them the worst torment﴾, such as humiliation and the imposition of the jizya (poll tax) and other things, because of their disobedience, their opposition to God's commands and His law, and their trickery regarding what is forbidden. God Exalted sent Bakhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babylon, after Solomon, peace be upon him. He destroyed their homes, killed their fighting men, took their women and offspring captive, imposed the jizya on those of them who remained, and exiled many of them to Babylon, the seat of his kingdom. They remained there seventy years. Then various kings held power over them, and they endured a long time of severe affliction, due to the continuous wars upon their lands, until, after the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, by seventy-one years, they all came under the authority of the Romans. They were uprooted from their land and scattered throughout the lands in every direction, humbled and subdued. From this, whoever deduced that they would never have a state or honor, and that their humiliation would be continuous, drew his conclusion. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is swift in punishment﴾ for whoever persists in his disbelief and casts aside His commandments, ﴿and indeed He is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, meaning for whoever repents, believes, and does righteous deeds."

Then He, exalted, informed of their dispersal throughout the regions, saying:

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, Exalted is He:

[168] ﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations; among them are the righteous, and among them are those short of that; and We tested them with good things and bad, that they might return.﴾

"﴿And We divided them in the earth into nations﴾ meaning: We dispersed the Children of Israel throughout the land, and We made each group of them to be in one of its regions, such that no part of it was free of them, as a completion of their humiliation, so that they would have no power (shawka).

﴿Among them are the righteous, and among them are those short of that﴾ meaning: those who fall below the degree of righteousness, through disbelief or wickedness. ﴿And We tested them with good things and bad﴾ meaning: with blessings and afflictions, which are examples of the reward of righteousness and of wickedness." ﴿That they might return﴾ meaning: from the causes of evil deeds to good deeds.

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[169] ﴿Then there succeeded them a successor who inherited the Scripture, taking the goods of this lowly world and saying, "It will be forgiven us." And if a similar offer of goods came to them, they would take it. Was not the covenant of the Scripture taken from them, that they would not say about God except the truth? And they have studied what is in it. And the Last Abode is better for those who fear God. Will you not then reason?﴾

"﴿Then there succeeded them﴾" means: after these who were mentioned. "﴿a successor﴾" means: a bad replacement. Those meant are the people who lived in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The word (khalf), an infinitive (maṣdar), is used to describe both the singular and the plural. It is commonly used for the bad, and with a vowelled lām, khalaf, for the good. Sometimes the reverse occurs.

"﴿who inherited the Scripture﴾" means: the Torah, inherited from their forefathers who differed. They read it and become acquainted with what it contains of commands and prohibitions, of what is lawful and unlawful, but they do not act upon it, as He said: "﴿taking the goods of this lowly world﴾" means: the trash of this lowly thing, meaning the worldly life and what is enjoyed from it.

In His saying "﴿this lowly﴾" there is belittling and disparagement. (ʿaraḍ), with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, is that which has no permanence. From it, the theologians (mutakallimūn) borrowed (ʿaraḍ) for the counterpart of (jawhar, substance).

(al-adnā, "lowly") is either from (dunuww), meaning nearness, because it is hastening and near in comparison to the Hereafter, or from the lowering (dunuww) of a condition, its decline and its scarcity. "﴿and they say, 'It will be forgiven us'﴾" means: they exchange the proclamation and spreading of the truth for the goods of the worldly life, and they pass judgement upon God, exalted is He, that He will not hold them to account for what they have taken. "﴿And if a similar offer of goods came to them, they would take it﴾": the waw is for the circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: they hope for forgiveness while they persist (p-٢٨٩٥) and return to the like of their deed, not repenting; whenever the like of the first came into view for them, they took it. "﴿Was not the covenant of the Scripture taken﴾" means: the covenant contained in it. "﴿that they would not say about God except the truth﴾" means: if what they pass judgement upon God with were correct, there would be no meaning to the taking of this covenant.

Then He, exalted is He, informed that their taking was not out of ignorance of that covenant, by His saying: "﴿And they have studied what is in it﴾" means: they read what is in the Book of the covenant time and again. "﴿And the Last Abode is better﴾" means: than that lowly exchange. "﴿for those who fear God﴾" means: taking this lowly thing in place of concealing the truth. "﴿Will you not then reason?﴾" means: that you may know this, so do not exchange the lowly, which leads to punishment, for everlasting bliss. It was also read with the letter yāʾ (ya‘qilūn, "they reason"), and the shift (iltifāt, a change of grammatical person) contains an intensification of rebuke.

Then He, exalted is He, praised those who hold fast to His Book, which leads them to follow His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), as it is written in it, by His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 170:

The discussion of His saying, may He be exalted:

[170] ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer — indeed, We do not allow the reward of the reformers to be lost.﴾

"﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾ — i.e., they cling to it in matters of their religion. It is said: massaka bi-l-shay' and tamassaka bihi (he held fast to the thing and clung to it). It was also read as ((yumsikūna)), from (al-imsak) (holding), and tamassakū and istamsakū (they held fast). ﴿And establish prayer — indeed, We do not allow the reward of the reformers to be lost﴾ — this is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, as an alert that reform acts as a preventer against loss, because attaching a judgment to a derived noun (al-mushtaqq) indicates the cause of the basis of derivation (ma'khadh al-ishtiqaq). It is as if it were said: We do not allow their reward to be lost because of their reform.

If you say: holding fast to the Book includes every act of worship, and among them is the establishment of prayer, so why was it singled out? It is answered: its singling out is to show the excellence of prayer, since it is the pillar of the religion and the distinguishing mark between disbelief and faith.

Al-Jushami said: The verse indicates the threat against one who turns away from the Book, and the promise for one who holds fast to it, as an alert to us and a warning against adopting their way. It also indicates that seeking forgiveness with the tongue alone, and wishing for forgiveness, do not benefit unless they are accompanied by repentance and action."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 171:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[171] ﴿And [recall] when We raised the mountain over them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it would fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination, and remember what is in it, that you may be righteous."﴾

"﴿And when We raised the mountain over them﴾" i.e., We lifted it up. "﴿As though it were a canopy﴾" i.e., a cloud. "﴿And they thought it would fall upon them﴾" i.e., that it would drop down upon them, because the mountain does not remain suspended in the air. "﴿Take what We have given you﴾" i.e., and We said, or saying: "Take what We have given you of the rulings of the Torah." "﴿With determination﴾" i.e., with resolve and earnestness. "﴿And remember what is in it﴾" i.e., by acting upon it, and do not abandon it like one who has forgotten. "﴿That you may be righteous﴾" i.e., that you may avoid evil deeds, or hoping that you will be counted among the righteous. This verse is like His saying, exalted is He: "﴿And We raised over them the Mount [Tur]﴾" [An-Nisa: 154].

It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and others among the early generations (al-salaf) that they debated with Musa concerning the obligations and laws of the Torah, until Allah raised the mountain above their heads. Musa said to them: "Do you not see what my Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is saying? If you do not accept the Torah with what is in it, I will surely throw this upon you!" So they fell down prostrate, out of fear that it would fall upon them. Narrated by al-Nasa'i and Sunayd.

﴿Wa-idh akhadha rabbuka min Banī Ādam min ẓuhūrihim dhurriyyatahum﴾ means: "And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring." It means that He brought forth their progeny from their loins, generation after generation, from the stage at which each was a drop of sperm propelled into the wombs of mothers, then became a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, and then He produced them as complete, living, responsible human beings. His creation of them in this way was a bringing-forth from their loins, because their origin came out of them. "From their loins" (min ẓuhūrihim) is a substitution (badal) for "the Children of Adam," a substitution of part for whole. It has also been read as dhurriyyātihim (their offspring, in the plural).

﴿Wa-ashhadahum ʿalā anfusihim﴾ means: "and He made them testify concerning themselves." That is, He made each of those offspring, taken from the loins of their fathers, bear witness against itself, as an affirmation to them of His complete lordship.

Al-Jashami said: That is, He made them testify against themselves through the proofs of His oneness that He placed in them, the wonders of His creation, and the marvels of His craftsmanship: sound limbs, perceiving senses, visible organs, nerves, veins, and other things that teach one who reflects on them. All of these point to Him, to His attributes, and to His oneness. Thus, through the testimony of the proofs, it became as though He had made them testify by His word.

His words, exalted is He, ﴿Alastu bi-rabbikum?﴾ ("Am I not your Lord?") are spoken with the sense of saying: "saying: Am I not your Lord, and the Owner of your affairs, and the one who nurtures you absolutely, with no one having any part in any of your affairs?" Thereby the entitlement to be worshipped is established, and His exclusive right to it, exalted is He, is implied. ﴿Qālū balā shahidnā﴾ ("They said: Yes, we have testified") means: against ourselves, that You are our Lord and our God, that there is no lord other than You. Because of the signs of the craftsmanship that became manifest in them, it was as though they had said "Yes" (balā), even though there was no speech with the tongue.

Thus the verse is of the kind of figurative representation (tamthīl) well known in the speech of the Arabs.
