"﴿Indeed, those who fear Allah, when they are touched by﴾" i.e., reach them, "﴿an impulse from Satan﴾" i.e., a whispering and a suggestion from him, "﴿they remember﴾" i.e., seeking refuge in Him, exalted is He, and placing their trust in Him, "﴿and at once they are﴾" i.e., because of that remembrance, "﴿seeing clearly﴾" i.e., the places of error and the snares of Satan, so they refrain from them and do not follow him. It has been read as ((ṭayf)) as a verbal noun (maṣdar), from the saying of them (ṭāfa bihi al-khayāl, yaṭīfu ṭayfan, "the phantom haunted him"), or as a lightened form of (ṭayyif), like (layyin) and (hayyin). This verse is an emphasis and confirmation of what precedes it concerning the obligation of seeking refuge in Allah, exalted is He, at the incitement of Satan, and that the God-fearing have this as their custom. And the words of Him, exalted is He:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[202] ﴿And their brothers push them further into error, and they do not relent.﴾

"﴿And their brothers﴾ means: as for the brothers of the devils, from the devils of mankind. Like His saying: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra': 27]. They are those who did not fear God, so remembrance did not benefit them, and seeking refuge (al-isti'adhah) does not help them, because the devils [...]" ﴿push them further into error﴾, meaning they become a support for them by multiplying doubts, adorning falsehood, and making error easy. That is, the devils assist them in sins, make them easy for them, and make them appear good to them.

(p-2932) ﴿Then they do not relent﴾, meaning they do not refrain from misleading them until they persist and do not return. That is, the devils push their allies among mankind further, and they never tire of supporting them in evil, because that is their nature and disposition. He also permitted the pronoun to refer to "the brothers", meaning they do not desist from error and do not refrain, even if they are admonished greatly with the signs of God, the establishment of proofs, the removal of doubts, and other means.

He also permitted that "the brothers" here refers to the devils, with the pronoun referring to "the ignorant", meaning: and the brothers of the ignorant, who are the devils, push the ignorant further into error.

al-Zamakhshari said: "The first is more appropriate, because ﴿their brothers﴾ stands in contrast to ﴿those who feared God﴾."

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 203:

Then Exalted God explained, among the kinds of their misguidance, their obstinacy in demanding specific signs and their stubbornness in proposing them, even though they had the greatest miracle and the supreme extraordinary sign, which is the Noble Qur'an. So He, glorified is He, said:

The discussion on the interpretation of the words of Exalted God:

[203] ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why have you not invented it?" Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe."﴾

"﴿And when you do not bring them a sign﴾" i.e., of what they proposed. "﴿They say, 'Why have you not invented it?'﴾" i.e., why did you not take the trouble to devise it and produce it from yourself? "﴿Say, 'I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord.'﴾" i.e., I do not fabricate signs, nor do I go ahead of Him, exalted is He, in anything of them. Then Exalted God guided them to the fact that this Qur'an is the greatest of miracles, the clearest of proofs, and the most truthful of arguments and clear evidences. So He, glorified is He, said: "﴿This﴾" i.e., the Qur'an "﴿is insights from your Lord﴾" i.e., it is in the position of insights for hearts, by which the truth is seen and right judgment is grasped. So the speech is in the manner of an eloquent metaphor (tashbih baligh). Or it is the cause of insights, so it is a metonymy (majaz mursal) or a metaphor for its guidance. Or the meaning is: clear proofs and luminous evidences. The plural of the predicate of the singular is used because it comprises verses and surahs, making each of them an insight. The mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) together with the attribution to their pronoun is to emphasise the obligation of belief in it. "﴿And guidance﴾" i.e., from misguidance. "﴿And mercy﴾" i.e., from punishment. "﴿For a people who believe﴾" i.e., in it, so that they reflect upon its realities.

Note:

Al-Jashami said: The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, sends down signs according to what is in the interest (maslahah), not according to their proposals, because that may be corruption. The words "﴿This is insights﴾" indicate that knowledge is acquired. It also indicates that everything the Messenger says and does of the Sharia is from His revelation, which is why he said: "﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾." If it is asked: does the verse indicate that he does not exercise ijtihad (independent reasoning) or qiyas (analogical reasoning)? We say: No, because qiyas and ijtihad, when they are a matter of worship, following them is following revelation, like the layman who accepts from the mufti, and the scholar who exercises ijtihad and follows revelation; so it is likewise here.

What is indicated is that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not do anything of his own accord until he is commanded to do it. — End of his words. Its unrestricted wording has a detailed treatment in another place.

The discourse on the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[204] ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾

"﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, i.e., from inner speech and other things," ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾. When the Exalted mentioned that the Qur'an is insights for people, guidance and mercy, He guided to the path of success through what it contains of its magnificent benefits. That is: when the Qur'an whose characteristics have been mentioned is recited, then listen to it, i.e., give it your ears so that you understand its meanings and reflect upon its admonitions, and be silent for its recitation until it finishes, out of glorification of it and reverence, so that you may attain the mercy which is its greatest fruit. Not as the disbelievers of Quraysh rely upon in their saying: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it﴾ [Fussilat: 26].

(p-2934) Points of note:

The first: The apparent meaning of the verse requires the obligation of listening and remaining silent when the Qur'an is recited, both in prayer and otherwise. This is the view of the people of the apparent meaning (Ahl al-Zahir), and it is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani. Muslim narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The imam was only appointed to be followed. So when he says the takbir, say the takbir, and when he recites, be silent." Likewise the people of the Sunan narrated it from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.

Imam Ahmad and the people of the Sunan narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished a prayer in which he recited aloud, and said: "Did any of you recite with me just now?" A man said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "I say, why am I being disputed in the Qur'an?" He said: So the people ceased reciting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in what he recited aloud in the prayer, when they heard that from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

At-Tirmidhi said: This is a hasan hadith. Abu Hatim al-Razi authenticated it. Indeed, the sound Sunnah has come with an exception for al-Fatihah alone for the follower. This is in what 'Ubadah narrated, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in the dawn prayer, and the recitation became heavy upon him. When he finished he said: 'I see you reciting behind your imam?' We said: 'Yes, by Allah, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Do not do so except with Umm al-Qur'an (al-Fatihah), for there is no prayer for one who does not recite it.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi.

In another wording: "So do not recite anything of the Qur'an when you recite aloud, except Umm al-Qur'an." Narrated by Abu Dawud, an-Nasa'i, and ad-Daraqutni, who said: all its narrators are trustworthy.

Ibn Hibban narrated from Anas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do you recite in your prayer behind the imam while the imam is reciting? Do not do so, and let one of you recite the Opening of the Book silently to himself."

As for the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned earlier, it is not used as evidence for the prohibition of the follower's recitation absolutely, but only aloud, because the disputing occurs only with the follower's audible recitation, not with his silent recitation. And even if it is granted that this is included in the disputing, the interrogative of denial there would be general to the entire Qur'an, or absolute in all of it.

The hadith of 'Ubadah is specific or restricted, and there is no contradiction between a general and a specific, or an absolute and a restricted, because the former is built upon the latter. The same is said regarding the generality of the verse. In this, the evidence of the Book and the sound Sunnah are combined, since the one who brought the Qur'an also brought these.

The second: It is narrated from many of the early generation (salaf) that the verse was revealed concerning the prayer. Some of them said: concerning it and the Friday sermon. Others said: concerning it and the sermon of the two festivals, al-Adha and al-Fitr. We have already mentioned in the introduction of the book the term of the salaf in their saying, "This verse was revealed concerning such-and-such," and we explained that by it may be meant that the verse includes that matter by its entry into its generality, not that it was the cause of its revelation; this occurs in some contexts, and what is here is of that kind.

By verifying this, what al-Razi said here falls away, namely that if it is said the verse was revealed to prohibit the follower from reciting aloud, the verse's coherence with what precedes it—of silencing the polytheists by having them listen to its recitation so that they may witness its inimitability—would be lost. Likewise what al-Khazin said, that the verse is Meccan, while the Friday and Eid sermons were legislated in Medina—so understand it.

The third: Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever listens to a verse from the Book of Allah, a good deed will be written for him multiplied, and whoever recites it, it will be a light for him on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Kathir said: Imam Ahmad alone narrated it, may Allah have mercy on him.

And His saying, exalted is He:

(p-٢٩٣٦)The interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[205] ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless.﴾

"﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings﴾ is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and the intended meaning is general. Or the meaning is: 'Remember your Lord, O human being.' The first is more apparent, because what is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and is not among his specific privileges applies to his community as well.

This is clarified by the verses: ﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 41) ﴿and exalt Him morning and evening﴾ (Al-Ahzab: 42). As for the command to remembrance, al-Zamakhshari (the commentator on the Qur'an) said: it is general, covering invocations, recitation of the Qur'an, supplication, glorification (tasbih), declaration of God's oneness (tahlil), and other things. Some of the Zaydiyya (a Shi'i school) said: this command may imply obligation if remembrance is interpreted as prayer; if it is meant as supplication or remembrance by the tongue, then it is to be taken as recommendation. He said: the verse has been interpreted in all of these ways.

Then, He, exalted is He, mentioned etiquettes for remembering Him:

The first: that it be within oneself, because concealment is more conducive to sincerity, closer to being answered, and further from ostentation.

The second: that it be in the manner of humility (tadarru'), which is submission, lowliness, and acknowledgment of shortcoming, so that the servant realizes the humbleness of servitude before the might of lordship.

The third: that it be with fear (khifa), that is, dread and awe before the authority of lordship and the greatness of divinity, lest one be held accountable for shortcoming in action, so that the soul may be humbled and the heart may submit.

(p-٢٩٣٧)The fourth: that it be without loudness, because that is closer to good reflection. Ibn Kathir said: therefore it is recommended that remembrance not be by calling out or by loud exclamation. In the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim), on the authority of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: 'The people raised their voices in supplication during some journey, so the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "O people! Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent. Indeed, the One you are calling upon is All-Hearing and near, nearer to any of you than the neck of his mount."' The imam (al-Razi) said: the intended meaning is that remembrance should occur at a middle point between loudness and secrecy, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer or silent therein, but seek between that a way﴾ (Al-Isra: 110).

The fifth: that it be by the tongue and not by the heart alone. This is derived from His words ﴿without loudness﴾, because its meaning is: 'speaking words without loudness.' So it is an adjective of an omitted circumstantial object (ma'mul hal) coordinated with ﴿humbly﴾; or it is coordinated with ﴿within yourself﴾, meaning: remember Him with remembrance within yourself, and with remembrance by your tongue without loudness.

The sixth: that it be in the mornings and the evenings, that is, in the early day and the late day. The verse thus indicates the excellence of these two times, because they are times of tranquility, ease, worship, and diligence, while what lies between them is generally given over to attending to livelihood. It has been related that the deeds of the servant are raised at the beginning and end of the day, so the seeking of remembrance at these two times is so that the beginning and conclusion of his deeds are with remembrance.

Then He, exalted is He, forbade heedlessness of His remembrance with His words ﴿and do not be among the heedless﴾, that is, among those who are heedless of the remembrance of Allah and are distracted from it. Within this is an indication of seeking the continuance of His remembrance, and of summoning His greatness, majesty, and grandeur, to the extent of human capacity.

(p-٢٩٣٨)Then He, exalted is He, mentioned what strengthens the motives for remembrance and rouses the resolve toward it, by praising the angels who glorify Him night and day, not slackening, so He said:

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 7, verse 206:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[206] ﴿Indeed, those who are near your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they exalt Him and to Him they prostrate.﴾

"﴿Indeed, those who are near your Lord﴾" means the angels who are in the highest ranks of nearness. "﴿do not disdain His worship﴾" means they do not consider themselves too great for it. And His saying "﴿and they exalt Him and to Him they prostrate﴾" means: so they should be followed in what is mentioned of them. There is in this an exhortation and a gentle encouragement toward that, because if those (who are of such nearness of station and protection) are in such a state in their worship of Him, exalted is He, and in glorifying Him as has been mentioned, then how should others be?

Remarks:

First: al-Razi said: Abu Bakr al-Asamm held onto this verse in preferring the angels over humans. He said: Because when He, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to worship and remember Him, He said: "﴿Indeed, those who are near your Lord﴾" and so on, meaning: you are more worthy and more deserving of worship. The matter is fully treated in the books of kalam. Whoever argued for the aforementioned preference derived from the verse that a servant should look to those above him in obedience to God, exalted is He.

Second: al-Razi said: The Mushabbihah held onto His saying, exalted is He: "﴿Indeed, those who are near your Lord﴾" and said: the word "near" (ʿinda) indicates a direction. Then he answered with what is well known among the later scholars. By "the Mushabbihah" he means—may God forgive him—the Hanbalites, who are free of anthropomorphism, as whoever has studied their creeds knows; they stop at the limits of the texts without anthropomorphism or negation of attributes. They were not alone in this, for countless scholars preceded them in this matter. Refer to the book (al-ʿUluww) of al-Dhahabi, and you will know what we have mentioned.

(p-2939) Third: al-Jashmi said: The verse indicates that the angels are obligated (mukallafun). It also indicates that they prostrated to God, and that Adam was the direction of prostration, because He described them as prostrating to Him.

Fourth: This is the first prostration in the Qur'an that, by consensus (ijma'), makes it obligatory for the one reciting it and the one listening to it to prostrate.

It has been narrated in a hadith related by Ibn Majah from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he counted it among the prostrations of the Qur'an.

Al-Shaykhan narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar that "the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the Qur'an, and he would recite a surah containing a prostration, then he would prostrate, and we would prostrate with him, until some of us would not find a place for his forehead, outside the time of prayer."

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When the son of Adam recites the prostration and prostrates, Satan withdraws weeping, saying: Woe is me! The son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so for him is Paradise; and I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so for me is the Fire."

Muslim narrated from Thawban, the freed slave of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said: I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "Keep to much prostration to God, for you do not prostrate to God a single prostration except that God raises you by it a degree and removes from you by it a sin."

Fifth: The legislated prostration, if it is for a verse in which prostration is commanded, then it is for the command; or if in it is related the refusal of the disbelievers toward it, then it is for opposing them and humbling them; or if in it is related the prostration of the prophets or the angels, then it is for emulating them. Thus said (al-ʿInaya).

This is the last of what was easily possible to comment upon concerning Surat al-A'raf. So praise be to God for this facilitation and assistance, and we ask Him, by His bounty and generosity, for help in completing it, for He is Possessor of Majesty and Honor.

The completion of that was at sunrise on Tuesday, 26 Ramadan, the blessed, in the year 1321, at the right upper window of the high platform of the Sananiyya Mosque, by the hand of the poor one Jamal al-Din al-Qasimi, may God forgive him, and his parents, and all the believers, and have mercy on him and them, for He is Most Merciful of the merciful.

The seventh part is complete, and following it, God willing, is the eighth part, which contains the commentary on Surat al-Anfal and Surat al-Tawba.
